en: Regarding the "Preface to the *Shun-zhu* (Correcting the Red Ink) of the *Chanlin Baoxun*":
Why is it called "Correcting the Red Ink"? It is because our own perceptions are coarse and superficial; we merely recognize the "bright and numinous" as companions of dreams and illusions.
We do not engage in authentic inquiry, nor do we attain genuine awakening; we do not follow the ritual laws of the ancient sages, nor do we maintain integrity and righteousness.
I have briefly set forth the intentions of former sages to admonish myself. Furthermore, I observe that among those of our own class who practice Zen, their insight is often shallow and limited;
as they continue their practice, they find no flavor and achieve no efficacy. Consequently, they turn to external classics, practicing poetry and prose merely to seek immediate gratification.
Suddenly they enter local schools, suddenly they become practitioners of medicine, and suddenly they become clerks in government offices. Thus it is.

The waves at the Three Gorges of the Yu Gate—how swift they are! I am pained by this deficiency; therefore, I have requested the Mountain Man of Qixia to compose a word-by-word commentary on the *Baokun*.
My intention was to first use worldly desires as a hook to entice them, leading them into the wisdom of the Buddha.

Unintentionally, however, the Mountain Man of Qixia, though possessed of lofty talent and vast insight, has failed to explain the scriptures with precision. Rather than providing clear and accessible metaphors, he has instead produced a commentary akin to that of Guo Xiang.
This is Zhuangzi. Those who see it find it distressing. I, for my part, could not bear to remain silent; thus, imitating the "grimace" (of the original), I have brought out my own ugliness.
Having applied the vermilion and ink, I do this first to lead others into the Buddha-wisdom according to their inclinations, and second to serve as a self-admonition.
Therefore, I do not fear the ridicule of those from all quarters. This draft was completed at the end of summer in the year Wumu (1898).
It remains here as a permanent record, awaiting the corrections of wise scholars. Recorded by Deyu.
*Chanlin Baoxun Shunzhu*, Scroll One.
Compiled by Ji’er Guansheng Ke of Huayan, Yuzhou, Shu; Deyu. Regarding the *Shunzhu*, Master Mingjiao Song said:
"There is nothing more venerable than the Way (*dào*); there is nothing more beautiful than virtue (*dé*). As for the locus of the Way and virtue..."

Existence: though one may be a commoner, it is not a state of destitution if the Way and its Virtue (Dao-de) abide within them. Non-existence: though one may rule all under heaven, it is not a state of fulfillment if the Way and its Virtue do not abide within them.
Boyi and Shuqi were once men who starved to death; yet when people today compare themselves to such men, everyone feels joy.
Jie, Zhou, You, and Li were once sovereigns of men. If one were to compare them with such figures today, everyone would be incensed.
Therefore, students worry that their moral virtue (*mòdé*) does not fill their persons; they do not worry that power and rank (*shìwèi*) are not in their own possession.
(From the *Xínjīn jí*; "Wáng" is pronounced as an oblique tone.)
Mingjiao, whose name was Qisong and courtesy name Zhongling, was the successor of Dongshan Xiaocong. "Upādhyāya" (Heshang) is a Sanskrit term;

here it is translated as "Power-Born," meaning that one gives birth to the life-force of wisdom and the Dharma-body through the power of the teacher. "Dao" (the Way) refers to the penetration of the mind.
Virtue is the rectitude of the person. Boyi and Shuqi were the two sons of the Lord of Guzhu. Their clan name was Motai;

Boyi’s given name was Yun, his courtesy name was Gongxin; Shuqi’s given name was Zhi, his courtesy name was Gongda. These two were men of integrity and righteousness. Jie’s name was Liu Gui; he was the son of Emperor Fa.
According to the *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles), one who harms many people and commits numerous killings is called "Jie. Zhou’s name was Xin; he was the son of Emperor Jie.
The son of Yi was styled Zhou; according to the *Shifa* (Methods of Posthumous Titles), "one who ruins righteousness and diminishes goodness" is called Zhou.
The son of Youming was styled Xuanwang; according to the *Shifa*, "one who obstructs and blocks so that there is no passage" is called You.

The son of Li was styled Yiwang; according to the *Shifa*, "one who slaughters the innocent" is called Li. These four kings were all tyrannical rulers; therefore, this is taught to clarify what was explained above.
A student should regard moral virtue as paramount; they should not take power or status as a source of honor.
Among all that is most weighty in the world, there are many such things, but which one can outweigh the principle of mental penetration?
Among all that is most excellent throughout the four seas, there are many such things, but which one can surpass the conduct of bodily rectitude? If...
This mind possesses the Way, and this body possesses virtue; when these two are ever-present and not lost, even if one is as lowly as a commoner, one does not consider oneself destitute.

Conversely, if the mental state is clouded and ignorant, if one acts contrary to the Way, and if one is selfish, depraved, and devoid of virtue—when these two are not known to exist within—one does not consider oneself illustrious or successful, even if one is as noble as the Son of Heaven.
The two scholars Boyi and Shuqi were ashamed to eat the grain of Zhou; they starved to death on Mount Shouyang as mere commoners.
Why is it that when these two scholars are compared to people of today, everyone feels joy? It is because they possessed integrity and righteousness.
What else could integrity and righteousness be but the Way and its Virtue? Kings Jie, Zhou, You, and Li were the successors of former days...
He occupied the position of the Son of Heaven under the Three Dynasties. Now, when people compare the Four Kings to those of the present day, they all feel resentment;
why is this? It is because those others practiced tyranny and cruelty. How can there be any morality or virtue in tyranny and cruelty?
For this reason, those who study should be concerned that their own moral cultivation is insufficient within themselves; they need not worry about other matters.
One should consider whether positions of power and high rank exist within oneself. A student must know what is truly important.
The study of the sages and worthies is certainly not something that can be mastered in a single day; when the daylight is insufficient, one must continue by night.
Accumulated over months and years, it will naturally be accomplished. Therefore it is said: "Study to gather [knowledge], and inquiry to discern it.
These words mean that study cannot be made manifest without inquiry and discernment. Yet among those who study today, there are rarely any who utter a single word of inquiry or discernment to others.
I do not know how they hope to assist their fundamental nature (*xingdi*) or achieve the benefit of daily renewal.
The Sage is unimpeded in all matters. The virtuous and worthy person is one who solidifies the foundation, possesses the vessel [of capacity], continues the lineage, and accumulates merit.
"Years and months" refers to their long duration; "gathering" (*jù*) means to assemble and collect; "discerning" (*biàn*) means to distinguish; "rare" (*hǎn*) means to be few;
and "aiding" (*bì*) means to provide benefit. The "nature-ground" (*xìngdì*) is the field of the mind. To clarify the teachings and instruct others, one must achieve daily renewal.
Gongsu said: "To become a sage or a worthy, the foundation of one's studies cannot be accomplished in a single morning or evening.
During the day, due to the distractions of affairs or social obligations, one may lack the leisure to complete a full day’s work.

At night, however, one must burn oil lamps and prolong the light of the sun to continue what was left unfinished during the day. It is by accumulating effort in this manner that one’s achievements are built up."
Through long years and many months of practice, the mind becomes penetrating and the body upright; every matter accords with principle, and spontaneous accomplishment ensues.

Thus it was said by the ancients: "If what is below the mind is not yet resolved, then study the past and examine the present to gather and accumulate [wisdom]. If there are doubts within the mind..."
Therefore, one must consult and question enlightened masters in order to discern them. These two sentences are precisely for the purpose of enlightening students.
If one does not inquire and discern, how can one distinguish what is correct from what is incorrect? How, then, could the mind be opened and the intellect become clear?
As for the students of today, wherever they go, not even one or half of one can be found who does so.
There are those who are willing to cite a single word or half-phrase and seek clarification and analysis from a wise person;
yet they do not know by what principle these students will benefit their own minds, so as to achieve the constant renewal of their nature and eliminate their beginningless habitual tendencies.
Mingjiao said: When Grand Historian Sima Qian read the *Mencius* to the point where King Hui of Liang asked, "How can I profit my state?", he unconsciously set down his scroll and sighed deeply:
"Alas! Profit is truly the beginning of disorder. Therefore, the Master [Confucius] seldom spoke of profit, constantly seeking to prevent it at its source.
'Source' means the beginning. If one honors the poor and lowly, how can the evil of craving profit be distinguished from them?"

Those who serve in public office, if they seek profit without impartiality, will cause the laws to fall into disorder. Those who act in private, if they seek profit through deception, will cause affairs to fall into disorder.

When affairs are in disorder, people contend with one another unjustly; when the laws are in disorder, the people resent them and refuse to submit. Thus, there arises rebellion, perversity, strife, and contention.

Those who disregard death set out from this very point. Is this not, therefore, the beginning of truly inciting disorder? Furthermore, the sages and worthies deeply cautioned against seeking profit and held benevolence and righteousness as supreme.
Yet in later generations, there were still countless instances of those who relied on profit to deceive one another, wounding social customs and subverting the teachings.
How much more so when one openly proclaims the way of seeking profit and puts it into practice—desiring to [govern] Heaven...?
To have the customs of the lower classes be upright, neither decadent nor coarse—is that possible? (From the *Xintin ji*; "qu" is read as the third tone.
The Grand Historian’s surname was Sī-mǎ, his given name Qiān; he was the son of Tàn, the Director of the Grand Historian. Mèng-zǐ’s given name was Kē.
His courtesy name was Ziyu. He composed the *Mencius* in seven chapters. Liang Huai Wang was Marquis Wen of Wei. He ruled from Liang, usurping the title of king;
his posthumous title was Huai. "Zhi" means to set down or relinquish; "juan" refers to the scrolls of the *Mencius*. "Jie" signifies lamentation and regret; it is the fundamental root.
The Master’s surname was Kong and his given name was Zhongni; he was the "Sovereign King" (*suwang*). "Fang" means a dam or embankment; it is the original source.

"Honored" refers to the Son of Heaven; "poor and lowly" refers to the common people. To be rebellious, contrary, perverse, and discordant, to be combative, headstrong, contentious, and competitive—these are the ranks of those who bring disorder.

Benevolence (*ren*) is the virtue of the mind; righteousness (*yi*) is the propriety of affairs. To rely upon and deploy [these virtues] is to counteract the decadence, corruption, and decline of the age.
Clearly instructing and showing people how to refrain from greed, he recounted that in the past, the Grand Historian observed:
At the very beginning of the first chapter of the *Mencius*, when King Hui of Liang asked Mencius, "Master, you have come from no less than a thousand li away;

will you perhaps provide some means to profit my state? Mencius could not help but set down his book and sigh deeply, saying, "This single word 'profit' (li) is truly the root and foundation from which disorder arises in a state."
Therefore, it is recorded in the *Analects* that the Master seldom spoke of profit (*li*).

This was his daily precaution, undertaken out of fear that [profit] might become the root of inciting disorder. Why did he guard against its source? Because he feared it would be the beginning of chaos.
As for this, whether one is as noble as the Son of Heaven or as lowly as a commoner, all alike suffer from the malady of attachment to love and profit. How can they be distinguished?
Distinguish between them. For those who stand above the people, if they extract wealth and profit without public righteousness, then the laws and institutions will fall into disorder.
For those who stand below, if they seek profit with a covetous mind, then the affairs of the world will fall into disorder.
Once affairs are in disorder, everyone will engage in contentious debate; when the Way is not equitable, the Way is lost. Once the laws are in disorder, the common people will harbor resentment.
Resentment. The mind is not pleased or submissive. From this state of affairs, many instances of unrest arise. They become perverse and rebellious;
they become contrary and erroneous; they become combative and fierce; they become contentious and vying for gain.
It is from this that those who cast aside death and life, regarding nothing at all, originate. Viewed in this light, this is one aspect of profit.
Are these characters not indeed the very root of disorder? Furthermore, the Sage Confucius and the Worthy Mencius issued deep and poignant warnings;

they sought to eliminate the disease of profit and sweep away the heterodox to return to the orthodox. Can it be said that they lacked the power to do so? They revered benevolence (*ren*) and prioritized righteousness (*yi*);
by replacing the heterodox with the orthodox, they may be said to have rendered great service. Yet, as for the people of later generations, regarding profit and disease—

It is difficult to eliminate. There are still those who rely upon wealth and profit, deceiving one another, harming social customs, and ruining the teachings—how could there be any limit to such people?
It does not stop at this alone; moreover, they even ostentatiously establish and widely implement systems for extracting profit.
This is the height of shamelessness. They desire to bring about a state where the customs of the world are upright...
To achieve such rectitude and avoid becoming corrupt, decadent, or diminished—how could this ever be possible? It is absolutely impossible. Mingjiao said:
"Among the evils committed by ordinary people, there are those that are manifest and those that are unmanifest. Unmanifest evil is that which harms others;
manifest evil is that which kills people. The evil that kills people is minor compared to the evil that harms others."
The evils therein are great. Thus, within one's leisure and banquets there may be hemlock poison; amidst talk and laughter there may be spears and halberds;
within the inner chambers there may be tigers and leopards; and in the neighboring lanes there may be the Rong and Di barbarians.
Unless one is a sage or a worthy, and cuts these off before they sprout and guards against them through ritual and law, will their harm not be exceedingly severe? (From the *Guangji of West Lake*)
That which has form refers to the hands and body; that which is formless refers to the mind and intentions. "Strolling and feasting" refers to wine banquets;

"poisoned chime" refers to the feathers of a poisonous bird. When these pass through one's food and drink, they can kill a person. The "hall" is the central hall; the "inner recess" is the corner alcove.
Five households constitute a neighborhood; twenty-five households constitute a lane. These are the locations of villages and fortresses. "Rong" refers to the Western Rong;
"Di" refers to the Northern Di, such as the Khans and their like. "Li" refers to ritual propriety; "Xing" refers to penal law. This clearly teaches the instructions for human defense against harm.
Generally, regarding the improper conduct of those in the world who do not learn what is good, there are two types of evil deeds. One type is...
That which has form and is visible is of one kind; that which is formless and difficult to see is another.
Formless and invisible evil consists entirely of secret plotting within the mind and cold-blooded harm to others.
Visible and tangible evil is the grasping of swords and halberds to kill people openly. When the evil of killing is seen coming with one's own eyes, it can be prevented and countered.

One may avoid it; it does not necessarily lead to death, and for this reason it is called "small. As for the evil that harms others, its arrival is unknown, and when one emerges from it unprepared, what path to life remains?
For this reason, it is called "great. Furthermore, the means by which it harms people are not limited to a single method.
There are those who, amidst the joyful banquets and feasts of guests and hosts, secretly administer lethal poison (gall-poison). There are also those who... [extreme cases].
When engaging in rational discourse, jesting, or playful banter, one secretly conceals weapons and spears;
in the manifest halls of the central court or in the deep, secluded corners and recesses, one harbors tigers and leopards;

in places where neighboring households are linked and streets and alleys intersect, one mingles with the barbarians of the Rong and Di. These four types of conduct—how could they not be considered evils that harm others?

Great indeed! Had it not been for the sage’s exercise of skillful means and the worthy official’s establishment of expedients—extinguishing [evil] before its sprouting and movement, and providing a dam with rites and laws—would not the resulting lingering poison and harm have been far more extreme?
One cannot fail to understand these principles for extinguishing evil and preventing harm. ○

The character for *zhèng* (鴆) is pronounced *zhèng*. Mingjiao said: "When the Great Awakened Master Liaan was residing at Yuwang Monastery, two monks were quarreling incessantly over the distribution of offerings.

The administrators were unable to resolve the dispute. The Great Awakened Master summoned them and addressed them with gravity, saying: 'In the past, when Lord Bao presided over Kaifeng, there was a citizen who...'"
Chen said, "The hundred taels of white silver that I entrusted to you have been lost. I am now returning it to your family. His son would not accept it.
He hoped that the Duke would summon his son and return the silver to him. The Duke marveled at this and immediately summoned the son to speak with him.

The son declined, saying, "During my late father's lifetime, there was no private deposit of white silver in another household. The two men continued to decline for a long time, until the Duke had no choice but to yield.
He was entrusted to a temple within the city to perform rites for the deceased in order to secure merit for the departed. I witnessed this with my own eyes;
yet even those mired in the dust of worldly toil can thus be generous with their wealth and admire righteousness. You, however, being a disciple of the Buddha, lack such integrity and shame as this.
Consequently, I have expelled you according to the laws of the monastic community. (From the *Guangji of West Lake*; "yu" and "guan" are pronounced in the departing tone).

Dajue (Great Awakening) was named Huailian; his courtesy name was Qizhi. He was the successor of Letan Huacheng. Yuyang Mountain is located in the territory of Mingzhou; it is Guangli Temple. "Hu" means to summon.
"Ze" means to reprimand. "Xia" refers to assigning responsibility. Bao Gong’s name was Zheng; his courtesy name was Xiren. His posthumous title was Xiaosu.
He served as the Governor of Kaifeng and administered excellent governance. "Fu" means to entrust. "Shou" means to bestow. "Bin" means to banish. "Zhu" means to expel.
Thus it was. To provide clear instruction to others, he used the story of Da Jue Lian’s detachment from wealth and his aspiration for righteousness.
From the second year of the Huangyou era of Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty, Da Jue Lian was summoned by imperial decree to reside at the Shifang Jingyin Chan Monastery in the capital.
Later, when he returned to reside at Ayuwangshan Guangli Temple, there were two monks who, lacking a sense of shame, quarreled over the money offered as alms.
Their pursuit of profit did not cease. The head administrators and those in charge were all powerless against them; it was difficult to reach a definitive judgment.
It was evident that these two men were exceedingly greedy for gain. Da Jue then sent someone to summon them and rebuked them, saying:
"In the past, when the Duke Bao Xiaosu was the Governor of Kaifeng in the Eastern Capital, there was a commoner named Zhang Huiming who personally submitted a petition."
He said, "Li Jue'an was once in Japan. Because his son was young, he entrusted me with one hundred taels of silver.
He has been deceased for a long time now; when his son grew older, I returned the silver to him, but he refused to accept it. I look up to Lord Bao for help."
He summoned the son of Gwak-an and returned [the items] to him. The Duke sighed in admiration and marveled at the wonder, saying, "Do I have such a righteous subject as this?
He then immediately summoned the son of Gwak-an and gave [the items] to him. The son also declined and would not accept them, saying:
During my late father’s lifetime, there was originally no silver. It had been entrusted to another family.
After the two parties repeatedly and firmly declined for a long time, Lord Bao had no choice but to see that his son was likewise righteous;

he therefore took responsibility for the matter and entrusted it to the eminent monk Guanzhong Gaodao at the temple within the city, charging him to make offerings to the Buddhas and deities and cultivate merit for the benefit of the netherworld.
This is beneficial, for it allows the deceased to attain awakening and peace. When I resided at Jingyin, I personally witnessed this matter with my own eyes.
Furthermore, Huiming and Anzi were both men of worldly toil and dust; yet even they were able to find no pleasure in wealth.
To admire integrity and righteousness is of such a nature. You two monks are disciples of the Buddha;
yet, failing to embody the Buddha’s mind, you have not practiced the perfection of giving as extensively as those two laymen, and you remain ignorant of integrity and shame.
Having reached such a state, you cannot be tolerated by principle; you should follow the regulations of the monastic community.
According to the rites and laws, he was expelled and not permitted to re-enter, lest he defile the assembly.
When the Great Awakened Master Liaan first traveled to Mount Lu, Chan Master Netuan of Yuan Tong saw him at once and regarded him as one destined for a great vessel.
Someone asked, "How did you know this? Netuan replied, "This man is centered and impartial; in both motion and stillness, he maintains dignity."
Furthermore, he was distinguished by his mastery of the Way and his integrity of conduct; his speech was concise yet exhaustive in its principles.
Among ordinary people, few who possess such endowments fail to become accomplished vessels (from the *Jiupeng ji*).
Mount Lu is the name of a mountain in Jiangxi. Yuantong’s name was Ju-ne, and his courtesy name was Zhong-min; he was the successor of Ziyong of Yanqing.
"Qi" (期) signifies expectation, while "you" (由) signifies spontaneity, and "yi" (誼) signifies righteousness. This refers to the initial period when Dajue first began his travels as a wandering monk.

He arrived at Yuantong Temple on Mount Lu. As soon as Master Zhongmin saw him, he knew at once that his character was extraordinary and that he was a man of great capacity who would surely meet with the expectations of the assembly.
Someone asked him, "Master, by what means did you know from the start that he was a man of such great capacity? Zhongmin replied: "This..."
Their minds are upright; their bodies are not crooked or biased. Their movements are not frivolous; their stillness is governed by method.

They are revered so that others look up to them; they are dignified so that others stand in awe of them. Furthermore, they augment this with the vertical study of the Way, practicing virtue and righteous conduct.
Their speech is simple yet exhaustive in its grasp of principle. Generally, those who possess such excellent natural endowment and fine innate disposition—this is it.
Among those of equal standing, there were few who did not become great vessels. After he became such a vessel, he indeed fulfilled the expectations of the multitude;
his audience with the Emperor was to the Emperor's satisfaction. Zhongmin may truly be said to have possessed foresight and the discerning eye for men of talent.

At the beginning of the Huángyòu era of Emperor Rénzǔ, a small envoy with silver seals was dispatched, carrying a decree written on green silk one chi in length, to summon Yuántōng Nè to reside at the Great Monastery of Xiàocí.
Nè declined on the grounds of illness and sent a memorial requesting Dàjué to respond to the imperial summons.

Someone said, "The Sage Emperor honors and exalts moral virtue, and his grace extends even to the springs and rocks; why does the Master so stubbornly decline? Nè replied, "I have unworthily occupied the ranks of the monastic community..."
Lun: My hearing and sight are no longer acute; I am fortunate to dwell in peace beneath these woods, eating vegetables and drinking water.
Even Buddhas and patriarchs have things they would not do, let alone others. As the ancient sages said, "It is difficult to dwell long under a great name.

Throughout my life, I have practiced the principle of contentment and have not burdened myself with fame or profit. If the heart is weary of them, when could one ever be satisfied? Therefore, to the east...
Sūshō once said: "To know contentment is honor; to know sufficiency is wealth; to avoid fame is to preserve one's integrity; to begin well and end well—this was attained by Yuántōng.
(Biographical Account) [Note: *tí* is pronounced as *tí*.]
"King Injo" refers to Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty. "Huangyou" was the era name of that state. "Silver-earrings" refers to minor eunuchs.
"Chi-il" refers to the imperial edict tablets. "Chaoji" (孝慈) was the ancestral name recommended by Yi Unnyeong. He petitioned for the construction of a monastery on his own private estate;
the Sovereign then bestowed upon it the plaque name "Sipang Jeongin Seonwon. "Garam" is a Sanskrit term, which in this translation means "assembly" (saṃgha).

"Yuan" (Garden) is an alternative designation for a "Conglin" (Forest Monastery); it signifies being honored and revered, and being protected by its shade. To decline firmly and resolutely means not to accept [an invitation].
To be "illegitimately included" refers to being cast among the profane and the defiled; the ancient sages pointed to Fan Li as an example of this. "Leying" means weariness and satiety.
Dongpo’s surname was Su, his given name Shi, and his courtesy name Zizhan. He received the Dharma from Donglin Changcong and was titled Dongpo.

Householder, at the beginning of the Huángyòu era of the Divine Ancestor (Emperor Rénzǔ), His Majesty dispatched a small eunuch with silver insignia, carrying an imperial edict written on green silk and mounted upon a tablet one chi long, to summon Wŏn-t'ong Nŏk to preside over the Great Monastery of Filial Compassion (Hyoji Dagaebam).
Nŏk declined the summons on the grounds of illness and did not respond to the imperial decree; he subsequently submitted a formal memorial.
The Preface: Recommending Dajue. He responded to the imperial summons of the Son of Heaven.
Someone asked Yuantong, "The Sage Emperor has honored and highly esteemed the Master’s wondrous Dao, virtue, and conduct; its gracious radiance extends even to the grasses and trees.
Why does the Master cling so stubbornly to his refusal and decline to accept? Nan replied, "I am but a person who has wallowed in the foul latrines of the monastic community."

I am now old and my years advanced; my eyes are dim and my ears deaf, and I am no longer very sharp-witted. Fortunately, I have found a precarious peace beneath these trees, eating simple vegetables and drinking from mountain streams.
As for the single word "Buddha," I do not even care to hear it. Even if it were the Buddha or a Patriarch himself, I would still be unwilling to become one;

how much less would I respond to an imperial summons to seek honor and renown? It is not that I am quoting Fan Li, but rather— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "大", which likely begins the phrase "大丈夫" [great man] or a similar expression.)
"Under a name, it is difficult to dwell long. Reflecting deeply on these words, one realizes that seeking fame and fortune is better left undone.
My own conduct throughout my life has been guided by the principle of contentment; I have not sought after reputation, profit, or sustenance to entangle myself in worldly burdens.

If one wishes for the heart to be truly satisfied, when will such sufficiency ever be attained? The above constitutes the practice of the Perfect and Universal Way (Yuan Tong Xing Shi). By means of this—
The following is the record of the scribe. Furthermore, he quotes the words of Dongpo (Suzhou Dongpo) to praise him, saying:
"To know contentment is honor; to know sufficiency is wealth. These two phrases perfectly mirror the conduct of Master Anetu.
Moreover, he did not seek honor or prominence but avoided great fame; he recommended worthy talents and preserved his great integrity. Having first come to know him...
He was a great vessel; in the end, he would surely preserve his illustrious reputation. As for Master Nǜ, he has mastered every single aspect of this.
Master Yuántōng Nǜ said: "The life of a cripple depends on his staff; without his staff, he falls. The life of one crossing a river depends on his boat."
If one loses their boat, they will drown. Generally, those who dwell beneath the forest trees have nothing of their own to rely upon;
those who rely on external power to establish their importance cannot avoid the calamity of falling and drowning the moment they lose that which they rely upon (from the *Lushan Yalu*).
"Lameness" means being crippled. "Falling" means tumbling down. "Drowning" means being submerged. "Supporting" means holding up or assisting.
Master Yuantong showed people that they must maintain their own internal integrity and not rely on external things as the basis for their practice. This refers to one who is lame and unable to walk.
It relies entirely upon a single staff; if one loses that staff, one will surely fall.
Those who cross rivers to seek their livelihood rely entirely upon a sturdy boat; if that boat is wrecked, they will surely be submerged.
Likewise, for those who dwell in seclusion among the mountains and forests to cultivate the Way, [they rely entirely upon themselves...]

If one lacks even a slight degree of steadfast integrity and relies entirely upon external power and influence for support, considering this to be true respect, how is this any different from the present case?
When fortune reaches its peak and karma exhausts itself, one loses that which supported them;
they will then be like a lame person who has lost their cane or a ferryman who has lost their boat—how could they avoid falling or drowning? From this...
Observe this: it is clear that external things cannot be relied upon.

Yuantong Ne said: "In the past, the Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang established monasteries and instituted rules and regulations, desiring to remedy the corruption of the Dharma during the Age of Semblance.
Little did he know that scholars of the Age of Semblance would steal those very rules and regulations to destroy Baizhang’s [legacy]."
Regarding monastic groves (*saṃghārāma*): In ancient times, though people lived in nests or caves, everyone disciplined themselves.
After the era of Great Sages, though there are high halls and vast mansions, everyone neglects themselves. Thus it is said: "Safety and peril depend on virtue; rise and fall depend on destiny.
If virtue can be sustained, why necessarily require monastic groves? If destiny can be relied upon, what need is there for rules and regulations? (From *Yelù*).
Baizhang’s name was Huaihǎi; his posthumous title was Dàzhì. He was the successor of Mázū Dàoyī. "To establish" (jiànzhì) means to set up or erect.

"Desiring to rescue" (yù jiāng jiùzhěng) means wishing to save and deliver. "Image" (xiàng) refers to the Semblance Dharma; "end" (jì) refers to the Final Age. "Decadence" (bì) refers to illness or decay. "Neng" (néng) is used as a particle of emphasis.
"Zhě" (zhě) points to a person. The compass is the tool for making circles; the square is the tool for making squares. These refer to the gong and mallet used to issue prohibitions and commands.
The text says: "Nest-dwelling" refers to dwelling in peace atop a tree; "cave-dwelling" refers to the place where one settles within a cavern.

Although these are words established as a pair, they carry the meaning of what is appropriate and what is inappropriate, and the sense of what is inappropriate yet appropriate. "Gai" (苟) means to abandon or destroy; "guo" (果) means to act with resolve;

"jiang" (將) means to rely upon or support; "shu" (數) refers to numerical principle; and "he" (曷) means how or why. Master Yuan Tong’s commentary on the *Zhuchi* (Dwelling of the Abbot) states that one who holds the office must necessarily...
This explains the principles of cultivating conduct and practicing virtue through the logic of the numerical sequence.

In the past, when Master Baizhang saw that the number of practitioners seeking instruction was great, he established a Chan monastery to provide them with a place of rest. Seeing that habitual defilements were difficult to eliminate, he established rules and regulations to govern and discipline them.
What is the meaning of this? It was intended as a means of salvation during this present age of the Dharma’s decline.
This is the failing of those who lack integrity; it may be called a manifestation of overzealous concern. However, if this persists for long, it breeds corruption.
Thus, one comes to realize that students of this degenerate age use public office to serve private ends, stealing the legal standards established by their predecessors.
To destroy the groves established by those who came before is precisely what is meant by "one law emerges and one villain arises";
it becomes, instead, a ladder for the passage of bandits. Have you not seen that in ancient times, even during the summer, people lived in tree nests to seek coolness?
In winter, people dwell in caves to seek warmth. At such a time, although there are strict regulations, everyone observes the law and each adheres to their own discipline.

However, after the era of Great Wisdom (the Buddha), even if one possesses a high hall of a hundred feet or a vast mansion of a thousand pillars, when faced with this situation, though regulations exist, everyone becomes lax and instead brings about their own ruin.
Master Zhi knows only that the tip of the awl is sharp, but he does not see that the head of the chisel is square; how could he have anticipated this? Therefore it is said:
"Peace and security, or peril and danger, depend entirely upon one's virtue and conduct (*de-xing*); prosperity and decline are rooted in the laws of principle and destiny.
If a person is truly willing to uphold virtue and conduct, they can practice even amidst burial mounds or beneath trees; why must they necessarily dwell in a monastic grove?

Lín: If a person is willing to thoroughly understand the principles of *lǐ* (principle) and *shù* (phenomenal patterns), then even those engaged in hunting, netting, or fire-raiding can practice the Way;

what need is there for formal regulations? Jì replied: "The intent of 'perfect penetration' (*yuántōng*) lies in teaching people to cultivate virtue, where the elucidation of principle is of primary urgency.
Future abbots must not use this as a pretext to neglect the monastic groves (*cónglín*) or to hold formal regulations in contempt."
Yuantong said to Dajue: "The ancient sages cultivated their minds before thoughts had sprouted and guarded their emotions before they were disordered.
This was because preparation prevents calamity; thus, one sets up heavy gates and strikes the wooden clappers to await violent guests, taking this from the hexagram Yù (Preparation).

When a matter is prepared for in advance, it is easy; to act upon it at the last moment is certainly difficult. Among the worthies and sages of antiquity, there were those who harbored lifelong anxieties."
That there is not a single morning of suffering lies truly in this. (From the Jiufeng Collection; "治" is pronounced as "池," "卒" is an entering tone, and "朝" is a level tone.)
This refers to speaking with them. "Treat" (治) carries the meaning of cultivation and repair. "Sprouting and moving" (萌動) refers to the stirrings of emotional consciousness (*qing-shi*).
"Yu" (豫) is the name of the *Yù* hexagram from the *I Ching*, consisting of thunder above earth; it signifies "previously. It means that by being prepared beforehand, one attains peace and joy.
"Double gates" (*chóngmén*) refers to the outer three lines of the hexagram *Zhèn* (Thunder), which resembles an overturned bowl with two yin lines on top, like double gates.
This is the image [of the hexagram]. Striking the wooden clapper represents one yang line at the bottom, like the image of striking a clapper;
it takes up the meaning of warning against indolence. "Violent guests" refers to fierce and wicked people. "Sudden" refers to a time of urgency. "Wise" means intelligent.
Master Yuantong Ne warned Da Jue, explaining it through the way of cultivating the mind. Since ancient times, the supreme sages have cultivated...
The mind and intention are entirely focused on a single thought; one must exert effort before any movement has arisen to restrain emotional consciousness.
The five desires are entirely the point where one must intervene before confusion sets in. Therefore, the *Book of Changes* says:
To prepare in advance, one naturally avoids calamity and affliction; this takes its image from the outer *Zhen* hexagram.

The two upper yin lines represent double gates, and the single yang line below represents the striking of the wooden clappers to ward off coarse and violent intruders, while the three inner yin lines naturally attain joy and contentment—it is precisely for this reason that the hexagram is so named.
Generally speaking, in all matters, if one thoroughly prepares and settles them beforehand, [one will succeed].
When faced with a sudden emergency, one naturally avoids panic and remains composed;

however, if one has not previously examined and prepared for such matters, and suddenly finds all affairs converging at once, attempting to settle them in haste is truly a great difficulty. This was the case even for the wise and talented men of antiquity.
There is not a single moment or instant when one does not worry, strive diligently, and remain alert to self-exhortation.
Only by doing so can one hope that not even a trace of misfortune shall befall oneself. What is the proof of this efficacy? It lies truly in making preparations in advance;
only then can one enjoy lifelong peace.
Master Da’jue Lian said: "Jade is not fashioned into a vessel unless it is carved; a person does not know the Way unless they study.
What is known today is derived from what was known in antiquity; what is known in later times is derived from what came before. The good can serve as a model, and the evil can serve as a warning.
Looking back through the generations of predecessors, those who established themselves and achieved renown in their time rarely did so without the cultivation of learning."
...it is so (from the *Jiupeng ji*; "xian" is pronounced with a rising tone).
"Carving and chiseling" refers to the sense of working and refining. This is observed by examining the successive stages.
Master Dajue instructed people through the discourse on diligent study: "If jade is not carved and polished, how can it be fashioned into vessels? If a person does not study diligently..."
Who among you can fully comprehend the wondrous Way? Those of the present day should study the ancients; those of later generations should emulate their predecessors.
Selecting the upright and virtuous teachings of the ancient sages and former worthies, one should take them as models and follow them in practice.
As for that which is base, vulgar, and evil, one should regard it as a warning and maintain reverent caution toward it. Such is the proper sequence.
When we look back upon our predecessors who were virtuous men— those possessed of outstanding insight and refined conduct,
whose noble reputations have been spread throughout the age— who among them was not one who diligently and earnestly perused the classics and consulted the wise?
It is from this that [the Way] first achieves fulfillment. Students should exert themselves in their own strength. The Great Awakened One said:
"The principle of the wondrous Way was once embodied by the Sages in the *I Ching*. When the Zhou dynasty declined, the laws of the former kings were destroyed and rites and righteousness perished;
thereafter, strange words and heterodox arts emerged sporadically to disorder the customs. This continued until our Śākyamuni appeared."
Entering the Middle Kingdom, he demonstrated the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) to people with sincerity, yet from beginning to end he established compassion to transform sentient beings;

this was also a means of responding to the times. Since the birth of the human race, when the primal simplicity had not yet dissipated, the teachings of the Three Augusts were concise and plain—this was like spring.
As the apertures of the emotions were gradually excavated, the teachings of the Five Emperors became detailed and ornate—this was like summer.
Furthermore, times differ from the age, and human sentiments shift with the passing days. Thus, the teachings of the Three Kings were subtle and rigorous—like the autumn season.
In the past, regarding the proclamations and oaths of the Shang and Zhou dynasties, scholars of later generations have indeed been unable to understand them;
yet when the people of those times heard them, they did not oppose them. How different, then, is the custom of today! When things reached their decline and became the Qin and Han periods, then...
There is nowhere it does not reach. Thus, there are those in the world who are unwilling to hear [this].

Therefore, our Buddha, the Tathāgata, once explained it through the principle of life and destiny (*xingming*). Winter is one of the four seasons of Heaven that circulate to generate and sustain all things.
When sages establish their teachings, they support one another in turn to transform and harmonize the world; it is precisely like this.
Yet, when these reach their ultimate limit, all inevitably suffer from defects. These defects are merely superficial traces;

it must be that sages and worthies arise in the world from time to time to rescue them. Since the Qin and Han dynasties, more than a millennium has passed, and social customs have become increasingly decadent and thin.

The teachings of the Sages were arranged so as to stand like tripods side by side; yet they have mutually disparaged one another, and the Great Way has become desolate with none to return to it—this is truly lamentable.
(The tone of "jiàn" is departing; the pronunciation of "dǐzī" is dǐ zī.)
"Yù" (寓) means to lodge or dwell temporarily. "Yì" (易) refers to the *I Ching* (The Book of Changes). To emerge secretly through an opening or gap is called "emerging from an interval" (*jiānchū*).

"Dài" (逮) means to reach or arrive at. To regard it as a single flavor is "pure" (*chún*). "Śākyamuni" is a Sanskrit term; this is translated as "Capable Benevolent One" (*Néngrén*). The primary meaning is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is not existent;

the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is not non-existent. Being neither existent nor non-existent is called the Middle Way Ultimate Truth (*madhyamā-pratipad-paramārtha-satya*). This is the instruction and teaching.
"Compassion (*maitrī*) is able to bestow happiness; pity (*karuṇā*) is able to extract one from suffering. This is also a term used to extend [the application] to others;
it means to proceed toward [a goal]. "The times" refers to the four seasons below; the intent includes the discourse on winter. "Pure and simple" (*chun-chih*) means plain and unadorned.

It signifies the fundamental essence, the original state, and the sense of not being embellished according to one's natural allotment. The "Three Sovereigns" (*san-huang*) are Fuxi, Shennong, and Youxiong. "Simplicity" (*jian*) is...
"Concise" means not being prolix. "Plain" (*su*) refers to being unadorned and simple. "Emotion" (*qing*) refers to the seven emotions; it is like a cavity or aperture.

"To bore" (*zao*) signifies the act of opening and penetrating the emotional consciousness. The "Five Emperors" are: the Lord of Jintian, the Lord of Gaoyang, the Lord of Gaosin, the Lord of Taodang, and the Lord of Youyu.
"Detailed" (*xiangshen*) means thorough examination. "Ornamentation" (*wenhua*) means beauty. The "Three Kings" are: King Yu of Xia and King Tang of Yin.

"Zhou" refers to King Wen of Zhou. "Mi" (密) means dense; it signifies that the net of the Dharma is dense. "Yan" (嚴) means strict; it signifies that the commands of the teaching are urgent. "Gao" (誥) means to proclaim; this refers to the *Five Gao* of the *Shangshu*.
"Shi" (誓) means an oath or covenant; this refers to the *Three Shi*. "Fo" (佛) means awakening; "ru" (如) refers to original awakening (*benjue*), and "lai" (來) refers to initial awakening (*shijue*).

Because the initial and the original are non-dual, one is called a Tathāgata. "Xing" (性) is Buddha-nature; "ming" (命) is [the life-force].** *(Note: The final character "ming" (命) in the source text appears to be an incomplete or archaic reference to the Buddha's life or the mandate of his teaching, as the sentence trails off.)*
"Destiny" (天命) refers to the principle of the Way (理道). "Circulation" (循環) means revolving and circling around. "Alternating" (迭互) means mutual succession.

"Traces and flaws" (迹瑕纇) refer to blemishes and defects. "Mimi" (靡靡) means gradually and progressively. "Triadic establishment" (鼎立) refers to the division into three legs, with one mouth facing heaven. "Calumny and exposure" (詆訐) refers to slandering and denouncing.
This is disparagement. It is desolate and silent. Regarding the Great Awakened Master’s letter to the Elder Cui, it explains the ultimate principle of the Supreme Way.
The hexagram texts of Fuxi and Wenwang, and the line-images of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius—Zeng Qi treated these as marvelous in his study of the *I Ching*, and they are indeed most manifest.

Yet, during the reigns of Kings You and Li of Zhou, the Way declined severely; once the laws and institutions of former kings had collapsed, ritual propriety and righteousness likewise [fell into ruin].
Consequently, they perished in succession. Thus, strange and clever rumors, as well as bizarre and heterodox arts, emerged in profusion to bring disorder;
the social customs and the lineage of the Way were nearly extinguished. It was only when our Buddhist teaching was transmitted from Western India to this eastern land that [order was restored].
He teaches people by means of the single flavor of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad-paramārtha*).
Yet, from beginning to end, he employs the two immeasurable minds of compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to gather and transform all sentient beings;

this is also why one proceeds along this path without missing the opportune moment. Since the birth of the myriad creatures by Heaven, their fundamental and simple nature has never been dispersed. Thus, the three...
The teachings of the Sovereigns were concise and simple, like the season of spring.
When the seven emotions had become fully manifest and their channels were daily being excavated, the teachings of the Five Emperors became detailed and ornate, like the season of summer.
As time passed and eras changed, human nature likewise underwent transformation, shifting day by day; therefore—
The teachings of the Three Kings were dense and majestic, like the autumn season. Among them are the "Announcement of Zhong Hui" and the "Announcement of Tang" from the Shang dynasty;
the "Kang Gao," "Jiu Gao," "Gan Shi," and "Tang Shi" from the Xia dynasty; and the "Qin Shi" from the Zhou dynasty.
Their principles are profound and subtle; yet among the scholars of later generations, there are those who can recite and practice them but fail to comprehend their meaning.
Thus, comparing the present with the past, the people of those times were simple and honest; they would listen to the concise instructions [of their rulers] and did not dare to transgress them.
How vast, then, is the distance between the ancient customs and the current mores!

As the habits of the people grew increasingly stubborn and corrupt, reaching the eras of Qin and Han, there was nothing they would not do—ranging from the lewdness of Lü Buwei to the cruelty of Empress Lü’s "human pig. Therefore, Heaven...
I lament for those inferior worthies who, moved by sorrow and compassion, cannot bear to hear such unrighteous matters.
For this reason, our Buddha, the Tathāgata, has also expanded and extended [this teaching] through the causal conditions of the Great Matter (*mahā-pratyaya*).

He has done so by means of the principle that the resonance [of the heart] accords with the mandate of Heaven, which is called *xing* (nature). It is like the season of winter; thus, these four aspects—how could they not [be understood]?

Is it not the case that there are no dharmas to be grasped? It is simply the Way of Heaven, manifesting through the four seasons of spring, summer, autumn, and winter, which causes all things—whether spiritual or material, moving or stationary—to sprout, grow, mature, and store away their essence.

The Sage established the teachings and laws so that they might mutually assist and sustain one another, transmitting the lineage of the Way to transform and perfect the great world under heaven, making it equal to that celestial realm.
The Way flows forth, generating and nourishing the myriad things; it is simply one and the same.

Nevertheless, when individuals practice this Way and reach its ultimate limit, none can remain entirely free from flaws and blemishes. What are these flaws and blemishes? They are deeds that do not accord with the exigencies of the times.
It is necessary for a sagely person of comprehensive penetration and a worthy person of vast virtue to arise during such a declining age and restore it.
If one arises to rescue it, the lineage of the Way may perhaps be restored.
Since the Qin and Western Han dynasties, over a thousand years have passed; human sentiments and dispositions have gradually become exceedingly shallow.
The teachings of the Sage, displayed throughout the world, are like the three legs of a tripod—this is the first impossibility.
As for those who are deficient: they instead take the "Sovereign King of the Eastern Land" and the "Holy Man of the Western Region," dividing them into factions and mutually slandering one another.
Consequently, the transmission of the Sixteen Minds of the Unsurpassed Great Way has become desolate and silent, passing away without returning.
This is truly to be lamented. [Note on pronunciation: *lèi* (纇) is pronounced as *lèi*; *láo dú* (嫪毒) is pronounced as *lào dǔ*.]

The Great Awakened One said: "Now, one who acts as a leader of a region and wishes to practice the Way he has attained to benefit others must first subdue himself and bestow kindness upon all things, lowering his heart toward everyone.
Only then, regarding gold and silk as mere refuse, will the fourfold assembly honor and turn to him."

Master Dajue wrote to Xiuxian of Jiuxian: "In general, one who acts as the master establishing a transformation in a particular region must seek to circulate the wondrous Way they have attained to benefit all sentient beings.
First, one must overcome one's own selfish mind so that its grace extends to both people and things, regarding all persons as Buddhas."

One regards oneself as if one were his servant. Then, viewing silver and coins as if they were foul excrement and filthy mud, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās revere that morality and take refuge in it.
(The character *xǔ* is pronounced *hǔ*.)
The Great Awakened One said: "Those of former generations possessed the capacity for intelligence yet lacked foresight regarding safety and peril;

those such as Shimen Cong and Qixian Shun are examples one should take as a warning. Thus, while it is indeed difficult to clearly discern the fixed karma of human life, if one examines its origins in detail, how could one not realize that it is the fault of negligence, arrogance, and a lack of reflection? Therefore it is said: 'Calamity and misfortune...'"
"Hidden in the most obscure recesses, yet manifested in what people overlook. Observing it from this perspective, one must be especially cautious and reverent.
(From the *Jiupeng ji*) Shimen named Yuncong was the successor of Shoushan Nianzu. Qixian named Xiaoshun was the successor of Dongshan Xiaocong.
He was indeed fundamental and preeminent. This was the admonition of Master Dajue to the abbots.

One should always maintain the principle of "being at peace without forgetting danger. There were those among the ancients who possessed the natural aptitude to hear the quarreling of ants with keen hearing and discern the finest tip of a falling hair with clear vision, yet lacked the far-reaching foresight to remain mindful of danger while in peace.
They were like Shi Men Cong, who failed to exercise self-restraint beforehand and suffered the humiliation of Xiangzhou; or like Xi Xian Shun, who did not discipline himself during his leisure time.
Despite their precautions, they suffered the same fate as [the monks of] Nankang. How could these two men not have been individuals of pure and refined natural endowment?
Yet, they nonetheless committed such errors; this truly serves as a warning for future generations.

Nevertheless, there are fixed karmic retributions from past lives that cannot be escaped, which are inherently difficult to discern or distinguish. One must examine these two cases with the utmost care and scrutiny.
Is the root cause of their misfortune not simply that, on days when they were at ease and had no affairs, they suddenly became negligent, failing to reflect upon or examine their conduct?
Therefore it is said: "Calamities and anxieties lie latent within the hidden and the minute;
they erupt during moments of carelessness and oversight. This may be observed through the cases of these two individuals.
Come! It is most fitting that you be reverent, cautious, and fearful; with a mind as careful as a child’s, you may proceed without negligence for even a single moment.
This is acceptable. Master Yunju Shun, who styles himself "The Old Man," while residing at Qixian on Mount Lu, [received this] from County Magistrate Huai Dugu.
"Out of private resentment, I suffered injustice and calamity. My people were left in rags. I traveled to the capital to visit Da-jue.
Upon reaching Shanyang (Chuzhou), I was detained by snow at an inn. One night, a guest arrived through the falling snow with two servants; seeing me, he treated me as an old acquaintance."
Thereupon, he changed his clothes and bowed before him. The old man questioned him, and the guest replied, "Formerly, while at Dongshan, I was the one who carried the master's belongings to Hanyang;
I am Song Rong, your servant. The old man conversed with him about their past, and the guest sighed for a long time.
At dawn, he prepared a meal and presented five taels of white silver. He then called for a servant. The guest said, "This boy has traveled to and from the capital many times;
he is thoroughly familiar with the hardships and obstacles of the road. There is certainly no need to worry about the Master’s journey.
By means of this, I, an old man, shall be able to reach the imperial capital. From this, I further recognize the character these two have maintained throughout their lives" (from the *Jiupeng ji*).
Yunju is a famous mountain in Jiangxi, renowned as the foremost in the region east of the Yangtze River. Master Shun resided there and adopted it as his own name, for it was his place of origin.
"Li" (罹) signifies to encounter; "zao" (遭) signifies to suffer. "Hengni" (橫逆) refers to violence and injustice that do not accord with principle.

"Minyi" (民衣) refers to secular clothing, meaning the robes of a layperson. "Jingdu" (京都) refers to the Eastern Capital. "Ludiqu" (旅邸) refers to a guesthouse or inn. "Yi'er" (已而) means before long. Furthermore—
"Because of these words. "To change" means to go elsewhere. "Chou" (疇) refers to the past. "Ling-chin" (凌晨) refers to dawn. "Shu" (數) means frequent.
"Kuan-guan" (間關) describes the appearance of being rugged, uneven, and winding. "Pei-si" (備悉) means to know thoroughly.
"Lian-xia" (輦下) refers to beneath the imperial carriage [of the Son of Heaven]. Yunju Shun Laofu, while serving as the abbot of Qixian Sanxia Temple on Mount Lu, because of—
Hui, the Official of the Department of Personnel for Nan’gang Prefecture, was greedy and corrupt; when his desires were not met, he became enraged and treated him with insolent abuse.
[Lao Shun] asked to return to secular life and went to the capital to seek out Dajue. Upon reaching Chu Prefecture, he was forced to stay at an inn due to heavy snow.
One evening, as it grew late, two messengers arrived through the snow with a guest, who saw Old Man Shun just as if they had never been apart.
An old acquaintance, he took this opportunity to change his clothes and prostrate himself before the old man.
The old man asked for the reason, and the guest replied, "In the past, when you were at Dongshan in Xiangzhou, I once carried your luggage for you."
The official servant sent to the Hanyang Prefecture was Song Yong. The old man then conversed with him about past events.
The guest sighed and lamented incessantly. At dawn, they prepared and ate breakfast;
he then presented five taels of white silver as travel expenses. Furthermore, he called for another servant to accompany and assist him, saying: "This..."
My son has traveled back and forth to Dongjing not just once. This route of the Master’s is rugged and winding;
he understands every detail thoroughly, so there is no need for concern. Because the old man Shun encountered no hardships on his journey, he was able to reach the imperial presence.
The Emperor bestowed upon him a letter and a fan, and he subsequently resided at Qixian. Reflecting upon this...
Regarding the causal conditions of this episode: ultimately, there was something that moved him in the past.
Observing how his feelings are pervasive and his intentions so profound, what he harbors within his breast becomes all the more manifest.
Dajo said, "Old man Shun is simple and straightforward by nature; he knows nothing of the arts of diplomacy, balance, or commerce.
His daily routine is fixed and has never changed. Even lighting lamps and sweeping the floor, he performs these tasks with his own hands.

He once said, 'The ancients had the precept that if one does not work for a day, one shall not eat for a day. What kind of person am I? Though I am advanced in years, my resolve grows ever stronger.'"
Jian said, "Why not employ your attendants? The old man replied, "Having endured the vicissitudes of cold and heat, my rising and sitting have been irregular;
I do not wish to trouble them."
"Fu" (賦) means to bestow. "Quan-heng" (權衡) refers to weights and balances, such as scales. "Huo" (貨) refers to buying, selling, and exchanging goods.
"Zhi" (殖) refers to accumulating and generating wealth. "Chui" (垂) means to approach or nearly reach. "She-li" (涉厲) means to cross over or traverse.
Master Dajue cites the former sages to encourage those who follow; one should not speak of indolence. Old Man Shun’s nature was simple and unburdensome, direct and straightforward without detours.
He was not concerned with matters such as weighing goods for trade; rather, each day he maintained a fixed regimen of practice that he never altered.
Although tasks such as lighting the Buddha-lamps and sweeping the temple grounds were performed, he always carried them out with his own hands.
Shun Laofu once cited an ancient precedent to exhort himself, saying:
"The Great Wisdom Master Baizhang would not eat for an entire day if he failed to perform his manual labor that day; he always took this as a precept.
What kind of person am I that I dare to be indolent and waste my time? Moreover, as I have reached old age, my conduct..."
He resolved his aspiration and made it even more steadfast. Someone advised him, saying, "Why not have your attendants perform this for you?
The old man replied, "Having endured bitter cold and traversed scorching heat, whether moving or at rest, there is no fixed rule;
I do not wish to trouble others with my own toil. Thus, that old man was diligent and persevering.
[The Master] withdrew. This is of such a nature.

Old Man Shun said, "In transmitting and upholding this Way, what is most precious is that everything be true and real; one must distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, and eliminate deluded sentiments."
To cultivate the mind is the reality of practice; to recognize cause and effect and clarify sin and merit is the reality of conduct.
To propagate the Way and virtue and welcome those who come from afar is the reality of abbotship; to assess talents and appoint officials is the reality of employing men.
To examine words and deeds and determine their acceptability is the reality of seeking the worthy. Without maintaining these realities, one merely displays empty fame, which is of no benefit.

This is the principle. Therefore, in a person’s conduct, the only thing that matters is sincerity. If one maintains this without wavering, then even the level and the steep can be made consistent (the two matters are then smooth and even).
(From the *Tán’rán Ān jí*). (Note: *qù* is pronounced as an oblique tone; *zhì* is pronounced as a level tone.)

To transmit from generation to generation is called *chuan* (transmission). To grasp and maintain with earnest devotion is called *chi* (retention). To maintain one's will without alteration is called *cao* (steadfastness).

To practice in accordance with principle is called *li* (conduct). There are many types of *zhuchi* (abbot); here it refers specifically to one who upholds the Dharma and serves as a teacher for others.
To "display" means to sell; it refers to the administration of principle. Elder Shun cautioned the holders [of the Dharma]: "It is essential that your conduct be truthful.
To transmit and uphold the Great Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is no ordinary matter; you must not be frivolous or disparage yourselves.
What is most precious is that there be nothing untrue and nothing unreal in every single thing. To speak briefly: Truth."
In reality, there are five [points], the first of which must be discerned: what is false and what is correct.
To eliminate delusion before it arises and emotion before it is stirred—this is the true cultivation of one's own mind.
Second, one must clearly understand that evil causes inevitably result in evil retribution, and good causes inevitably result in good retribution; one must distinguish between sin and merit.
From what does it arise? From what is merit born? This is the reality of maintaining one's conduct and practice.
Third, one should broaden and penetrate one’s own mind and maintain the rectitude of one’s person with vast equanimity;
one should welcome those who come from the four quarters, causing them to advance and not retreat. This is the reality of upholding the Way of the Dharma. Third...
Fourth, one should exercise due measure: who possesses talent and refinement? Who possesses capability and diligence?
Please appoint them as administrators and leaders so that they may harmonize and manage affairs; this is the true way of employing the multitude.

Fifth, one must scrutinize whether their words can be put into practice and whether their actions can be truly implemented, thereby determining definitively whether they are fit for use or not; this is...
This is to select and seek out the true integrity of worthy men.
If these five realities are discarded and not cherished, and one instead vainly peddles a hollow reputation for fame, what benefit does this bring to the Way?
Therefore, it is said that a monastic administrator must ensure their conduct and practice are invariably sincere and substantial. If one indeed adheres to this without wavering—
Transformation: Although there are levels and obstacles, all may return to the same track, for there is no second principle.
Those who propagate the Way should examine this thoroughly. (The pronunciation of 燮 is xiè.)

Shun Laofu said to Master Fushan Yuan: "If one wishes to investigate the unsurpassed, wondrous Way, then in times of adversity one should become even more resolute, and in old age one should become even more vigorous.
One must not conform to worldly customs or merely seek after fame and profit, thereby losing one's supreme virtue. For jade is valued for its purity and luster;
thus, vermilion or purple cannot alter its substance. The pine stands out in the cold of winter; frost and snow cannot wither its integrity."
Thus we know that integrity and righteousness are the greatest virtues in the world. Only you, sir, possess a character worthy of admiration; how could you not exert yourself?
As the ancients said: "The soaring wings fly alone; solitary wind has no companion. This is surely fitting for you (from the *Guǎnglù*).
Fushan was the name of a district in Shuzhou Prefecture. Master Yuanlu, whose name was Yuanjian, was a successor of Guisheng of Yexian.

*Xun* means to follow and obey; *yu* means to change; *diaoshang* means to wither and suffer; *jiecao* means integrity and操守 (moral character); *yi* means propriety and suitability; *shanggui* means to honor and value.
"De" (得) is used here as "qí" (豈), meaning "how could it be that. "Yì" (逸) means to transcend and roam freely. "Hé" (翮) refers to strong feathers; it denotes soaring flight.
"Lǚ" (侶) means companions. It is thus: when Old Man Shùn saw that Master Lù was worthy of being recorded for his talent, he spoke these words to uplift him.

I wish to investigate this further; there is nothing more that can be added. This most refined and subtle, wondrous Way requires that even if one’s physical condition is utterly impoverished, one must further augment the seeds of the Vajra Path.
Though one’s years may be advanced in age, one must further augment an indomitable and courageous resolve.
One must not merely conform to the common crowd, nor engage in the expedient and selfish pursuit of fame, profit, reputation, or material support.
One loses one's own great virtue. Now, that which makes jade precious lies in its purity and luster;
therefore, even cinnabar and purple grass cannot stain or alter its natural substance. That which brings out the excellence of the pine lies in enduring the cold of year’s end;
therefore, even bitter frost and harsh snow cannot damage its verdant shoots. By this, one knows that a person must not be without [virtue].
The integrity of a jade-like nature and a pine-like resolve is the foremost and most vital matter in heaven and earth;
it is no trivial affair. Your exemplary character and refined bearing are truly praiseworthy and noble.
How could you fail to exert yourself with unceasing diligence? As the ancients said: "The Peng bird spreads its wings and flies alone to the very summit of existence."
The lofty horn of the sheep transcends the flock within the sky of non-obscuration; it is only fitting that it be so.
You, sir, ought not to fail to exert yourself with fierce vigor to investigate this Way.
Master Fushan Yuan said: "The ancients attended their teachers and chose their friends with such diligence that they did not dare to be idle even for a morning or an evening.

Even when performing menial tasks such as tending the hearth or carrying grain on their backs—sinking into lowly service—they never shrank from the labor. While I was at Ye County, I personally tested this through experience."

However, as long as one harbors a mind that calculates利害 (li-hai, benefit and harm) and weighs得失 (de-shi, gain and loss), one will resort to equivocation and indulgence to such an extent that there is no limit.
Furthermore, if one’s own person is not upright, how can one study the Way? (The character 爨 is pronounced cuàn.)
To perform manual labor and cook, to carry stones and pound rice—these are ascetic practices for seeking merit.

To remain submerged where there is no water, to serve in menial and lowly capacities—these are means of concealing one’s traces and shrouding one’s brilliance; they are by no means absent [from the path].

This was stated by Master Fushan Yuan as he exhorted Attendant Yue: "The seekers of the Way in ancient times drew near to enlightened masters and chose virtuous friends, being diligent from dawn until dusk."
I was vigilant, maintaining mindfulness in every thought and not daring to seek personal ease. As for tasks such as tending the hearth or carrying grain for milling, I did not decline the labor;
even when performing lowly service and sinking into obscurity, I felt no shame. All of this arose from my own spontaneous resolve toward the Way;
how could there ever have been a single thought of indolence or weariness? While I was at Guangjiao in Yechuan, I drew near to and examined [my practice].
During my time as a monk, I have experienced being pursued and driven away two or three times.

Had my footing not been firm, had I entertained a single thought of changing my course, or had I been unwilling to swallow my grievances and endure my hardships out of regard for personal gain or loss, [I would not be here].

If one compares gains and losses and develops a calculating mind, then one will turn toward good while turning away from evil; yet if one compromises merely to secure personal safety, there is nothing one will not do.
Furthermore, since your physical form is not upright, how could your mind be free from bias and depravity?
How then can you be resolute in your studies to attain the Way transmitted from Buddha to Buddha and Patriarch to Patriarch? You must exert yourself!

Master Yuan said: "Between heaven and earth, there are indeed things that grow easily; yet if one exposes them to the sun for but a single day and subjects them to the cold for ten days, it is not seen that they can grow.
The unsurpassed, wondrous Way is brilliantly manifest within the space between one's heart and mind, and thus it is not difficult to perceive.
It simply requires firm resolve and diligent practice; its realization may be awaited whether sitting or standing."

Perhaps one may believe for a single day and then doubt for ten; one may be diligent in the morning and weary by evening. It is not merely that these things are difficult to perceive before one's eyes;
I fear that by the end of one's life, one will have turned one's back upon them entirely.
Master Yuǎn encouraged the Head Seat Yún, exhorting him with words of firm resolve and diligent practice:
"Now, Heaven is Yang and Earth is Yin; within their embrace, there are indeed plants that can easily grow.
Yet, were they subjected to warm vapors for but a single day, followed by cold rain for ten days, one would not see them easily flourishing."
This unsurpassed, wondrous Way is perfectly clear within the very midst of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; fundamentally, there has never been any obstruction whatsoever.

Although it is not difficult to see, one must nonetheless establish a firm and resolute aspiration—one forged like cast iron—and possess the power of practice without weariness or fatigue. If you do so, you will surely attain Buddhahood on the spot.
If it were otherwise, one might have a little faith for a single day but harbor much doubt for ten days; one might exert oneself diligently in the morning but become indolent in the afternoon.
This is like treating a plant with one day of exposure to the sun followed by ten days of cold.

If this continues, not only will success be difficult to achieve in the present, but I believe that even if one spends an entire lifetime in such restless agitation, when the time comes that both feet are about to leave this world, nothing will have been accomplished.
Yet one would still not be able to see his face.
Master Yuan said: "The essential point of maintaining a monastery is nothing other than first examining what to accept and what to reject.
When acceptance and rejection are resolved within, the sprouts of safety and peril are determined without. However, safety is not safety for a single day, nor is peril peril for a single day."
All things arise from gradual accumulation; this must not fail to be examined. By maintaining oneself through the Way and Virtue, one accumulates the Way and Virtue;

by maintaining oneself through ritual and righteousness, one accumulates ritual and righteousness; by maintaining oneself through oppression and exploitation, one accumulates resentment. When resentment accumulates, those both within and without will turn away in alienation.
When ritual and righteousness accumulate, those within and without become harmonious and joyful. When the Way and its virtue accumulate, those within and without are moved to sincere submission.
Therefore, when the Way, virtue, ritual, and righteousness are pervasive, those within and without rejoice; when oppression and resentment reach their extreme, those within and without grieve.
Such responses of grief and joy bring about the corresponding manifestations of calamity and fortune.
Master Yuanyou, you who maintain the precepts, must carefully examine what is to be adopted and what is to be discarded when preaching.

When governing the essential principles of a monastic community, nothing takes precedence over careful investigation. What constitutes an urgent duty that ought to be adopted? What constitutes unrighteousness that ought to be discarded?
This adoption and this rejection represent the ultimate and definitive principle; one must be able to uphold this within the mind, thereby attaining peace and stability.
Danger! A certain sprout of fortune or root of calamity will inevitably manifest in one's external circumstances.
Yet, this security is not the security of a single day, nor is this danger the danger of a single day; both arise from long-term accumulation and gradual immersion.
One must examine this. If one examines it, there are three aspects. The first is that the mind does not penetrate [the truth].

1. When the abbot maintains himself upright and not deviant, then everyone will accumulate merit and practice, realizing the Way with a single-minded sincerity, purifying their persons and cultivating virtue.
2. When the abbot ensures that dignified deportment is orderly and his actions are reasonable, then everyone will be modest and courteous, generous with wealth and righteous in conduct.
3. When [the abbot] refrains from encroaching upon the community's benefits or causing harm through exploitation...
When a worthy and virtuous abbot resides, everyone utters evil words with venomous intent in their hearts.
Once resentment has accumulated, then from those within the monastic community to those among the fourfold assembly, there are none who do not become estranged, rebellious, and treacherous.

When propriety and righteousness have accumulated, then both internally and externally, all are harmonious and joyful. When virtue and the Way have accumulated, then internally and externally, there are none—

It is not that they fail to be moved or to submit. This is the way it is: if one adopts the two principles of the Way (Dao) and Ritual (Li), and causes them to be universally harmonized and pervasive throughout a region, then those both far and near will take refuge [in them], and every person will rejoice; they will apply themselves diligently to the Way and find peace.

However, if one does not abandon oppression and resentment, and instead intensifies exploitation and encroachment in one's conduct, then the relations between superiors and subordinates will fall into disorder.
Chaos! Every person grieves and withdraws from the Way, yet remains in peril. Now, grief and joy are stirred within one when they encounter their respective objects;
thus, calamity and blessing respond to them in the time that follows. One must therefore examine with great care what is to be accepted and what is to be rejected.

Master Yuan said, "There are three essentials for a *zhuchi* (abbot): benevolence (*ren*), wisdom (*ming*), and courage (*yong*). The benevolent person practices morality and virtue to promote transformation and education;
they bring peace to those above and below and bring joy to those who come and go. The wise person adheres to ritual and righteousness and recognizes security and peril;

they discern the worthy from the foolish and distinguish right from wrong. The courageous person acts with decisiveness and without hesitation; they must eliminate the treacherous and remove the sycophants. If one is benevolent but not wise..."
It is like having a field but not plowing it; one may be enlightened yet lack courage. It is like having seedlings but not weeding them; one may be courageous yet lack benevolence.
It is also like harvesting without knowing how to sow. When these three factors are complete, the monastic community flourishes; if one is missing, it declines; if two are missing, it is in peril;
if not even one of the three is present, the way of sustaining the Dharma is abandoned. (These two points were from a letter to Venerable Jingyin Zhen).
"Essential" (*yào*) means the core principles or guiding tenets. "Teaching" (*jiào*) refers to instructing others through the Way.

"Transforming" (*huà*) refers to practicing it oneself from above, so that it moves like a wind below, causing others to transform their natures and dispositions. "Fawning" (*nìng*) refers to being skillful in speech and quick in debate, adept at catering to others.
