"Weeding" (*yún*) is the act of pulling out weeds; "reaping" (*yì*) is the harvest. Master Yuǎn’s admonition to the abbot was expressed in terms of these essential points. The abbot—
Dhāraṇīdhara, there are three dharmas that are most essential. They are like the "Three Essentials" of Sima Guang’s memorial to Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty.
Buddhist Dharma is no different from worldly dharma; a human king is indeed a Dharma King. These three dharmas are likewise indispensable for a monastic community (saṅghārāma).
The first is benevolence (ren); the second is clarity (ming); the third is courage (yong). As for benevolence, it is purely...

Heavenly Principle is devoid of even a hair’s breadth of private desire. A benevolent person such as this can fully practice and uphold the Way and its Virtue, promote and spread transformation and instruction, bring peace and comfort to those above and below, and bring joy to all who come and go; this is one essential point. The wise understand this.
He thoroughly illuminates the principles of nature; there is not a single matter he dares to neglect.

A man of such clarity can fully observe ritual and righteousness, discern safety from peril, distinguish between the worthy and the foolish, and differentiate right from wrong—these are two essential points.
The brave person sees what is right and acts upon it, never retreating or showing cowardice for even a moment.

Only such a courageous person can carry out deeds with boldness and resolve, making judgments without hesitation; they know that the treacherous must be eliminated and the sycophantic must be removed.
These are the three essential points. If one possesses benevolence yet lacks clear insight into things, it is like being empty...

To possess a field but not plow it is one kind of failure; to possess clarity of understanding yet be weak and cowardly, refusing to be courageous and resolute, is like having sprouts but failing to weed them.
To possess courage yet act with partiality instead of practicing benevolence and love is like knowing how to reap the harvest but not knowing how to sow the seeds.
Generally speaking, if these three essentials are fully present, the monastery will certainly flourish.
If even one essential is lacking, it will certainly decline. If two are lacking, it will certainly be in peril.
If all three are entirely absent, the Buddha-dharma will be swept away and the monastic communities will fall into desolation; even if there is an abbot, he will be of no benefit. And...
This has long been neglected and abandoned. How can one who serves as the master of a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*) fail to possess these three essentials? Master Huiyuan said:

"The wise and the foolish, the worthy and the unworthy, are like water and fire—they cannot occupy the same vessel; cold and heat do not coexist at the same time. This is simply their inherent nature.
When men of wisdom and virtue are pure, refined, upright, and grave, they deliberate according to the Way, its Virtue, Benevolence, and Righteousness. When they speak..."

In conducting affairs, one must only fear that they do not accord with human sentiment or accord with the principles of nature. Those who are unworthy are treacherous, villainous, deceitful, and sycophantic;
they boast of themselves and flaunt their abilities, indulging in desires and seeking profit at all costs, disregarding everything else.

Therefore, when a Zen monastery gains a worthy person, its moral character is cultivated and its discipline is established, thereby forming a true seat of the Dharma. Yet, if even a single unworthy person is placed among them, they will stir up the multitude and bring disorder to the assembly.

Both within and without, there is no peace. Even if one possesses great wisdom and knowledge of ritual propriety, what use is it? Whether wise or foolish, worthy or unworthy, superior or inferior—the difference is exactly like this.
How can one not exercise discernment?
The wise and virtuous are gentlemen; the ignorant and unworthy are petty people. When a single color constitutes the whole substance, it is called "pure" (*chún*).

To be gentle and capable of attaining sagehood is called "excellent" (*yì*). "Guile" (*zhà*) means deception. "Self-importance" (*jīn*) refers to arrogance and self-conceit. "Taste" (*shìhào*) refers to private desires and depravity.

"Total ropes" are called the "mainstays" (*gāng*); the "many eyes" are called the "subordinates" (*jǐ*). "Superiority and inferiority" point toward what is preferred. To speak in reverse is called "wù."
Why is this? Master Huiyuan cautioned that when elders practice the Way, they must strive to accord with human sentiments.

Furthermore, one must distinguish between the gentleman and the petty person, the wise and the foolish, and the virtuous and the unworthy. This is like the nature of water, which is characterized by moisture, and the nature of fire, which is characterized by dryness;
when placed in the same vessel, they mutually inhibit and overcome one another. It is also like the arrival of cold, which brings chill, or the heat of summer...

When they meet, they are hot; when simultaneous, they are contrary. This is a fixed and inherent distinction. The virtuous and wise gentleman is refined and accomplished in his dignity and respectfulness;
he is upright, solemn, and grave. His every thought dwells upon the Way and its Virtue, and his every moment is occupied with benevolence and righteousness.
He plans and speaks with care, acting personally in accordance with his principles, for he fears that his own nature and character might not harmonize with those of others.
He was unable to fully comprehend the principles of phenomena and reality; yet he remained ever-vigilant and diligent, as if walking upon jagged ice or treading on the edge of a sword.
His resolve to pursue the Way is truly admirable. As for the ignorant and unworthy, their private and depraved intentions are unfathomable;
they are treacherous, wicked, deceitful, and false—clever, dexterous, and sycophantic—priding themselves and harboring self-importance while flaunting their supposed abilities.
They are self-exalting, greedy for private desires, and will do anything for the sake of wealth and profit; yet they are overly concerned with appearances.
How pitiable is their heart of self-deception! Therefore, if one finds a man of virtue within the monastic community, it is easy to cultivate his aspiration for the Way and his moral conduct;
it is not difficult to establish the general principles and all the specific regulations.

Thus, a fine Dharma community is established. However, if a person who is not a vessel for the Way is allowed to enter among them, they will disturb the monastic grove and confuse the assembly, such that the entire monastery can find no peace.
Even if Baizhang’s protocols were fully prepared and the legal regulations were already in place, they would be of no use; for whether one is wise or foolish, virtuous or... [the same applies].
Whether one is superior or inferior, the fundamental principle remains the same. How could the power of grace (*hui-li*) not require discernment? Master Yuan said:
"The abbot dwells in a position of authority and should receive those below with humility and courtesy; the attendants dwell in subordinate positions and must serve those above with total devotion.
When those above and below are in harmony, the Way of the abbot is realized. If those in authority are arrogant and haughty..."
"Venerable Sir, those below become indolent and distant; when the relationship between superior and subordinate is not communicated, the way of maintaining the monastery is obstructed.
When ancient masters held office, they were at leisure and had no pressing affairs, engaging in relaxed discussion with their students on all manner of topics."
For this reason, even a single word or half a phrase recorded in biographies is still cited to this day. What is the cause for this?

First, it is to ensure that the sentiments of those above reach those below, so that the Way remains unobstructed. Second, it serves to allow prospective students to know in advance whether their talents and capacities are sufficient.

In all matters of advancement and retreat, he acted with perfect propriety; naturally, those above and below were harmonious and solemn, and both the distant and the near turned toward him with reverence.
It was through this that the flourishing of monastic communities was brought about.
Arrogance; haughtiness; indolence and negligence. "Negligence" means a lack of reverence. "From-rong" (zìrōng) means being relaxed and slow, without urgency.
"Ōng" (yōng) means obstruction and blockage. "Bì" (bì) means screening and concealing. "Yōng-sù" (yōngsù) means harmony and reverence. Master Yuǎn cautioned Qīng regarding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
When one guides others with humble radiance, the superior sentiment flows downward; this is the discourse.

The Abbot, occupying the highest position, ought to be humble, reverent, and cautious in receiving the assembly. Those holding subordinate offices must exhaust their sincerity and etiquette in serving the master.
When the sentiments of those above and below are thus harmonized, the Way of the abbot’s governance is realized.
Thus, the circulation [of the Dharma] becomes unimpeded. Those above are arrogant, extravagant, and haughty;
lacking genuine virtue, they exalt themselves. Those below are indolent and disrespectful; they indulge in deception and distance themselves.
When the relations between those above and below are neither harmonious nor open, then the Way of the Abbot naturally becomes obstructed and fails to flow. From this...
In antiquity, those who were practitioners of the Way maintained the framework of the Dharma assembly and governed the great multitude primarily during their leisure and moments of inactivity.
At such times, they would engage with students who loved the Way, using gentle words and affectionate speech, delighting in discussion and commentary, reaching every point of inquiry.
For this reason, there are those who utter a full statement while seated upon the ground, or those who, like testing the "fishing pole," speak only half a phrase.
These have been recorded within the biographies, chronicles, and registers;

that they have been praised by people from antiquity to the present day surely suggests there is a certain underlying cause. What, ultimately, is it? Let us further expand upon the intent of the ancients.
There are two [purposes]. First, it is to cause the master’s mind to descend and communicate with the student, so that the lineage of the Way flows without obstruction.
Second, it is to first understand the student’s capacity, strength, and temperament, to see whether they are fit or unfit;
whether they advance to engage in practice or retreat to preserve the Way—in all such matters between these two, [the master must act accordingly].
This accords with what is appropriate. Naturally, those above and below, internal and external, become harmonious, dignified, and solemn.

News spreads far and wide, and there are none who do not come to take refuge. When monasteries flourish, is there any method other than this? It is simply because of this that such a state is brought about.

Master Yuǎn said to Dàowú Zhēn: "Those whose learning has not yet reached the Way, who flaunt their见闻 (what they have seen and heard) and race about with their intellectual acumen, seeking to overcome one another through the sharpness of their verbal eloquence, are like a latrine house painted with vermilion and cinnabar;
it only serves to increase its stench. (From *Xīhú Jìwén*; *chěng* is pronounced in the upper tone, and *yù* in the departing tone.)
Daowu’s name was Zhen. He was a successor of the Venerable Shichuang Chuyuan. "Chengchi" (galloping) refers to the rapid running of a horse;
it describes how he boasted of his own "head-golden-ghouls" (kōan-style talk), which was like the galloping of a horse. "Danhua" is a general term for colors and pigments.
Master Yuanlüe cautioned Daowu that his portrait should be authentic to its original substance and function, and must not be artificially adorned.

Let me speak from my own breast. Those who study the Way, before they have reached the ultimate pinnacle of the sublime path, often polish what they have not seen until they claim to see it, and embellish what they have not heard until they claim to hear it.
They boast of their own sharp wit and take intellectual understanding as the sole flavor;
they merely make a living out of verbal cleverness, sharpening their tongues with forceful sophistry. What is truly precious is to possess more than this.

Sentences are Zen. To harbor such a view—that they are like a person who, out of a competitive spirit, applies five-colored pigments to the wall of a public latrine, even though that person has no intention of defecating therein—is a delusion.

If one voids excrement inside, the filth will only increase and the stench will only spread further. For those who truly study the Way, it is fitting that they hold their own authentic nature (ben-se) as precious.
Master Yuan said to the senior monk Yan: "The mind is the sovereign of the single body and the foundation of the myriad practices.

If the mind does not attain wondrous awakening, deluded emotions arise spontaneously. Once deluded emotions have arisen, one’s vision of the principle is obscured. When the vision of the principle is obscured, right and wrong become confused and disordered.

Therefore, to cultivate the mind, one must seek wondrous awakening. Through awakening, the spirit becomes harmonious and the breath tranquil; the countenance becomes reverent and the expression dignified. Regarding delusion...
"Thoughts and emotions are all melted away into the true mind. By using this to govern the mind, the mind becomes naturally numinous and wondrous.
Only then can one guide beings and point them toward the Way; who would not follow such transformation? (From the *Fushan Shilu*).
Yan Shouzuo was Wuzu Fayan, the successor of Baizhang Yuanzhu. Master Yuan said of Wuzu:
"In the cultivation of the mind, one must seek wondrous enlightenment. He taught that the mind is the sovereign of the four limbs, the hundred bones, and the entire body;
the hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable gates of practice all arise from this. Therefore, he regarded it as the root."
Fundamentally, if this mind is not investigated until it is thoroughly penetrated, then deluded thoughts and emotional consciousness will continue to arise in succession.
Once such false imaginings have arisen, how can one clearly discern and reflect upon the underlying principles?

When one does not clearly perceive these principles, it is not that one fails to recognize what is right as being right, nor that one fails to recognize what is wrong as being wrong; rather, it is a state of muddled confusion and error. This is precisely the point.
For this reason, one should repair one’s own mind with diligent and tireless effort, seeking only great penetration (*dàchè*).
One who has attained such great awakening will have a harmonious spirit, tranquil breath, a respectful countenance, and dignified appearance.
Should any delusive thoughts or anxieties arise at this stage, they will vanish like snow falling upon a red-hot furnace, requiring no effort at all.
By the power of the Dharma-nature, it transforms itself spontaneously, such that all become the true essence of the mind-body.
Using this method to cultivate this mind, the mind becomes naturally spiritual, penetrating, and exquisite.

Thereafter, one expands and extends this principle to illuminate the nature of phenomena and guide the ignorant and deluded, causing them all to attain awakening. Who would not come to take refuge in and follow what they have been transformed by?
The Fifth Patriarch, Master Yuan, said: "In these times, those among the monastic communities who study the Way fail to have their reputations spread and are not trusted by others.
This is generally because their pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) is not clear and white, and they do not act with sincerity.

They hastily and improperly seek fame, reputation, profit, and sustenance, and thus extensively display their superficial adornments; consequently, they are censured by those who possess discernment, and their [true nature] is thereby obscured."
This is essential and profound. Even those possessing the Way and its Virtue like the Buddhas and Patriarchs may hear of this and yet doubt it, failing to believe.
On a future day, should any of you take up a thatched roof for your dwelling, you ought to encourage yourselves by means of this.
The Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*) is itself the Buddha-faring. To be examined and true is called "Truth" (*satya*). To be central and right is called "Appropriate" (*yathābhūta*).
"Ever so" means that in every matter it is thus. "To hear" refers to reputation; "to strive" refers to the diligent practice of the Way.

Master Wuzu Yan exhorted Fojian and Foguo to cultivate genuine virtue and not to pursue fame, profit, or flowery adornments in speech. Among those who study the Dharma through inquiry in recent times—
Why is it that a person fails to acquire a fine reputation that spreads abroad, and is not respected, trusted, or admired by all?
It is because such a person does not value the precepts; their physical conduct is neither pure nor clean;
they are insincere and unreliable in their dealings with others; and in every action and movement, they act with negligence and expediency.
Out of greed for fame, reputation, wealth, profit, and sustenance, they excessively display their brilliance and use artifice to deceive the ignorant;
consequently, those with clear vision see through their very root and subject them to ridicule and criticism, thereby obscuring their true excellence.
Even if they possess realizations and spiritual powers equal to those of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, or—
Whether heard or seen, you harbor doubts and refuse to believe with sincerity. When you, in the future, at some other time,
emerge from this world to become human beings and establish thatched huts to guard your own minds and subdue the intentions of others,
you should constantly exhort yourselves by means of these words of mine.
The Patriarch Yan said: "When my late master first resided at Yangqi, the old house had broken rafters that barely shielded against wind and rain.

It happened to be the end of winter, and snow and sleet filled his bed; he had no place to dwell. A monk came with sincere devotion, wishing to provide funds for repairs. My late master declined him, saying:
'The Buddha has said that we live in an age of decline (the *saṃvarta-kalpa*). High cliffs and deep valleys shift and change without constancy. How could one [expect stability]? "
"Your wishes are fulfilled; you have attained what you sought for yourself. You have left the household life to study the Way, yet your practice is not yet stable.

Already at forty or fifty years of age, how could you afford the leisure to concern yourselves with building fine houses? They still would not comply. On the following day, he ascended the hall and said:
"Yangqi has newly settled in, and the walls of my house are thin; the entire bed is strewn with snow-white pearls. [I] shrink my neck. (He remained silent.)
Alas! I am reminded once again of the ancients who dwelt beneath the trees (Guǎnglù; *mò* is pronounced like *xiàn*; *chēng* is pronounced with the departing tone).
Fānghuì of Yángqí was the dharma heir of the patriarch Címíng Yuán; he was merely somewhat capable. It happened that he arrived.

"Mò mù" (莫暮) means the same. "Xì" (霰) refers to the falling of sleet mixed with snow and rain. "Bù luáng" (不遑) and "bù xiá" (不暇) are similar; "luáng" (遑) pertains to the mind, while "xiá" (暇) pertains to affairs.

When affairs are numerous, one is said to be "without leisure" (不暇); when the mind is diligent, one is said to be "without rest" (不遑). "Jù" (詎) means "how could it be" (豈). "Yì" (翌) means "the following day" (明).
The Patriarch Yen admonished people, saying: "Do not strive after external conditions, lest you lose your original allotment.
When the Master first resided at Mount Yangqi, his dwelling was a dilapidated house with rotten rafters that could barely shield against the wind and rain.

By late winter, when snow and rain fell together, everyone lay upon their single mats; because everything was covered in snow, they had no leisure to find rest even in their quarters. Among the patch-robed monks...
There were those who, having conceived a sincere resolve, wished to act as the presiding master and sought out donors everywhere to repair and manage the monastic community.
The Master-Grandfather declined their request and forbade it, saying: "Our Buddha spoke in days of old that the present era coincides precisely with the *kṣaya-kalpa* (the age of decline).

In ancient times, the human lifespan was incalculable; now it has diminished to a mere few years. When the earth was level as the palm of a hand, all beings dwelt there; [now] it has shifted entirely."
Furthermore, it transforms into steep cliffs, high embankments, deep ravines, and abysses, such that it no longer resembles its former state at all.
Moreover, even the heavens and the moon have their waning and waxing; even the terrestrial sphere has its deficiencies and limits.
How could anything ever be as perfect as one’s desires? How could one seek self-sufficiency to fill the pit of insatiable craving? You who are monks, contemplate this!
This is the principle. One’s hands do not know who is grasping, nor do one’s feet know who is running;
before one has attained stability, forty or fifty years have already passed. Realizing that the time ahead is gradually diminishing, how can there be any leisure?
Whether it be managing external affairs or repairing the monastic groves—in the final analysis, such construction and renovation are not permitted.
Having attended to these matters, on the following day he ascended the hall to preach the Dharma. He presented a verse to the assembly, saying:
"When Yangqi first occupied this place, the walls and roof were in ruins and extremely leaky. Snowflakes fell everywhere, drifting onto the beds and seats.
Cowering against the cold, I shrank my neck; steadying my thoughts, I sighed in lamentation. As I turned this over in my mind again and again, I recalled those of old..."
In ancient times, those who sought the Way in the Zen groves did nothing but dwell peacefully among graves and beneath trees. One should attend urgently to one’s own affairs;
be careful not to long for external things. "Mù" (慕) means to yearn or think of. [Note: The character 葺 (qì) is pronounced jí.]
The Patriarch Yan said: "A patch-robed monk guards the city of the mind and upholds the precepts. He contemplates them day and night and practices them morning and evening.
His practice does not exceed his contemplation, and his contemplation does not exceed his practice. Having its beginning and completing its end, it is like a farmer who has well-defined boundaries."
Such faults will be few indeed.
Our founding ancestor taught people that one must practice what one preaches.

Zen practitioners should guard their own sovereign mind like a fortified city and like sturdy weapons, ensuring that the six thieves do not invade from within. You must strictly observe the *Vinaya* and the root precepts, making your very body...

The Vinaya: take the body as the means of deliverance, ensuring that not a single thought wanders outward. If one contemplates in this way during the day, one should likewise contemplate in this way at night;
if one practices in this way in the morning, one should likewise practice in this way in the evening.
Practice does not go beyond contemplation, and contemplation does not go beyond practice. Furthermore, there must be a beginning, and there must also be a conclusion—just as, for example:
When that farmer tills the field, once the center has been made clean, he likewise makes the four borders of the field equally clean.
In this way, having both a beginning and an end, with the head straight and the tail straight, he naturally avoids the faults of negligence and indolence.

The Patriarch Yan said: "What is called a 'congregation' (saṃghārāma) is a place for forging both sages and ordinary people, a ground for nurturing and cultivating talent, and the source from which transformation and education emerge.

Although they dwell together in large numbers, they are led and harmonized so that each has their own lineage of teachers. Yet nowadays, those in various quarters do not strive to uphold the laws and regulations of the former sages;
driven by partiality and favoritism, they mostly seek to reform others based on their own correctness, causing later generations..."
How should one grasp the Dharma? (The two matters are gathered in tranquility.
"Tao" refers to the kiln for firing earthenware; "zhu" refers to the mold for casting iron vessels. These serve as metaphors for the meaning of the *conglin* (monastic community).
Master Yuanwu admonished the various quarters, saying that one must uphold the laws and regulations of the ancient sages. This is what is meant by the so-called *conglin*.
What is this teaching? It is precisely the place that molds and refines the ordinary and the ignorant to become sages and wise men;
it is the ground that nurtures and raises up the beautiful vessels of human talent. The teachings and transformations of the Dharma all issue forth from here. Even among a vast multitude of people...
Categorized and gathered together, they are unified and brought into order. Each has its own lineage of transmission and succession.
Lately, the elders of various quarters have not specialized in practical application, but have instead exerted themselves toward the fundamental source.
Following what was left behind and circulated by the Great Wise Sages of antiquity, the rules and regulations of today are for the most part merely left to the individual practitioners.
With a one-sided disposition characterized by likes and dislikes, they insist that only their own views are correct.

They arrogantly assume the role of sovereign, inventing everything from scratch and arbitrarily altering established precedents. By disregarding old regulations, they leave later generations without a standard upon which to rely;
by what method, then, should they be emulated?

The Patriarch said: "In propagating the Way and benefiting sentient beings, the primary concern is to find the right person; yet, discerning people is a difficulty that has been a source of concern even for the sages.
If one listens only to their words, one cannot guarantee their conduct; if one seeks only their conduct, one fears overlooking their talent.

Unless one has previously associated with them and thoroughly understood their background, having probed their aspirations and examined their capacities, one should not preserve the Way while concealing its practical application."
This can be known. Those who peddle their names and gloss over their appearances cannot conceal their hypocrisy; even if they remain hidden and secret, their origins will still be revealed.
Indeed, the principle of observing, investigating, and listening attentively is certainly not something that can be accomplished in a single morning or evening.
This is why, after Nan-yueh Huai-ang met the Great Mirror (Huineng), he still served him for fifteen autumns; and when Ma-tsu met Nan-yueh...

We have also followed one another for over ten years. From this, we know that at the time of the transmission between former sages, it was certainly not something that those of shallow virtue could dare to uphold.
It is like water from one vessel being poured into another; only then can one truly succeed to the grand regulations. It is like the cultivated plants of one's own house.
This is the clear and verified principle of careful observation and detailed listening. How could it allow for clever words, insincere countenances, or fawning behavior?
How could those who are selected through flattery and sycophancy [attain this]? (From the writings of Yuanwu; "biàn" is pronounced in the level tone. Nanyue’s name was Huairang;
he was the successor of the Sixth Patriarch Dajian. The Sixth Patriarch’s name was Huineng; he was the successor of the Fifth Patriarch Hongren.
Mazu’s name was Daoyi; he was the successor of the Patriarch Nanyue Rang. This is the grand model and great Dharma.

"Du" (度) means to cross over. "Dangjiazi" (當家子) refers to one who receives the paternal vocation and is able to succeed to the family lineage. "Zhongcao" (種草) refers to speaking of the succession of the vocation;

it means that when good people act as the seeds for good grass, it is like good fields producing good grass. "Bian" (便) refers to being artful and eloquent. "Pi" (僻) means partial, biased, and heterodox.

"Chen" (諂) refers to words of flattery and sycophancy. "Mi" (媚) means to be affectionate toward and compliant with one's kin. The Patriarch’s admonition to those who transmit the Way is that they should be meticulous in... [the text continues].
Shixian said: "To benefit sentient beings and transmit the ancestral Way, the most urgent requirement is first to find a person with correct understanding;
yet it is difficult for a teacher to know people thoroughly and examine them with precision."
Even among those who are sagacious, holy, wise, and virtuous, there are those who suffer from the ailment of not knowing others. To clarify the four methods below, one may come close to success:
listen to what they say; it may seem as though they possess virtue, yet one must fear that their actual conduct may not be guaranteed to accord with reason.
First, one seeks to examine their conduct, ensuring that it ultimately accords with reason, while fearing at the same time that one might overlook the person's talent and capability.

Second, unless one has been in constant association with them, traveling together and scrutinizing them thoroughly to know their fundamental nature and understand their history from beginning to end. Third, one probes their aspirations and tests their actual practice.
Fourth, observe their capacity and examine their talents. Then you will see those who maintain the Way with sweet composure and withdraw from worldly affairs;
those who conceal their utility and hide their brilliance, yet do not delight in making themselves prominent. These qualities cannot be hidden and are easily recognized.
On the other hand, there are those who peddle empty fame to deceive the ignorant masses, who merely adorn their countenances to pose as false Chan masters.
These are all exposed as falsehoods and easily seen through. Even if one were to remain deeply hidden and circumspect, it would still be easy to see the clarity and depth of their fundamental source.

This principle of first listening, second examining, third probing, and fourth observing is not something that can understand a person's conduct in a single morning or a single evening; therefore, one must allow time for observation.
The Sixth Patriarch: What thing comes thus? This is the karmic occasion for awakening to one’s own mind.

After attaining the Dharma, he still served the Sixth Patriarch in menial labor for fifteen years. When Mazu met Huairang, Huairang said, "One who has attained my mind is skilled in the past and present.
After receiving this certification, he continued to serve him for over ten more years. This is that which comes.

By examining this, one knows that at the moment when the successive sages transmitted mind-to-mind, with the higher conferring and the lower receiving, it was originally not something that could be maintained by those of shallow roots and meager virtue;
it required, rather, to be like a vessel of water passed from one vessel to another.
Only by being neither deficient nor excessive can one continue the great dharma’s grand regulations and serve as a worthy vessel for the ancestral legacy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
This principle of careful observation and detailed listening is clear and its efficacy is manifest;
how could one allow oneself to gloss over words with clever artifice or refine appearances with superficial polish, thereby distinguishing between the heterodox and the sycophantic?

How could such as these be those who are selected and appointed for office? Thus we know that those who benefit sentient beings and propagate the Way must make the discernment of men their primary task.
(Note: *shèng* and *shèng* are homophones.)
The Patriarch Yan said: "The great handle of the abbot lies in kindness (*hui*) and virtue (*de*). These two must be practiced together; it is not permissible to neglect either.
If one possesses kindness but lacks virtue, people will not respect them. If one possesses virtue but lacks kindness, people will not feel affection for them.

If one knows that kindness can evoke affection, they should augment it with virtue to complement it; then the kindness bestowed will be sufficient to bring peace to those above and below, and to guide the four quarters."

Come! If you recognize that virtue is worthy of reverence and augment it with kindness to support one another, then the virtue you uphold will be sufficient to succeed those who have awakened first and to guide the ignorant and deluded.
Therefore, one who skillfully maintains [the Dharma] nurtures virtue to practice kindness and proclaims kindness to maintain virtue.
When virtue can be nurtured, it does not falter; when kindness can be practiced, it brings grace. Thus, virtue and...

Wisdom and appearance accumulate one another; wisdom and virtue proceed in tandem. If this is so, then virtue need not be cultivated through effort, yet reverence will be equal to that for Buddhas and Patriarchs;
wisdom need not expend labor, yet affection will be like that for parents. Thus, among those with aspirations for the Way across the lakes and seas, who would not come to take refuge?
When a *zhuchi* (abbot) intends to transmit the Way and its virtue and promote the teachings and transformation, if they do not understand this essential point, they shall find nothing to attain.
"Handle" (bǐng) means authority. "Wang" (罔) means non-existence. "Xu" (蓄) means to nurture and sustain.
In a letter from Yanzu to Foyan, he spoke of the great authority of the abbot in the dharma-way of the monastic community (*sōnglín*): it lies in both benevolence and virtuous conduct.
These two matters should be practiced in conjunction; if even one is lacking, it is not permissible. If one possesses the grace of benefiting others while failing to cultivate oneself...
If one possesses virtuous conduct but people do not revere them, or if one has cultivated virtue themselves yet does not bestow benevolence upon others, then people will not hold them in high esteem.
One must realize that benevolence can cause people to look up with devotion; therefore, cultivate virtue even further to provide mutual benefit and relief.
In this way, the benevolence you extend shall be sufficient to bring peace and comfort to the entire monastery, enabling those above—
With a compassionate heart, he reached down to guide the fourfold assembly toward their destined ground.
He realized that when one’s cultivated virtue inspires the respect of others, one should further bestow upon them kindness and grace to provide mutual benefit.

Thus, the virtuous conduct he maintained was sufficient to succeed the awakened ones and cause the lineage of the Buddha to flourish. Through skillful means, he led and supported ignorant and deluded sentient beings; therefore, he was able to—
The person who maintains the essence of the Dharma nurtures all virtues and practices the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).

By practicing the perfection of giving, they preserve their full virtue. When virtue is thus nurtured, its application is inexhaustible; when benevolence is thus put into practice, its grace is overflowing.
In this way, virtue and benevolence mutually sustain one another, and benevolence and virtue are unified as one.
It is thus. In this way, virtue is already fully contained within benevolence; what need is there for further cultivation?
It naturally causes people to revere and serve one as they would the Buddhas and patriarchs. Benevolence is already inherent within virtue; there is no need for excessive expenditure.
It naturally causes people to cherish and long for one as they would their own parents. Thus, throughout the four seas—
Among those throughout the five lakes who possess the aspiration for this Way, who would be unwilling to come and take refuge? It is like water flowing downward;
nothing can restrain it. The abbot wishes to cause the transmission of the Way and its virtue to endure and to promote the flourishing of the teachings.
"You do not yet penetrate the subtle essence of virtue and grace; I believe you certainly cannot [attain it]. Foyan urged him thus.
After Zen Master Yuan (Yanzu) moved from Haihui to Dongshan, two men—Fojian of Taiping and Foyan of Longmen—went to the mountain head to pay their respects.
Yuan gathered the senior monks and administrators for a night conversation served with hot water and fruit. Yuan asked Fojian, "Shuzhou..."

"Is it ripe? he asked. He replied, "It is ripe. The Patriarch said, "Is it ripe throughout the entire realm? He replied, "It is ripe. The Patriarch asked, "How much rice have all the manors harvested together?
While Fojian was deliberating, the Patriarch assumed a stern countenance and raised his voice sharply, saying, "You have usurped the position of master of this monastery.
Whether a matter is great or small, you must investigate it with a focused mind. The annual provisions of the Sangha estate depend upon the entire community; yet you remain ignorant of them."
This is understood. Other minor matters need not be mentioned; they are evident. You who serve as administrators in this mountain gate should know cause and recognize effect.
Do you not consider that the property of the Sangha is as heavy as a mountain? Master Yan was always sharp and swift in his wit and eloquence;
yet when Fojian observed the etiquette of a disciple, his responses became so measured and slow as to reach such a state.

As the ancients said: "Only when the teacher is revered does the Way one studies become honored. Therefore, among the disciples under Master Dongsan, many descendants have been virtuous and transcendent;
this is truly because the source is distant and the stream is long.
Fojian’s name was Huiqin; Foyan’s name was Qingyuan. Both were successors of the Fifth Patriarch, Fenyang Wude Yan. *Yi* means to go toward; *sheng* means to visit and inspect.
To have an audience with [a superior] in autumn is called *jin*. Ciming’s name was Chuyuan; he was a successor of the founding patriarch Fenyang Shanzhao.
Record of Geng Longxue. A letter to Gaowan Shanwu states:

"When Master Wuzu Yan moved from Baiyunshan Haihui in Shuzhou to Dongshan, both Fojian of Taiping Temple in Shuzhou and Fuyan of Longmen Temple went together to Dongshan to pay their respects to Wuzu and joined the assembly."
The elderly acquaintances, along with the administrators and others, prepared tea, soup, and fruit snacks, sitting through the night in conversation.
Zuzo then asked Fojian, "This autumn, in the region of Shuzhou, have the rice crops ripened? Fojian replied, "They have."
The Patriarch asked him again, "Is the rice in the monastery's permanent fields ripe? Jingian replied, "It is ripe.
The Patriarch asked again, "As for all the rice harvested from the various manors and fields, how many *shuo* (measures) do you have in total?"
The Buddha, unable to discern everything at once, hesitated to deliberate and reflect, not daring to answer recklessly.
The Patriarch then displayed the majestic power of a lion’s spring, his countenance stern as he roared, raising his voice to a great height.
He rebuked him, saying: "You have been the master of Taiping Temple for so many years.
Regarding all matters, whether great or small, you ought to investigate them thoroughly and bring them clearly to mind;
this alone is what is expected of you during your tenure as abbot and what concerns the entire assembly. Yet you still do not understand these things—let alone the other trivialities."
Do not concern yourself with trivial matters; there is no need for further words, for your deeds will reveal themselves.

To truly realize the essence within the mountain gate and serve as an administrator, one must understand causes and recognize effects—just as the Venerable Master [Furong Daokai] assisted the Patriarch Ciming.
Beginning at Nanyuan and ending at Xinghua, you must be able to preside over the affairs of the monastery; are you capable of this? You.
He no longer reflects on it; he dwells constantly in the realization that a single grain of rice is as heavy as Mount Sumeru.
This and what follows are the actual facts of a dialogue between a father and son from the Dongshan lineage. What follows below are all the appreciative words of Master Geng.
Indeed, the Master’s ordinary speech, his pivotal eloquence, and his lofty wisdom were swift and incisive. Once Fojian had...
As a gatekeeper and disciple, one must remain composed and gentle, not daring to respond with haste or superficiality; such is the proper principle.
Thus, the *Xueji* (Record of the Learning) states: "Only when the teacher is reverent does the Way become honored; only when the Way is honored do people come to respect learning."
Therefore, among the descendants of the founding patriarch, every individual possesses talent and virtue;
those who transcend their peers and surpass the multitude demonstrate that the true source is profound and remote, and its transmission shall likewise endure for a long time.

When the Patriarch Yeonju encountered monks who possessed integrity and were capable of establishing themselves, he would sternly reject them in his quarters, refusing to grant them even a word or a look.
Yet, when he observed those who were biased, sycophantic, or whose conduct was so base and trivial as to be beyond instruction, he treated them with even greater affection and respect.
No one could fathom this; alas, there must surely be a profound principle behind the Patriarch’s choices.
"Věi" means base and vulgar; "xiè" means to stoop to the trivial. In the postscript to the *Yanzu Fayu* (The Dharma Words of Master Yanzu) by Geng Longxue, it is said:

Whenever Master Yanzu encountered a Chan monk whose conduct was steadfast and reliable, whose actions were reasonable, and who could become a truly good person, he would often treat them with solitary severity and rejection within his quarters, refusing to employ harmonious words or a pleasant countenance. He did so to examine whether they possessed the true resolve.

Those who act with partiality and deviance, practicing flattery and sycophancy, whose every deed is base and contemptible, and who are unworthy of even being struck by the *gandi*—these he cherished and protected all the more. People did not realize that Master Yan’s skillful means were inconceivable;
truly, they are difficult to fathom. Alas! Indeed, whatever Master Yan accepted or rejected was necessarily...
There is indeed a certain principle inherent herein; it is not something that those who lack superior faculties and sharp wisdom can recognize.
Master Yuanyan said: "The ancients delighted in hearing their own faults, took joy in doing good, were long-suffering in embracing the chaotic, and generous in concealing others' evils.
They were humble in their friendships and diligent in aiding the multitude. They did not allow gain and loss to divide their minds; thus they were luminous."
Magnificent! Its brilliance illuminates both the present and the past.

In the *Record of the Patriarch’s Reply to Lingyuan*, it is said that in ancient times, the supreme sages were like Zilu, who would feel joy in his heart when others pointed out his faults and would immediately reform them;
even King Yu of Great Yu was so delighted to hear virtuous words that he would bend his body in humility.
He bowed and accepted the good. When the Duke of Zhou spoke of the gentleman abiding in *tai* (tranquility), he referred to his capacity to embrace the vast and chaotic;
thus, what he excelled in was the greatness of his will. Great Shun concealed faults and promoted goodness, and the Master praised him for his great wisdom.
Yan Pingzhong was humble, deferential, and compliant; he excelled at forming friendships with others.

Duanmu Ci was magnanimous in bestowing benefits upon the people and capable of aiding the masses. As for these ancients, none allowed their will or conduct to be altered by the two mentalities of gain and loss.
Therefore, throughout the ages, from past to present, their brilliance remains clear and penetrating. Great!
Vast and far-reaching, its illumination reflects both the present and the past without end.
The Patriarch Yan said to Fojian: "The essentials of abbotship are these: when presiding over the assembly, value abundance; in your personal conduct, strive for simplicity.
As for all other trivial matters, do not concern yourself with them at all. In employing others, extend deep sincerity; in choosing your words, you must be deliberate."
One must value respect. When one’s views are held in high esteem, the leader naturally gains self-respect; when people offer sincere devotion, the hearts of the multitude are spontaneously moved.

If one is respected, the multitude submits without the need for sternness; if they are moved, things are accomplished without the need for commands. Thus, both the wise and the ignorant naturally express their inner sentiments.
Both small and large alike exert their strength; compared to those who follow out of necessity—compelled by force and driven by threats—is this not more than ten thousand times greater? (As seen).
The Patriarch Yan’an wrote a letter to Fojian, explaining the essential principles for a monastic administrator: when presiding over the assembly, one must value abundance and fullness;
when abiding in self-composure, one must strive for moderation, simplicity, and frugality. Beyond this, there is nothing else.

Do not set your mind upon trivial matters at all; this is the way one should practice the Path. It is not comparable to the previous practice of merely overseeing and collecting during times of peace.
When employing people, examine and select them most carefully, choosing those who are authentic and free from falsehood. In employing them, choose their words with discernment.
One must understand the nature of their mental disposition; therefore, one should select those who are sincere, steadfast, and prudent, and employ them based on their insights.
If one selects those who are grave and substantial, then even if the leader does not personally hold them in high esteem, they will naturally command respect.

If one selects those who are trustworthy and honest, then even if the masses do not feel moved by them, they will naturally be inspired with loyalty. Once the leader is thus respected, there is no need for the exercise of stern authority.
The multitude will naturally submit out of their own accord; once they have been moved, there is no need for commands, and all matters will spontaneously be accomplished.
Reaching this point, there is no longer any forced effort; it is the natural way of things (*dharmatā*). Whether wise or foolish, each person will understand their own mind.
Those with great capacity and those with small capacity will all rouse their resolve, exerting their strength rather than maintaining a hollow pretense.

If you employ power and influence to turn the banner of ego-clinging and drive it away, yet still find yourself compelled to follow it, how could this be anything less than "leaving Zhengzhou to enter Cao’s gate"? It is far, far removed from the truth.
The Patriarch Yeonju said to Gwak Gongbu: "The nature and temperament of human beings are inherently without fixed constancy; they shift and change with the passage of time.

Since ancient times, although the rise and fall of the Buddha-dharma has followed a fixed pattern, there has never been a case where the principles of its flourishing or decline were not brought about by means of instruction and transformation.
In the past, when the various patriarchs of Nanyue in Jiangxi benefited sentient beings, they fanned them with a pure wind and regulated them with purity."

They were clothed in morality and virtue, and instructed in ritual propriety and righteousness. This caused students to withdraw their sight and hearing, block out depravity and deviation, sever carnal desires, and forget gain and sustenance.
Thus, they daily progressed toward goodness and distanced themselves from transgression; the Way was perfected and virtue was complete, yet they remained unaware of it themselves.
People today are far inferior to those of antiquity. If one truly desires to investigate this Way, one must resolve with firm determination and not allow the mind to waver.
One should take awakening as the goal. Thereafter, let fortune and misfortune, gain and loss, be entrusted to the Creator; they cannot be avoided at will.
How could one refrain from acting out of preoccupation with the fear that it might not succeed? Should even the slightest trace of such concern sprout within the breast, [the path is lost].
"Not only will there be no realization in this present life, but even through a thousand lives and ten thousand kalpas, there will be no time of accomplishment" (*Tantan'an ji*).
"Fengyin fan" (the sound of wind turning) means *si*; it describes how the pervasive wind moves all things. Guo Gongfu was Guo Zhengxiang, a Provincial Surveillance Commissioner;
his courtesy name was Gongfu and his style name was Jingkong Jushi. He received the Dharma from Baiyun Yuanwu.
Furthermore, regarding the Creator: Confucians speak of the "Mandate of Heaven" (*tianming*), while Buddhists speak of "fixed karma" (*dingye*). Master Yuanzong addressed Guo Gongfu, saying:

"You must resolutely determine your will and cultivate your conduct, vowing that you shall certainly attain awakening. Indeed, the dispositions of all people have no fixed nature that can be maintained;
they change and shift according to the teachings and transformations they encounter. Since ancient times, although the Buddha-dharma has at times flourished greatly, [it has also declined].

At times, these traditions may fall into decline; this is indeed subject to the laws of number. Yet, as for the principle of flourishing and decay, there has never been one that was not established through the power of teaching and transformation.
Have you not seen how the various patriarchs of the past—Mazu of Jiangxi, Shitou of Nanyue, and others—benefited sentient beings and engaged with the world?
They fanned the flames of the Dharma by maintaining themselves with simplicity and purity, moving all things like a sweeping wind, and exercising precise regulation.

He purifies the mind through freedom from desire and cleanses the body so it remains unstained. He provides shelter by means of the enlightened mind and the realization of the Way, rectifying the person and cultivating virtue.
He instructs and transforms others through the Vinaya, discipline, and propriety, harmonizing principle with practical affairs and meaning, so that students may exercise self-restraint:
their eyes do not gaze recklessly, their ears do not listen heedlessly, and they shut away private, depraved thoughts and the tongue of perverse sophistry.

They have utterly severed their cravings for flavors and sensual desires; their defiled minds are entirely forgotten. They no longer greedily seek wealth and profit, nor do they flatter others for the sake of maintenance.
Thus, day by day and moment by moment, people transform themselves toward goodness, distancing themselves from faults and transgressions.
Their Way is accomplished and their virtue is perfected, yet they remain unaware of it. In this way, customs and traditions are transformed, and people forget themselves within the Way.
If one is a person of the present day, one falls thousands of miles behind the people of antiquity.
If you are truly determined to engage in genuine inquiry and earnest investigation into this Way, you must further ensure that your resolve is firm and certain, as solid as an iron wall.
Stable as a silver mountain, it must not be altered. Make awakening the ultimate goal;

thereafter, whether it be calamity or harm, suffering or hardship, gain or loss, entrust them all entirely to the natural heavens, as well as to those fixed karmic debts that are certain and cannot be evaded.
One must not seek to avoid them through expediency, nor should one harbor premonitions of fear.
Is it that one fails to achieve accomplishment because one refuses to apply diligence and strives to seek thorough realization?

If there is even the slightest trace of attachment that one does not relinquish, if discursive thoughts do not cease, and if the stirrings of the mind are not eliminated, remaining within the heart-mind—then not only will one fail to attain awakening in this present life, but alas! Saṃsāra.

"One retribution for five thousand kalpas—when will one emerge from it? I fear that until a thousand births and ten thousand kalpas have passed, there will never come a time of awakening to the Way, realizing the fruit, and achieving fulfillment."
Gongfu crossed the Yangtze River from Dangtu (the prefecture of Taipingzhou) to visit Master Baiyun Chuan at Haihui Monastery.
Baiyun asked, "Is your ox pure? Gongfu replied, "It is pure. Baiyun rebuked him. Gongfu stood with his hands clasped in reverence. Baiyun said:
"How pure! How pure! Nanquan and Dayang were no different from this. He then presented a verse, saying: "When the ox comes into the mountains, there is plenty of water and plenty of grass;
when the ox leaves the mountains, it bumps into things to the east and to the west. He further said: "The 'Superior Man' transforms three thousand people;
one may know that they understand propriety" (from the *Xingzhuang*).
He crossed the river by cutting through the current. Baiyun’s name was Shouduan; he was the successor of Yangqi Hui’an. Nanquan’s name was Puyuan;
he was the successor of Mazu. Dayi’s name was Lingyou; he was the successor of Baizhang Hai’an. This records Guo Gongfu:
as a minister of state, he was steadfast and upright; worldly affairs were hurried and pressing, yet amidst his busyness, he found a moment of leisure. From Tai...
He crossed the river at Pingzhou and visited the ancestral master Baiyun at Haihui Temple.

Truly, he can be called one who had planted the roots of virtue in past lives and did not fail the entrustment of Vulture Peak. When Baiyun saw him, he perceived that although he was amidst desire, he was free from desire.
Dwelling in the dust yet unstained by it, he followed a separate path and proceeded to move among the heterodox. When asked, "Is the ox pure?
the Master, having reached this state where thought and speech are severed and the mind’s path is blocked, let go completely as if from a precipice.
Responding with self-acceptance, he said, "It is pure. Baiyun feared that his entry into the Way was crude and that his realization was shallow.
When [the Master] drew near, he struck him deeply with the awl and prodded him with the probe, exerting the full majesty of a lion to lash and spur him.

Yet the Master was like a steady herder of the mountains and rivers who has long since cast off his tether and halter; though the thunder rolls for a hundred li, he neither startles nor is surprised, but simply stands with hands clasped.
Truly, one may say that the iron ox fears not the roar of the lion. Baiyun saw this again.
"Entering and exiting with freedom, moving vertically and horizontally without hindrance—this truly constitutes attaining mastery.
He then conferred certification upon him, saying: "How pure! How pure! You may walk hand-in-hand with the thousand Buddhas and breathe from the same nostrils as all the Patriarchs;
Nanquan and Dayu were no different from this. He further presented him with a verse, which began: "When the ox comes into the mountains, the water..."
It is sufficient; it is sufficient. It is permitted that the needle and the mustard seed meet, and water and milk blend together.
When the ox leaves the mountain, whether it bumps into the east or the west, let it be dragged by the plow or pulled by the harrow as it repays the grace of the sovereign.

Worldly phenomena are themselves the Buddha-dharma. Furthermore, it is said: "The Great Man above transforms the three thousand, and one may know the rites. Although this is an old story, it is clear.
Yun used it most aptly; yet one does not know what its ultimate meaning is. Ji'er once offered this verse:
"Shaking head and wagging tail, he goes straight into the white clouds. Tender grass and cold spring water are fine, but alas, what can be done about a full belly?
This verse seems to have an abundance of merit in assisting [the original], yet the "white clouds" are actually insufficient. Why? Because it merely seeks the head.
While Ji was in his hand, Baiyun said to Gongfu, "In the past, Cuoyan Zhen Dianxiong was so enamored with the flavor of Chan meditation that he used his eloquence to revile those from all quarters;
yet none could satisfy his mind, for he did not truly understand the Great Dharma. One day..."
The attendant Jinluan laughed upon seeing him and said, "Brother, though you have practiced Zen extensively, you have not attained wondrous enlightenment;
this may be called 'dull Zen.
Cuoyan Mingzhen was a successor of Shishuang Chuyuan; he was fond of music and pleasure, and his Zen practice merely resulted in mental distraction."
Observing that the mind was dull, Jinluan Ciming’s eminent disciple, Chichan, fell into a stagnant concentration devoid of right wisdom.
In the *Baiyun Yehua*, it is said that Gongfu valued the discourse on actual realization in the study of the Way.
Formerly, Cuoyan Zhenke merely embellished his own mind with a single flavor; he delighted in taking up a withered and silent concentration and was fond of the "samādhi of the lips."

He beats two pieces of hide and plays with sharp-witted repartee, scolding and reviling the elders of all quarters, claiming that none have attained a height surpassing his own, while truly patting his chest [in self-assurance].
Yet, regarding the one point that transcends, he has never actually realized it through thorough penetration.
One day, while wandering in the mountains with the attendant Jinluan Shan, Shan picked up a piece of tile and placed it—
[The Master] was on a rock. [Xuefeng] asked, "If you can utter a single word here, I will grant that you have personally seen the former master.

As soon as [Xuefeng] hesitated, [Shishuang] sharply rebuked him, saying, "To pause for thought and stop the mind means the barrier of emotion has not been penetrated; when have you ever even dreamed of seeing the former master?"
"Brother, although you have practiced Zen extensively, you do not understand the ultimate point beyond. Consequently, you will never reach a profound realization from beginning to end;
you may truly be said to be mired in a deluded Zen that clings to aridity and guards silence. What benefit does this bring to the True Path?
The Way prizes genuine awakening free from doubt; insight prizes clarity free from confusion. It does not depend on many words."
Baibyun said: "Is the flourishing or decline of the Way not constant? It depends on people to propagate it. Thus it is said: 'If one maintains it, it remains; if one abandons it, it perishes.
Yet, it is not that the Way departs from people, but rather that people depart from the Way. Those of antiquity dwelt in mountain forests or remained hidden from the marketplace;
they were not entangled by fame and profit, nor deluded by sounds and colors. Consequently, they were able to cause their purity to resound for a time and their excellence to flow on."

For ten thousand generations, how could it be that what was possible in antiquity is impossible in the present? It is simply because instruction has not yet reached its mark and practice has not been exerted with sufficient vigor.
Some may argue that people of antiquity were so simple and honest they could be instructed, whereas people of today are so frivolous and superficial that they cannot be instructed.
These are indeed words intended to mislead; they are truly not worth examining.
In his *Reply to Guo Gongfu*, Baiyun explains that whether the Way flourishes or declines—how could there be any fixed, constant law for this?
It depends on individuals personally practicing it themselves and inspiring later students to propagate it on a grand scale.
Therefore, Ziyu said: "If one constantly maintains this Way from moment to moment, it will certainly remain forever without declining.
If one becomes lax and abandons it, it will certainly perish and not flourish. Yet, this Way is not something external to humanity."

In reality, it is people themselves who stand outside the Way. People of antiquity either dwelt in the secluded and tranquil places of mountains and forests, or remained hidden within the bustling markets and city centers.
Whether in the mountains and forests, they were not led astray by fame or wealth;
whether in the cities and markets, they were not deluded or disturbed by sounds, laughter, or artificial expressions. Thus, they were able to maintain pure reputations and achieve great renown.
Their excellence was celebrated for a time, and their beauty has spread its fragrance through ten thousand generations. Yet, they were but single individuals;

so too is this present individual. Is it that those of antiquity were pure, natural, and free from eccentricity such that they could act as they did, while those of today are cunning, artful, full of pretense and deceit, and thus incapable of such deeds? This is not so. It is because [the ancients] were guiding the ignorant and deluded.
There are things that have not been reached. Those who practice and uphold the Way of the Dharma simply lack sufficient diligence.

Some people say that because the ancients were pure, simple, and plain, they could be transformed; whereas because people today are frivolous, agitated, and of meager virtue, they cannot be transformed.
Such words truly stir the hearts of men and delude their minds; they are the talk of commoners, and their speech does not encompass the classical canons.
Truly, there is nothing here to be verified by evidence. One who possesses right view will naturally not listen to the delusions of others. Baiyun said to Wuzhi:
"If something can be spoken but cannot be practiced, it is better not to speak it. If something can be practiced but cannot be spoken, it is better not to practice it.
When speaking, one must consider its ultimate consequence; when establishing a course of action, one must examine its potential obscurations. Regarding this:

These were the ancient sages. They were cautious in speech and selective in action. When they spoke, it was not for the sake of mere expediency, but to clarify principles and awaken those students who had not yet attained enlightenment.
When they established their conduct, it was not merely to perfect themselves, but to instruct those students whose cultivation was not yet complete.

Thus, their speech followed certain patterns and their conduct adhered to ritual propriety; consequently, their words did not bring about calamity, nor did their actions invite disgrace. Their speech then became...
The Sūtra says: "To practice is to embody the Dharma. Therefore it is said: "Words and deeds are the pivot of the gentleman and the fundamental basis for governing oneself.
They move Heaven and Earth and stir the ghosts and spirits; how can one not be reverent? (From the *Baiyun Guanglu*; "zhi" is pronounced as a level tone).
Wuwei Zi’s surname was Yang, his given name Jie, and his courtesy name Cigong; he styled himself the Layman Wuwei.

He served as an official in the Ministry of Rites and received the Dharma from Master Tianyi Huai. His categories were like the mechanism of the law; his pivot-gate turned like the trigger of a crossbow.
Baiyun said to Wuwei Zi: "Be cautious in your speech and conduct. That which can be spoken but cannot be practiced, the gentleman does not speak."
If one says while looking back at one's conduct, then one's words do not contradict one's actions. If something can be practiced but cannot be spoken, the gentleman does not practice it.
If one acts while looking back at one's words, then one's actions do not contradict one's words. The words of Master Ma are truly worthy of emulation.
Therefore, whenever one speaks or utters words, one must first reflect upon them to see whether they are practicable. Once they can be put into practice, there must also be a sense of restraint.
In all established conduct, one must examine oneself to see whether it may serve as a model for others. Only when it can serve as a model should it be followed.
Furthermore, there must be no obstructions. For this reason, the sages of old were always cautious regarding their speech and constantly discerned in their practice.

Thus, when they spoke, it was never done with superficiality; rather, they manifested the underlying principles, truly desiring to enlighten those students who had not yet attained realization, so that they might ultimately achieve awakening. Their establishment of practice was not for their own sake alone.
With one body, he truly desires to instruct and guide those students who have not yet attained completion, so as to ensure they ultimately achieve it.
Therefore, every word he utters must ultimately serve as a model for others; every practice he establishes must ultimately possess a fundamental standard of propriety.
Only then can his words fill the world without verbal transgression, and his conduct fill the world without resentment or malice. Thus he spoke.
Thus, one may serve as a constant standard for others; in practice, one may serve as a model for others. Therefore, the *Yijing* says: "Words and deeds are the pivot of the gentleman.
A single movement and the door opens; a single movement of the trigger and the arrow is released.
This is the great fundamental root of governing the person. If words and deeds are truly good, Heaven bestows blessings and Earth...

If one’s conduct is not good, Heaven will send down calamity and Earth will bestow disgrace; yet if one’s words and deeds are good, ghosts will secretly support them and spirits will covertly assist them.
If they are not good, ghosts will extinguish their glory and spirits will seize their allotted lifespan. Such are the ways in which movement and response manifest.
Since what is tied to one’s speech and action is no small matter, how can one not be careful about wherefrom it issues?
Baoyun said to Zen Master Yan: "Zen practitioners are often able to perceive what has already occurred, but they cannot perceive what is yet to come.

Stopping, contemplating, concentration, and wisdom (*śamatha-vipaśyanā-samādhi-prajñā*) guard against the unmanifest; ceasing, maintaining, relinquishing, and extinguishing (*zhi-zhi-ren-mie*) awaken one after the fact has occurred.

Therefore, the application of ceasing, maintaining, relinquishing, and extinguishing is easy to see, whereas the function of stopping, contemplating, concentration, and wisdom is difficult to know. Only the ancients..."

A person’s aspiration lies in the Way. One should sever all thoughts before they have even sprouted. Although there are practices such as *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), as well as concentration and wisdom, the categories of "activity and cessation," "effort and spontaneity," and "arising and extinction" are all merely discourses concerning the primary and the secondary.
Thus it is said: "If there were so much as a hair’s tip of talk regarding the primary and the secondary..."
All these are forms of self-deception. This is the point where the ancients attained thorough insight and were no longer self-deceptive:

*śamatha* (calm abiding) is the cessation of all discursive thoughts; *vipaśyanā* (insight) is contemplation through reflection on reality as it is; *samādhi* (concentration) is the immobility of the inner mind; *prajñā* (wisdom) is the clear illumination that accords with conditions;
"forming the mind" refers to the activity of mental construction; and "stopping" means that when delusion ceases, it is precisely the True. To simply let things be...
"Relying on circumstances" means following one's own whims. "Extinction" (mie) means the cessation of birth within quiescence. "Deception" (qimān):
to deceive oneself is to deceive both others and oneself; it signifies a lack of self-authenticity. Master Baiyun said to Master Yuan:
"In terms of the actual work of cultivating the Way, the wisdom and capability of Chan practitioners often see only that which exists after things have already taken form."

One cannot illuminate that which is yet to come before any trace appears; rather, one must cease discursive thought, bring [the mind] to rest, investigate principle through contemplation, and settle the mind in tranquility to attain wisdom through illumination.
These four are precisely the means of proactive defense against what has not yet occurred.
When encountering the good, act; when encountering evil, stop. When encountering the True Principle, embrace it; when encountering affliction, extinguish it. This...

Fourth, this refers precisely to the state of awakening and illumination after [the action] has already occurred. Therefore, one performs good and ceases evil, allowing conditions to exhaust transgressions.

That which is employed has form and is thus easy to perceive; however, the cessation of thought, the contemplation of principle, the stabilization of the mind, and the illumination of wisdom leave no trace of their activity and are therefore difficult to know.

This is possible only for those of antiquity who were resolute in their aspirations, applying themselves with earnestness to the Way, and who had utterly eliminated the outflows of discursive thought.

Before even a single thought has sprouted, this is the ultimate state of effortless ease. Although there are the eight methods of *śamatha* (calm abiding), *vipaśyanā* (insight), concentration, wisdom, cessation, application, naturalness, and extinction, where could they possibly find a place to settle? These eight methods all arise because of a fundamental basis;
thus, they possess a beginning and an end. This is merely a discourse on remedial countermeasures. Therefore, the ancients said: "Before a thought has yet sprouted..."
What kind of realm is this? If there were even so much as the tip of a single needle, and one spoke of "beginning" and "end," it would all be self-deception.
This is the place where the ancients saw through from top to bottom; therein lies why they did not deceive themselves.

Baizhen said, "I have often observed that many monastics have never contemplated plans for the distant and the great. I fear that from this point on, the monastic communities will decline and become impoverished.
My late master Yangqi used to say that 'superiors and subordinates seeking only mutual comfort' is the greatest affliction of the Dharma gate."
In the past, while I was living in seclusion at Guizong Shutang, I perused the classics and histories more than several hundred times;

their scrolls and bindings have become extremely worn and tattered. Nevertheless, every time I opened a volume, I invariably felt as though I were gaining something new. Reflecting on this, I thought:
Learning that does not fail one is like this.
The name of Guizong Monastery is located to the south of Mount Lu; it was the place where Wang Xizhi lived in seclusion.
Master Baiyun’s exhortation for people to study diligently states: "Whenever I see the current monastics, their aims are narrow and petty, as they have never yet experienced..."
I have reflected deeply upon this and considered eternal, far-reaching strategies.
I fear that from now on there will be no hope for future generations, and that the monasteries will undoubtedly decline and fall into ruin. Has not our late master Yangqi often said:
"Superior [monks] seek personal ease and fail to instruct their juniors; inferior [monks] seek personal ease and fail to resolve [matters]?"
To choose between birth and death is, among all the afflictions within the Dharma-gates, the most grievous of calamities.
In the past, while I was living in seclusion at Guizong Shuyuan, I would daily peruse the scriptures and examine the historical records.

It has passed before my eyes more than several hundred times. Although the texts and scrolls contained therein are already extremely worn and dilapidated, every time I open a volume and encounter the words and contemplate their principles, they enter my mind as soon as they pass my eyes;
there is invariably a fresh and inspiring realization. Reflecting on this, I have come to the conclusion that extensive learning does not fail the person, but rather... [the text ends].
In the end, there was great benefit. It was like this:
when Baiyun first resided at Jiushang Chengtian and subsequently moved to Yuancong, he was still very young in years.

At that time, Huītáng was at Bǎofēng, and he said to Master Yuègōng Huì, "The new abbot of Yuancong has a profound and penetrating insight into the fundamental source; he is truly no disgrace to the lineage of Yángqí."
"What a pity that his active career began so early; it was not a blessing for the monastic community. Gonghui then asked the reason for this.

Huītáng said, "Fame and office are precious vessels that the Creator cherishes and does not bestow in their entirety upon a person. If a person firmly desires them, Heaven will surely snatch them away.
When Báiyún finally passed away at Shū’s Hǎihuì, he was only fifty-six years old. Those who discerned the truth remarked that Huītáng knew the subtle signs of destiny."
He knew the subtle; he was truly a sage (from the *Zantang Jiwen*).
Jiǔjiāng is the name of a prefecture. Chéngtiān is the name of a temple. Yuántōng is also the name of a temple. "Chǐ" refers to age.
Huìtáng’s style name was Zǔxīn and his given name was Bǎojiào; he was a successor of Huínán of Huánglóng. Bǎofēng is the name of a temple. Yuègōng’s style name was Huì. His given name was...

Xiao Yue, whose courtesy name was Gonghui, was the dharma heir of Huijue of Langye. "Tianruo" (忝辱) means to receive an undeserved honor; "zhongjin" (終盡) means to reach the end, which signifies entering *parinirvāṇa*.
This record concerns Master Baiyun’s initial residence at Chengtian Temple in Jiuyang Prefecture, whereupon he subsequently accepted an invitation to Yuan Tong Temple.
At that time, he was still young and immature. Huaitang was also there at that time.
Baofeng then spoke with Yue Gonghui, saying, "Xin Yuancong and Baiyun have attained profound and penetrating realization;
they have seen the fundamental root of the Way and are not mistakenly the successors of Yangqi Hui’an.

However, it is to be regretted that their manifestation of spiritual efficacy seems premature; I fear this may not be for the benefit of the monastic community. Gonghui then questioned him about this.
Therefore, why is it that seeking blessings too early is not auspicious? Huìtáng said: "In antiquity, those who possessed fame and rank lacked the vessel of excellence;
those who possessed the vessel of excellence lacked fame and rank. This is the fixed decree of the Way of Heaven; they cannot both be present at once.

Thus, the Creator cherishes these qualities and does not grant them to a person in their entirety. Who among men does not love them and wish for them to be fully realized? Yet Heaven may snatch them away."
Yet it was not necessarily complete. Later, Baiyun entered nirvana at Shouzhou Baiyunshan Haihui Temple at the mere age of fifty-six, which is but a middling lifespan.

Those with discernment remarked that Master Zu’s ability to know the subtle before it becomes manifest and his divine capacity for knowing the signs of change truly mark him as a person of profound wisdom.
Master Huitang Xin went to study under Master Yuegong Huì at Baofeng. Huì was profoundly enlightened regarding the deep principles of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and was peerless on the sea of Dharma.
Whenever Huitang heard a single phrase or a single word from him, he felt as though he had obtained a most precious treasure, his joy beyond measure.
Among the assembly of patch-robed monks, some raised private criticisms. Hearing this, Huìtáng said, "I shall strike at their strengths to sharpen my own weaknesses;
what cause for regret is there? Yīng of Shǎowǔ remarked, "Master Huìtáng’s cultivation of the Way is that which the Zen monks take as their model."

If one still considers it strength to surpass others through one's own venerable virtue, and feels shame for what one has not yet seen or heard, then one will cause the monastic community to broaden itself while remaining humble toward others;
this provides a model for emulation—how could this be anything less than a small but vital contribution?
*Lengyan* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "ultimate solidity. *Kou* (扣) means to strike or test;
*li* (礪) means to grind or sharpen, carrying the sense of augmentation. *Mian* (慊) means resentment; it contains the meaning of being without shame or deficiency.
*Ying* (英) refers to Hongying of Shaowu, who was a successor of Huinang of Huanglong. *Qiang* (強) means robust or vigorous; *jin* (矜) means respect; *shi* (式) means model or method. Record.
Master Huìtáng Xīn went to visit Gōnghuì at Bǎofēng. Gōnghuì was fundamentally well-versed in the scriptural teachings;
he had thoroughly penetrated and clearly understood the profound and subtle purport of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Among the masters in the monastic communities throughout the region of Hǎiyáng, none could equal him. In the eyes of others, Gōnghuì was like a celestial being. Whenever Huìtáng...
To hear a single phrase is like obtaining the precious jewels that fill a trichiliocosm;

to hear each individual word is like attaining the rank of a universal monarch (cakravartin). One’s joy reaches its ultimate limit. Among the patch-robed monks (śramaṇas), there are occasionally those who discuss this in private:
"He is already one who has transcended the masses and attained the ground; he should not be forced to submit."
"Furthermore, this only benefits me and remedies my deficiencies; what could I possibly lack? When Master Ying of Shaowu heard of this, he praised him, saying:
'Brother Huìtáng’s realization of the Way is stable and secure, and his mastery of the teachings is profound and refined.

He has already become an object of veneration for the Chan community, yet he still strives to excel himself through the cultivation of human conduct and virtue, as if there were still something he had not yet seen.'"
There is nothing he has not heard. To feel shame and remorse for this—is it not meaningful?
