This is precisely what causes the banner of pride to be raised within the monastic community and the parasol of arrogance to be turned back, such that those who are narrow-minded and deficient in humanity find something to revere in the Dharma.
This will be of immense benefit to the gateway of the Dharma and can serve as a model for future students.
Huìtáng said: "The essentials of being an abbot consist in prioritizing what is far-reaching and grand while setting aside what is immediate and minor.
If a matter is not yet resolved, one should consult those who are mature and experienced; if doubts still remain, one should further question those with true insight.
Even if there are points left unaddressed, they will not be excessive. However, if the leader is fond of indulging their own private whims and acts solely for their own gain or loss,"
Once one is plotted against by a petty person, to whom shall the blame be attributed? Therefore it is said: "Planning rests with many; decision rests with the solitary.
By planning with many, one can observe the ultimate limits of benefit and harm; by deciding for oneself, one can determine right and wrong within the thicket of complications.
Huitang’s Letter to Caotang on the Great Outline of the Dharma Path for Abbotship:
One must select those who can serve as eyes for the monastic community for a thousand or ten thousand years and who can eliminate the afflictions of countless kalpas for future students.
For such far-reaching and grand individuals, one should set aside minor, trivial matters that lack essential importance. Such [matters] are merely proximate.

As for those of lesser capacity: should there be matters that ought to be undertaken, yet which they obscure through ignorance and lack of clarity, unable to reach a decision, they should consult and inquire of those who are mature and experienced.
Or, if they still harbor doubts and fail to discern the truth, they should further consult and inquire of learned gentlemen.
Even if there remains something not fully understood, it must not be neglected or treated with excessive laxity.

It is a mistake. Should one who acts as a leader be fond of self-aggrandizement and the display of ability, being partial and arbitrary, acting solely according to his own whims, and refusing to listen to the admonitions of others;

should he take all matters upon himself and grant them according to his own will—then if, all of a sudden, he becomes a petty person and is watched for by those seeking his vulnerabilities, he brings this calamity upon himself. To whom can he then turn? Therefore it is said:
In planning all matters, one must certainly do so among a great multitude. One must recognize those who possess discernment;
when deciding upon all affairs, one must take personal responsibility. Choose what is virtuous and follow it. Why is it that planning matters must ultimately involve many people?

It is by means of this that one can observe the ultimate principles of distance and proximity, benefit and harm, gain and loss. As for what is essential when dissecting affairs to reach their conclusion:
it is by means of this that one can adjudicate the right and wrong of the elders and juniors within the entire monastery and its various communities.
When Huìtáng did not accept the invitation to reside at Míshān, Chén Yíngzhōng of Yánpíng sent him a letter exhorting him, saying:
"In the past, those who held the office of abbot had no formal administrative duties; they were selected to dwell there because of their virtue.

One who assumes such a responsibility must surely seek to awaken the people through this Way, never allowing power, status, fame, or profit to alter their resolve. Today, students have not yet clarified the Great Way, and each..."

They hasten toward heterodox studies and flow into the realm of names and forms, eventually becoming moved by sounds and sights. Thus, the worthy and the unworthy become intermingled, impossible to distinguish clearly.
This is precisely the time for those who are mature and experienced to take up the Way with a heart of compassion;
to stem and turn back the hundred rivers would surely not be difficult. As for those who withdraw to seek tranquility and make ease their primary pursuit, this is merely to perfect themselves alone.
This is what [the Master] favored. It is not what the monastic community expected of you (from *Lingyuan Shiyi*; *jiù* is pronounced *róu* with an upper tone;
*mì* is pronounced *mì*). Chen Yingzhong, Chen Liaoweng of Yanping County, whose given name was Jie, courtesy name Yingzhong, and style name Huayan Jushi.

"Miù" (糅) means mixed; "mì" (謐) means peaceful. When Huìtáng did not accept the invitation from the resident community of Mount Guǎng to serve as abbot, Chén Liǎowēng, the Magistrate of Yánpíng County, sent a letter urging him, saying:
"In the ancients' upholding of the Buddha-dharma, there were originally no formal positions or administrative offices.
One simply selected those of virtuous conduct to reside in that place; this was their responsibility."
It is necessarily of a single flavor; one simply takes the path of one’s own awakening to enlighten sentient beings who have not yet awakened.
One must never allow oneself to be altered by power, high status, fame, profit, or sustenance.
Those who study today have not yet thoroughly penetrated the Great Dharma; each pursues their own eccentric practices and follows the current, becoming mired in mere reputation.
Within the sphere of sensory instruction, the ears follow the shifting of sounds and the eyes pursue the changing of forms.
Thus, gentlemen and commoners become intermingled and disordered, such that their distinctions cannot be discerned.

It is precisely those of profound virtue and high reputation, mature and experienced, who give rise to immeasurable kindness and immeasurable compassion; they feel this so keenly and so deeply that they apply their attention to benefiting others.
When one is born into this world, if one takes up this Way upon one shoulder and braves the turbulent waves to propagate it above and transform those below, what difficulty could there be?

But as for those who loathe clamor and seek quietude, withdrawing to dwell in tranquility; who decline toil and cherish ease, devoting themselves solely to a life of petty security—what benefit do they provide to the world?
Such individuals, who merely cultivate their own virtue, may enjoy what people generally prefer, yet they are not the true spirit of the monastic community (saṃgha).
The reason the vast multitude looks up to you, Master, is that when you emerge from seclusion, you ought to do good for all under heaven.
One day, while Huanglong was in seclusion, he appeared somber. Huitang questioned him about this, and Huanglong replied, "I have not yet found a person to serve as *jian-shou* (supervisor of stores).
Huitang then recommended Gan, the assistant steward. Huanglong said, "Gan is still impetuous; I fear he will cause trouble."

When people discussed this, Huìtáng said, "Attendant Huà is somewhat upright and cautious. Hónglóng remarked, "Although Huà is upright and cautious, he is not equal to Zhǔzhǔ Xiù, who possesses great capacity and is loyal.
Língyuán once asked Huìtáng, "Hónglóng appointed one person as a supervisor (*jiānshōu*)."
"Why such excessive concern? Huìtáng replied, "Those who possess a state or a family have never failed to take this as their foundation;
it is not only so for Huánglóng, but the former sages also once cautioned against it" (Tōngān Bìjì).
"Yu" (豫) means joy. "Ni" (逆) means to welcome or receive. Huanglong Huinam was the successor of Ciming Chuyuan. Cigan was the name of the head cook (fu-si) who was moved by his spirit;
Bi-hua was the name of the attendant (shi-zhe) who underwent transformation; and Huixiu was the name of the steward (zhuang-zhu). All were successors of Huanglong Huinam.
"Lian" (廉) means integrity. "Liang" (量) means to measure; it signifies the capacity to accommodate others. "Zhong" (忠) refers to inner loyalty.
He exhausted his heart’s sincerity and was not deceitful. Lingyuan, whose name was Weiqing, was the successor of the Patriarch Huitang Xinzhi.
It is recorded that one day Huitang saw that Huanglong had a look of displeasure on his face; he therefore went to meet him and asked the reason for it.
Huanglong replied, “It is because I have been supervising the collection of coins, spreading grain, and gathering rice.”
[The Master] said: "This position is a vital administrative office within the monastic community.
Until one finds a person who truly understands cause and effect, Huitang then recommended Gan Tie-mian, the Vice Steward of the East Wing, to fill it. Huanglong said:
Regarding the character of Gan-zhi, his nature was prone to abruptness and violence. I fear he might be harmed by a petty person taking advantage of a vulnerability;
this would not do. Huìtáng then cited the case of the attendant Shuānglǐng Huà of the western wing, saying, "This man is somewhat upright and cautious;
would he be suitable? Huanglong replied, "Although Huà is upright and cautious, he is still not equal to Dàméi Xiù."
The Master of the Hall possesses the capacity to accommodate others; yet, it is better to ensure that one’s inner heart is not deceitful.
Nan Gong’s Dharma descendant, Lingyuan, once raised this matter and questioned Zu Xin. The Master replied, "Using a single supervisor—what difficulty is there in that?
Why over-analyze it? This being the case, Hei Tang answered Lingyuan, saying: "In all..."

Within the imperial court, those who rule over the world, as well as the gentry and commoners who possess households—how could they ever fail to regard this as the fundamental basis for their planning and management?
How difficult such a matter is! It is not only our venerable teacher who holds this view;
the sages and worthies of antiquity also repeatedly exhorted and cautioned others regarding it.
Huitang said to Imperial Secretary Zhu Shiying: "When I first entered the Way, I relied on my own judgment and thought it would be very easy.

However, after meeting the late Master Huanglong, I reflected upon my daily conduct and found that it contradicted the Principle in many respects. Consequently, I practiced with all my might for three years;
even amidst bitter cold and humid heat, my firm resolve never wavered. Only then did I come to realize that every matter accords with the Principle. And so it is now.

"Coughing and spitting, swinging one's arms—this too is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West" (from the *Zhangjiang ji*; "dùn" is pronounced like "qún," "qí" is pronounced like "qí," and "rù" is pronounced like "ròu").
The Imperial Secretary Zhu’s name was Xianmu, his courtesy name Shiying. He served as an Imperial Secretary and received the Dharma from Master Nan.

[The Dharma] consists of the spear and the shield—the *máo* (spear) and the *qiāng* (lance), along with the *dùn* (shield) and the *hùshēn pái* (body-protecting plaque). In the past, people sold these two items together, each boasting of its own excellence.
A buyer said: "I shall buy your spear and use it to pierce your shield; whether it is sturdy or not, whether it is sharp or not, depends on you. Not so.

"It is so even for me; how much more so for those who contradict themselves. This means "how much greater [is the offense]? "Qi-da" (祁大) means "exceedingly great. "Prushu" (溽暑) refers to intense heat.
Huìtáng addressed Official Zhū, saying: "In studying the Way, one must be firm in resolve and diligent in practice. At the beginning, I had a slight understanding of some principles;
relying on my own clever disposition, I held the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs in low esteem, thinking it was not...

It is difficult to reach. After meeting the late Master Huanglong, I withdrew to reflect upon my daily activities, both in motion and stillness, and found that there was not a single instance where my conduct did not contradict the Way.
Thereupon, I exerted all my strength in my practice, ensuring it was uninterrupted from moment to moment.
I maintained this for three years; even during the most extreme cold or the most intense dampness, I did not cease.
Exert yourself with fervor and make your resolve firm and unshakable; only then will you achieve a state of total integration where every action accords with principle.
Even now, a cough, a sneeze, or the swinging of an arm—these are the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West. But tell me:
when one does not cough, does not sneeze, and does not swing one's arms, where is the Patriarch’s coming from the West? When he finally reached the point of providing the commentary...
At this, he set down his brush.
Zhu Shiying asked Huitang, "When a gentleman unfortunately commits a slight transgression, people are so preoccupied with pointing it out and scrutinizing him that they cannot stop.
Yet when a commoner spends the whole day committing evil, no one considers it so. What is the reason for this? Huitang replied:
It is said: "The virtue of a gentleman is comparable to fine jade. If a flaw exists within, it must manifest on the outside.
Therefore, when people see it, they remark upon its uniqueness and cannot help but point at it. As for the petty man, whatever he does daily is nothing but transgression and evil;
why then would one even bother to speak of it? (Zhang Jiang)
Zhu Shiying asked Huitang, "Why do you not speak of the faults of the gentleman and the petty man in the same way?

When a man of great virtue unfortunately commits some minor transgression, there are those who, upon merely hearing of it or catching sight of it, immediately point it out and ceaselessly criticize him.
Yet when the unworthy commit evil day after day throughout their entire lives, people see it and [remain silent]."
"Nor do they find it strange; they regard it as something ordinary. Why is this so? Huìtáng replied, "The virtuous conduct of a gentleman is like a fine jade.
If even a single thread of flaw arises within it, it will inevitably manifest on the outside.
Therefore, whenever it comes before the eyes of others, it naturally evokes wonder. Dao... [text ends]
This is indeed an excellent object. How could it have such a flaw? One cannot help but gaze upon it and sigh in ceaseless lamentation.
As for those of the lowest and most ignorant sort, whose every gesture, movement, and stillness is nothing but fault wherever they go—what is there even worth speaking of them?
Huìtáng said: "The Way of the Sage is like Heaven and Earth nourishing the myriad things; there is nothing that is not fully provided for within the Way.

The Way of the common person is like the Yangtze, the Yellow River, the Huai, and the Ji rivers, or like mountains, rivers, hills, valleys, plants, trees, and insects—each merely exhausts its own capacity and knows nothing beyond it.
Yet, outside of this, there is nothing that is not fully provided for. How could the Way be two? It is simply a matter of whether one attains it."
Is there a distinction of shallow and deep, or small and great?

The "rivers" refer to the Three Rivers, Four Rivers, Six Rivers, Eight Rivers, Nine Rivers, Hundred Rivers, and Ten Thousand Rivers—all of which denote the various paths of the Yangtze, the Yellow River, and the many provinces.
"Lingfu" refers to the hills and mounds. "Kun" means the multitude. This is from Huitang’s reply letter to Zhang.

It is inexhaustible. This must be explained according to the great principle: the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is supremely vast and expansive, like the height of heaven and the depth of earth, which nurture all things alike.

Among all sentient and insentient beings in the world, what single thing is not encompassed within this Way? The Way of ordinary people, however, is narrow and limited in its scope; it is, for example, like—

The nine provinces and the four seas, the Tong and Huai rivers and the Chang and Ji rivers, the various mountains and rivers, the high ridges and deep valleys, the flora and fauna, and all crawling insects are all alike; each merely exhausts its own capacity.
Furthermore, how could they know that beyond the limited scope of each individual, there exists that which encompasses all and sustains all—namely, the Buddhas and Patriarchs who abide in the Way?
How could the Way, which is most expansive and most vast, truly consist of two distinct types?
It is simply that according to what each individual has attained, there are degrees of shallowness and depth; thus, what they establish is either small or great.
Huìtáng said: "What has long been neglected cannot be perfected quickly; long-standing abuses cannot be eliminated all at once; one must not linger too long in leisurely ease;

human relations can never be perfectly harmonious; and calamities cannot be evaded by mere expediency. If a true spiritual friend understands these five matters, they will be able to navigate the world without weariness."
Huitang’s Letter to Master Xiang: On the Method for a Knower of Reality to Engage with the World.
There are five matters regarding a knower of reality engaging with the world. First, long-neglected affairs cannot be accomplished in haste.
Second, accumulated maladies cannot be eliminated in a sudden rush. Third, one should not remain attached for long to leisure and contentment.
Third, human sentiments and worldly affairs cannot always be perfectly executed. Fourth, calamities and hardships cannot be avoided through mere negligence.
Fifth, as a master of the monastic community, one who transforms others and benefits sentient beings must thoroughly understand these five matters.
By engaging with the world while understanding these points, one can benefit all people and ensure that there is no cause for anxiety or distress.
Huìtáng said: "The former master’s deportment was grave and dignified; those who saw him felt awe and reverence. When monks requested leave for various reasons, he would often sternly refuse them.
Only when he heard that they were going to attend to their elderly parents did his countenance become serene and his expression reveal his affection; he would see them off with full courtesy.
Such was his love for others and his respect for filial piety."

The inner sincerity of the profound [Master] was manifested in his countenance. In a letter from Heitang to Jingwen, discussing the master’s teaching on loving others, reverence, filial piety, and propriety, it is said:
"Our late Master’s deportment—whether advancing or withdrawing—was majestic, solemn, and dignified.

Merely beholding his features caused one’s worldly thoughts to dissolve, giving rise to a heart of reverence, humility, caution, and awe. Often, when Zen practitioners requested leave on various pretexts, [he would grant it only with such gravity]."
He sternly and resolutely refused, not permitting it. Only upon hearing that she wished to return home to attend to her parents, he observed her demeanor;
her sincerity was manifest in her countenance, and her expression was serene and dignified.

Consequently, he provided her with all the necessary gifts and provisions for her journey, sending her away without delay. Such was his profound love for others and his respectful obedience in providing filial support.
He possessed a majestic presence that inspired awe and a dignified demeanor that served as a model; how could those who study not take this as their standard?
Huìtáng said: "In the past, our late teacher Hónglóng resided together with the Venerable Yúnfēng Yuè at Fènglín in Jīngnán during the summer retreat."
Yue was fond of debate. One day he engaged in a heated argument with some monastics, while the Master was reading a scripture as usual, appearing as though he neither heard nor saw anything.
After a while, Yue went to the Master’s desk and, glaring at him, rebuked him, saying, "Are you here practicing the 'measurement' of a *shanzhishi* (a virtuous spiritual friend)?
The Master bowed his head in apology and continued reading the scripture as before. (The above is recorded in the *Lingyuan Shiyi*).
Yunfeng was named Wenyue; he was the successor of Dayu Shouzhi. Huaitang Baonan assessed his capacity and established him as a model for others in terms of teaching and exposition.
My late master Huanglong once studied together with Master Yunfeng Yue.
During the summer retreat at Fenglin Temple in Jingzhou Prefecture, Yue was fond of discussion and delighted in speaking incessantly;
he would engage in loud disputes with the assembly of practitioners. Yet, when the Master read the scriptures, he remained as usual—as if his eyes could not see and his ears could not hear.
After a short while, Master Yue went once more to the Master’s side.
Leaning over his desk, he opened his eyes wide and rebuked him, saying, "Are you here merely putting on airs and practicing the mannerisms of a *kalyāṇamitra*?
My late master never spoke a word; he simply lowered his head and offered an apology for his shortcomings.
Yet you continue as before, reading and reciting the scriptures without ceasing. Later, he once remarked to others:
It is said that Master Yue was narrow-minded and impetuous, failing to match the measured composure of Master Nan. I say this is not so.

Master Nan indeed possessed a chest as vast as mountains and seas, yet Master Yue also possessed a direct insight that cut through all obstructions; each had his own strengths. Otherwise, [this would not be the case].
"How could one dwell in Tuṣita Heaven and yet strike the sun with one's hand?
Master Nanyuan Huanglong said: "In the past, I traveled through Hunan with Wenyue. We saw a monk carrying a travel basket on his back.
Wenyue was struck with wonder and knit his brows; he then rebuked him, saying: 'This is something from within your own inner chambers; you are unwilling to let it go.'"
"Down! To return and involve others in carrying this heavy burden—is it not a great toil?
'Crowning the brow' refers to knitting the eyebrows and pinching the nose. 'Things of the inner chambers' refers to those objects of the heart and mind that are privately indulged in.
'Carrying on the back' means to bear them upon one's shoulders. Master Nanyuan of Huanglong used past events to exhort present-day practitioners."
People say: "In the past, while Wen-yue and I were traveling on foot together, we arrived south of Huguang and saw a monk carrying a trunk and traveling from place to place.
Wen-yue was struck with astonishment and admiration, yet felt pity; he knit his brows and frowned, feeling both regret and resentment.
Consequently, I looked upon him and gave rise to a heart of compassion, employing fearless eloquence to uplift him."
He rebuked them, saying: "What kind of gourd or ladle are you people carrying within your own inner chambers?
You refuse to let it go, and with your vast, deluded consciousness of karma, you instead bring trouble upon that person, forcing them to carry the burden on their shoulders and back.
Is this not far too exhausting? How earnest is the 'old woman's heart' of Yue-zhi!"
Huanglong said: "The success of an abbot depends on winning over the assembly; winning over the assembly depends on understanding human sentiments.

The Buddhas of old said that human sentiment is the field of merit for the world, for it is from this that the Way of principle arises. Thus, whether times are in decline or prosperity, and whether affairs are diminished or enhanced, must depend upon human sentiment.
When sentiment is either open or obstructed, decline or prosperity arises; when affairs are either substantial or meager, diminution [or increase] follows."

Benefit reaches its ultimate. Only the sage can penetrate the sentiments of the world. Therefore, in the differentiation of the hexagrams of the *Yi*, when Qian is below and Kun is above, it is called Tai (Threatening);
when Qian is above and Kun is below, it is called Pi (Obstruction). As for their symbolic significance, when the upper is diminished and the lower is increased, it is called Yi (Benefit).
"To diminish the lower and benefit the upper" is called *Dun* (Diminution). Now, Qian represents Heaven and Kun represents Earth;
Heaven is below while Earth is above, so their positions are indeed contrary. Yet it is called *Tai* (Peace/Prosperity) because the upper and lower interact.
When the host is above and the guest is below, the principle is indeed harmonious; yet it is called *Pi* (Obstruction) because the upper and lower do not interact. This is so.
When heaven and earth do not interact, the myriad things cannot flourish; when human sentiments do not interact, all affairs fall into discord.
The principles of increase and decrease are likewise derived from this. Now, those who stand above others can restrain themselves to enrich those below;

the subordinates will surely be joyful and serve their superiors. Is this not what is called "increase"? When those above hold the subordinates in contempt and act with self-indulgence, the subordinates will surely...
To harbor resentment and rebel against one’s superior—is this not called diminution? Therefore, when the superior and the subordinate interact, there is prosperity (*tai*);

when they do not interact, there is stagnation (*pi*). He who diminishes himself is benefited by others; he who seeks to benefit himself is diminished by others. Is the attainment or loss of such conditions not a matter of no small importance?
The former sages once used the metaphor of man as a boat and emotion as water. Water can carry a boat, yet it can also overturn it. When the water follows the boat...
If one floats with the current, one rises; if one goes against it, one sinks. Therefore, when an abbot wins the hearts of the people, the temple flourishes;

when he loses their hearts, it falls into ruin. If he fully wins them, there is full prosperity; if he fully loses them, there is total decline. Thus, shared goodness brings abundant blessings, while shared evil brings severe calamity.

Good and evil follow one another as surely as beads on a string; the rise and fall of the institution mirror its conduct as clearly as observing the sun. This is the fundamental principle of successive generations.
"Gui" (tortoise) refers to this.
"Pi," "Tai," "Sun," and "Yi" are all names of hexagrams in the *I Ching*. "Pi" means obstruction; it signifies that human relations are not in accord.
"Tai" means penetration; it signifies that human relations are in accord. "Sun" means diminution; it means diminishing and suppressing the multitude to benefit oneself.
"Ji" (己) means that both those above and below are diminished. "Yi" (益) means to increase. It signifies diminishing one's own wealth to augment the masses;
it means that both those above and below are simultaneously increased. "Shu" (庶) refers to the common people. "Pan" (叛) means to rebel or act in a defiant and unruly manner.
"Guan" (貫) means to thread through; it expresses the sense of continuity without interruption. "Yuanyin" (元龜) refers to a great tortoise; it is capable of foreknowledge.

This concerns future fortunes, misfortunes, calamities, and blessings. In the letter from Huanglong to Huangbo, he states that a monastic administrator (zhuchi) must first win over the hearts and perceptions of the assembly when expounding the Way of the Abbot and governing the great multitude.

The most critical point is first to gain the support of the assembly; once the assembly is won over, one must further discern the person's temperament and character. Without this, [one cannot succeed].
The Buddha spoke of human sentiment (*mānasa*) as being one of the great fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) in the human world.
This is because all principles and phenomena—there is not a single matter that does not arise from human sentiment.
Therefore, whether the times are obstructed or flourishing, and whether affairs are diminished or increased, if one examines the cause of these conditions, it will ultimately be found to be so.
This arises from human sentiment. If human sentiments accord with one another and flow freely, then prosperity (*tai*) naturally arises and there is no stagnation (*pi*).
If they cannot accord and remain obstructed, then stagnation naturally arises and there is no prosperity. When matters are profound and substantial, both parties mutually benefit.
When the four classes of people gather like clouds, yet their affairs are meager and thin, they will diminish and encroach upon one another until they part ways.

This human sentiment—how could it be understood by an ordinary person? Only a Great Sage endowed with heavenly talent, a person of supreme realization appearing once more, might be able to comprehend it.
This is the fundamental principle of human nature throughout the world. Therefore, the *Yi* distinguishes...
The hexagram states: When Qian (Heaven) is below and Kun (Earth) is above, it is called Tai (Threatening).
When Qian is above and Kun is below, it is called Pi (Oppression). As for deriving the hexagram images, it involves diminishing the ruler to benefit the people.
When the people are wealthy, how could the ruler alone be poor? Thus, both those above and below benefit; this is what constitutes "benefit" (yì).
To diminish the people's resources to serve the ruler, the people become poor; how could the ruler alone be wealthy? Thus, both those above and below suffer loss;
this is what constitutes "loss" (sǔn). Now, Qian represents Heaven; its origin is above, yet it now resides below. Kun represents Earth; its origin is below, yet it now resides above.
Is it not a contradiction for their positions to be thus disordered? Yet you instead call this "penetration and harmony. For what reason?
It is because the celestial qi descends and the terrestrial qi ascends, and these harmonious energies meet one another; therefore, there is penetration and harmony.
The ruler ought to be above by nature, while ministers and guests ought to occupy the lower positions by nature. How is it that the principles of righteousness are so perfectly suited?
Furthermore, as for what is called "obstruction" (*pi-sai*), by what cause does it arise?
Because those above are haughty and arrogant, while those below are likewise negligent and disrespectful, human sentiments do not interact; thus there is obstruction.

For this reason, when the Way of Heaven and Earth no longer provides mutual nurturing through its seasonal cycles, how could the spiritual and the insentient, the moving and the stationary, be able to grow and flourish?
This develops from the way of human emotion. If mutual care and protection are not thorough and complete, how can the various offices and ranks, whether east or west, be harmonized and managed?
As for the principles of diminution and augmentation, they are just like the principles of *tai* (prosperity) and *pi* (stagnation);
they are of one and the same nature. Indeed, those who stand above others must truly be able to exercise restraint and practice humility.
It shall accommodate the fourfold assembly; the fourfold assembly will surely be harmonious and joyful, following and supporting their leader with reverence to serve him above.

Is this not the same principle as that of Naya? If those in superior positions were to disparage and belittle the great assembly, acting with unrestrained license and self-indulgence, the assembly would surely become resentful, rebellious, and defiant, thereby deceiving those above.
Is this not indeed the same principle as that of "diminishing" (sun)?
Therefore, when the sentiments of those above and below accord with one another, it is necessarily *tai* (prosperity); when they do not accord, it is necessarily *pi* (misfortune).
To diminish oneself to benefit others certainly results in mutual benefit; to diminish others to benefit oneself certainly results in mutual loss. From this...
When one observes this, is it not difficult for human sentiment to attain its goal?
Therefore, when Confucius answered Duke Ai of Lu, he spoke through a parable: he compared humans to a boat and human sentiment to water.
When the wind is calm and the waves are still, the water can certainly support the boat; yet even when white waves surge to the heavens, it can likewise do so.
When a boat capsizes, if the water flows smoothly and unimpeded, the boat will certainly float and remain safe;

however, if the boat goes against the current or in a contrary direction, the water will surely submerge it and cause disaster. Using this as a metaphor for human relations, would it not be difficult to manage them?
Therefore, when a monastic administrator wins over people's hearts, the Way and the Dharma flourish easily; if he does not win them over...
If human sentiments are disregarded, then the Way and its teachings will easily fall into ruin. When human sentiments are fully realized, the transformative power of the Dharma flourishes;

when human sentiments are entirely lost, the transformative power of the Dharma is utterly destroyed. Therefore, if every person accumulates goodness, the resulting blessings will surely be manifold—how could this not be a full flourishing?
If every person accumulates evil, the resulting calamities will surely be extreme—is this not a total collapse? Such is the nature of good and evil.
To align with their respective categories and reach the ultimate point is like threading beads on a rosary; it is a continuous succession.
Whether in prosperity or decline, one acts in accordance with these patterns, as clearly as one gazes upward at the sun.
This is thoroughly understood without omission; it is truly the great mirror for understanding human nature throughout the ages.
Huanglong said to Lord Jing: "In all matters undertaken with the mind, one must always ensure that the path before one is wide open, so that all people may pass through;

only then is this the application of the mind of a great man. If it is narrow, treacherous, and impassable, not only will others be unable to proceed, but even for oneself there will be no ground upon which to set foot" (*Zhangjiang ji*).
The Duke of Jing’s surname was Wang and his given name was Anshi; his courtesy name was Jiefu. He served as a Chancellor of the Song Dynasty.
He received the Dharma from Huanglong, who said to the Duke of Jing: "In all your actions, you must prioritize being upright and grand.
Whenever a person sets their mind upon performing any undertaking, they should always ensure that the direct path before them is clear, open, and expansive, leaving nothing obstructed."
Without the slightest obstruction, it enables those of superior wisdom and inferior folly, whether noble or base, to practice it all.
This is precisely what a true man employs: a mind of public righteousness.
If there were obstacles, narrowness, or a lack of openness and ease, not only would it prevent everyone from practicing it, but I fear that even I myself could not practice it.
"It shall not depart.

Huanglong said, "A person’s speech and silence, their conduct and movements—when they claim above not to deceive Heaven, outwardly not to deceive others, and inwardly not to deceive their own heart—they may truly be said to have attained it.
Yet, one must still remain cautious and reverent even in the solitude of private and hidden moments."
If there is not even a hair’s breadth of deception in the result, this may be called "attainment.
As Huanglong said in his letter to Lord Jing: "A person may either display words and phrases, or keep their mouth sealed with three silences."
Whether in the movement of one’s countenance and gestures, or in the conduct and disposition of one’s person, does one not speak to oneself of being free from deception?
Is one not free from deception toward Heaven above? Is one not free from deception among the multitude within?
This is truly that which can be taught to those who are capable of practice. Nevertheless, one must further guard and warn this mind before it has yet encountered external objects.
Regarding the priority of reception: it is that which others do not know while one alone knows;
one must be cautious of this thought at the very moment before it has even sprouted. It is that which others do not see while one alone sees;
it must be precise and exact, without the slightest hair’s breadth of delusion. Only then can one hope to truly practice this teaching.

Huanglong said, "The office of an elder is the vessel for the Way and its virtue. When the former sages established the monasteries, set forth the regulations, and instituted ranks and titles, they selected those monks endowed with the Way and virtue, appointing them as 'elders' so that they might practice that Way and virtue;
it was not for them to merely usurp this title at will. Our late master Ciming once said: 'Rather than remaining old and dying while merely guarding the Way...'"

To dwell in mountain retreats is not as good as practicing the Way and leading the assembly within the monastic groves; for is it not the case that the moral virtue of the Buddhas and Patriarchs endures only in those who excel at fulfilling the duties of an elder?
Huanglong and Cuoyan spoke in their true script: "The office of the elder is the vessel for carrying the essential path of the Three Mysteries and the measure of virtue of the Four Integrations.

Formerly, when Mazu first established the monastic groves (conglin) and Baizhang set forth the regulations, the titles of 'Knowledgeable One' (zhishi) and the position of 'Hall Head' (dangtou) were established; these were positions selected and chosen through careful deliberation."

One who truly practices and embodies the Way, possessing its entirety and perfection, is what a patch-robed monk calls a "Name-Teacher" (mingjiao). As for those who act as elders (*zhǎnglǎo*), how can they do so?
If you wish to practice the Way and virtue of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, it must not be done with negligence or expediency, nor should you privately usurp the empty title of "Elder.
Have you not seen that our late master Ciming once said: "It would be better to embrace the Way and die in obscurity than to die in the dust of worldly fame"?

To dwell in mountain streams and ravines as one who has attained self-enlightenment, yet fail to practice the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs or to govern the great assembly within the monastic groves—

is this not to be unworthy of one’s name? Is it not the duty of those who can maintain their conduct and uphold their integrity in the position of an elder to ensure that the virtue and teachings of all Buddhas and Patriarchs endure forever without loss?
Huanglong said to the recluse Pan Yanzhi: "The learning of the sages and worthies cannot be accomplished in a moment; it must depend upon accumulation.
The essentials of accumulation are nothing other than single-mindedness and diligence. One must eliminate all personal indulgences and practice without weariness.
Only then can one expand and fulfill this learning, thereby exhausting the subtle mysteries of the world."
The hermit Pan Yanzhi did not care for holding office; he delighted in the Way for himself. His courtesy name was Xingsi, and his style was Qingyi Jushi.
He received the Dharma from Master Nan (Huanglong Nan), who said to him:
"The study of attaining sagehood or worthiness lies in the value of practicing with vigor and diligence; it cannot be achieved through haste or negligence."
Success lies in daily accumulation. As for the essential method of this accumulation, it consists solely in being single-mindedly earnest and diligent.
One must eliminate what the mouth desires, sever what the heart loves, and practice with vigor without giving rise to a mind of indolence.
Thereafter, one expands and applies this principle to fill this mind completely, exhausting it without remainder;
thus, one thoroughly understands the ultimate limit of all under heaven—is this not magnificent?
When Pan Yanzhi heard that Huanglong’s method of the Way was strict and profound, he asked for its essential points. Huanglong said, "If the father is strict, the son will be respectful.
Today's discipline and instruction are tomorrow's model and standard. It is like leveling various terrains: that which is high is lowered, and that which is low is leveled.
When he ascends a mountain a thousand *zhang* high, I shall go with him; when he is exhausted, [I shall support him]."
"Reaching down to the depths of the Nine Abysses, I am likewise there with it. When skill is exhausted and delusion is ended, that [state] naturally rests.
It is further said: "To nurture and foster—this is how spring and summer bring forth life.
To frost and snow—this is how autumn and winter bring things to maturity. How could I wish to remain without words? (Linjian Lu).

"Lóng" (隆) means high and elevated. "Wá" (窪), pronounced as *wa*, means deep. "Xǔ" (姁), pronounced as *xǔ*, refers to the warmth of the sun; "xù" (煦) means gentle warmth. "Yù" (嫗), in the departing tone (*qùshēng*), refers to the nurturing of a mother.
This expresses the intent that Heaven nurtures all things with its vital energy (*qì*) and Earth nurtures them with its physical form (*xíng*).
It records how Pan Yanzhi saw a yellow dragon. His practice and maintenance of the Way were exceedingly strict and meticulous; there must have been a specific cause for this.
He asked for the essential principles. Huanglong replied to him, saying: "It is like a secular family teaching their child;
if the father is majestic and stern, the son will likewise be filial and respectful. The rules and admonitions established today in my Dharma gate are just like this."
This is indeed a ready-made model and standard for those who come after.
Its essential point is just like the way a worldly family teaches its children. It is also like a farmer leveling the soil:
he lowers the high places to make them low, and fills in the deep hollows to make them level. My strict regulations are likewise not without purpose; it is simply because of people.
And so it is with giving. If he wishes to ascend to the highest mountain peak, I shall go there with him.
If he becomes exhausted and sinks to the very bottom of the deep ocean, I shall go there with him as well.
Once his skillful means are exhausted and his deluded thoughts are spent, he will naturally come to rest. The essential point is also like that of a farmer.
Human beings are generally like the level ground. It is further said: Heaven nurtures with its vital energy (*qi*), while Earth nurtures with its form.
In spring, it is warm so that sprouts may grow; in summer, it is hot so that branches and shoots may develop. With frost, they wither and fall.
The snow is piercingly cold; when autumn is complete, fruits are gathered as a sign of contraction;
when winter ripens, both the moving and the stationary enter hibernation. How could I wish to remain silent and fail to bestow instruction and admonition?
Such is the essential point. (Note: *pèi* is pronounced *bài*; it means extreme exhaustion.)
Within the chamber of Huanglong, there were three "gate" sayings. Among the monks, few were able to accord with his spiritual mechanism;

even when some offered a response, he would merely sit upright with eyes closed, showing no sign of approval or disapproval. When Yan repeatedly pressed him for further clarification, Huanglong said, "Those who have already passed through the gate."

He flung his arms and departed. He went to ask the customs official whether it was permissible; this refers to one who has not yet passed through the barrier (*Linjian Lu*). As for the "Three Barriers," they are:
"Everyone has their own karmic affinity of birth," "What is my hand like compared to the Buddha’s hand? and "What is my foot like compared to a donkey’s foot?
The word *tuō* (脫) is a particle used to express possibility or uncertainty. This records that when Huanglong entered the room [of his master], he constantly used these three [barriers].
Regarding these critical words used to examine Zen practitioners: few are those who achieve resonance or penetrate the essential point.

Even when some offer a response, Huanglong remains entirely silent; he merely sits with his eyes closed and his mind vacant. Whether they are capable or incapable, he never grants them his seal of approval.
Pan Yanzhi could not fathom its application, so he requested further instruction and questioned him.
Huanglong did not keep his application secret, but laid bare his heart and soul, speaking to him directly.
Those who have traversed this path walk on with arms akimbo, proceeding without the slightest doubt or obstruction. To those guarding the pass, they ask: "May I pass through?"
One must not go there; this is a path that even those who have never traveled it have not traversed. Zen practitioners do not understand this principle.
They seek clarification from the mouths of their teachers, yet they speak no differently than those who have not yet passed through the barrier.
One can see, then, what more could be said to them?
Huanglong said: "The Way is like a mountain: the higher one ascends, the higher it becomes; it is like the earth: the further one travels, the further it extends.

Those who study it with shallow and limited understanding stop as soon as they have exhausted their own strength. Only those who are resolute in their pursuit of the Way can exhaust its heights and distances."
"What else could it be compared to? (Recorded Sayings).
"Yù" means "together with" or "to permit. Huanglong encouraged people, saying: "One must exert all one's strength to bring this teaching to its ultimate conclusion.
The Great Way is like a mountain of extreme height; having ascended one level, there is yet another level beyond. Furthermore, it is like...
It is like the vast expanse of the great earth. Having traveled one *li*, there is yet another *li*.
The understanding and insight of the learner are humble, limited, and shallow; they merely come to rest according to the capacity of each individual.

Only those who possess the faculties and aspirations of the Mahāyāna, and who are single-mindedly and earnestly devoted to this principle, are able to exhaust its heights and reach its furthest reaches.
When one reaches the ground where there is no doubt, who among those of inferior vision and shallow understanding would grant their approval?
Huanglong said: "The heaven, earth, sun, and moon of antiquity are the same as the heaven, earth, sun, and moon of today.

The nature and characteristics of the myriad things of antiquity are the same as the nature and characteristics of the myriad things of today. Heaven, earth, sun, and moon certainly do not change; the nature of the myriad things..."
Sentiment is inherently unchanging; why then would the Dao alone be subject to change? Alas for those who have not yet attained it:
they grow weary of the old and take pleasure in the new, abandoning this to grasp that. They are like one traveling to Yue who goes north instead of south;
truly, they may be called different from others. Yet they merely exhaust their minds and toil their bodies; the more diligent their will becomes, the further away their Way grows.
It lies across the lands of Yue and Zhe, situated south and north of Shaoxing Prefecture. "Er" (two) here signifies "going. Master Huanglong cautioned his students:
"Do not grow weary of the old or take pleasure in the new; you should take the ancients as your model. He said:

"The heavens above and the earth below, and the passing of days and coming of months in the past, are just like the heavens above and the earth below, and the passing of days and coming of months today. The ancients...

The myriad things among the moving and the stationary, and the natures and dispositions of those that fly and those that hide, are just like the myriad things among the moving and the stationary, and the natures and dispositions of those that fly and those that hide, today.
Since the heavens, the earth, the sun, and the moon—the natures and dispositions of the myriad things—have existed from antiquity until now, they have fundamentally never changed or been altered.
For what reason, then, would this principle alone be subject to change? How painful!
It is a pity that those who have not yet reached the Way loathe what is old and familiar while delighting in what is new;

they discard their own strengths and adopt the weaknesses of others. This is like someone intending to travel to South Yue who does not proceed southward but instead heads north—it can truly be called being alienated from the past and alienated from the present. Yet, it is all in vain to labor...
If one’s mind and will are distracted, though one may exhaust oneself in practice, one’s aspirations will be doubly arduous and one’s path doubly remote.
Huanglong said to Ying Shaowu: "Your will must be focused on a single point; persevere for a long time without retreating. In days to come, you will surely know where the wondrous Way leads.
If, however, the mind harbors likes and dislikes and the emotions indulge in depravity, then even if one possesses the ambition and spirit of the ancients," [it will be of no avail].
"I fear that in the end I shall not be able to see its Way. (From the *Biji*; "hào" and "è" are pronounced in the fourth tone. Huanglong said to Ying of Shaowu:
"In establishing one's resolve, what is valued is purity and single-mindedness without ceasing. When an ordinary person establishes their resolve, they should simply look at this 'one' and ask:
'Where does it return? No matter how many thousands of thoughts and ten thousand imaginings there may be, when one reaches this point, it is like placing something upon a red-hot furnace."
Snow. It does not return to the one, yet it naturally returns to the one. Practice this for a long time, with diligence and without regression.
When the day is finally complete, with a single sound from the earth, there will surely be a sudden breakthrough. This is the ultimate treasury of the unsurpassed, wondrous Way.

Should one harbor likes and dislikes in the heart or indulge the emotions in depravity and perversity, then a thousand heads and ten thousand threads of confusion will arise from this. How can one [attain it]?

Even if you possess ambition and the spirit of an ancient master, I fear that by the time your eyes fall to the ground and your two feet vanish into the void, it will be difficult for you even to perceive the Way.

Master Baofeng Ying said: "The old masters of various quarters who critique the words of the predecessors and present public cases (gong'an) are like those who carry soil to build Mount Tai or scoop water to fill the Eastern Sea.
Yet how could the mountain rely on such efforts to become high or the sea on them to become deep?
Observing their intent, they aim to augment these things, yet they do not realize that what they do is inappropriate."
A *kōan* (gong'an) consists of the questions and answers of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past, through which one attains awakening and meets the essential point beneath a single word.
The seventeen hundred ancient *kōans* transmitted in the *Jingde Record of the Lamp* are not merely legal documents from government offices within the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
When Master Ying was abbot at Baofeng, he critiqued the views and understandings of various quarters.
One should not speak of criticizing and analyzing the words of the ancient sages, nor of picking up and proclaiming the public cases (gong'an) of the predecessors;

this is like trying to increase the height of Mount Tai by scooping away soil with both hands, or like trying to fill the vast ocean by ladling out water with both hands—it is exactly the same. Yet, how could those ancient public cases rely upon such efforts?
To critique and extract [the essence] is to cultivate what is lofty, fertile, and deep.

Observing the intent of the venerable elders of various quarters, their former aim lay in supplementing the public cases (gong'an), yet they were entirely unaware of what they were employing; indeed, this was inappropriate.
Whenever Master Ying Shaowu encountered scholars who acted with unrestrained license and showed no fear of cause and effect, he would sigh deeply for a long time and say:
"This toilsome life is like a temporary lodging; one stays according to conditions, and when one departs, it is gone. What can such people truly gain?
You lot lack a sense of integrity and shame, violating social hierarchies and defiling the religious teachings to such an extent. The resolve of a true man lies in—"

To expand the ancestral Way and guide future generations, one should not privately indulge one's own desires without restraint, thereby inviting calamity upon oneself and creating misfortune for ten thousand kalpas.
To suffer in the three realms and the hells is not yet the ultimate suffering;
to lose one’s human form beneath the *kāṣāya* is truly the greatest suffering (from the *Biji*).

To dwell in a guest inn is called "journeying" (*lǚ*); to moor a boat by a riverbank is called "anchoring" (*pò*). These terms denote expansion and magnitude. To lead from the front is called "guiding" (*yòu*);

to support from the side is called "assisting" (*yè*). These terms denote caution and fear. "Mediator" (*méi*) and "enzyme" (*mài*) are the same as "ferment" (*jiào*) used for wine; they refer to brewing or bringing about one's transgressions.
Master Ying of Shaowu remarked that he frequently observed students who were unrestrained and arrogant, showing no regard for sin, merit, or the law of cause and effect.
He then sighed deeply and, after a long pause, revealed to him: "This body born of one's parents cannot transcend form in what it sees, nor can it transcend sound in what it hears.
Day after day, one busies oneself in vain, never attaining mastery; how exhausting this is!"
You do not realize that you possess by nature the original state of truth, which is merely temporarily lodged within this body—like a guest staying in a lodging, or like a boat moored at a shore.
While you dwell here, you may enjoy things according to conditions; yet when you no longer dwell here, they will certainly not be yours.
What value is there in what you have acquired? Even if you were to acquire much, what benefit would it bring? You people are ignorant of integrity and lack a sense of shame.

How shameful! To thus presume to offend the names and ranks of the lineage, to defile and profane the rites and laws, and to bring the ancestral wind and the gates of instruction to such a state—is this truly fitting?

A man of great character ought to establish a lofty ambition, making it his concern to expand and propagate the Way of the Patriarchs, and making it his heart’s intent to guide, inspire, support, and assist future generations. One must not privately indulge in personal desires or harbor greed.
Without satiety and without restraint, they indulge their cravings without relinquishing them, thereby brewing the sins of a single lifetime and creating calamities for ten thousand kalpas.

Among the three miserable realms—the hungry ghosts, animals, and hells—those who suffer by wearing iron bits, carrying saddles, being sawn, burned, ground, crushed, or forced to swallow flames do so not because they were taught to seek such suffering;
it is only those who have left the household life, beneath these very *kāṣāya* robes, [who must take heed].
To lose this human body is truly what is called undergoing great suffering; how can one not stand in awe? How can one not stand in awe?
(The character *yǐ* is pronounced *yǐ*; *méi* is pronounced *méi*; *niàng* has the departing tone.)

Ying Shaowu said to Huitang, "Those who are called 'good knowledge-holders' (śāstrins) assist the Buddhas and Patriarchs in propagating the transformation [of beings], causing monastics to turn their minds toward the Way and changing customs and transforming social mores; this is certainly not something that those of shallow virtue can accomplish.

Monks of the Final Dharma do not cultivate morality or virtue and possess little integrity or righteousness; they often engage in the corruption of bribery and are filthy, wagging their tails to beg for pity. He continued: "To pursue..."
He sought fame and profit at the gates of those in power. Once his karma was exhausted and his merit had faded, the devas and humans grew weary of him;
he defiled the orthodox lineage and became a burden to his teachers and friends—could he not have avoided such deep regret? Huìtáng nodded in agreement.

"Bhikṣu" is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "Beggar" (qǐshì). This means that above, he begs from the Buddhas and Patriarchs to sustain his life of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*), and below, he begs from sentient beings to nourish his physical body.

"Bāo" (苞) means to wrap or enclose; "jū" (苴) means to mat or provide a base. These characters refer to the practice of wrapping things to present them with flattery, seeking to entrust one's affairs [to others].
"Āngzàng" (骯髒) describes an appearance of being straightforward through sheer luck or audacity. "Hàn" (頷) refers to nodding the head; it means to be mute in speech yet... [the text is incomplete].
This is my sincere conviction. Ying of Shaowu told Huitang that those who are named "Good Knowledge" (Śāstr) are those who assist the Buddhas and Patriarchs and aid the propagation of the Dharma;
they cause monastics to turn back their deviant minds and incline toward the Right Path, shifting base customs and transforming them into virtuous ones.
This is certainly not something that can be accomplished by those of shallow roots or meager practice.

Monks of the Final Dharma do not realize the Way through genuine awakening, nor do they cultivate virtue through authentic practice. They lack integrity in their dwelling and their conduct is unfitting;
they constantly engage in the offering of bribes and flattery, behaving with sycophancy and contortion, leaning upon the gates of others and huddling against the walls of others.
Like a dog fawning upon humans, shaking its head and wagging its tail, it begs for pity and compassion;
likewise, one pursues and solicits fame, reputation, wealth, and profit at the gates of those with power, influence, and high status. This is the height of shamelessness.

One day, when one's sinful karma has reached its full measure and present blessings wither away, Heaven will loathe them and the world will despise them; not only does one bring calamity upon oneself, but one also brings disgrace [upon others].
"This defiles the Dharma-gate; it brings disgrace upon the lineage of teachers above and casts a burden upon our Dharma friends beside.
How could we not feel deep regret? When Huitang heard these words, he nodded silently in his heart and gave his consent.
Ying Shaowu said to Pan Yanzhi: "In ancient times, scholars cultivated the mind; in the present day, scholars cultivate outward traces.
Yet, the distance between the mind and outward traces is as vast as that between heaven and earth."
The late Mr. Shao Wu cited the words of Pan Yanzhi, saying: "In ancient times, those who studied the Way made it their primary task to sever all external conditions and cultivate their own minds.
Nowadays, those who study the Way instead seek outwardly, making it their primary task only to cultivate ritual matters and historical traces.
However, the Dharma of the mind is formless and has no creator; ritual matters and historical traces, by contrast, possess form and are conditioned."
The difference between the Way and its manifestations is as vast as the distance between heaven and earth.
Ying of Shaowu said to Master Zhenjing Wen: "That which grows rapidly will surely wither and die;

that which is accomplished too quickly will surely be easily destroyed. To pursue immediate success without devising a long-term plan for enduring growth is never a far-reaching or great undertaking."

The resources for this are vast. Now, even Heaven and Earth—the most spiritual of entities—require three years and an intercalary month before their work is completed and their transformation perfected.

How much more so the mystery of the Great Way; how could it be accomplished in haste? It depends on the accumulation of merit and the layering of virtue. Thus it is said: "He who seeks speed will not reach his goal;
he who attends to minute details shall not fail. Beauty lies in long-term completion. Consequently, there arises a lifelong plan for the Sage.
It is said: "Trust it to maintain it; be diligent to practice it; be loyal to bring it to completion. Though a task be great, it will surely succeed.
Formerly, the attendant Zhe sat through the night without sleeping, using a round log as a pillow. When he dozed off, the pillow would roll away;
upon waking, he would rise again and sit back down as before. He made this his constant practice. Some remarked that his mental exertion was excessive, to which Zhe replied: "As for me..."
One’s affinity for Prajñāpāramitā is naturally slight; if one does not exert oneself with bitter diligence and resolve, there is fear that one will be led astray by deluded habits.
How much more so when dreams and illusions are not real—how could they serve as a long-term plan? In the past, while I was in Xiangxi, I witnessed his conduct firsthand.
Therefore, the monastic community honored his reputation and revered his virtue, praising him as such (from *Lingyuan Shiyi*).
Zhenjing’s name was Kewen; he was a successor of Huanglong Nan. *Cangcu* means urgent or pressing. *Lei* means to increase or accumulate.
*Jing* means agile or swift. *Qi* means illness. The attendant Zhè’s name was Muzhè; his style name was Zhenru. He was a successor of Cuoyan Zhenke.
*Prajñā* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "wisdom. [This refers to] Xiāngyī County in Xiāngyīn Prefecture, Changsha, Huguang.
To the west [of this place], Ying of Shaowu told Zhenjing Wuheshang:
"Generally, those things that grow up suddenly and violently will inevitably be fragile and tender, and thus easily perish prematurely.
Those whose achievements are rapidly established will inevitably lack solidity and are easily ruined. One must not refuse to investigate long-term strategies for enduring stability."
This is a strategy for the distant future, yet you seek only immediate gratification and expect success on the spot.
Such a perspective is entirely lacking in the long-term vision and noble character required. Now, consider that Heaven is Yang and Earth is Yin;

they are most subtle and wondrous, yet even they wait three years to provide moisture again, and even the months and days must be adjusted for their greater or lesser lengths, as well as the surplus days of the year.

The seasons are fixed to complete the year, thereby enabling the achievement of the "one moistening every three years" when the celestial breath is slightly complete, and the "moistening every five years" when the celestial breath is fully complete. Such is the case here;

how much more so for the ultimate, most refined, and most subtle point of the Unsurpassed Great Way? How could it be achieved through haste, negligence, or superficiality? This is what I have observed.
To achieve and fulfill this, it lies in accumulating merit daily and accumulating virtuous conduct monthly.
It is just like the most spiritual force of Heaven and Earth: after accumulating for three years, its functions are modestly complete;
after further accumulating for five years, its transformations are fully perfected. Therefore, the ancients said: "If one desires haste, there will be no penetration. If one can...
If one acts with meticulous care, there will be no error or loss; things will be beautifully established and remain stable for a long time.
This is why one plans for the distant future: it requires lifelong deliberation. The Sage said: "Maintain it with firm faith, carry it out with agility, and establish it with loyalty and generosity.
If one proceeds in this manner, no matter how great the undertaking may be, rest assured that it will surely succeed.
In the past, when Zen Master Che was a *śrāmaṇera*, he applied himself to his practice. During the night, he sat upright for long periods without lying down.
Whenever he felt sleepy, he would use a round wooden block as a pillow; as soon as he dozed off slightly, the pillow would roll away.
He would then wake up, rise again, and sit calmly and steadily, returning to his original state. He took this as his standard. Some have said of Che: [text continues].
"If an attendant applies their mind in this manner, would that not be a great error? Zhe said, "Regarding the principles of Chan, I have never attained complete penetration;
my wisdom has not become clear. My karmic conditions and destiny are fixed, and my past merit has been meager.
If I do not exert myself with diligent effort in this way to advance my initial resolve, I fear I will be led astray by the habitual tendencies of deluded thoughts. Moreover..."
Dreams and illusions are but faint forms; they are provisional and not real. To grasp them as substantial and to cherish them—how could this possibly be a strategy for permanence or the long term?
In the past, while I was in Xiangyin, I witnessed with my own eyes how the attendant Zhe maintained and practiced these principles.
Therefore, throughout the monastic community, both veteran practitioners and newcomers alike were moved to submission.
As for this man, his virtuous conduct was held in high esteem, and he was praised and lauded everywhere.
Zen Master Zhenjing Wen had long studied under Huanglong; initially, he maintained the vow of never appearing before others.
Later, having accepted an invitation from Dongshan, he traveled through the Western Mountains to visit Zen Master Xun of Xiangcheng. Xun teased him, saying: "In years past, Zhuge..."

He was called the Recluse. Though invited from his thatched hut to emerge from the mountains, if the pine blossoms receive the power of spring, they will surely bloom even though their roots lie deep within the crags.
Thus Zhenjing declined and withdrew. (From the *Shun Record*)
Xiangcheng Shunming (Jingshun) was the successor of Huanglong Nan. Zhuge bore the compound surname [Zhuge]; his given name was Liang, and his courtesy name was Kongming.
While he was personally tilling the soil in Nanyang, Liu Xuande was stationing his troops at Xinye.
Xu Shu went to see him and reported, saying: "Kongming is the Sleeping Dragon. Your Excellency may go to visit him, but you must not seek to compel him. Xuande—
Because of this virtue, Emperor Liang thrice visited his thatched cottage and appointed him as Prime Minister. Master Zhenjing Wen had long studied under Huanglong;
from the beginning, he had expressed a reluctance to enter the world to serve as a teacher for others. Later, he suddenly accepted an invitation to head the ancestral monastery of Dongshan.
On his way, he passed directly through Xishan, whereupon he entered the mountains to pay his respects and inquire after the incense.
Master Chengshun composed a verse to playfully mock him, saying: "Zhuge Liang of old was called a recluse; At first, Zhenjing had no intention of appearing in the world.
The thatched cottage earnestly invited him to leave the mountains; Today, you instead accept the invitation of Dongshan.
If the pine blossoms receive the power of spring, It is due to the influence of his virtue. Dongshan... [text ends]

The mountain came to welcome him; his roots lay deep within the crags. This implies that even though he had entered the monastic order, there was a man of the Way who ultimately remained in seclusion and would not stay.
The first two lines contain a tone of irony, while the latter two lines are words of sincere praise.
Zhenjing expressed his thanks and withdrew to Xiangcheng.
When Zhenjing appointed Guangdao to reside at Wufeng, Yuguang was considered blunt and lacking the talent for worldly affairs.

Upon Guang’s arrival as abbot, he governed himself with discipline and treated the assembly with broad magnanimity; before long, all neglected matters were restored, and monastics came and went in great numbers.
Rumors were spreading about the competition. When Zhenjing heard of this, he said, "How can scholars be so easily swayed by praise and blame?

Whenever I observe the private discussions in the monasteries, they say: 'That elder practices the Way and brings peace to the assembly; that elder does not misappropriate the permanent property and shares both joy and hardship with the community.
To be called a *shanzhishi* (a true spiritual friend) and the master of a monastery, one must practice the Way and bring peace to the assembly."

Not encroaching upon the permanent property of the Sangha and sharing both sweet and bitter experiences with the assembly are things one ought to do as a matter of course; what is there to say about them?
It is like a scholar-official serving in government to secure the state and pacify the people, who then says, "I do not accept bribes and I do not harass the people.
Now, is it not merely doing one's duty not to accept bribes and not to harass the people? (From *Shantang Xiaocan*).
Guangdao (Broad Way) was named Xiguang (Rarely Broad) and styled Guang Wuxin (Broad No-Mind). He was the dharma heir of Zhenjing Wen.

"Yuzhong" (Carrying the Multitude) is a title used for elders of venerable virtue. The record states that when Zhenjing Wen appointed Guang Wuxin to reside at Wufeng, everyone said that Guang was dissipated, clumsy, and dull-witted, yet possessed the talent and refinement of one destined for transcendence. When Guang arrived at Wufeng, he became diligent...
He advanced himself through diligent cultivation and presided over the great assembly with magnanimity.
Before long, all that had fallen into neglect within the monastic grove was fully restored. Monks passing by vied with one another to spread the news, all saying it was excellent.
When Zhenjing heard of this, he said, "Why do students so lightly disparage or praise others? I have always..."
Whenever I observe within the monastic communities (conglin) those who engage in private discussions, saying: "That monk’s conduct and Dharma practice are such that he comforts the assembly;

that monk understands causes and recognizes effects, never encroaching upon or misappropriating the communal funds, but sharing both the sweetness and the bitterness with the assembly"—such individuals may truly be called *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friends), for they shoulder the heavy responsibility of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

As the host of the world for all quarters, he practices and upholds the Great Way, guides and disciplines the great assembly, and does not treat the monastery’s permanent property as his own private possession.
He shares in joy with the community; such conduct is only right, so what is there to say? It is like a gentleman who enters public service to become a local official:
above, he serves his sovereign with loyalty; below, he benefits the people with integrity. Thus one may say: "I am not greedy."
Seeking wealth and profit without harming the common people, and being neither greedy for bribes nor encroaching upon the populace—all these are entirely appropriate.
How could they be considered extraordinary? What is there to say about them? Let students not rashly disparage or praise others.
Zhenguan resided at Guizong. Every year, when the fundraising master received the petitions for donations, bolts of cloth and silk arrived in great abundance.

Zhenguan looked upon them with a frown and then sighed, saying, "This is the blood and fat of the faithful's devotion; I am ashamed that I lack virtue. How can I be worthy of this? (Recorded by Li Shanglao in the *Ri she ji*).

A Record of Zhenjing’s Stay at Guizong Temple: Every year, when the fundraising master returned to the monastery, he would hand over offerings of donated documents, cotton cloth, and silk fabrics that had accumulated like clouds. Upon seeing them, Zhenjing knit his brows and frowned;
after a long while, he sighed and said, "The faith of the donors and the very marrow and blood of the patrons—how can I feel anything but shame for my own lack of substance?"
"Virtue! What could you possibly bring that would be worthy of receiving his spirit of renunciation?

Zhenjing said, "In the age of the Dharma’s decline, monks rarely possess integrity and righteousness. Whenever I see them engaging in lofty talk and grand discourse, they claim that no one can equal them;
yet when it comes to the kindness of a single meal, they first express suspicion and ultimately assist it, having previously disparaged it."

Later, he praised them, saying: "Few are those who, when seeking what is right, declare it to be right, and when facing what is wrong, declare it to be wrong—those who are impartial and do not conceal the truth" (from the *Biji*).
When Zhenjing instructs people, he maintains a sense of impartiality and possesses a settled perspective.

In this age of the Dharma’s decline, there are few monks in the monasteries who possess integrity, nor do they have a sense of righteous spirit. I often observe their daily conduct; [their thoughts] arise like clouds.
They engage in lofty talk and expansive discourse, surging like waves, claiming that among the multitude, none can equal them.
Yet, when it comes to the kindness of a single meal, they first show dissension and finally offer compliance; they first slander and later praise. Thus, they lack any fixed principle.
If one seeks their inner core, they are unable to exercise mastery over themselves. This is not a settled path; it is neither right nor wrong—it is simply unsettled.
Regarding the Way: there are few who do not conceal their partiality and selfishness while claiming to be upright and impartial.
Zhenjing said: "The dharma of a bhikṣu is that one's enjoyments should not be excessive; if they are excessive, they will overflow.

Matters that accord with one's desires should not be over-schemed; over-scheming leads inevitably to ruin. That which is about to be accomplished will surely be brought to destruction. I have observed Huang...

Master Longxian lived for forty years in this world. In his speech and silence, his movements and stillness, he never attempted to ensnare the monks of his time with mere countenance, etiquette, or literary talent.
Rather, he was solely intent on guiding those who possessed genuine insight and practiced the truth through action, providing them with detailed instruction and correction.
His solemnity in upholding the authentic style of the ancients was rarely equaled by anyone else in all quarters; thus, even today—
Facing the multitude, there is nothing that does not take the Dharma as its standard (from the *Risheri*).

"Wei-qu" means to be thoroughly compliant; "wei-shun" means to bring things to completion through adaptability. "Ti" (pronounced "chi," with the phonetic component "chi") refers to accomplishment. "Cai-ge" refers to structural form and stylistic format.
Zhenjing showed people that one should speak with caution regarding one’s conduct.

According to the dharma of the monastic community, one’s daily life should not be characterized by excessive abundance or fullness. If things are too abundant and sufficient, a mind of overflow will arise.
In worldly affairs, one must not engage in excessive scheming or greedy seeking. If there is excessive scheming and seeking, the calamity of ruin and injury will arrive. [Desire]...
There is that which is established; there is inevitably that which is destroyed. This is an invariable principle.
I have observed the former master Huanglong for forty years as he benefited sentient beings and received the assembly.

Whether through unimpeded speech or through the samādhi of silent stillness—whether in motion or at rest, throughout the four modes of deportment—he never once relied upon his own physical appearance or countenance. He did not [seek] prostrations...
He maintained the solemnity of the temple’s appearance; his literary works and scholarly erudition were such that he bound and ensnared the monks of his time within his influence.
Yet, for those who possessed true inquiry and genuine realization, whose practice and understanding were in accord, he would employ every means—subtle and artful—to bring them to fulfillment.
His sense of caution and secrecy, as well as his dignified and grave demeanor, truly embodied the standards of the former sages; few in all quarters could be compared to him.
"Lièi" (類) means that which can be compared or modeled after. Therefore, when I preside over a great assembly today, there are none who do not take me as their standard of conduct.
*Bìgàn* (狴犴): Pronounced *bèi'àn*.
When Zhenjing was residing at Baoning in Jiankang, Prince Shu offered him a roll of plain silk as a donation for his vegetarian meal.

He asked an attendant monk, "What is this? The attendant replied, "It is spun silk gauze. Zhenjing asked, "What will you do with it? The attendant said, "It is suitable for making a *kāṣāya* (monastic robe).
Zhenjing pointed to the *saṃghāṭī* he was wearing and said, "I usually wear this; those who see me do not find it particularly offensive. Thereupon, [the attendant] folded [the silk].
[The items] were sent to the storehouse to be appraised and sold for the benefit of the community; such was his lack of concern for finery (from the *Ri-shek-ji*).
Jiankang is Jinling. Baoning is the name of a temple. "Prince Shu": Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty conferred the title of Prince Shu upon the Duke of Jing (Wang Anshi).
The Duke served as Chancellor during the Xining era; because he established the New Laws which harmed the people, his son Wang Pang...
While serving as a scholar-official, Fan Ping suddenly died of a violent illness. Prime Minister Fan Zhongyan was also dismissed from office at the same time.

Sitting idly as if in a trance, he saw a ghost messenger leading Ping, who was burdened with an iron cangue and weeping before him. Ping said, "My father was intent on the New Policies; that is why I have come to this state. Zhongyan asked the messenger for a way to save him.
The messenger replied, "Only by building a monastery and providing food for monks can you be spared. Zhongyan subsequently established a monastery in Jinling.
The residence was converted into a temple, and an imperial edict granted it the name Baoning. He requested that Zhenjing take charge of it.
"Kāṣāya" is a Sanskrit term; here it means "dust-detaching robe. "Kāṣāya" is a Sanskrit term; here it means "great robe," or alternatively, "variegated robe.
"Gū" means to sell; the matter is still favorable. While Zhenjing was serving as the abbot of Baoning Temple in Jinling, Prince Shu hosted a vegetarian feast and made offerings.
He presented one roll of white raw silk as an offering. He then asked an attendant monk, "What object is this?
The attendant replied, "This is spun-silk gauze. Zhenjing asked again, "What is it used for? The attendant said, "It is suitable for making robes that transcend the mundane world.
Zhenjing pointed to the *kāṣāya* robe he himself was wearing and said, "I usually..."
When they don this cloth robe, those who see it feel no sense of revulsion, disdain, or malice;
immediately, it is sent to the storehouse for appraisal and sale to provide for the community. Such is their lack of interest in ornamentation.
