Zhenjing said to Prince Shu: "In daily life, exert yourself to practice where it is right; if it is not so, firmly cease from it.

One should not allow ease or difficulty to shift one's resolve. If, because of today’s difficulties, you shake your head and disregard them, how do you know that tomorrow will not be as difficult as today? (From *Risheng ji*).
Zhenjing refers to King Shu. This means that what is valued is swift action, not swift cessation.

Among the four modes of deportment, whenever one encounters a situation where action is appropriate, one should immediately apply diligent effort to act swiftly; when encountering a situation where action is inappropriate, one should immediately resolve the mind to cease swiftly.
One must not allow the will to fluctuate or shift based on whether circumstances are difficult or easy. As previously established:
Perhaps because of the hardships of today, you are unwilling to proceed and unwilling to stop; you cast everything aside without a second thought.
But how do you know that at some other time or on another day, things will not be more difficult than they are today?
When Zhenjing heard that a man of the Way from another region had passed away, he sighed with deep sorrow until he wept.
At that time, Zhantang was serving as his attendant and said, "All things born between heaven and earth possess a single form and substance; they wither and die, leaving behind only remnants."
"It seems impossible to escape this. Why inflict such pain upon yourself? Zhenjing said, "The flourishing of the Dharma depends on those of virtue to sustain it.
Now that they have all passed away, the monastic communities are in decline; by this, one may predict the future. (Recorded in the Rishen ji)
Zantang’s name was Wenzhun; he was a successor of Zhenjing. The term "beings" (*wu*) encompasses both the animate and the inanimate, signifying the multitude.
When Zhenjing heard that a man of the Way from another region had passed away, he felt deep compassion and sorrow, sighing aloud in lamentation.

As for weeping in such a way that tears flow down, at that time Zhan Tang was serving as an attendant. Seeing that [the Master] was grieving for others to such an extreme degree, he admonished him, saying:
"Of all things born between heaven and earth—whether one person or many people, one object or many objects—all possess this decaying form and fragile substance.
Withering, drying up, death, being mangled, or being infested by insects—all these are things from which there is no escape."
[All] cannot escape this. Why suffer such self-inflicted injury? Zhenjing said: "The physical form of a person ultimately returns to decay;
how could I not know this? That which I lament is the Dharma. When a person who preserves the Way exists, the Dharma also exists with them.
When a person of virtue passes away, the Dharma also passes away with them. Now they are both gone; the Dharma [is likewise lost]."
On whom does the Way rely to be revitalized? By observing this, one can foresee the decline or prosperity of the monastic communities.
*Cane Lin Bao Xun* (Jade Instructions for Zen Forests), Volume One, with Red Annotations.
*Shun Zhu Juan* (Second Volume of the *Chanlin Baoxun*), compiled by Ji'er Guansheng Ke of Huarayan in Yuzhou, Shu; edited by Deyu. Regarding Master Zhantang Zun’s initial study under Zhenjing:

Once, while reading by the light of a lamp inside his mosquito netting, Zhenjing rebuked him, saying: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omission of the specific content of the rebuke as per the source text.*
What is called "learning" is the pursuit of governing the mind. Though one may study much, if the mind is not governed, what benefit is there in such study?
This is especially true for the heterodox teachings of the hundred schools, which are as lofty as mountains and as deep as the ocean;

were you to exhaust yourself in mastering them all, you would now be abandoning the fundamental to pursue the peripheral—like a lowly servant serving the noble—and I fear this will hinder your progress on the Way. You must simply cut off all external conditions and seek the sublime.
He attained enlightenment. Later, when he contemplated this, it was as if pushing open a door to enter a mortar; thus, it was not difficult for him.

Zhandang immediately cast aside his previous studies and concentrated exclusively on Chan meditation. One day, hearing a monk reciting Zhuge Kongming’s "Memorial on the Dispatch of the Army," he experienced a sudden and vast awakening.
His mental stagnation was instantly released, and his eloquence became unimpeded; among his contemporaries, few could surpass him.
"Du" (杜) means to shut off. "Zhuan" (專) means to focus the mind on one point. "Xu" (續) means to continue without interruption. "Chan" (禪) refers to a concentrated mind that does not waver.

"Guan" (觀) refers to the illumination of wisdom that does not sink into dullness. "Chushi biao" (出師表) is the memorial presented by Zhuge Wuhou to the Later Emperor, expressing his desire to dispatch the army to campaign against Wei;
the details of this matter are found in the *Yinyi* (Explanations of Sounds and Meanings). This records the initial encounter of Master Zhantan Zun.
Zhenjing would constantly light lamps within his curtains to read and study; he could truly be called a person of devoted learning.
When Zhenji saw this, he rebuked and admonished him, saying: "One who is called a practitioner of Zen seeks to cultivate and rectify their own mind.
Though your reading and studies may be extensive, if you do not cultivate your own mind, what benefit will there be, no matter how broad your learning?"
How much more so regarding the divergences among the various schools and the hundred masters, whose learning is as lofty as mountains and as deep as the ocean;
how could you possibly exhaust it all? Now, instead, you abandon your own root and pursue its branches and leaves, like a lowly servant attending upon the noble.

I fear that regarding the path of practice, they may instead become mutual hindrances. You must simply cut off external conditions and, knocking upon your own self, seek true inquiry and genuine awakening.

When you suddenly achieve thorough understanding of your own nature, it will be like pushing open a door hinge or entering a *dou* (a measure of volume)—vividly alive and agile, opening and closing as you please; what difficulty could there be? Zantang was a man of decisive resolve.
A man of resolute character who hears this and puts it into practice will immediately sever and eliminate all habitual activities.
He will focus his mind with single-mindedness, maintaining a continuous succession of thoughts without falling into distracted delusions or sinking into indolent indifference.

One day, he suddenly heard a Chan practitioner reciting the "Memorial on Sending Out the Army" by Zhuge Liang (Wuhou). When the passage reached the line, "The palace and the government offices shall be regarded as one body," he was struck with sudden insight.
However, when the mind-ground is awakened, the congealed and accumulated stagnations dissolve like ice melting in the sun;
one’s speech and dhāraṇīs then flow freely and without obstruction. Among one's peers, few can surpass such a person.
This is why practitioners of Chan value genuine awakening.
Zantang said: "Those who possess virtue and morality delight in the assembly; those who lack virtue and morality delight in themselves.
He who delights in the assembly endures; he who delights in himself perishes. Nowadays, those who hold the position of abbot mostly treat the assembly with favoritism and resentment;
thus, the multitude repels them. It is rare to find one who seeks out their virtues while knowing their faults, or who recognizes their faults while knowing their virtues. Therefore it is said:"
To share in the sorrows and joys of the multitude, and to share their likes and dislikes, is righteousness (*yi*).
Wherever righteousness resides, who in all under heaven would not turn toward it? (From the *Ershi Lai Ke Zhewou Ji*).
Zantang’s Admonition to the Abbot: One should speak of likes and dislikes in common with the assembly. Those whose Way is complete and virtue perfected greatly prefer a vast multitude;
the more numerous the assembly, the greater their joy in their hearts. Those whose Way is slight and virtue meager do not delight in a vast multitude;
they seek only their own pleasure and do not share in the joy of others. Little do they realize that...
Those who share joy with the assembly endure for a long time; those who seek only their own pleasure perish.
Most abbots today act according to their own likes and dislikes when presiding over the assembly; thus they do not harmonize with the people, and the people do not submit to them.
Yet they brush this aside and act contrary to it. They seek what is good for themselves, yet they know little of what others do not like;

they know what they dislike, yet they know little of what others do not dislike. Cold, heat, hunger, and thirst are what all share as concerns; ease, leisure, satiety, and warmth are what all share as joys;
morality, virtue, and righteousness are what all share as preferences; while cruelty and meanness are what all [share as aversions].
This is what all people alike detest. Therefore, it is the principle that the abbot must be able to identify with the assembly.
Since this principle lies therein, who among the fourfold assembly throughout the world would not come to take refuge in him?
Zantang said: "The Way is the true authority of antiquity and the present. One who skillfully propagates the Way must rely on adaptability and transformation.

Those who do not understand transformation cling to the literal text and fixed teachings, becoming mired in appearances and fettered by emotions; these are all cases of failing to comprehend the transformative power of expedient means. Thus, a monk asked Zhaozhou:
"The myriad dharmas return to the One. To what place does the One return? The Master said, "I am in Qingzhou, making a cotton robe that weighs seven *jin*.

This shows that the ancients were not ignorant of skillful means; they were able to respond with such eloquence. The Sage said, "In the deep valley there is no partiality, and thus this resonance is produced.
A great bell receives the frame; when struck, there is nothing it does not answer. Thus we know that the superior man who penetrates all directions, taking...
"Returning to the ordinary is to accord with the Way; it is not to cling to the One while failing to respond to change" (Letter to Li Shanglao).
*Tì* (pronounced as in *tì*) means the height of exhaustion. When a guest reports to the host that there is vinegar, the host replies to the guest by saying "in return.
Zhaozhou’s name was Congshen; he was a successor of Nanquan Puyuan. *Jù* (with the second tone) refers to the frame for bells and drums; the horizontal beam is called *xǔn*.

The term *zǒng* refers to the stand upon which bells and drums are suspended. This is from the letter by Zhantang to Li Shanglao, discussing the principle that propagating the Way requires adaptability and transformation.
The Way is the fundamental principle and provisional essentials that have existed from antiquity until the present.

One who can expand and manifest this Way must accord with circumstances to harmonize with its meaning and transform according to human emotions. Therefore, it is said that one who does not know how to adapt and transform [cannot propagate the Way].
Such people are bound by words, attached to scriptures, obstructed by names and forms, and mired in the consciousness of the intellect.
None of these are those who possess sovereign mastery and the power of transformation, nor those who have attained thorough penetration and adaptability.
Thus, a monk asked Zhaozhou, "All phenomena return to the One; where does the One return? Zhaozhou said, "I am in Qingzhou, making a cotton robe that weighs seven... (sheng).
If one were to say that Zhaozhou lacked mastery of skillful means (*upāya*), how could he have been capable of such a dialogue?
A Sage said: "In deep and secluded ravines, there is no private mind; thus, when called upon, it responds with resonance.
It is like a great bell suspended high: when the frame receives it and a mallet strikes it, there is no sound that does not respond. Zhaozhou’s response was just so.
It is like an empty valley that has no mind of its own, or like a great bell suspended upon its stand.

Thus we know that the Great Being who penetrates all directions, wishing to turn his back on ordinary principles and harmonize with the wondrous Way, employs inconceivable and skillful expedients (*upāya*) that are certainly not obstructed.
He does not cling to a single dharma, nor does he fail to adapt or exhaust his potential. In the end, he accords with the crimson [of transformation].
Whenever one encounters a *gong'an*, why is it that the brush is often dragged straight across without the addition of annotations?

It is because *gong'an* are valued for their investigation to give rise to the "doubting mind" (*yi-qing*) in order to seek thorough awakening. If they were annotated and explained away, they would be of no benefit to the person.
Zhandang [Zhaojue] used the story of the monk’s cassock to demonstrate the exercise of skillful means, the reversal of the ordinary, the accord with the Way, and the non-abiding.
There is one Dharma. It is for the sake of responding without end. Let us set aside for a moment the matter of not remaining fixed and being inexhaustible;
consider this: when the monk’s robe and the single return are presented, where is it? How is it? Turning back, how is it? You should try to speak on this.
If you cannot speak, then as before, you will once again be stuck in appearances and bound by emotions. There was once a verse that said: "The question is like an iron wall; the answer is like..."
Yingshan said: "How lamentable are those who have not yet awakened! Ten difficulties and ten thousand difficulties—how can they possibly endure them?
This is like washing clods of earth in the mud. Zantang said:
"When a student seeks a friend, it must be one worthy to serve as a teacher; at all times, one should maintain a heart of reverence. He then composed [a verse].
In dealing with people, one should seek what is beneficial. If their wisdom and insight are superior to my own, it is appropriate to follow them so as to be alerted to what I have not yet attained.
If they happen to be similar to me, then it is better not to associate with them at all (from the *Baofeng Shilu*).
Zhantang instructed people that in seeking friends, one must seek those who surpass oneself. A student seeking to choose a virtuous friend must find one who can act as a true teacher and mentor.
Such a person should be cherished and held in mind at all times—day and night—and treated with constant reverence and respect.
In all matters one undertakes, one should adopt the methods of each [teacher] and wait for their future benefit.
Even if someone’s wisdom and insight are slightly superior to one's own, it is still appropriate to follow them with vigilance regarding what one has not yet attained.
If they were merely identical to oneself, it would be better not to have them at all; what benefit would there be?
Zantang said: "In these late autumn days at the ancestral temple, it is truly difficult to find those among the forest-dwellers who are not frivolous and superficial.
Formerly, when Zhenru resided at Zhikai, he once remarked that while there were not many people at Daowu on the west of Xiangxi, there were still several veteran monks who had practiced this Way.
Since I came here from Daguangzhai, there have been no fewer than nine hundred monks, yet not one in seven or five."
People understand my words; by this I know that those who have attained [the Way] are not many (Shilu).
Zantang taught people that they must practice this path. Having reached the gateway of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, it is now like autumn in a forest, like the setting sun;
it is nearly withered away. Those who dwell beneath the trees do not engage in clamor or frivolity.
Those who are earnest are still few indeed. Formerly, when Zhēnrú was at Zhùzhī Temple, he once remarked:

"When I was on the road in Western Xiān, although my assembly was not particularly large, there were still several elderly monks and practitioners who walked the path with sincerity and practiced this Way with integrity. Since I came from Dàméishān, the assembly here has grown."
There were as many as nine hundred people. Of all the words I spoke, not even seven or five people could understand them.
From this I know that although one may have many followers, if they do not practice, what difference is there between having them and having none? It does not depend on the number of people.
Zhantang said: "In the conduct of men, one cannot fully know them through a single response or a single interrogation.
For those whose speech is eloquent and clever, their actions may not yet be trustworthy; those whose words are clumsy and stammering, their principles may not yet be exhausted.
Though one may exhaust their words, I fear one has not exhausted their principles; though one may subdue their mouths, I fear one has not subdued their hearts. Truly, man is difficult to fathom."
This is known to be the ailment of the sages; how much more so for the monks of recent times who, though clever, do not strive to understand human nature.

Their sight and hearing are mostly occupied with watching for flaws, acting in opposition to the multitude and deviating from the Way. They compete with one another in deception and deceive one another with fraud.
This causes the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to decline and grow ever more thin, to the point that it is perhaps beyond salvation (Letter to Lu Zhi).
In the *Danzhang’s Letter to Lu Zhi*, the difficulty of knowing others is discussed:

"Ordinary people cannot be fully known through a single encounter or a single interrogation, even when they have practiced and exerted themselves; for there are those who possess eloquence and swift verbal skill."

As for those who are beneficial, their affairs may be either true or false; they cannot be trusted implicitly. As for those whose speech is coarse, clumsy, and dull, their principles may be sound and appropriate;
they cannot be dismissed as insignificant. Though one may exhaust a person’s words, one fears that one has not yet exhausted that person’s principles.
Though one may subdue a person’s mouth, one fears that one has not yet subdued that person’s heart. Truly, people are difficult to know.

This is why even sages have cause for concern: they do not know the illnesses of others, let alone the fact that contemporary monastics pride themselves on their cleverness and are deeply obscured by what they perceive. They do not strive to master Buddhist principles or the ways of human relations;
rather, with eyes and ears attuned only to observing the faults and vulnerabilities of others, they stand in opposition to the multitude. Their preferences, moreover, run contrary to the True Path.
There are deviations and discrepancies. Those who pursue external signs and appearances are deceitful and insincere; those who delude one another are fraudulent, sycophantic, and disloyal.
Consequently, the Dharma-path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs from above gradually declines and becomes ever more decayed and thin.
Then it can no longer be saved. Such is the difficulty of knowing others. Zhandang said to Miaoxi:
"In this age of the Semblance Dharma, bhikṣus mostly pursue external objects while failing to clarify their inner minds.
Even if they engage in grand deeds, none of them reach the ultimate goal. This is because that which they rely upon is base and vulgar, making it so—like gadflies flying about a fat ox."
It takes but a few steps; yet if one clings to the horse's tail, one immediately gains the power to chase the wind and overtake the sun. This is the excellence of relying upon another.
Therefore, a student must choose their dwelling carefully and seek out scholars in their travels; thus they can sever the path of depravity and draw near to the correct mean.
It is by hearing these orthodox words that this is achieved. Formerly, the Venerable Fuyan Ya always admired the refinement of Zhenru Zhe, for his character was truly commendable.
However, he did not yet know who those with whom he was associated were. One day, he saw him traveling together with Da-ning Kuan, Jiang-shan Yuan, and Cui-yen Zhen;
he rejoiced beyond measure and said to Zhe with composure, "These great beings are the dragon elephants of the Dharma-gate."
You have been able to follow him in his travels. On another day, you shall witness the decline of Zhiguang’s Way and the manifest salvation brought by the Patriarch’s teachings;
truly, this does not depend on my many exhortations (from the *Rishen ji*).
Miaoxi, whose name was Zonggao, was a senior disciple of Zhantang and later succeeded Yuanwu as his dharma heir; he was like a "thousand-li steed.
Foyan, whose name was Liangya, was a successor of Dongshan Shouchu; he was one who relied upon [the lineage].
Danning, named Daokuan, and Jiangshan, named Zanyuan, were both successors of Shishuang Chuyuan; they were companions. Among those from Longshui—
"Those of great strength": among land-dwelling creatures, the elephant possesses the greatest strength;

this serves as a metaphor for the intent of a patch-robed monk (*bhikṣu*) of great insight and realization, who is able to provide support. Zhantang said that when Miaoxi was studying, he should have relied upon virtuous people.
In this age of semblance, monks mostly conform to external matters while remaining internally ignorant of their own minds; even if they possess something vast and grand...
As for these actions, none of them reach the ultimate or final goal; this is because they rely upon that which is base, small, and vulgar.
They are like a swarm of mosquitoes and gadflies on the back of an ox, unable to fly more than a few paces—how could they ever travel far?
If, however, one were willing to rely upon the tail of a noble steed, then one would immediately be able to pursue the wind and chase the sun.
As for the ability to travel a thousand *li*, how could a mosquito possibly overcome it? It is rather through relying upon and entrusting itself [to a larger being] that it succeeds.
For this reason, those who study must choose to reside where there are people of knowledge; they must travel to those who practice the Way.
Only then can they eliminate private, depraved, and biased tendencies, draw near to upright and auspicious gentlemen, and hear correct and excellent words.
In the past, Master Fuyan was always fond of Zhenru Zhe for his outstanding character and refined integrity, deeming him worthy of admiration.
However, he did not know which of the other elders Zhe associated with.
One day, he suddenly saw Zhe traveling together with the venerable masters Danning Kuan, Jiangshan Yuan, Cuiyan Zhen, and others. Fuyan was filled with joy.

It was truly beyond measure. Yet, with a composed and gentle air, he said to Cheol, "Among the great practitioners who traveled with you, there were those of great capacity, like dragons and elephants. You have had the opportunity to associate with them;
as the saying goes, 'near vermilion one becomes red, near ink one becomes black,' and you will surely come to resemble them. Now, let us go."
In times to come, this shall support the decline of my Way and Dharma and manifest the benefits and salvation provided by our ancestors;
it does not depend on my repeated exhortations and warnings. When choosing a place to serve as a scholar, how can one not know upon whom to rely?
Zantang said to Miaoxi, "In the practice of Chan, one must have lofty discernment and far-reaching vision, with a spirit that transcends the mundane.
In one's speech and conduct, one must maintain integrity and inspire trust in others; do not yield to power or profit through deceitful compromise.
In this way, you will naturally not be subject to the fashions or the arbitrary judgments of your peers" (*Baofeng Jiwen*).
Zantang said that Miaoxi’s words were those of one with lofty discernment and great ambition. A person who studies Chan must have high insight and understanding;
their reflections must be far-reaching; their aspirations must be transcendent; and their spirit and momentum must be surpassing. Even when they utter a single word...
Alternatively, one may practice a single matter: to maintain sincerity and integrity, not to deceive others, and not to follow the influence of power or seek profit through expediency.

One must not be swayed or led astray by such matters as dishonesty. Naturally, one should not allow oneself to be painted or modeled after others by those who form factions, nor should one’s discernment shift and change with the times, easily rising or falling.
Zantang said: "In the past, I was with Lingyuan, attending Huaitang at Zhangjiang Temple.
One day, Lingyuan went into the city with two monks and did not return until evening. Huaitang asked him, 'Where have you been today?
Lingyuan replied, 'I just came from Danning. At that time, Sishin was standing nearby; he rebuked him in a stern voice, saying, 'If you wish to practice Chan to escape birth and death, [you must...]"
It is said that one must first be sincere. How could my elder brother Qing have uttered a falsehood? Lingyuan’s face turned red with shame, and he did not dare to respond.
From then on, he no longer entered the city gates nor spoke recklessly. I knew well that both Lingyuan and Sishin were men of excellent capacity (from the *Ri-seki-ki*).
Sishi, whose name was Wuxin, was the successor of Grandfather Huichang. Zantang said:
"In the past, I was with Lingyuan, attending upon Master Huichang at Zhangjiang Temple.
Lingyuan and two other monks went into the city for a leisurely stroll and did not return to the temple until dusk. Huichang therefore asked, 'Where have you been today? Lingyuan—"
He replied, "I had just been to Daining Temple when I returned. At that time, Sishin was by my side;

seeing that Lingyuan’s response was not truthful, he shouted at him in a loud voice, rebuking him: 'If you wish to transcend birth and death through Zen practice, your speech must first be sincere and free from deception.
Elder Qing, how can you fail to uphold the fundamental principle and instead utter empty, false words?'"
Yes. Linyuan’s face flushed with heat; he realized his error and did not dare to argue further. From that time forward, he reformed his ways and turned toward virtue;
he no longer entered city walls nor uttered idle words. As I see it, Linyuan recognized his fault and corrected it swiftly.
Sishin, Zhengjian, and Zeshan were all men of refined character and possessed the spiritual capacity for the Mahayana.
Zhantang remarked, "Lingyuan is fond of reading the classics and histories; he never rests even during eating or sleeping, only ceasing when he can recite them from memory.
Huitang therefore rebuked him. Lingyuan replied, "I have heard that those who exert great effort will achieve far-reaching success. Thus, Huang..."
Taishi Luzhi said: "My elder brother Qing is fond of learning as if he were starving and thirsting for food and drink;
he regards worldly gain and ostentation as if they were a foul odor. This is simply the natural expression of his sincere heart, and not merely a matter of habit" (*Zhuwou ji*).
This means "to rest. Huang Taishi’s name was Tingjian; his courtesy name was Lushi; he styled himself the Layman Shangu.

He received the Dharma from Huanglong Zuoxin. This phrase, "specifically and insistently so," refers to Zhantang borrowing Lingyuan’s "love of learning" to exhort the assembly. Lingyuan loved reading the scriptures; for a single meal—
"At every moment, even for the duration of a single breath, he refuses to rest. Furthermore, he insists that he must master the text through recitation before he will stop.
Because Lingyuan was excessively devoted to his studies, Huichang scolded him to cease; Lingyuan replied:

I have heard that those who possess courageous strength and vigor, whose diligence is spirited and robust, and who exert themselves without ceasing, will find it easy to achieve *samādhi*, easy to reach the other shore (*pāra*), and will also attain the fulfillment of merit for all eternity.
Therefore, Imperial Historian Huang Lu-zhi praised him, saying: "Your brother Qing’s devotion to study is like a person suffering from hunger."
To one who suffers from a parched throat and thirst, a meal is like tea;
to him, observing the worldly affairs of wealth, profit, and elaborate offerings is like foul-smelling excrement.
This is because he is both true to his nature and true to his lot; it is simply due to his innate disposition, not something he has intentionally sought to be so.
When Master Lingyuan Qing went to Taiping in Shuzhou, he observed that every time Foyan presided over the assembly, he was thorough and meticulous, never failing in his duties.
Consequently, Lingyuan asked him for the essential principle behind this. Foyan replied: "In managing affairs, it is better to err on the side of leniency than on the side of haste;
it is better to err on the side of brevity than on the side of excessive detail. What is hasty cannot be rescued; what is overly detailed leaves no room for anything else. You should maintain this."
Regarding the Middle Way, one should treat it with patience and leniency; this may serve as a method for managing the affairs of the assembly (from the *Shiyi*).
This is a near-approximation of the words [spoken by] Master Lingyuan Qing while he was at Taiping Temple in Shuzhou.
Whenever he saw Fuyan presiding over the great assembly, his conduct was thorough, meticulous, and detailed; everything he did was perfectly executed without error. Because of this—

how much more so for those inferior to him? Furthermore, turning back to examine the Buddhist sūtras, it is said: "One need not fear mental outflows."
When these arise, one only fears that awakening and illumination will be slow. Moreover, from the ancient sages and worthies downward, who among them has been without faults?
It is for the spiritual teacher to guide with patience and skillful means to bring them to completion.
Thus, whether one is wise or foolish, noble or humble, sharp-witted or dull, great or small, one will not be cast aside. Therefore it is said:
when a skilled carpenter follows the principle that wheels must be round and rafters square, then even warped ends are materials that can be used;

when a skilled charioteer adapts to the requirements of mountainous terrain or level ground, then both the blunt and the sharp possess the nature of convenience. Since this is the case for the carpenter and the charioteer, [it is so for all].
Knowledge should likewise be appropriate. However, if one acts as a "friend" (knowledge) in such a manner—advancing according to attachment and retreating according to aversion;
indulging in one's own temperament; separating when things differ and joining when they agree;
and lacking any regard for the ultimate goal—then this is like abandoning the rules of measurement to determine what is crooked or straight, or discarding the balance scale to compare weights.

Weighing by the *jin* (catty): although one may be thoroughly proficient in the subtle and profound, it is difficult to guarantee that there will be no error or deviation in their final determination.
○ *Lin* is pronounced *lin*. Lingyuan said: "A capable abbot takes the minds of the assembly as his own mind; he never treats his own mind as private. He [takes] the assembly...

A person’s ears and eyes serve as ears and eyes; they have never been treated as private. Consequently, one is able to communicate the will of the multitude and exhaust the sentiments of the multitude.
For when one takes the hearts of the multitude as one’s own heart, then one’s own likes and dislikes become the likes and dislikes of the multitude.
Thus, what is liked is not perverse, and what is disliked is not erroneous. Furthermore, why rely on private confidants as one’s innermost heart? And why indulge in... [the rest of the text follows].

How one serves such flattery! Since you have already employed the ears and eyes of the multitude as your own, then the intelligence and wisdom of the multitude are all your own intelligence and wisdom.

Thus, there is nothing clear that is not reflected in your vision, and nothing subtle that is not heard by your hearing. Furthermore, why would you privately entrust your ears and eyes to others, thereby stubbornly inviting obscuration and delusion?
As for laying bare one’s innermost thoughts and entrusting one’s ears and eyes, this is something sought only by the worthy and enlightened.
He rectifies his own faults and shares the same desires as the multitude, without partiality or private bias; thus, there are none among the people who do not turn their hearts toward him.
That the Way, Virtue, Benevolence, and Righteousness spread so far and wide is only to be expected.

Conversely, those who are foolish and unworthy strive to seek out the faults of others, act in opposition to the will of the multitude, and wallow in partiality and private bias; consequently, there are none among the people who do not turn their hearts away from them. Therefore...
That ill repute and perilous conduct spread so far and wide was indeed to be expected. Thus we know that a monastic administrator who shares the desires of the community is called a worthy sage;

one who opposes the desires of the community is called a common person. Generally speaking, while their intentions in entrusting their hearts and minds or relying on the eyes and ears of others differ, the resulting good or evil, and success or failure, are as opposite as this. Is it not because they seek out faults?
The sentiments of these people differ; how could the way they entrust themselves to others not be different?
Master Jingzhu of Lingyuan should take the hearts of the assembly as his own heart when preaching.
One who can manage the permanent property and uphold the Dharma and its transformation must ultimately take the hearts of the broad masses as their own heart, without private bias.
To employ one's own biased mind to broaden the ears and eyes of the multitude, while regarding them as one's own ears and eyes—
rather than using one's own private and solitary perceptions as one's ears and eyes— in this way,
one may come to understand the aspirations of the multitude and fully comprehend their dispositions. For when one takes the minds of the multitude as one's own, [one attains this].
As for the mind, my likes and dislikes are not different from those of the multitude; therefore, what is liked is not perverse, and what is disliked is not erroneous.
Why, then, must one take the trouble to privately instruct one's closest confidants so that they may willingly submit to and find pleasure in flattery and sycophancy?
Since one already takes the ears and eyes of the multitude as one's own...
If one’s own ears and eyes are joined with the intelligence of the multitude, one’s wisdom will become increasingly cultivated.
Thus, being enlightened, there is nothing that is not illuminated; being discerning, there is nothing that is not heard.
Why, then, must one petty-mindedly entrust one's ears and eyes to others and remain obstinate, thereby inviting obstruction and delusion for oneself? Indeed, to unfold and spread [this truth]...
There may indeed be those who entrust their closest confidants or their ears and eyes with such a request; these are surely men of virtue and refinement.

Fearing that there may be matters in their human relations that are obstructed or improper, they entrust others to seek out their own faults so that, should such exist, they may be corrected promptly.
This means that one’s likes and dislikes must accord with those of the multitude, without being biased or partial.
Therefore, all people turn toward them and find their hearts in harmony; thus, their spiritual aspiration is lofty and their virtuous conduct is esteemed.
To be benevolent and compassionate toward all things, to extend righteousness to others, and to circulate and proclaim these virtues in the four quarters—this is precisely how it ought to be.
Yet, the thoughts of the ignorant and unworthy are solely intent on scrutinizing the faults of others;

they act contrary to the common good, differing from the masses in their likes and dislikes, and remain submerged in partiality and self-interest. How could such people possess even a single iota of what benefits the human heart?
Consequently, there are none among the multitude who do not become estranged and harbor divergent intentions.
Thus, ill repute and treacherous, perverse conduct also circulate and spread, being propagated throughout the four quarters; this is entirely consistent with reason.

From this we know that a person who maintains the community should see what the multitude desires and share those same desires with them; only then can they be called a worthy and sagacious gentleman.
To see that the desires of the multitude are contrary to one's own is what defines a common and petty person. For the most part, they appear identical on the surface;
they disclose their innermost thoughts and entrust their ears and eyes to others, yet the intentions harbored within their hearts are entirely different.
Thus, auspiciousness and calamity, establishment and ruin, are opposites. Is it not the case that such differences arise from seeking out faults and having divergent intentions?
Since there are discrepancies in how people apply the principles of the human way, those who hold the position of abbot must certainly recognize this truth.
Lingyuan said: "In recent times, those who serve as elders are involved in two kinds of conditions;

for the most part, their wisdom and understanding are not clear, and being struck by these two winds, they lose the integrity of the Dharma-body. First, responding to adverse conditions, they are mostly struck by the wind of decline.

Second, responding to favorable conditions, they are mostly struck by the wind of profit. Once struck by these two winds, the vapors of joy and anger intermingle within the mind, becoming stifling and turbulent."
A haughty expression on one’s face is a gateway to inviting humiliation and being ridiculed by the wise and accomplished.
Only the intelligent are well able to transform this into a method for gathering and converting others, providing an excellent guide for those who follow.

For example, when the Monk of Langye went to Suzhou to visit Fan Xihun, he received offerings totaling over a thousand strings of cash. He then dispatched someone to secretly calculate the number of monks in all the temples within the city.
Everyone secretly sent money. On that same day, he established a vegetarian feast for the assembly of donors. He immediately took his leave of Master Fan.

That morning, he set sail before dawn and reached the next day's break of light; the crowd realized he had already departed. Some pursued him as far as Changzhou, where they were able to meet him. Having received the benefits of the Dharma, they returned.
Observing this single act of the Elder, all the clergy and laity of Gusu were moved to give rise to faith, and their devotion deepened.
The "seeds of the Way" (mārga-vidyā)—this is what is called the method for transforming and gathering [disciples].
It is as utterly different from those who pilfer the rank of the Dharma for the sake of mere gain and sustenance—as the distance between heaven and earth (Letter to Master De).
"Body of Dharma" refers to the Dharmakāya. "Bursting with color" means a change of facial expression; it denotes rebuking through verbal demeanor. Langye’s name was Huijue;
he was a successor of the Patriarch Fenyang Wude. Fan Xiwen’s name was Zhongyan; he was a worthy man of the Song dynasty, posthumously titled Wenzheng.
"Mian" refers to a string of cash. Lingyuan, responding to conditions and alerting people, should extensively practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) in order to inspire them.
People hold him in high esteem and speak of him with reverence. Among the elders who have practiced the Way in recent times, many have encountered two kinds of causal conditions;
while they often observe the wisdom of others, their own discernment is not particularly clear. When touched by the two winds of decline and gain, they immediately lose the true nature of the Dharma.
In one type of case, amidst unfavorable and contrary conditions that do not accord with their wishes, much affliction arises within the mind.
This is the wind of misfortune (*hāni-vāyu*). When one encounters two kinds of conditions that are contrary to one's wishes, much craving and attachment arise within the mind;

this is the wind of fortune (*lābha-vāyu*). Once one is struck by these winds of misfortune and fortune, the vapors of joy and anger will inevitably enter between the heart and the chest, and the colors of suppressed agitation and violent transformation will likewise manifest.
His arrogance was clearly manifest upon his countenance. For this reason, he brought disgrace upon the gateway of the Dharma;
he was reviled, censured, and ridiculed by the worthy and the enlightened, becoming a most fitting object of karmic conditions. O Elder, you alone are a man of great wisdom.

Only then can one possess great skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to transform one's conduct for the benefit of others, gathering and transforming those in all directions, and skillfully guiding future generations—such as the Venerable Master of Langye in Xuzhou, who may be taken as a model for the Dharma.
He once went to Suzhou Prefecture to visit Fan Wen Zheng Gong; there, he received over nine hundred strings of cash in offerings from a donor, which he then... [he then dispatched].
He went to a secluded place to perform his calculations; the number of monks in all the temples within the city was clearly accounted for.
He secretly sent money to them, ensuring no one knew of it, as he had no love for fame or profit. On that same day, he prepared a vegetarian feast and took leave of the various donors.
He first bid farewell to Fan Xingwen. The following day, before dawn, he set sail early in the morning.
When the sky grew bright and everyone realized he had already departed, those who did not cherish his reputation followed him as far as Changzhou Prefecture, where they were finally able to meet him;
having received the gift of the Dharma, they returned. Such was his lack of stinginess regarding the Dharma.
Observing these actions of the Elder Langye, one sees how his engagement with the world was driven by the conditions of the times.
It caused both the clergy and the laity of Gusu to all give rise to unsurpassed faith and deepen their seeds for the unsurpassed Way.
Can this not be called Zhiyi’s skillful employment of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), serving as a great and ingenious expedient (*upāya*) for conversion and transformation?

Compared to those who secretly usurp the position of the Dharma and greedily seek gain and sustenance, plotting only for their own single selves, there is truly as vast a difference between heaven and earth; they cannot be compared at all.
Duke Wenzheng said to Langye, "Last year when I arrived here, I was thinking of finding someone among the recluses with whom I might converse.
I once asked an official whether there were any fine monks among the various mountains. The official replied that the two monks Ruiguang and Ximao of Beisi Temple were excellent.
I asked, 'Are there no others besides these among the various Chan and Vinaya masters? The official answered me, 'The Confucians honor the conduct of the scholar.'"
The monks discussed their virtuous achievements, noting that those such as Xi and Mao had for thirty years trodden the path without ever crossing its threshold;

they wore only plain cloth and hemp, remaining entirely unattached to fame, profit, or worldly sustenance. Consequently, the people of the land held their conduct in high esteem and revered them as teachers.

If one ascends the seat to preach the Dharma, acting as the Buddha’s representative to propagate the transformation of beings, possessing spontaneous eloquence and being hailed as a true *kalyāṇamitra*, this is not something a dull-witted official can understand.
On a day of leisure, I visited the two venerable masters Xi and Mou and observed their long-standing conduct; it was exactly as the official had described.

I reflected on the old reputation that the customs of Suzhou and Xiu are excellent, and now, observing even this aged official, I see he is still capable of distinguishing between the gentleman and the commoner.
If this is the case for petty men, how much more so for those of true discernment? Langya said: "What the official has said is truly a lofty discourse.
I request that it be recorded so as to enlighten those who have not yet heard it. (From the *Langya Bie Lu*)

The name of Rui Guang Temple (Auspicious Light Temple) derives from four auspicious omens: the bells and drums rang spontaneously; the precious pagoda emitted light; auspicious bamboo grew intertwined;
and a white tortoise listened to the Dharma. Thus it is called Rui Guang. A "gatepost" (*kūnmen*) refers to a wooden stake.
An "upper person" (*shangren*) is one who possesses wisdom within and virtuous conduct without, standing above others; hence they are called an "upper person. "Xiu" refers to Jiaxing Prefecture.
Furthermore, Lord Fan Wenzheng said to the Monk of Langye, "A beautiful land produces fine people.
Last year, while staying here, I reflected upon finding a man of the Way among the forest-dwellers with whom I might discuss this matter.
I once questioned an experienced senior clerk regarding whether there were any monks among the various mountain monasteries who were truly devoted to practice.
The clerk replied that these two—Xieguang and Ximao of Beisi Temple—were good monks. I said:
"Beyond these two individuals, are there not others among those who practice Chan meditation and uphold the precepts within these two dharma-gates?
The official replied once more: "Among those held in high esteem within the Confucian gate are the virtuous conduct of scholars;
among those held in high esteem within the Buddhist gate are the spiritual practices of monks. As for individuals such as Xi and Mao, they have not stepped outside [their chambers] for thirty years."
Regarding his threshold [of conduct]: as for his clothing, he wore only undyed cloth. He did not seek fame or reputation, nor was he greedy for gain or offerings.

Within his breast, there was no obstruction whatsoever. Therefore, the people of the entire region held his integrity and practice in high esteem, serving him as their teacher and honoring him with reverence.
This continued until he ascended the precious Flower-King Throne (*padmavajrāsana*) to propagate the Dharma on behalf of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, manifesting his spiritual power.
Their sharp edges met; their eloquence was unimpeded. Moving freely across all eight directions, they were everywhere sovereign.
Those called "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra) are not something that can be understood by ignorant, stubborn, or dull-witted officials.

When I had some leisure time and no other affairs, I visited the two superior men, Xi and Mou, to observe their conduct and examine their natural character and practice; every single detail accorded with what the official had said.
I withdrew and reflected: the ancients praised Gusu as a place where oranges and peaches produced fine men and possessed excellent customs.
Now, observing even an elderly clerk who can distinguish between the noble and the base, or the good and the bad, in his cross-examination—how much more so those with great insight?
When Langya heard Wen Gong speak thus, he likewise commended him, saying:

The words of this official are truly a lofty discourse. I request that they be recorded in writing to inform those who have not yet heard them in the future, so that they may take them as a model for emulation.
Lingyuan said: "Master Yuan of Mount Zhong spent his life never associating with high officials and never seeking fame or profit.

He cultivated himself through humility and delighted in the Way. When scholars and gentlemen first urged him to engage with the world, Yuan said: 'If one possesses good fields, [one need not seek elsewhere].'"
"What need is there to worry about late success? I only fear a lack of talent and ability. When Lord Jing heard this, he said: "When they see color, they take flight;
they wheel about and only then settle. This is what Master Yuan has attained" (Zhouyou ji).
Zhongshan is the name of Mount Jinling. Yuan refers to Master Zanyuan. Lingyuan borrowed Master Yuan’s life and conduct to admonish later students;
one should deeply store and richly nourish oneself before speaking of transcending the world.

As for Master Yuan of Zhongshan, throughout his life his natural disposition was such that he did not cultivate friendships with the Three Ducal Ministers or the Nine High Officials, nor did he seek fame, reputation, wealth, or profit in a fickle manner.
One should cultivate oneself through humility, modesty, and compliance; one should attain profound mastery of the Way to find personal peace and joy.
When scholars and officials take pleasure in his actual lowliness, they initially urge him to exert himself so that he might transcend the mundane world. He replies:
"If there were fine, excellent, and fertile fields from which to sow good seeds, one need not worry about a poor harvest; success does not depend on being early."
It is simply that one fears there is no Secret Mara’s fork, Heoshan’s drum, Deshan’s staff, Linji’s shout, or such discernment regarding the profound and the essential.
When Lord Jing heard this, he praised it, saying: "The *Analects* states:
'When a bird sees that a person’s countenance is not benevolent, it flies away; yet it circles back and hovers to examine it, until it is finally shot.'"
"Where it does not reach, then one gathers and stops. Looking at these two lines of speech, they correspond exactly to the conduct of Master Yuan; he has fully realized them.
Lingyuan said: "The sages of old have said that it is difficult to attain awakening through the study of the Way; once awakened, it is difficult to maintain that state;
and once maintained, it is difficult to put it into practice. Now, when it comes to the time of actual practice, the difficulty exceeds even that of awakening and maintenance.

This is because while awakening and maintenance require only diligent effort and steadfast resolve applied to one's own person, practice necessitates the equalizing of the mind and the making of a death-vow to diminish the self."

Taking the benefit of others as one's primary responsibility, if the mind is not impartial and one's vows are not firm, then benefit and harm will be inverted, and one will fall into the ranks of a common worldly teacher; this is something to be feared.
Lingyuan shows the Way-seeking person the sequence for maintaining practice. A former sage said: "In studying the Way, there is nothing else;
it culminates in certain awakening. It is truly difficult not to awaken. After days and years have passed, one suddenly awakens in a single morning.
Once awakened and entered, it is also difficult not to lose what has been attained by failing to maintain it long-term. Having already secured a firm and secret grasp of it,"
It is already difficult to practice what one upholds; now, at the time when one must actually walk the Path, the difficulty is doubled.
It is even more difficult than awakening to and maintaining the Way. Indeed, awakening to and maintaining the Way involves nothing other than:

being diligent and never retreating, remaining steadfast and unwavering, applying oneself with sensitivity and effort, and putting it into practice through the body. Only upon reaching the time of actual practice must one certainly maintain these qualities.
The mind of equanimity arises and continues until death. This great vow is of a single flavor;
it takes the sacrificing of oneself to benefit others as its primary task, bearing this burden upon one shoulder.

If the mind is not impartial and the vow is not firm and certain, then the intention to harm oneself to benefit others will become inverted and misplaced, and one will fall into the ranks of base, vulgar teachers—neither for oneself nor for others.
"What benefit is there in this? This is precisely why one should instead treat him with reverence and approach him with cautious awe.

Lingyuan said, "Brother Dongshan was exceptionally gifted by nature; his speech and silence were always measured. Whenever he ordinarily presented a saying or phrase, its underlying principle was naturally superior.
When others elsewhere sought to imitate him, they could never reach his level—either they became artificial and vulgar, or they fell into vulgarity and meanness."
Even when sought among the ancients, such a person could not be found. Yet, he remained humble and radiant in his guidance of others, as if driven by nothing less than hunger and thirst.
He once said: "I possess no Dharma; how can I fail to encourage my disciples? I am truly a sinner within the gates of the True Dharma."
Lingyuan borrowed the humble brilliance of Master Yuan to guide sentient beings, thereby encouraging those in all quarters to speak.
As for my elder brother from Dongshan, his innate nature and character were exceptionally outstanding; whether speaking or remaining silent, he always accorded with the Dharma.
Whenever he would casually present his recorded sayings, the principles within them were naturally transcendent and superior. Now, those in all quarters wish to imitate him.
It is neither deceitful nor vulgar; it is not the kind of worldly excess or narrowness that ultimately leaves one unable to reach its heights.
Even when sought among the ancient sages of antiquity, few can compare to it. Yet, it remains humble and harmonious with the light of the world, guiding and benefiting all beings.
It was as if he were hungry and longing for food, or thirsty and longing for drink. He once said, "I have no Buddha-dharma to give to others;
how could I possibly encourage my disciples? I am truly a sinner within this Dharma-gate. Such was his humble brilliance in benefiting others.
If this were so, could it not be taken as a guiding principle?
Lingyuan’s Daoist learning, conduct, and righteousness were characterized by pure sincerity and profound virtue, possessing the spirit of the ancients.

He was composed and spoke sparingly, earning the highest respect from scholars and officials. He once said: "What the multitude neglects, the Sage treats with caution; how much more so for one who..."
O masters of the monastic groves, to assist in proclaiming the Buddha’s transformation is a task that can only be undertaken by those whose practice and understanding are in accord;
how could anyone else do so? It is essential that you examine yourselves at all times, ensuring that fame, profit, or sustenance never sprout within your minds.

Should there be aspects of the Dharma that have not yet been fully realized, or disciples who have not yet been won over, you must withdraw in reflection to cultivate virtue, awaiting those who will come in the future. I have never seen one whose own person is upright [who can lead others].
Regarding the failure to govern the monastic community (chónglín): it is said that by observing the countenance of a man of virtue, one causes the turbidity of another’s mind to dissolve;

this is truly what is meant here (*Jìwén*). That which is not mixed is called "pure" (chún); that which is not false is called "sincere" (chéng). If one uses such words, they signify trustworthiness and faith. This records the source of spiritual power.
The Way of learning has its origins; the practice of righteousness has its methods. His pure sincerity is worthy of emulation, and his profound virtue is worthy of veneration.
He truly possessed the spirit of the ancients, being composed, cautious, and sparing in speech; he was further held in high esteem by Confucian scholars and government officials.
He once said: "That which the multitude neglects is what the sages treat with caution. How much more so for one who...

Good friends, those who assist in proclaiming and disseminating the Dharma-transformation of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are not merely those whose practice accords with their understanding, nor those whose understanding accords with their practice;
they are those for whom practice and understanding are unified. How could such people possibly act recklessly?
They must, at all times, constantly examine and reproach themselves, ensuring that these matters—status, reputation, wealth, profit, and offerings—do not arise in even one of them.
A mere thread or hair’s breadth stirs within the breast and heart. If this were merely a formal rule, it would not be trusted by people once put into practice;
nor would the patch-robed monks, having come here, find satisfaction in it. One must not force others, nor suppress them to make them follow one's own will.
You should withdraw to cultivate self-reflection and deeply nurture your virtue, waiting for a transformative influence to move you and allowing it to come of its own accord.
I have never seen one who is upright themselves yet fails to bring the temple community into order.

It is said that beholding the countenance of a person of virtue can cause one’s mind to sink into humility and the stains of habitual defilement to melt away like ice; the reality of this indeed lies herein.

Lingyuan said to Yuanwu, "Although a monastic may possess the potential for insight into the Way, if they do not store it deeply and nurture it thickly, their manifestation of it will inevitably be abrupt and violent.
Not only will this fail to benefit the teachings, but it may even invite calamity and disgrace."
Yuánwù, whose name was Kèqín, was the son of the Lù family of Pénghōu. He resided at Zhāojié Monastery in Chéngdū Fǔ.
He was a successor of Wǔzǔ Yuǎn. Língyuán remarked to Yuánwù’s disciples: "A Chan practitioner possesses the natural capacity for insight into the Way;
if they do not conceal their brilliance and obscure their luster, but instead remain submerged in quietude to nurture their cultivation, their realization will inevitably manifest."
Ultimately, being harsh, sharp, and violent is not only of no benefit to the precincts of the Dharma teachings;
it is feared that it will also be disadvantageous to oneself, inviting misfortune, harm, and disgrace.
Students should know this as the way to cultivate themselves.
Chan Master Yuanwu said: "The study of the Way depends upon faith; establishing faith depends upon sincerity. When sincerity is maintained within, one can then cause others to be free from delusion.
When faith is maintained within oneself, one can teach others without deception. Only through faith and sincerity is there benefit and no loss.
Thus we know that if sincerity is not constant, the mind cannot be preserved; if faith is not constant, words cannot be relied upon."

Practice. An ancient said: "One's clothing and food may be dispensed with, but sincerity and trustworthiness must not be lost. Only a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) should teach others through sincerity and trustworthiness.
Furthermore, if one’s mind is not sincere and one’s actions are not trustworthy, can one truly be called a spiritual friend? The *I Ching* says:
Only those who possess the utmost sincerity in the world are able to fully realize their own nature. Being able to fully realize one's own nature, one can then fully realize the nature of others.
Yet, if one cannot first fully realize it within oneself while desiring to realize it in others, the multitude will surely view this as deceptive and refuse to follow.

If one is not sincere in what precedes while claiming to be sincere in what follows, the multitude will surely view this with suspicion and fail to believe it. This is what is meant by "cutting the hair" [and leaving the scalp].
It should reach the skin; when clipping one's nails, they should be trimmed close to the flesh. This is truly because if sincerity does not reach its object, then things will not respond;

if diminution [of self] does not reach its limit, then benefit will not arrive. It is clear, therefore, that sincerity and trustworthiness must never for a moment depart from oneself. (Letter to the Vice-Prefect Yu)

The reality of the mind is called sincerity (*cheng*); the reality of speech is called trustworthiness (*xin*). Trustworthiness is the substance of sincerity; sincerity is the function of trustworthiness.
When one possesses the utmost sincerity in the world, this describes the sage’s virtue reaching the pinnacle of sincerity and freedom from falsehood, such that none in the world can surpass it.
"This" refers to the distinction made here; "a moment" refers to the waiting for that. Distinction implies separation; waiting implies union. This is what is meant by "this very moment."
This is the moment of parting from one and uniting with another. Yuanwu taught his disciples: "One should maintain sincerity and preserve faith.
When studying to master the principles of the Way, first establish sincere faith; establish practice upon sincere faith. The essential point lies in being truly sincere.

Once you are able to maintain sincerity within your own heart, you can then cause the hearts of all others to likewise be free of doubt. Since you yourself are able to maintain sincerity in your mind, [you may then lead others].
Maintain faith within yourself; only then can you teach others not to deceive.
Thus, sincerity and truthfulness—these two—provide great benefit to both oneself and others, and are free from error.
Know that if sincerity is not single-minded, the sincere heart will easily become false and one will be unable to preserve it; if faith is not single-minded, then sincerity...
Words are also easy to feign, yet one is unable to act accordingly. The *Analects* says: "Clothing is essential to the body;
it can relieve the cold. Food is essential to life; it can stave off hunger. These things seem as if they could not be dispensed with, yet they can still be set aside.

Regarding the single matter of sincerity and trustworthiness, one would rather die than depart from it. Therefore, a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) must certainly teach people sincerity and trustworthiness.
If one’s mind is already deluded and insincere, and one’s actions are already deceitful and untrustworthy, how could such a person be fit to act as a spiritual friend?
The *Appended Statements* of the *I Ching* say: "Only the utmost sincerity in the world..."
This is the ultimate of sincerity; nothing in the world surpasses it. It is just as when one speaks of the unsurpassed, wondrous Way:

the wonder of that Way cannot be added to beyond the "One. When a person possesses this sincerity, they are able to eliminate habitual defilements, falsehoods, and delusions, thereby penetrating the original nature of the person. Since one is thus able to remove habitual defilements, falsehoods, and delusions...

One must realize one's original nature. Furthermore, one should extend this principle of utmost sincerity to others, so that whether noble or base, wise or foolish, virtuous or otherwise—every person throughout the world—may each be able to eliminate habitual defilements and delusions, thereby penetrating through to their own original nature.
If even one cannot personally remove these defilements and clarify one's fundamental nature, [how can one lead others to do so?]

If one’s nature desires to lead others to abandon their habitual defilements and clarify their original nature, yet everyone surely regards this as deception and does not believe it—since you yourself have not participated in it from the outset, but instead claim to practice sincerity only after having already acted with deceit toward the ignorant masses—this will only further give rise to doubt and lack of reverent faith. Thus it is said: [The text continues: "If one wishes to cause others to abandon their habitual defilements and clarify their original nature, yet everyone surely regards this as deception and does not believe it; since you yourself have not participated in it from the outset, but instead claim to practice sincerity only after having already acted with deceit toward the ignorant masses, this will only further give rise to doubt and lack of reverent faith. So it is said: [The text continues: "If one wishes to cause others to abandon their habitual defilements and clarify their original nature, yet everyone surely regards this as deception and does not believe it; since you yourself have not participated in it from the outset, but instead claim to practice sincerity only after having already acted with deceit toward the ignorant masses, this will only further give rise to doubt and lack of reverent faith.
