So it is said: [The text continues:]
When one shaves the hair according to the Way, it must necessarily reach the skin; when one trims the nails, they must necessarily penetrate the flesh.
This is because if sincerity does not reach its ultimate limit, people will not feel moved. It is just as when removing hair that does not reach the skin:
if the reduction does not reach its ultimate limit, the resulting benefit will not attain excellence. It is also like trimming the nails without penetrating [the flesh].
Their essence is one. For sincerity (*cheng*) and trustworthiness (*xin*) are one substance and one function; how could they be separated for even a moment?
It is clear that one must not depart from them for an instant. This is why it is said that a person of the Way should hold sincerity and trustworthiness as most precious.
Yuánwù said: "Who among men is without fault? To err and yet be able to reform—there is no goodness greater than this.

Those of antiquity all praised the correction of faults as being worthy, rather than regarding the absence of faults as a virtue. Therefore, in the conduct of people, errors and deviations are frequent;
even those of superior wisdom and the lowest folly cannot avoid them. Only the wise are able to correct their faults and shift toward goodness, whereas the foolish mostly conceal their faults."

To gloss over one’s faults while shifting toward goodness causes one’s virtue to renew daily; such a person is called a gentleman (*junzi*). To gloss over one’s transgressions causes one’s evil to become ever more manifest;
this is what is meant by a petty man (*xiaoren*). Therefore, to hear of righteousness and be able to move toward it is difficult for ordinary people;
to see goodness and joyfully follow it is what the virtuous esteem. It would be appropriate, Mr. Gong, for you and I to forget each other beyond words (as with Assistant Magistrate Wen).
Yuanwu’s Letter to Magistrate Wen: I instruct you not to scrutinize the faults of others.
Throughout the entire world, among the wise and the foolish, the noble and the base, who is able to be completely pure and entirely without fault? For even the virtuous and wise nobleman—
Because one is able to quickly reform even the slightest transgressions, this constitutes goodness, and no goodness is greater than this.
All the sages of antiquity praised those who reform their faults as being virtuous; they did not consider those who have committed no fault to be admirable.
Consequently, everyone busies themselves with social interactions and worldly affairs, and for the most part...
There are faults. From the sons of heaven down to the common people, from the sages to the ordinary folk, none can escape them.
Only those possessed of wisdom are able to reform themselves and begin anew; they shift toward goodness and clarify their principles.
As for the ignorant and dull-witted, they mostly conceal their own faults and gloss over their errors. When it comes to shifting toward goodness, their...

If one’s virtuous deeds advance and renew daily, is this not teaching one to become a gentleman? If one merely adorns over one’s transgressions, then one’s evil karma increases and becomes ever more manifest;
this is teaching one to become a petty person. Therefore, Confucius took it as a cause for concern that one hears of righteousness yet cannot shift toward it.
To be able to shift is truly what ordinary circumstances find difficult; only the Sovereign Yu delighted in taking [the good] and acting with others for their mutual excellence.
To do good is truly what the worthy and virtuous esteem. Viewed through the lens of the Two Sages, such faults are indeed beyond scrutiny.
I hope you will not ride upon words nor be hindered by phrases; it would be well for us to forget one another beyond the realm of words and forms.
Yuánwù said: "The former master spoke of those who become elders: there are those who move others through their virtue and character, and there are those who subdue others through their power.
These are like the flight of the phoenix, which all birds love, and the prowling of the tiger and wolf, which all beasts fear.
In their ability to move and subdue others, they are one and the same; yet their natures are as different as heaven and earth. (From the *Zhuìyòu jí*)
Yuanwu instructed the Elder: "One should move others through virtue. The Fifth Patriarch, our former teacher, once said:
"Among those who serve as elders, there are those who move others by clarifying the mind, awakening to the Way, and cultivating virtuous conduct;
and there are those who subdue others out of pride in their status and power, relying on their own might. These are like the soaring plumage and feathers of divine birds and auspicious fowl."

...these and their like all follow him in groups, loving and cherishing him. Furthermore, as for fierce tigers, greedy wolves, and those with long, curling fur and horns, each of them is startled and avoids him, fearing and trembling before him. The way they are moved and subdued is fundamentally the same;
yet the application of virtue versus the application of force, and the categories of fur and feathers, are like the heavens above and the earth below.
Below. From this point on, the distinctions between the honorable and the humble naturally differ.

Yuanwu said to Attendant Administrator Long: "If one wishes to manage a monastic community (conglin) but does not strive to understand the sentiments of its people, then the community cannot be managed.
If one strives to understand the sentiments of its people but is not diligent in receiving those below, then the sentiments of the people cannot be grasped."
It is possible. If one strives to engage with subordinates but does not distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy, then subordinates cannot be engaged.

If one strives to distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy but loathes speaking of their faults while delighting in compliance with oneself, then the worthy and the unworthy cannot be distinguished.
Only the sagely and enlightened person does not loathe speaking of faults nor delight in compliance with themselves; they follow only the Way. This is how one attains the hearts of others and—
"The management of the monastic community (*saṃghārāma*) is a matter of principle" (from the *Guǎnglù*). The Abbot Lóng was named Shàolóng; he was a successor of Yuánwù Qín.

When Yuánwù instructed Abbot Lóng on managing the monastic community, he emphasized that it is vital to obtain the right person for the task, while also insisting that taking the Way as one's primary duty is essential. He then spoke of the methods for rectifying the monastic community.
Even if one follows the standard of the compass and square, if one does not first single-mindedly strive to win the hearts of people, then the monastic communities will likely not be well-ordered.

If one single-mindedly strives to win the hearts of people, yet does not diligently and earnestly apply oneself to receiving those who come from the four quarters, then human sentiments will likely not be fully won over.
If one single-mindedly strives to receive those who come from the four quarters, yet fails to distinguish between the gentleman and the commoner...
As for petty people, even if they come from all four directions, they may not necessarily be worthy of being received.

If one focuses solely on distinguishing between the noble and the petty, while refusing to hear of one's own faults and delighting only in those who are compliant with oneself, then slanderers, flatterers, and sycophants will arrive;
yet the noble and the petty will not necessarily be distinguished. Only those of virtuous excellence and broad, penetrating wisdom do not harbor such aversion.
One speaks of one’s own faults and is surely able to reform them; one does not seek to please oneself but remains straightforward, sincere, and without artifice.
Taking only the fundamental matter as the singular flavor, one upholds its great principles as a support.
By doing so, one wins the hearts of people, and the various aspects of the monastic community will naturally fall into proper order.
Yuánwù said: "The abbot takes the wisdom of the multitude as his own wisdom and the mind of the multitude as his own mind.

He constantly fears that even a single matter may not exhaust its true circumstances or that a single affair may not accord with principle. Thus, he diligently seeks counsel and pursues only what is good.

One should inquire whether a principle is right or wrong; why should one debate whether an affair is large or small? If the principle is right, even if the expenditure is great, why should it not be undertaken?"

It is regrettable. If a matter is improper, even if its expenditure is small, what harm is there in eliminating it? For the small is the precursor of the great, and the minute is the sprout of the manifest;
thus the worthy are cautious at the beginning, and the sages maintain their vigilance. If a tiny stream is not dammed, it will eventually transform a mulberry field;
if a fierce fire is not extinguished, it will ultimately consume the plains and wilds. Once the spreading flames have become intense and the calamity is already complete, though one wishes—
To save him was certainly beyond reach. As the ancients said: "If one does not take care in small matters, it will eventually bring ruin to great virtue.

This is precisely what that means. To distinguish between right and wrong is called wisdom; it is to master all principles and govern all things. *Zi* (孜) means diligent. *E* (遏) means to stop or restrain.

*Yan* (炎) refers to fire blazing upward. *Yuandi* (原地) refers to a broad and level place. *Shan* (煽) means to kindle or intensify. *Jin* (矜) means to pity or feel compassion. *Xi* (惜) means to cherish or regret.

This is the intended meaning. It concerns the accumulation of matters, conditions, and circumstances. In a letter to Fozhi, Yuanwu stated that a monastic administrator (*zhuchi*) should take the mind of the assembly as his own mind.
He emphasized the importance of seeking what is good and being careful at the outset.
An administrator should regard the wisdom of the multitude as his own wisdom and the sentiments of the multitude as his own sentiments, constantly fearing that even a single thing might be lacking.
Exhaust their sincerity so that every single matter is treated with full sincerity; attain the principle so that every dharma accords with the principle.
With diligent and earnest devotion, seek out the worthy and embrace the good, making this alone your pursuit.

You must inquire whether the underlying principle is correct or not, regardless of whether the matter at hand is great or small. When it accords with the principle, it is appropriate for the monastic community.
If it brings benefit to a vast assembly, even if one acts with great extravagance, what harm is there in doing so?
If the matter were otherwise and brought no benefit to the vast assembly or the monastic community, then even if the expenditure were but slight, it would be improper.
To eliminate them—what harm is there in this principle? For the small is the gradual progression toward the great, and the minute is the sprouting of the manifest.
Do not say that a good deed is too small to perform; do not say that an evil is too slight to remove.
Therefore, those of supreme virtue are cautious in their conduct from the very beginning; the widely enlightened Great Sages maintain their minds as a constant restraint.

This is like water in its subtle state: if one does not stop it at the first drop, it will eventually breach the embankments and overflow the fields, ultimately transforming the mulberry fields into a vast blue sea.
It is also like fire in its smallness: if one does not [extinguish] it at the first spark...

Extinguish it! When fierce winds and blazing fires suddenly consume the plains and wilds until they become a charred wasteland, and when the flow of water and the fanning of flames have already reached such magnitude—that human calamity and celestial disaster have already fully matured—at this point, though one wishes to reach out a hand to save them, it is too late to bite one's own heel.
As the ancients said: "If one does not cherish and guard against minor actions, there will ultimately be a failure."
"To be burdened by conditions and by one's own lofty virtue—these two phrases are precisely what is meant by 'being cautious at the outset' and 'maintaining the precepts.
How can they be neglected? Yuanwu said to Yuan Budai:
"In all matters pertaining to the office of an Elder, you must assist in proclaiming the Buddha’s transformation; always reflect upon this."
To take the relief of others as one’s primary concern and to act without self-conceit ensures that those reached will be far-reaching and those aided will be numerous.

However, if there arises even a single thought of self-importance or the desire to display one's own abilities, the notion of seeking personal gain will emerge, and the mind of the unworthy will take birth.
Yuan was originally named Jingyuan; his style name was Cican. He was a successor of the patriarch Zhaojue Qin.

He was full of self-importance and maintained a sense of self-reliance, manifesting his pride through his own displays. Yuanwu remarked, "As for 'Bagua Yuan,' he should take the salvation of others as his primary concern."
Be careful not to indulge in self-conceit regarding your teachings. The office and rank of one who is called an Elder (sthavira) is no ordinary matter;

it is to assist and facilitate the propagation of the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' Dharma-transformation. You should constantly reflect upon this in every thought, taking the benefit of sentient beings as your primary aim.
Exert yourself with diligence, instructing others without weariness, and never harbor self-importance. Only then will the Dharma-transformation you disseminate—
Furthermore, those whom one reaches out to will surely be many; those who are rescued, gathered, and brought to take refuge will likewise be numerous.

However, if one possesses even a single thought of self-conceit, self-importance, or the display of one's own abilities and loftiness, the desire for gain through mere chance will arise, and the mind that refuses to learn from others will follow suit.
Yuánwù said to Miàoxī, "In general, one’s conduct must be careful from beginning to end;

therefore, those who excel at initiating a task will surely excel at completing it, and those who excel at the start will surely excel at the finish. To be as careful at the end as at the beginning ensures that no failure occurs. As the ancients said:

'Alas, the robe was not finished when it was turned into a skirt,' and 'The last ten li of a hundred-li journey are equal to the whole ninety. These were all lamentations regarding having a beginning..."
There is no end [to such lapses]. Thus it is said: "There is nothing that does not have a beginning, yet few are able to reach the end. Long ago, the elder master Huìtáng said:

"The monk Héshèng of Huangbō was also a remarkable patch-robed practitioner; however, he was mistaken in his later years. Judging by his initial attainment, one cannot fail to call him worthy (from the *Yúnmén Ān jí*).
Huangbo’s name was Weisheng; he was the successor of Huanglong Nan. "Ban" means "half" or "to stop. "Mi" means "none. "Xian" means "few. "Ke" means "able.
Yuanwu said that Miaoxi taught that one should be as careful at the end as one was at the beginning. Generally speaking, in all movements and actions, one must be cautious from the very start.
This is why it is called "shaguo" (stopping short); it is because one must act in this way to be able to accomplish a task.
One who acts thus will surely accomplish their task; one who can provide a beginning will surely be able to reach the end.
Therefore, one must be cautious and maintain the same diligence as when first starting out; in this way, one may hope to avoid failure. As the ancients said:
"It is a pity that the upper garment was left unfinished and transformed into a lower robe," or as it is said: "To travel a hundred li on a journey and then stop."
There is no such thing as "concluding" (sha-ge). Thus, a poem says: "There is nothing that does not have a beginning; few are able to reach the end.
This poem also speaks of that which has no starting point, yet few are able to bring it to a conclusion. Formerly, the elder Huitang said:
"When Master Huangbo Sheng was first studying under Huanglong, everyone called him extraordinary."
"O patch-robed monks! This is merely a later error of omission. Observe its starting point:
does it not teach that one becomes a worthy person who has attained something? Half of a hundred *li* is fifty *li*. This means that it is not only fifty *li*;
even if it were ninety-nine *li*, lacking but a single *li*, it would still be half."

Yuanwu said to Fojian, "Master Baoyun’s every movement and action was invariably modeled upon antiquity. He once said: 'If one does not examine antiquity in their affairs, it is called being contrary to the Dharma.
I have studied many ancient words and past deeds, and thus I have fulfilled his aspiration. However, this was not merely a fondness for the ancients;
rather, it was because people of the present day are insufficient as models. My late teacher often remarked that Master Baoyun clung to antiquity and did not realize—"
"Change of time. The Master said: "To change the constant for the sake of novelty is the great affliction of people today;
I shall never do so. 'The former words' are the words of the ancient sages; 'the past conduct' is the conduct of the ancient sages. 'Detailed phonology and meaning' refers to antiquity.
'The constant' refers to the classics—the eternal and unchanging canonical laws. This points to the former words and past conduct."
This is my intention. Yuanwu said that Fojian should emulate the ancient masters of former times. Master Baiyun, in all four modes of deportment, would invariably examine past precedents;
he once said, "If one does not examine the ways of antiquity when performing a task, the instruction will be rootless—what standard can there be for emulation?
I have extensively studied the words of the sages of old and the conduct of the saints of yesteryear.
Thus, it became my own aspiration. However, it was not that I personally loved antiquity so much; rather, it was because people of the present day are insufficient to serve as a model.
My late teacher often remarked that the Master [Linji] was overly rigid regarding the ancients and failed to adapt to the changing times.
The Master replied: "To alter the ancient canons and change the constant classics—this is a grievous affliction."
This is no small matter; it is, in fact, a great affliction for people of the present day. I have already made a firm resolve and sworn an oath that I must ultimately follow the ancient ways.
Even if circumstances change and the usual order is overturned, I shall never dare to act contrary to them.
When Fojian was serving as abbot at Zhihai, having moved there from Taiping, District Magistrate Cen Yuanli asked him, "Who would be capable of succeeding you as the presiding abbot?
Fojian recommended the head seat, Mingben. The Magistrate wished to meet him; Fojian said, "Mingben is a man of stern integrity who remains aloof from the world and has no worldly attachments.
Even if we were to invite him, I fear he might not comply; how much less would he ever come of his own accord?"
Lord Ye earnestly invited him. Baoying said, "This is what is called a 'long-lived elder who presents his body [to the world]'"; he ultimately fled to Mount Sīkong.
Lord Ye looked back at Fojian and said, "One knows one's son better than one's father. He immediately ordered the various monasteries to press their invitation;
with no other choice, Baoying finally complied (from *Chansi Zhe Rilü*).
Zeng Gongyuanli was the Prefect of Shuzhou. The Head Seat (Shouzuo) Ming was named Zhibing; he was a man of stern integrity and was known as "Bing the Iron-Faced.
He was a successor of Fojian Qin. As Head Seat, he served as a model for the monastic community, acting as the eyes for the human and celestial realms.
He shares his seat to preach the Dharma and provides guidance for future generations; as the head of the administrative staff, he holds the primary position of the West Hall.
"Miao" means distant, or alternatively, it implies looking down upon others. "Yao" means to invite or summon. "Chengmei" refers to acting as a go-between or self-promotion;

it signifies the intent of using one's reputation to advertise oneself. Sīkōng Mountain belongs to Tàihú County in Ānqīng Prefecture; it was the site where the Second Patriarch transmitted the robe to the Third Patriarch.

This was the site of the ancient Minister of Works. It is said that Li Bai once sought refuge here during his travels. (The particle "yi" is used here as a discourse marker. This records how the Venerable Fojian Qin moved from Taiping to Zhihai. When the Prefectural Governor, Zeng Yuanli, asked, "Which monk is this? [the Master replied: "He is the one who has just arrived. [The Governor] asked, "What is his name? [The Master] replied, "His name is 'Not Yet. [The Governor] asked, "Where is he from? [The Master] replied, "From the place where the wind does not reach. [The Governor] asked, "How old is he? [The Master] replied, "He is as old as the sky. [The Governor] asked, "What is his style? [The Master] replied, "His style is 'Unobtainable. [The Governor] asked, "What is his dharma-name? [The Master] replied, "His dharma-name is 'No Name. [The Governor] asked, "What is his lineage? [The Master] replied, "He is the one who has just arrived. [The Governor] asked, "What is his teaching? [The Master] replied, "It is the teaching of 'Not Yet. [The Governor] asked, "What is his robe? [The Master] replied, "It is the robe of 'Unobtainable. [The Governor] asked, "What is his bowl? [The Master] replied, "It is the bowl of 'No Name. [The Governor] asked, "What is his staff? [The Master] replied, "It is the staff of 'The Place Where the Wind Does Not Reach. [The Governor] asked, "What is his seat? [The Master] replied, "It is the seat of 'As Old as the Sky. [The Governor] asked, "What is his meditation hall? [The Master] replied, "It is the meditation hall of 'The Teaching of Not Yet. [The Governor] asked, "What is his kitchen? [The Master] replied, "It is the kitchen of 'The Robe of Unobtainable. [The Governor] asked, "What is his bathhouse? [The Master] replied, "It is the bathhouse of 'The Bowl of No Name. [The Governor] asked, "What is his latrine? [The Master] replied, "It is the latrine of 'The Staff of the Place Where the Wind Does Not Reach. [The Governor] asked, "What is his sleeping quarters? [The Master] replied, "It is the sleeping quarters of 'As Old as the Sky. [The Governor] asked, "What is his lecture hall? [The Master] replied, "It is the lecture hall of 'The Teaching of Not Yet. [The Governor] asked, "What is his dining hall? [The Master] replied, "It is the dining hall of 'The Robe of Unobtainable. [The Governor] asked, "What is his washroom? [The Master] replied, "It is the washroom of 'The Bowl of No Name. [The Governor] asked, "What is his privy? [The Master] replied, "It is the privy of 'The Staff of the Place Where the Wind Does Not Reach. [The Governor] asked, "What is his abbot's quarters? [The Master] replied, "It is the abbot's quarters of 'As Old as the Sky. [The Governor] asked, "What is his main hall? [The Master] replied, "It is the main hall of 'The Teaching of Not Yet. [The Governor] asked, "What is his treasury? [The Master] replied, "It is the treasury of 'The Robe of Unobtainable. [The Governor] asked, "What is his storehouse? [The Master] replied, "It is the storehouse of 'The Bowl of No Name. [The Governor] asked, "What is his gate? [The Master] replied, "It is the gate of 'The Staff of the Place Where the Wind Does Not Reach. [The Governor] asked, "What is his courtyard? [The Master] replied, "It is the courtyard of 'As Old as the Sky. [The Governor] asked, "What is his path? [The Master] replied, "It is the path of 'The Teaching of Not Yet. [The Governor] asked, "What is his bridge? [The Master] replied, "It is the bridge of 'The Robe of Unobtainable. [The Governor] asked, "What is his well? [The Master] replied, "It is the well of 'The Bowl of No Name. [The Governor] asked, "What is his pond? [The Master] replied, "It is the pond of 'The Staff of the Place Where the Wind Does Not Reach. He could succeed him as the abbot of this Taiping Monastery. Fojian then proposed the head seat, Zhenbing.
When Lord Zeng wished to meet him, Fojian said, "As for the man Bing, he is firm, vigorous, upright, and balanced.
He regards worldly affairs with great detachment and takes no pleasure in fame or reputation. Even if one were to invite him, I fear he might not come; how could he ever come of his own accord?"
Lord Ye firmly intended to invite him. Baoming said, "This is what is called a 'manifest-body' monk who seeks fame by self-promotion.
How could I do such a thing? Ultimately, he evaded him and took refuge in Mount Sengkong. Lord Ye looked toward Fojian and praised them both, saying, "There is such a father;
there is such a son. It is not without a father that his son is born; one must know the son to know the father."
Nor was there anyone like his father. Master Zeng Gongru then charged the senior monks of the various mountains to insistently request him.
Although Ming declined, he could not prevail; constrained by necessity, he responded to the summons of Taiping.
Fojian said to Foxun: "A person of lofty character does not take fame or rank as a source of glory;

one who has mastered the principles is not distressed by suppression or humiliation. Those who accept favors to exert their strength or offer their sincerity for the sake of profit are all the behaviors of those inferior to the average man" (Daily Record).

Xun asked about the name Fodeng, which is Shou Xun. He was a successor of Fojian. "Yi" means to suppress grievances. "Cuo" means to crush. "Xiao" means to bring about. "Shu" means to offer sincere words;
it signifies the exhaustion of one's reverence. Fojian said to Fodeng: "One must understand the mind of the eminent person and the man of attainment.
His insight and vision are lofty and far-reaching. He is a man of the highest and greatest ambition who does not regard fame or status as [the ultimate goal]."
Those who are illustrious and renowned, who have thoroughly mastered the ultimate principles, and who are upright and resolute, are not brought to exhaustion by suppression or frustration.
When they encounter kindness, they respond with deference; when they perceive profit, they exert themselves to offer their sincere devotion.
These two types of persons are both the conduct of those of middling or inferior capacity; they are not the conduct of the noble who have attained the ultimate principles.
Buddha-jian said to the head seat, Ming-bing: "In being called an Elder, one must have nothing for which one has a preference.
If there is anything for which one has a preference, one is plundered by external things. To prefer sensual desires gives rise to a heart of greedy attachment; to prefer gain and sustenance..."
Then the impulse for vying and scrambling arises. If you favor compliance and submission, sycophantic flatterers will gather around you.

If you favor victory and defeat, the mountain of "self" and "other" will become high. If you favor plunder and exploitation, the sounds of lamentation and resentment will arise. To investigate these matters in their entirety, they do not depart from the single mind.
If the mind does not give rise [to delusions], the myriad dharmas naturally vanish. Nothing that you have attained throughout your life exceeds this. You should exert yourself accordingly.
*Zhan*: To rectify those who come to study (according to the Nanhua stone inscription).

It means to harm; it means to love and admire; it means to be crooked; it means to flatter and comply with the surface. *Pouke*: To plunder and amass wealth. *Qiangjian*: To exert oneself with effort.
*Zhan*: To approve of or choose. Fojian addressed the Head Seat, Ming: "An Elder should have nothing toward which he feels attachment."
It is said: To be called an "Elder" (sthavira), one must have nothing in the breast that is cherished, being like the great void of space.
Do not allow even a hair’s breadth of cloud or mist to arise. An Elder must also be like this.
If it is not so, and there is even the slightest thing cherished, it will be like a single speck of dust rising to obscure the sky; one is then harmed by external objects. The breast...
The interior will then no longer be pure. There are five such thieves: first, when one gives rise to a mind that relishes sensual desires, one is beset by the thief of greedy attachment;

second, when thoughts arise that favor gain and offerings, one is beset by the thief of competitive striving; third, when one favors compliance and submissiveness, one is beset by the thief of sycophantic flatterers;
fourth, when one favors victory and defeat, one is beset by the thief of the high mountains of self and other; fifth, when one favors... [the text here is incomplete].
Amassing and plundering, they are met with cries of lamentation and resentment. These five thieves encompass these five pleasures;

yet, when one thoroughly investigates these five thieves, they do not lie outside of the single mind. If the mind truly gives rise to not even a single thought, it will be like empty space—stable and secure.
Then, regarding every phenomenon and every dharma in the world, there will be neither right nor wrong; there will be no need for rejection or elimination. And...
It has naturally dissolved away. Among all that I have investigated, studied, and attained throughout my life, nothing surpasses this.
You should practice it with diligent effort; by means of these regulations, you shall rectify those who come after and have not yet studied.
Fojian said, "My late master was frugal; his single alms-bowl bag and shoe-sack had been patched a hundred times and mended a thousand times, yet he could not bear to discard them.
He used to say, 'These two items have accompanied me across the pass for barely fifty years; how could I ever cast them aside midway?
There was a senior monk named Wuzhe from Quannan who sent him a coarse cotton robe, saying it had been obtained from overseas. When worn in winter..."
"Warm. If worn in summer, it is cool. My former teacher said: "For this old monk, when cold there are firewood, charcoal, and paper quilts;
when hot there are pine trees, wind, water, and rocks. For what purpose do I store these? In the end, I reject them" (*Nikkanroku*).
"Frugality" means restraint. "Austerity" means abandoning luxury and following simplicity. A "bag" (nang) is the bag for carrying an alms bowl; a "sack" (dai) is the sack for storing shoes.
"Sewing" (zhuì) refers to patching and mending. "Quannan" refers to Quanzhou Prefecture. The identity of the Venerable Wù is not yet known.
A "coarse cloth robe" (hèbù duò) is a robe made by stitching together cloth woven from the fur of the two mice, the "Ice Mouse" and the "Fire Mouse. [The text ends with] "Buddha."
To instruct people, he taught them to abandon extravagance and follow frugality. Throughout his entire life, our late master’s conduct was never luxurious;
he cherished only simplicity and economy. He had but a single alms-bag and a single shoe-sack, mended with hundreds of threads and stitched together with thousands of needles.
Yet he still cherished them, unable to bear parting with them. He would often say: "These two items have accompanied me."
It has been nearly fifty years since I departed from Kuiguan Pass. How could I possibly abandon my journey halfway, cast it aside midway, and fail to persevere until old age?

There was a Venerable Wuzhuo from Quanzhou who presented me with a *zhiduō* (monastic robe) woven from the fur of two mice—one of ice and one of fire—saying he had obtained it from overseas to signify its distant provenance; when worn during the winter, it provides warmth.
When worn in the summer, it is cool and refreshing, manifesting its extraordinary value. My late teacher said:
"In winter, this old monk has firewood, charcoal, and paper quilts with which to ward off the cold; in summer, he has pine trees, water, wind, and rocks with which to dispel the heat.
What is the use of possessing these? Ultimately, he rejected them and would not accept them. Such was his frugality.
Fojian said: "When my late master heard that Zhenjing had passed away, he prepared a seat and offerings for him and wept with excessive grief. He sighed, saying:

'Such a person is hard to find—one who has seen the very root of the Way and is devoid of branches and leaves. It is a pity he died so young; it is particularly regrettable that I have not yet heard of anyone who can succeed to his Way.
From this point on, the monastic communities of Jiangxi will fall into silence. (From the *Rilü*).
When Fojian mentioned the Fifth Patriarch, he lamented that the Way had no one left to transmit it.

Upon hearing that Zhenjing had entered nirvana, the Master prepared an altar for offerings and wept with such profound grief that his prostrations were excessive. He then sighed, saying: "Zhenjing—such a person as this will be difficult to find again.
His realization of the source of the Way was thorough to its very roots; his preaching of the Dharma was like the trunk of an old tree, yet remained free of branches."
[The Master] Ye lamented that his natural lifespan had not yet reached its end, yet he grieved that he passed away so early.

However, it has not been heard that there was a son who could have depicted his likeness and succeeded him in the Dharma-way. Consequently, the Dharma community of the Jiangxi school has fallen into desolation from this point on; how tragic!
Fojian said: "My late master said that Master Baoyun was throughout his life open and unreserved, without the pretensions of a citadel.

Whenever there was a righteous cause worth pursuing, he would leap forward and take the lead with his own person. He delighted in drawing forth and promoting the worthy and capable, and did not favor sycophancy or fickle alliances."
Secluded on a single mat, he sat upright throughout the entire day. He once said to Attendant Ning, "To preserve the Way and remain content in poverty is the natural lot of a monk.
One who shifts their steadfastness because of success or failure, gain or loss, cannot yet be said to speak of the Way" (Daily Record).
"To clear" means to unblock; it means to penetrate and reach through. "To clear" in this context expresses that there is no stagnation or obstruction within a person's breast.
"To have no citadel or storehouse" means to have no concealment, barriers, or defensive restrictions. "To leap and bound" refers to raising the entire body upward.
This refers to the meaning of courageous and vigorous diligence (*vīrya*). "Xuān" (翛然) means to act with natural spontaneity.
The Buddha-mirror [of the patriarchs] cites the conduct and deportment of the ancestral masters as a teaching for later students. The Five Patriarchs and former teachers say:

"Master Baiyun, throughout his life, was open and unobstructed within his breast; he never practiced self-restraint and possessed no hidden depths or artifice. Observe how he acted when it was appropriate..."
Regarding matters that ought to be done according to principle, he personally applied himself with courageous diligence, leading by example and putting them into practice.

He drew others in with great affection and recommended them for advancement; he promoted the worthy and employed the capable. He took no pleasure in celebrating victory or lamenting defeat, nor in seeking a mere superficial harmony.
He remained as he was on his single mat, sitting alone throughout the day. He once said to the attendant Ning, "I embrace and maintain the Great Way."
To dwell peacefully in poverty is the fundamental allotment of the patch-robed monk; it should be understood as such.

If one is a person without roots—who easily advances and easily retreats, and who alters what they practice according to the vicissitudes of poverty and success or gain and loss—they cannot yet be said to speak of the Way of the Sage.
[Note: *Ní* (pronounced *nǐ*) refers to the ancestral temple of a father.]

The Buddha-jian said: "If one does not worry while practicing the Way, the mind will not be directed toward distant goals. If one dwells in constant ease, the application of one's will will not be great.
The ancients underwent hardships and experienced perils before enjoying lifelong peace; for when matters are difficult, the will becomes sharp, and through austerity, one’s deliberation deepens.
Thus, they were able to transform calamity into fortune and transform worldly things into the Way. I have often seen those who study..."
Such a person pursues external things and forgets the Way; they turn their backs on light and cast themselves into darkness.
Thus, they gloss over their own inadequacies while deceiving others by pretending to possess wisdom; they force others to follow what they cannot reach while insulting them to appear superior.

By means of this, they deceive others, yet remain unaware that there are those with prior awakening who cannot be deceived; by means of this, they conceal themselves, yet remain unaware that there are those whom they cannot conceal.
This is the public consensus. Therefore, those who claim to be wise are treated as fools by others; those who exalt themselves are looked down upon by others.
Only the truly worthy are not like this. They recognize that affairs are dispersed and inexhaustible, while human capacity has limits and is finite.
To desire to encompass inexhaustible affairs with finite wisdom results in a partiality of consciousness and a frustration of the spirit. Thus, regarding the Great Way, there will necessarily be...
[From the "Letter to Xiu Zizhi"]: "Fojian, when instructing others, one must maintain deep integrity and far-reaching foresight;

only then can one transform external things into the Way. If one investigates this Way thoroughly yet refuses to conceal one's inner anxieties, then one’s resolve for self-cultivation will not be broad or far-reaching, and one’s own conduct will remain constantly unsettled."* *Note:

The final phrase "自己處身，常安" (zìjǐ chǔshēn, cháng'ān) appears to be a scribal error or a later interpolation, as it contradicts the preceding critique. A more likely reading based on the context would be "自己處身，常不安" (zìjǐ chǔshēn, cháng bù'ān), meaning "one's own conduct will remain constantly unsettled. However, as the instruction is to translate the provided text, the literal rendering is given above.*
If one is indolent, even the will for active engagement will not be vast or great.
How many hardships did the ancients undergo, and how many perils did they endure, before they were finally able to enjoy a lifetime of ease?
This was not obtained by understanding no dharma or doing nothing at all; rather, it was because they had experienced many difficult matters.
Then one’s aspirations become ever more courageous and sharp; through diligent effort and austerity, one’s contemplation becomes increasingly profound.
Only through such valor and such diligence can one transform calamity into blessing and transform stubborn matter into the wondrous Way.
How could those who do not worry about the Way, or who always keep their persons at ease, ever reach this state? Much indeed!

Observing scholars of recent times, they externally pursue material things while internally failing to maintain the Way; they turn their backs on awakening and illumination to instead unite with worldly defilements.
Consequently, they constantly cultivate their own inadequacies to deceive the ignorant, regarding themselves as wise and striving to outshine others.
Thinking that others have not reached their level, they treat them with contempt and arrogance, considering themselves superior.
Little do they realize that all people possess a spiritual essence that cannot be deceived;
yet, by using this to deceive others, they fail to recognize the enlightened ones who cannot be deceived. All people possess eyes that cannot be obscured;
yet, by using this to obscure others, they fail to recognize the public consensus which cannot be obscured. To hold such views is nothing but the fault of one’s own ignorance.
Because fools deceive themselves in this way, how could they possibly deceive others? Therefore, those who possess self-knowledge are treated with disrespect and regarded as fools by others;
those who are self-exalting are met with lack of reverence and are brought low.
Only those who possess virtue are never like this. For all things in the world are diverse and infinite; as for human beings—

Intelligence has boundaries and is limited in measure. To attempt to encompass all-pervasive matters that have no limits or surface with such limited intelligence results in a partiality and deficiency in perception and cognition, and a state of exhaustion and fatigue within the spiritual consciousness.
Therefore, regarding the unsurpassed Great Way, there will inevitably be aspects that are not fully perfected.
(The character *bèi* is pronounced *bài*. Master Fajian said to Dharma Master Longya Cai: "If one wishes to reform the failings of predecessors, one must not attempt to remove them too abruptly.
One must reform by means of specific circumstances so that commoners do not become suspicious; in this way, there will likely be no resentment. I have often spoken of the duties of an abbot.
There are three essential points: discerning the matter, being able to act upon it, and exercising resolute judgment. If any one of these three is lacking, then one's discernment will be unclear;
ultimately, one will become a petty person characterized by negligence and arrogance, and the leadership of the monastery will fail to flourish.

Longya’s name was Zhicai. He was a successor of Fojian Qinqing; "ge" (革) means to reform, and "gai" (改) means to change. "Shu" (庶) means to hope for proximity, and "jueyao" (訣要) refers to essential methods.
"Que" (缺) means to lack, and "ka" (乏) means to have little. Fojian told Longya: "When appearing in the world, you should take the Three Essentials as your primary teaching.
When presiding over a monastic community (*senglin*), if you wish to reform and eliminate the improper ailments of those who came before, you must not act with haste."
One must immediately change it; however, one must rely on a skillful means, borrowing some pretext or circumstance to effect the change so that the common folk do not give rise to doubt or confusion.
In this way, they will harbor no feelings of resentment nearby. I have often said: for one who acts as the master of a monastic community (chónglín),...
There are three methods. First, regarding the perception of all phenomena: it is like the bright sun in the sky, vast and complete, leaving nothing minute or subtle unperceived.
Second, regarding what should be practiced: it is like a great elephant crossing a river, cutting through the current and proceeding straight ahead.
Third, regarding the discernment of right and wrong: it is like a clear mirror set upon its stand, wherein beauty and ugliness appear naturally.

These three methods cause others to be convinced and submit. If even one of these methods is lacking, then affairs will not be clearly understood, and ultimately one will be treated with contempt and disdain by petty people; thus, the way of the abbot cannot be revitalized.
"Are these three dharmas not essential?

The Buddha observed and said: 'In general, for one who serves as the master of a monastery, what is most precious is pure conduct. One must maintain great integrity to welcome monastics from the four quarters.
If there is even the slightest trace of vulgar or impure matters that has not been removed from oneself, one will consequently be taken advantage of by petty people.'"
To "peek" (kuī) and "spy" (chù): even if one possesses the virtue and realization of the ancients, students will remain suspicious and lack faith (from *Shantang Xiaocan*).
"Věi" means base and vulgar; "bǐ" means to defile through intimacy; "kuī" means to look with a narrow or petty gaze; "chù" means to watch and observe. Fojian cautioned the abbot, saying:
"You should maintain pure conduct, uphold trustworthiness, and treat others with sincerity. Whenever you act as an elder, you must uphold the Great Dharma."
As the master of a monastery, what is most precious is that you personally exert yourself in practice, keeping body and mind pure.
You must respond appropriately to others and maintain trustworthiness so that practitioners from the four quarters have a standard by which to emulate you.
If, as the leader, you commit even the slightest act of vulgarity or disrespect, you will fail to remain pure within yourself and will instead be corrupted by petty people.
In the depths of the earth, one peers in from the side and sees it shattered.

Even if there were masters like Linji or Deshan in terms of the Way, or Xuanzang, Vinaya Masters, or Xianshou in terms of virtue, students would still harbor doubts and refuse to believe with deep conviction. (The characters for "vòu xiè" [猥媟] are pronounced wěi xiè.)
Therefore, as an abbot and elder, one must value the cultivation of one's conduct. Fojian said:
"Among the disciples of Foyan, only Ga’nan was upright and resolute, refusing to accommodate worldly sentiments. He had no personal indulgences and acted without seeking partisan support.
Pure, austere, reverent, and cautious, he established himself through integrity and reputation from beginning to end; he was a man of antiquity."
This is his style. Among the monks of recent times, few can compare to him. "Jingjian" (勁健) means vigorous and robust;
"zhengzhi" (挺直) means upright and straight—it refers to the sense of being frank and outspoken. "Yi jingtíng" (宜徑庭) is taken as a description of being distant and remote.
Zhuangzi’s words are profoundly unconventional. "Fang" (方) connects with the following phrase; it means "faction" or "party," and by extension, "to cite" or "to invoke.
This refers to the letter from Master Fojian to State Councilor Geng Longxue, which describes how Gaoshan was upright and possessed integrity, thereby inspiring later students.

Among the dharma heirs of Foyan, only Gaoshan was truly enlightened and straightforward; he would not curry favor with others or comply with their whims for the sake of human relations. As a person, he was... [text ends]
Free from craving, he supported himself alone; in his conduct, he did not form cliques or seek mutual recommendation.
Thus, he was pure through non-attachment, dignified through distance, upright yet respectful, and cautious without partisanship.

From the time he first became a Zen monk until his engagement with the world, he maintained a single flavor throughout his life, establishing himself through the integrity of his reputation and principles.
Truly, there is the spirit of the ancient sages and worthies. Among the monks of recent times, there are many;
yet if one were to compare them with their kind, few could equal him.

Master Foyuan said: "The demeanor when presiding over the assembly must be more solemn than on days of leisure; the speech when addressing guests must be more dignified than during moments of intimacy.
When one who dwells beneath the forest trees speaks, acts, or undertakes any measure, they must first deliberate thoroughly before putting it into practice.
Do not act with haste or recklessness, and if you are unable to reach a decision yourself, you ought to..."

Consult the elders and inquire widely of the former sages to broaden your见闻 (knowledge and experience), thereby supplementing what you have not yet mastered and illuminating what you do not yet understand.
How can you vainly display your prestige and solely indulge in arrogance, thereby manifesting your own ugliness?
If one single action fails at the outset, then a hundred subsequent virtues will not be able to conceal it. (From a Letter to Zhenmu)

"Attending" (*lì*) means to be present. "Solemnity" (*sù*) means to be composed and restrained. "Dignity" (*yán*) refers to gravity and majesty. "Intimacy" (*sīnì*) refers to the time of private and secluded dwelling.

"Violence" (*bào*) means ferocity. "Deliberation" (*chóu*) means calculation. "Candlelight" (*zhú*) means illumination. In the *Letter from the Buddha-Eye to the Worthy and True Herdsman*, it is said:

"When attending to the assembly, one must be cautious at every moment and every instant. Regarding the deportment when facing the assembly, it is entirely dependent on the state one maintains even when not yet facing the assembly.
Prior to this, there is no fixed time or occasion; one should practice withdrawal at all times. Even when responding to guests, it must be done before the guest has arrived.
During moments of solitude, one must maintain self-respect at every instant. Generally speaking, for those who dwell in the forest, this is the single word they proclaim.
Regarding the execution of any single matter—whether it be an action, a measure, a provision, or a deed—one must ultimately calculate and settle it beforehand.
Only after one has reflected clearly and understood the situation should one proceed; one must not act with haste or recklessness, thereby losing one's own beneficial advantage.
Alternatively, if one’s own talent is insufficient and one’s learning shallow, such that one cannot reach a decision on one’s own, one should... [not act].

One should not feel shame in asking questions of those below oneself. Instead, one should consult those of long-standing virtue and extensively seek counsel from senior practitioners, so as to broaden what I have not yet seen and verify what I have not yet heard.

This shall supplement my weakness and cowardice and illuminate my ignorance with the light of wisdom. How could I possibly act like one who hangs up a goat to sell dog meat, or like a fox borrowing a tiger’s prestige?
It would be improper to falsely project an air of authority, merely flaunting the banners of arrogance and the parasol of conceit.
One thus reveals one's own ugliness. If a single matter is handled wrongly, the foundation of what preceded it is lost;
even if one attempts to embellish it with a hundred virtuous deeds, it cannot be concealed or covered up afterward. This is true for those who preside over a community.
"Is this not something to be deeply cautious about?
Foyan said: 'When human beings are born between heaven and earth, they receive the qi of yin and yang to form their physical bodies.
Unless one is a true sage who appears in the world through the power of compassionate vows, it seems impossible to suddenly eliminate the mind of profit and desire; only a saint can do so.'"
People know that one cannot eliminate others' desires for profit and pleasure; therefore, one first rectifies their minds through the Way and its Virtue (*Dao-de*).

Only then does one use benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and wisdom to instruct and establish defensive barriers against them. Through this gradual progress day by day and month by month, one ensures that their desires for profit and pleasure do not overcome their benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and wisdom, thereby preserving their integrity of the Way and its Virtue.
A letter from Foyan to Geng Longxue. He spoke of how profit and desire are difficult to guard against, and said that one must rectify the mind through the Way and its Virtue (*dào-dé*).
Human life is established within the realm of heaven and earth (*qiān-kūn*); having received the blended and pervasive breath of Yin and Yang, these four limbs and hundred bones were formed.
If this physical form were not for the sake of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who ride upon the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*)...
With a compassionate heart, he gave rise to the Four Great Vows and practiced the vast Ten Powers, appearing in the human world.
His mind of greed for profit, craving desire, hatred, and delusion seemed as if it could not be quickly removed.
Only the Sage, who is unimpeded in all things, knew that these cravings for profit and desire were difficult to eliminate; therefore, he established various skillful means to open [the way].
First, one may rectify the mind through the Way, or cultivate the person through virtue.

Thereafter, through benevolence characterized by compassion, righteousness that accords with principle, ritual that provides refinement and pattern, or wisdom that involves discernment, one guides others well and gradually, teaching them in successive stages and providing them with protection. Thus they achieve accomplishment day by day and month by month.
It assists the generals so that the three poisons and sharp desires accumulated over immeasurable kalpas cannot surpass the four beginnings— benevolence, righteousness,
propriety, and wisdom— which fully embody the two methods of the Way and its Virtue that opened the way in the past.
Foyan said: "A student must not become mired in words and language. For words and language are based on others' interpretations;
they obstruct the gate of self-awakening and prevent one from transcending the realm of speech and symbols.
In the past, Daguan Ying initially saw Master Shimen Cong in his room and displayed his verbal eloquence and dialectical skill. Cong said: 'What you have spoken is merely paper.'"
The Master said: "As for the subtle and profound essence of the mind, one has not yet beheld its depths; one must seek wondrous awakening.
Once awakened, one stands preeminent and transcendent, neither riding upon words nor lingering in phrases. It is like the roar of the lion king, at which all beasts are struck with terror.
When compared to the study of mere texts, this is more than ten to one, or even a thousand to ten thousand. (Recorded in *Ryūkan Kikwan*)
Daguan, whose name was Tanying, was the successor of Shimen Yuncong, who in turn was the successor of Shoushan Niangu.
Foyan instructed people: "You must truly awaken to your own mind; do not rely on others for explanations.
Students should strike at their own selves in inquiry; you must not be mired in historical texts, words, or speech, nor rely upon others."
To take what is known innately and form intellectual interpretations of it creates an obstacle to the gateway of one’s own awakening;
one cannot thereby sever the tangles of conceptualization or transcend the realm of words, phrases, and mental images.

Long ago, when Daguan Ying first met Shimeng Yuncong, as he entered the room, he galloped about with sharp wit, flapping his lips and wagging his tongue, speaking at will with forceful sophistry. Yuncong said:
What you have spoken does not flow from your own breast; it is merely the language upon paper.
As for the profound and subtle depths of the mind-dharma (*cittadharma*), you have not yet personally and clearly realized them, nor have you penetrated their mysterious mysteries.
You ought to seek direct great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). If one is truly a person of authentic great enlightenment, they will transcend and be heroic.
Magnificent! He stands out in solitary excellence. He does not rely on words, yet his expression is unimpeded; he does not linger in phrases, yet his meaning is unimpeded.
Having reached this stage, he is free in both speech and silence. It is better not to open one’s mouth at all;
but if one does open it, it is like the roar of a lion king—a single cry that splits the skulls of the hundred beasts, such that none fail to tremble with awe and alarm.
Even after awakening, one’s majestic authority remains just as it was. When one turns back to examine that study of words and letters, how could it possibly compare—how could it even approach it?
It is not merely a matter of ten to a hundred or a thousand to ten thousand; how could it ever reach it?
Foyan said to Gao’an: “The *Baizhang Qinggui* is, in its general outline, intended to distinguish the correct from the deviant and to provide a model for regulating things and unifying the assembly.

It establishes regulations according to the times to accommodate the dispositions of later generations. Now, human dispositions are like water; rules, measures, and ritual laws serve as the embankments.
If the embankments are not firm, flooding and breaches will inevitably occur. If human dispositions are not restrained, they will run wild and lead to disorder. Therefore—”
One must eliminate passions and cease delusions, restraining evil and halting deviance; one cannot for a moment dispense with rules and standards.

Thus, while rules and ritual laws can never fully restrain the human heart, they nonetheless serve as the steps leading toward the Way. The establishment of these rules is as manifest as the sun and moon;
those who look up to them will not lose their way. They are as expansive as the Great Way; those who walk within them will not falter.
Delusion! Although the institutions established by the former sages differ, they are no different in their ultimate source.

In recent monastic communities, there are those who labor to establish rules, those who cling dogmatically to rules, and those who hold rules in contempt. All of these turn their backs on the Way and lose propriety;

it is because they indulge their passions and pursue evil that this has come to pass. They never consider that the former sages established these prohibitions to remedy the defects of the Dharma-ending age and to restrain negligence.

Sentiment. To block the source of lustful desires and sever the path of depravity; this is why it is established (*Donghu ji*). *Gui* (軌) means law. *Xun* (循) means to follow. *Qi* (齊) means to rectify.
*Zheng* (正) means to regulate. *Yu* (御) means to govern. *Benji* (奔急) means rushing and changing. *Tong* (突) means to collide.

*Kuo* (擴) conveys the sense of expanding and promoting. *Mie* (蔑) means to slight. *Shu* (殊) means extraordinary. *Yi* (異) means different. *Zhi* (致) means to cause to reach. *Fo yan* (佛眼) means the Buddha-eye.
This refers to Gaoan. One should know that rules, regulations, and ritual propriety are taught to guard against the emotions and remedy abuses.
The *Qinggui* (Pure Rules) composed by Baizhang is, for the most part, intended to manifest right mindfulness in gentlemen and to restrain the deviant minds of petty men.
By acceding to the nature of things, it rectifies the great assembly; thus, it is employed according to the times to regulate the mental consciousnesses of later generations.
Furthermore, the nature of human beings is like the nature of water. Water uses earth and stone to form embankments for its defense;
humans rely on rules, rituals, propriety, and laws as their embankments for defense.
If these embankments of earth and stone are not firm, they will inevitably cause the skin’s pores to become loose, leading to sudden surges and breaches. Such is the nature of human beings.
If one does not restrain oneself with ritual propriety and law, one will become licentious and suddenly give rise to disorder. Human emotion and the nature of water are surely no different;

therefore, when one wishes to eliminate emotional consciousness and cease deluded thoughts, and to prohibit evil conduct and halt deviant intentions, one must never for a single moment or instant neglect these rules and regulations.
Yet how could rules and regulations, as well as ritual propriety and law, ever be sufficient to contain [the mind] entirely? They can only serve as a dyke.
It serves as a defense; it accords with the emotional consciousness of human beings.

These rites and laws can also assist people in ascending the stages toward the Way, allowing them to reach the vermilion steps and enter the gate. The establishment of these rules and measures is perfectly clear.
It is like the sun and moon adorning the heavens; all who possess eyes will lift their heads to see them without fail and will not be deluded by them—how vast they are!
Again, it is like a great highway with four branches; all who possess feet will trustfully walk upon it without being confused.
Although the gateways established by the ancient sages differ from one another, they all converge back to the same source, leaving no room for doubt.
Second, regarding principle: In the monastic communities of recent times, there are those who focus exclusively on ritual practice while rigidly adhering to formal regulations;
those who, despite being rebuked and corrected, stubbornly cling to these regulations; and those who show no respect for rites and laws, treating the regulations with contempt.
Such views as these all contradict the correct principle, result in the loss of established systems, and lead to unrestrained license.
Sentient consciousness follows and pursues evil demons, causing them to act in such a manner.

It has never occurred to them to contemplate the Great Wisdom Master’s salvation of the maladies of the Final Dharma—restraining the sentient consciousness of those who are heedless, blocking the very beginnings of sensual desire, and cutting off the paths of deviance and heterodoxy; for this reason, he has established this [teaching].
Foyan said to Gao’an: “One who can see the tip of an autumn hair cannot see his own eyelashes;
one who can lift a weight of a thousand *qun* cannot lift his own body. This is like a student who is clear-sighted when criticizing others but dim-sighted when exercising self-compassion.”
"Not a little different" (from the *Zhēnmù jí*).
"Cilia" refers to the eyebrows. "A *jūn*" is thirty *jīn*. Foyan addressed Gao'an, saying: "One should hold oneself to the standard of blame and extend forgiveness to others.
There are those in the world with eyes who are extremely clear-sighted, able to see even the finest details down to a single autumn hair; yet [they...]

They do not see the eyebrows on their own faces. In this world, there are those with great strength who are most powerful and capable of lifting a weight of a thousand *jin*, yet they cannot lift their own bodies.
Tell me, how are these two types of people alike? It is just like those scholars who devote themselves exclusively to scrutinizing the faults of others, while regarding themselves—
Those who are ignorant of extending forgiveness to themselves are no different from this.

Master Wugao An said: "When I first traveled to the ancestral mountains, I witnessed Master Fojian’s small-scale sermon (xiaocan), in which he stated that greed, desire, anger, and hatred are as harmful as vengeful enemies and must be countered with wisdom. Wisdom is like water; if it is not used, it stagnates, and if it stagnates..."
He did not flow [into worldly attachments]. When one does not flow, wisdom does not function.

As for what of greed, desire, hatred, and anger—though I was young at that time, I knew in my heart that he was a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). I then requested to be enrolled as a resident monk (according to the *Yunju Shilu*).
Gaofeng showed this to others, saying it should be explained with the eye of discernment (*dharmapravicaya*).
When I first set out on my travels to Mount Zu (Nanyue), I met the Venerable Fojian Qin, who said in a small assembly: "People's minds dwell underground;
greed and anger—these two kinds of poison—are as harmful as enemies or bandits. Once everyone has recognized these poisons, they should employ wisdom."
To resist them—what is this but wisdom? It is like water: if it is not set in motion, it will surely become stagnant;
once stagnant, it will certainly not flow. Since it does not flow, one knows that the water is not circulating.
What can be done about the two poisons of greed and hatred? At that time, my age was still...
Zhuang said, "My heart is settled; I now know that Master Jian is a true *kalyāṇamitra*. He then requested to be enrolled as a resident monk and took him as his teacher.
Gao'an said, "If a student maintains a mind of central rectitude, even if they undergo a hundred setbacks, they will remain vast and free from anxiety. However, if..."
Your inclinations are biased and deviant; from dawn until dusk, you are preoccupied with schemes for profit and gain.
I fear that this magnificent body of yours will find no place within heaven and earth (from the *Jinmujip*).
"Qiao Xiao's Appearance" expresses the sense that one's insight and understanding are not extensive. "Gao'an’s Instruction on Maintaining the Mind in the Center" states:
"What the student harbors within their breast should be centered and not biased; it should be upright and not deviant."
Even when calamities, harms, disgrace, and all manner of misfortunes arrive, and one is subjected to a hundredfold setbacks and humiliations,
such a person remains vast and expansive, entirely free from anxiety or fear. Should their aspirations happen to be biased and off-center, crooked and improper,

or if they spend their days and nights in trivial pursuits with narrow views and limited understanding— constantly preoccupied with personal gain and utterly lacking in grand strategy— I fear this kind of person [will fail].
A person with such a magnificent and beautiful physique will find no place of rest within heaven and earth.
Gao-an said: "Virtue, Way, benevolence, and righteousness are not possessed by the ancients alone; modern people possess them as well.

It is because their wisdom and understanding are not clear, their learning is not broad, their spiritual capacity is impure, their will and spirit are narrow and inferior, and they do not practice with vigor."

Consequently, one is moved by sounds and forms, rendered unconscious of this process. This is because deluded thoughts and emotional attachments have accumulated through long habituation and cannot be suddenly eliminated;
for this reason, one fails to reach the level of the ancients.
Gao’an’s Letter to Lord Geng: In instructing others, one should maintain great resolve and practice this Way with vigor.

Do not be moved by the allure of sound and color. The Way of rectifying one's character, the virtue of humility, the benevolence of compassion, and the righteousness of conforming to principle—these were possessed not only by the ancients, but by people of the present day as well, through the wisdom that serves as their guide.
The transmigrating consciousness is chaotic and indistinct. Its study is confined to external scriptures; its inquiries are not directed toward the Way.
It is narrow rather than expansive, and the faculties lack a foundation. The physical vessel loses its integrity, becoming defiled and impure.
One’s aspirations are cramped, one’s constitution is weak, and one’s conduct lacks diligence. With an unstable mastery, one is consequently overcome by...
One is carried away by the various sensory objects of sound and form, yet remains unaware of it oneself.

This is because of the dense forest of delusive thoughts, the wilderness of emotional attachments, and the accumulation of heavy habitual tendencies; these are as deep as the ocean and as vast as the earth, and cannot be abandoned all at once.
For this reason, one does not reach the sublime stages of the Ten Sages and Three Worthies.
When Gao’an heard that Cheng Kumu was residing at Jinshan and indulging in luxury and extravagance, he sighed for a long time and said:

"The dharma of a bhikṣu prizes purity and frugality. How could it be appropriate to act like this? It merely causes those among the younger generation who are accustomed to light food and fine clothing to increase their insatiable desires. Are they not ashamed of the ancients?"
Cheng Kumu (成枯木), whose name was Facheng (法成), was a successor of Furong Kai (芙蓉楷). "Chi" (侈) means extravagance;
"mi" (靡) refers to a state of decadent luxury. "Qingfei" (輕肥) conveys the sense of wearing light furs and riding fat horses.
The Record notes that when Ga’ān (高菴) heard that Cheng Kumu was residing at Jinshan Temple in Runzhou, his daily enjoyments and expenditures were magnificent and abundant, he sighed in lamentation.
Having done so, he said: "The dharma of a bhikṣu values abiding peacefully in pure poverty and maintaining frugal expenditure.

How could one act like this? To needlessly set a precedent for later generations and those who have recently entered the path, teaching them to practice riding in light furs and on fat horses, thereby increasing insatiable greed—what face do you have? To construct [such a life] would not befit the ancestors."
As for the lineage: having been listed in the *Dengpu* (Lamp Records), can one not feel shame?

Gao’an said: "The fundamental principle of a *zhuchi* (abbot) is to regard the monastic community as his home; he must distinguish [his disciples] appropriately and entrust [the Dharma] to those who are worthy vessels."
One's conduct is the principle by which safety and peril are determined; success or failure is the source of transformation and instruction. As a model for others, how can one be casual?

It has never been seen that a *zhuchi* (abbot) could cause his disciples to submit while remaining lax and unrestrained, nor that he could forbid arrogance within the monastic community while the laws and regulations were in decline.
In the past, Yuyang Shen dispatched his head seat, and Yangshan Wei demoted his attendant monk. These matters are recorded [in the histories].

Regarding the classical texts, they were sufficient to serve as models; yet now, everyone pursues their own private desires, causing the regulations and rules established by Baizhang to fall into great ruin.

They are negligent in rising early, and many fail to observe the ritual laws of communal assembly. Some indulge in greed and gluttony without restraint, while others provoke clamorous strife for the sake of gain and offerings.
As for sycophancy and depravity, there is nothing that does not exist among them. Alas! How can one look toward the Dharma-gate?
How could the flourishing of this [teaching] and the prosperity of its religious tradition be far off? (From the *Longchang ji*; "shen" is pronounced "chen").

"Qu-fen" means to distinguish; "fan-fang" means to provide a model and restraint; "mo" means a standard; "gui-ju" means a rule. "Chi" means to neglect or abolish; "zong-fang" means to let loose or abandon.
*Línglí* means to wither and decay. Master Yùchén was styled Jiàchén and titled Wúshì. He was by nature firm and resolute;

his conduct toward the assembly conformed to ancient standards, earning him the reputation of being "Chén with the Iron Face. He was the successor of Zhǎozhǎng Zǎozhuó. Master Āngyán was styled Xíngwěi.

By nature he was stern. When facing affairs, he followed established methods. He was the successor of Huanglong Nan. Regarding the matter of dispatching the Head Seat, both the phonetic glosses and the annotated meanings are contained therein.
As for the dismissal of the attendant monk at Yangshan, it is unknown for what reason; both accounts remain undetailed. "Huīhuǐ" means to ruin or destroy. "Sùxīng" means to rise early in the morning.
"Cānhuì" refers to the evening small discourse (xiǎocān) held during the assembly. To say that one seeks yet finds nothing sufficient is called...
Greed. To crave insatiably is called *tāo* (greed). Gao’an instructs those who serve as abbots: you must prioritize the monastic laws and regulations;
treat these matters with the gravity of a great undertaking. A *conglin* (monastic community) is the ancestral legacy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
In planning and organizing it, you must ensure that everything accords with principle and is handled with precision and propriety. This requires one of truly great capacity to manage its affairs.

In managing affairs, what is good brings peace; what is not good brings peril. What is at stake here is truly great. One must understand this principle: to attain it leads to prosperity; to lose it leads to ruin.
It concerns the transformation of people through education. One must recognize its fundamental source. Since you have become a teacher of men, you must grasp this.

The scale of such precautions cannot be treated as a mere incidental matter. One has never seen a leader who, while being lax, negligent, and indolent, was able to cause the great assembly to submit with joy and obedience.
When rules and regulations have fallen into decay, one cannot expect to restrain the arrogance and insolence of the monastic community.
In the past, King Śātavāhana sent forth his head seat (śrāmaṇera), and Yaoshan Wei did the same.
The demotion of the attendant monk is recorded in detail within the scriptures and literary records; this serves as a model for the Dharma-gate. Is it not indeed praiseworthy?
Those who preside over the Dharma today are not so; each follows their own private sentiments and accords with the desires of others.
They utterly ruin the ritual laws of Baizhang, being indolent and fond of sleep, refusing to rise early. Superiors and subordinates alike seek only a stolen peace; those below do not...
They diligently attend assemblies for consultation and deliberation. Yet those in superior positions do not maintain ritual propriety, textual precedents, or legal standards;
some are licentious, greedy, and depraved, addicted to drink and devoid of shame; others pursue wealth and profit for their own sustenance, giving rise to the notions of "self" and "other.
As for flattery, depravity, impurity, and evil conduct—there is nothing they do not possess. Alas! To look upon the gateway of the Dharma and the Path!
The flourishing of the school at Mount Nanyue through the teachings of its patriarchs, or the prosperity of the tradition in Jiangxi—such things are certainly not to be obtained by chance.
As for the ritual laws of the presiding master, how could they be treated with contempt and left unpracticed? (Note: The character *wěi* [韙] is pronounced *wěi*.)

Whenever Gao’an was at Yunju and encountered a monk in his quarters whose mind was not in accord with his own, he would immediately seize him by the sleeve and, with a stern expression, rebuke him, saying:
"Your parents raised your body; your teachers and friends have cultivated your aspirations. You are not pressed by hunger or cold."

"There is no labor of conscription or corvée service here. If you do not resolutely and vigorously accomplish the work of the Path at this time, what face will you have when you see your parents, teachers, and friends on another day? When the monastics heard these words, some wept incessantly.
Such was the strictness and order of his commands (from the *Qian'an Yishi*).
"Mani" refers to the sleeve. "Zheng" refers to military conscription; "yi" refers to corvée labor for commoners.

It is recorded that when Gao'an was serving as the abbot of Yunju, whenever he saw a Zen practitioner enter his room and their dialogue failed to reach accord, he would immediately seize the person by the sleeve with his hand.
Bestowing the Samādhi of Vigorous Agility, he employs both gentle and stern speech to subdue and gather them, saying: "Your parents raised this body of yours;
your enlightened teacher and virtuous friends have fulfilled your aspirations. Within, you are free from the oppression of hunger and cold;
without, you are free from the toil of military service and corvée labor. Having reached this point, do not stand idly."
With firm resolve, arouse a mind of diligence and establish yourself in the practice of the Way.
Otherwise, when you return home one day, what face will you have to show your parents, as well as your teachers and friends?
When the monks in the assembly heard such an exhortation, some were moved to the core of their hearts and wept and wailed without ceasing; this was Gao’an.
Issuing proclamations and disseminating orders, he was both orderly and meticulous, yet capable of moving others to tears. It was thus:
when Gaofeng resided at Yunju, hearing that a monk had fallen ill and been moved to the Yanshou Hall, he sighed with deep lamentation as if it were his own affair.
He inquired after him morning and evening, even going so far as to personally prepare his food; he would not eat until he had tasted what the monk had consumed. This continued whenever the weather...

If it is slightly cold, he pats the person’s back and asks, “Are you not wearing too few layers? If they encounter the heat of summer, he observes their complexion and asks, “Are you not suffering from excessive heat?
If someone dies unexpectedly and cannot be saved, he does not inquire whether the deceased has any property; rather, the monastery funds are used to provide full funeral rites and escort the remains.

If an administrator attempts to offer excuses, Gao’an rebukes him, saying, “In the past, Baizhang established the monastery funds for the sake of the elderly and the infirm. You [do not act accordingly].”
He did not die of his illness. Scholars from the four directions held him in high esteem as a man.
When he retired to Yunju and later passed through Tiantai, there were barely fifty disciples who followed him; some who were unable to go with him wept as they parted.
Such was the way his virtue moved people (from the *Sandang Xiaocan*).
The Yanshou Hall is a place for comforting the elderly and the sick. Its height signifies the reverence [due to them] and expresses the intention of honoring their excellence.
When Chan Master Ga’ān was abbot at Yunju, he heard that a monk was ill;
he moved his bedding into the Yanshou Hall to nurse him, weeping and lamenting with great emotion as if it were his own illness.

At dawn and at dusk, he went in person to inquire after his health. He even prepared medicines and cooked porridge with his own hands for his close relatives, never tasting them himself to check their temperature, lest they be too cold or hot and fail to meet the patient's wishes.
He would not share his own food with others, fearing it might not satisfy the patient’s preferences.
When it was midwinter and the weather was bitterly cold, he would stroke the patient’s back and ask, "Is your clothing not too thin? Or when it was...
When the weather was hot and people suffered from heatstroke, he would observe the faces of the sick and ask, "Is your body not too feverish?
He was thus diligent in tending to the ill. Should a death occur unexpectedly and it be difficult to provide medical treatment, he would not inquire whether the deceased had clothing or bedding;
regardless of their presence or absence, he would perform the full rites of cremation according to the monastery’s resources, rich or meager, to escort the soul on its way.
There was one who, knowing that the monastery’s permanent assets were being protected and cherished, firmly declined to contribute toward the expenses. Gao’an then rebuked him, saying:
"In the past, Master Dazhi specifically established this permanent property for those who are old and have nowhere to turn, or who are sick and have no one to rely upon.

If it is not used for this purpose, for what else is it intended? Have you attained a vajra-body so that you do not suffer from illness? Have you mastered the arts of longevity so that you do not die?"
