Indeed, those throughout the various regions who possessed insight all praised Gao’an’s character as being most excellent.
When he retired from the monastery and traveled to Tiantai, the monastic disciples were so reluctant to part that fifty of them followed him there.
Among them were some whose physical constitutions were frail and whose legs were too weak to keep pace; these could not follow along, and they all lamented with tears.
They parted with tears; such was the depth of his benevolence and virtue that he moved and won over others in this way.
When Gao’an retired from Yunju, Yuanwu wished to restore Fo-yin’s Wolong Hermitage as a place for him to rest in retirement.
Gao’an said, "For one who dwells among the groves, if there is the joy of the Way and righteousness, the physical form may be cast aside. As for me, I follow my heart's inclination."
"Like the morning moon at Changgeng, how long can its light and shadow endure? Moreover, the forests and springs of Mount Lu in the western mountains are all places where I may retire in my old age.
Why must one possess these things personally before they can be enjoyed?
Not long after, he took up his staff and traveled to Tiantai, where he eventually passed away on Huading Peak (from the *Zhenmu ji*).
Gao’an retired from Yunju Monastery, and Zen Master Yuanwu Qin succeeded him. Yuanwu wished to repair Wolong Hermitage, which had been built by Foyin, to establish a place for leisurely rest.
Gao’an declined this, saying: "For one who dwells beneath the forest trees, if they possess virtue, moral integrity, and righteousness, they can find sufficient joy.
Yet, the physical form inevitably ends in decay; it must certainly [be understood as such]."
If even these are being consumed by fire, what need be said of Sleeping Dragon?

At this age of seventy, as my heart follows its natural course, it is like the rising of the sun at dawn, with the long-tailed Venus (Chang-geng) vanishing and the morning moon no longer appearing. My shadow and light are likewise;
how could they endure for long? Furthermore, the mountain hermitages of West Mountain and Mount Lu, along with all their forests, springs, and wells, are all [in harmony].
"Even these places where I have looked forward to visiting are all grounds upon which I may rest, enjoy myself, and grow old in leisure.

Why must I insist that they be definitively 'mine' before I can find peace and happiness? After some time, he took up his staff and traveled to Mount Tiantai, eventually passing away on the summit of Huading Peak.
His influence spread throughout the Way, and his conduct regarding his entry into and departure from the world was exemplary.
This can well be imagined.
Gao’an said: "Among the monastics, there is no distinction between the worthy and the foolish; it depends entirely upon the *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend).

One must guide them with tact to exalt their virtue and deeds, test them through experience to bring forth their capacity and talent, honor them with commendation to give weight to their words, and show them generous affection to preserve their integrity. Year after year...

As the months accumulated, both his reputation and his actual accomplishments flourished. Indeed, all people possess the spirit of enlightenment; it is only through diligent guidance that they are brought forth.

Like jade within its ore: if cast aside, it is but a mere brick or stone; yet if polished and refined, it becomes a *gui* or *zhang* vessel. Like water at its source: if obstructed, it becomes mud; yet if dredged and cleared, it becomes a river or marsh.
Thus we know that in this age of the Dharma’s semblance (*xiangji*), it is not merely that the worthy are neglected and left unused; rather, regarding their cultivation—
The way of nurturing, encouraging, and rewarding has also not yet reached its full potential.

During times when monastic groves were flourishing, those who were considered discarded timber in an age of decline became the pillars of the community when that era rose. Thus it is said: "All people possess the spiritual essence;

it is only through diligent guidance that they are brought forth. We know from this that the talents of scholars rise and fall with the times: if they are cherished, they arrive; if they are rewarded, they are exalted.
If it is suppressed, it declines; if it is cast aside, it is severed. This is how the moral character, virtue, and talent of scholars wax and wane.
(Yē is pronounced ě; jùn is pronounced jùn.)
"Jingbiao" (旌表) means to honor and encourage. "You" (優) means harmonious and gentle; it conveys a sense of magnanimity. "Zhuomo" (琢磨) refers to the treatment of jade:
once it has been carved, the craftsman further polishes it, making it increasingly refined. "Gui-zhang" (圭璋): the *gui* is round at the top and square at the bottom, made of auspicious jade;
the *zhang* is half a *gui*, held by the high officials and ministers. "E" (閼) means to obstruct or restrain. "Jun" (濬) means deep.

"Zhi" means "to approach. "Yin" means "great. In a letter from Gao'an to the Provincial Transport Commissioner Li, he states that regarding the saying that "patch-robed monks have no distinction between the worthy and the foolish, as it depends on the patriarchal master to guide them," there are no fixed categories of who is worthy and who is foolish among patch-robed monks; this depends solely upon the one who presides over the Dharma.
Accomplish things through indirect and subtle means, honoring and respecting them so that they may advance in virtue and cultivate their studies.

Put them to the test through practical experience and observation to bring out their potential, thereby molding them into excellent vessels of talent. Commend and encourage them to ensure the gravity of their words;
treat them with harmonious kindness and affection to preserve the integrity of their conduct. Year after year, month after month, let these qualities accumulate.

Long has his fragrant reputation and virtuous practice flourished; these two excellences are both abundant. This is due to no other reason than that every person possesses the wisdom, virtue, and marks of a Tathāgata.

It rests solely upon the Master to instruct others without weariness, using diligent effort to guide them, so that they may awaken to and realize it for themselves, reaching the ultimate state. It is like a precious jade still within its rough stone; one must strike it—

If one throws it down, it is truly no different from a tile or a stone; yet if it is chiseled and polished, it becomes a *gui* or *zhang* jade vessel, employed by the Three Dukes and the Nine Ministers.
It is like water flowing from a spring source: if it is obstructed or blocked, it remains no different from muddy silt;
but if it is diverted and deepened, it becomes a great river or marsh, upon which all things and the myriad people depend. Thus it is with all things.
It is thus. How could it be otherwise for human beings? One can thus know that in this age of the Semblance Dharma, it is not only that good people have been lost and cannot be recruited;
even regarding the methods of nurturing, raising, exhorting, and encouraging them, there has been much that falls short of perfection.
During the time when the monastic groves were flourishing and magnificent, these were all instances of the Semblance Age.
Material discarded and left unused during a period of decline would certainly seem foolish; yet when it is brought forth and employed today when the time for prosperity has arrived, it is wise.

This is precisely why it is said that every person possesses the wisdom of the Tathāgata, which exists only in the guidance of a master to reach this very state. Thus we know that the talent of the student—
It is possible; it depends entirely on how the presiding master employs them. If they are employed, one ascends; if not employed, one descends.

If the presiding master loves and cherishes others, people will come from the four quarters of their own accord without being summoned. If he encourages and rewards them, everyone will turn toward the Way and honor it spontaneously.
Is this not ascending in accordance with the times? Conversely, if he suppresses and obstructs them, he will cause their will and strength to decline and cast them out.
To exclude others is to sever their aspirations; is this not descending in accordance with the times?
This is truly the origin of why the virtue, conduct, and talent of a student flourish when employed and diminish when not employed. Those who preside over the Dharma must understand this.
Gaoyuan said: "In the great task of teaching and transforming others, nothing takes precedence over morality, virtue, propriety, and righteousness.
If the abbot honors morality and virtue, then students will esteem respectfulness; if he practices propriety and righteousness, then students will feel shame for greed and competition.

If the abbot displays the arrogance of improper demeanor, then students will fall into the vice of aggression; if the abbot displays the strife of emotional agitation, then students will likewise [fall into discord]."

Regarding the calamities of strife and combat, the ancient sages foresaw them before they occurred. They consequently selected men of wisdom and sagacity to preside over the monastic groves, so that all might look up to them with reverence and be transformed through understanding without being told.
Thus, during the time when the Way of Shitou and Mazu flourished, eminent and heroic figures emerged;

their deportment was gentle and refined, and they were harmonious and solemn. Whether issuing commands or speaking, they would convey their meaning by a mere glance of the eyes or a raising of the eyebrows.
That all these may serve as models for future generations is only to be expected (as stated in the Letter to Sishin).
Shitou’s name was Xiqian; he was the successor of Qingyuan Xingsi. He was harmonious and gentle, solemn and reverent.
To blink one's eyes is a momentary movement. Gao’an Xian was a master of the Dharma who taught that one must be careful regarding the four modes of deportment.
Among the great points of instruction, nothing precedes using morality and virtue to govern the mind, and ritual propriety and righteousness to cultivate the person.
If the abbot respects morality and virtue, then the students will also respect morality and virtue, and their hearts will harbor thoughts of reverence. Thus, the abbot brings about [this state].
If one practices ritual propriety and righteousness, then students will likewise follow these rites and feel personal shame regarding greedy and competitive pursuits.
If the abbot is narrow-minded and lacks decorum, showing arrogance and impoliteness, then the students will lack moral cultivation and suffer from the maladies of insolence and violence.
If the abbot lacks gravity and displays agitation and strife, then the students—

Such people lack propriety and righteousness, yet they engage in the wrongs of attacking, fighting, and litigating. The sages of antiquity possessed the clarity of foresight; they provided for the unmanifested state of affairs.
Consequently, they selected and appointed those who had awakened their minds and were diligent in practice to preside over the monastic communities (*conglin*).

This caused people’s intentions to dissolve upon merely beholding their countenances; without the need for verbal instruction, they underwent transformation of their own accord. Thus, [the masters of] Nanyue, Shitou, Jiangxi...
During the time when Mazu’s great Way and Dharma-transformation were flourishing and widespread, men of heroic talent and noble character arrived in dense ranks and flocked together like herds.
Their majestic bearing and decorum were gentle, compliant, and admirable; they were harmonious and concordant.
With solemnity and restraint, he might utter a single word, issue a single command, cast a single glance, or raise a single eyebrow;
yet each of these could serve as a model and a standard for the cultivation of students in future generations. It was only natural that it should be so.
This is the master of the Dharma who is careful in his deportment; thus he acts as a superior and those below follow his example. (The character for "deer," *jūn*, is pronounced *jūn*.

Gao'an said: "My late teacher once remarked that when traveling on pilgrimage beyond the mountain passes, there are often many disagreeable matters encountered at the smaller monasteries one visits.")
I recall that when Fayen went to study under Dizang, and Mingjiao saw Shending, they no longer perceived the existence of afflictions (*kleśa*).
(Recorded Oral Tradition). Fayen’s name was Wenyi; he was a successor of Dizang. Dizang’s name was Guichen; he was a successor of Xuansha Shibei.
Gao’an cited the words of these masters to enlighten students, saying: "My late teacher once said: 'From Linqiong...'"
When he first set out on his travels and passed through the Kuiguan Pass, almost every small temple he visited was highly unsatisfactory;
often it was difficult even to find news of others. He then thought of how in the past Fayan had been blocked by snow at Dizang’s monastery.

While Fayan was warming himself by the hearth, Dizang asked him, "Where are you going, Upasaka? Fayan replied, "I am traveling on pilgrimage. Dizang asked, "What is the matter with this pilgrimage? Fayan—
He replied, "I do not know. Facheng said, "Not knowing is most intimate. At these words, Fayuan’s eyes suddenly opened and he attained realization.

This was when Fayuan was studying under Dizang; Mingjiao saw Shending sitting in the hall. When Fayuan entered and performed his prostrations, Shending pointed to a small jar on the platform and said, "When you first arrived, there was no sauce yet;
it is only now that there is some. The next morning, as they were eating congee, he saw one [of the monks].
A person holding a basket took some items and placed them into the monks' alms bowls. Huìsōng observed that among the assembly, some ate while others did not.
He slipped his sleeve under the hall to look and saw that it was merely crushed rice cakes. He then questioned the senior monk, who replied, "The permanent provisions of the monastery are meager."

Those who attended the meal collect the leftovers and, upon returning, deposit them in the storehouse. On days when there is no communal meal, they are dried and distributed equally for consumption, manifesting the sharing of both sweetness and bitterness.
This was said by Mingjiao when he saw the divine cauldron; it was precisely at a time of adversity.
How could the habitual tendencies accumulated since beginningless time be suddenly brought to rest?

It was when I reflected upon the two Great Beings—Fayan Ming and Miaojiao—that, during their times of enduring the snow and sharing rice cakes, the habitual tendencies and afflictions within my breast were like ice melting under the sun or darkness dispelled by a lamp; they simply ceased to exist.
Ga’ān was upright and firm both inwardly and outwardly; his demeanor was majestic and awe-inspiring. Whether in motion or at rest, he never forgot the rules of propriety.

Throughout his life, he frequently encountered harassment from those within the assembly, yet he took no offense. To the end of his days, he maintained a life of simplicity and frugality for himself. Within his quarters, he did not grant permission to anyone lightly.

Whenever there was even the slightest lack of accord, he would invariably assume a stern countenance and speak with direct words to rectify the situation; thus, all the monastics were filled with faith and submission.
He once said, "In the study of the Way, my learning is no superior to others'; it is simply that throughout my life, in all I have done, I have had nothing to feel ashamed of in my own heart."
The record notes that Gao’an’s outward appearance was dignified and upright, while his inner character was firm and honest.

His bearing and demeanor were so majestic and awe-inspiring that they struck one with reverence. Whether in motion or at rest, he conducted himself according to the Vinaya and the sacred precepts, never failing in propriety and ritual law.
Even before he entered the monastic order, while still among the common crowd, he frequently encountered those who would insult, deceive, or harm him; yet he remained utterly unmoved.
Throughout his life until old age, he maintained his mind with unwearied diligence and without disparagement, using it to examine and restrain himself.
He bound his body and disciplined himself, never nodding lightly at others even within the quarters.
Should anyone fail to accord with him, he would invariably display the swift majesty of a lion, letting out fearless roars to subdue them; thus, all the monastics placed their trust in him.
I respectfully take these words to heart. He once said: "I have no Way to transmit and no Dharma to teach; there is nothing in me that surpasses others.
It is simply that throughout my life, whatever I have done, I feel not the slightest sense of shame before my own mind."
When Gao’an was residing at Yunju, he encountered a monk who was exposing the hidden faults of others. He immediately spoke to him with composure, saying: "The matter is not as you think.
For those who dwell beneath the forest, the cultivation of the Way is the primary duty; harmony is the means by which one refines oneself.
How can one recklessly indulge in likes and dislikes to ruin another’s conduct? His tactfulness was of this nature (Recorded Sayings).
When Gao’an was serving as the abbot of Yunju, he observed that some monastics failed to cultivate themselves and instead exposed the hidden faults and failings of others.
To these individuals, he would respond with composure and gentleness, admonishing them: "This matter should not be handled in such a manner.
For those who dwell beneath the forest, the single-minded investigation of principle is the urgent task; only then can the dharma of the six harmonies be realized."

In cultivating oneself, how can one afford to be negligent or licentious? To harbor partiality, love, and hatred, thereby destroying the conduct of others—is this not surely to lose righteousness and forfeit one's virtue?
Such is the manner in which one should be tactful and complete one's cultivation of others.
When Gao’an first declined the summons to Yunju, Foyan sent a letter urging him, saying: "Yunju is preeminent among the monasteries of Jiangzuo;

it is also a place where you may settle the assembly and practice the Way. It seems there is no need for such firm refusal. Gao’an replied: "Since the very beginning of the forest-monastery tradition..."
Among those who study the teachings, there are not a few who, having been ensnared by such labels, have ruined their integrity and righteousness.
When Fojian heard of this, he remarked, "The conduct of Gaoyuan in leaving or staying is something that other patch-robed monks cannot match" (Jiwen).
At the outset, Gao’an refused to accept the invitation to go to Yunju. Foyan sent a letter urging him, saying:

"Yunju is the ancestral seat of the school, preeminent in the region east of the Yangtze. It is fitting that you settle there to lead the great assembly and practice the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
it would seem inappropriate to decline so firmly. Gao’an did not agree with this view, saying: "Since the very first establishment of monasteries..."
Among the students, every single one’s conduct is yet unstable; they all desire to seek out a fine dwelling place.
Yet, because of such titles and reputations, their integrity and sense of honor are ruined beyond counting.
When Fojian heard Gaoyuan speak in this manner, he praised him, saying: "The conduct and actions of Gaoyuan in his daily life are truly exemplary for these times."
"Monks, this is truly something we cannot hope to attain.
Gao'an’s 'Exhortation to Elderly and Ailing Monks' states: 'I, the poor monk, have often perused the Tripitaka and carefully examined the Buddha's intent.
He did not permit bhikṣus to sit and receive food without labor, for that gives rise to a mind of indolence and the view of a self. Every time morning arrives...'"

In the morning, the Buddha and his disciples went out with their alms bowls to beg for food. They made no distinction between the noble and the lowly, nor did they harbor thoughts of superiority or inferiority;

thus, those who were able to provide merit received it all equally and universally. That which was later called "permanent property" (sanghika) was originally established for the sake of elderly or infirm bhikṣus who were unable to go begging;
it was not something that those in the prime of youth could consume. This remained so until after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the era of the True Dharma.
It is likewise so. Since the age of the Semblance Dharma, the Zen monasteries (*cān-lín*) of the Central Kingdom have not ceased the practice of almsround (*piṇḍapāta*).

However, they merely appoint those deemed capable to perform it, and whatever gains and offerings are obtained are pooled together to support the *caitya-vihāra* for the peace of the broad assembly; thus, the rule of daily begging has been abandoned.
Now I hear that the abbots of several monasteries do not recognize cause and effect, do not provide for elderly monks, and act in opposition to the Buddha’s teachings.
The purport is this: as the Dharma-gate has declined and weakened, if one does not reside in the monastery, where will an elder go for refuge?
Furthermore, one must reflect again upon the property of the Sangha: for whose sake was it originally established? What state of mind should one cultivate to accord with the Buddha’s mind?

What practice should one cultivate to accord with the Buddha’s conduct? In the past, when the Buddha was alive, he would sometimes decline invitations and remain at the vihāra, wandering through the monks’ quarters to look after the elders.
He was ill. [The Master] questioned him one by one and attended to his needs one by one;
he then exhorted the bhikṣus to respect one another, to follow skillful means, and to eliminate resentment and animosity. This Teacher of Men is the model for governing the great assembly.

Yet nowadays, people recklessly consume the permanent property of the monastery to provide for their own physical comforts, curry favor with the powerful and influential, and furthermore, exclude the elderly.
The sick are the property of the Sangha; yet [the monks] conceal them as their own. Of the Buddha’s mind and the Buddha’s practice, not a single trace remains.
How tragic, how tragic! An ancient worthy said: "An elder monk is the banner of the mountain gate. Yet in the Chan forests of today, among a hundred monks, there is not one who is old.
Even when they are old, they are not admitted. This only serves to increase their longevity without providing any benefit; it is truly no better than—

They died prematurely. We pray that you shall now take their place, each of you following the Buddha’s words to perpetuate the ancestral position, provide comfort to the elderly and the infirm, and manage the monastery's assets—both those present and those acquired—providing for all needs as appropriate.
Do not allow ignorant individuals to monopolize power and act with negligence, thereby inviting the retribution of a short life in future existences.
You must examine this matter most earnestly.

"Di" (諦) means detailed examination. "Pu" (溥) means universal salvation. "Bian" (徧) means pervasive. "Zhao-ti" (招提) is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "permanently abiding" (*cāturdiśa*). "Chuo" (輟) means to cease or stop.

"Xue" (削) means to thin or pare down. "Ruo" (弱) means weak or feeble. "Di" (遞) means to alternate or succeed one another. "Jingshe" (精舍) refers to a place for the refined cultivation of pure conduct (*vihāra*).

*Vināyaka* (Tuner/Controller). "Tune" is like tuning a stew of a hundred flavors so that all tastes are exquisite; "control" is like a skilled charioteer driving horses, ensuring that both the slow and the swift are managed appropriately.
When a Bodhisattva attains this *vināyaka-samādhi*, they are called a *vināyaka-puruṣa* (Tamer of Men), which is one of the Ten Epithets [of a Buddha].
It is the Teacher’s Dharma; it is the model for humanity. *Nirodha* (Cessation). *Bheda* (Cleaving/Breaking). Record.
Gao’an’s Exhortation to the Monastic Community: A Text for Consoling Elderly and Ailing Monks, which states:
"I, this poor monk, have examined the scriptures and treatises of the Tripitaka and scrutinized the Buddha’s original intent.

It was never permitted that young bhikṣus should sit idly and enjoy food obtained without merit, thereby giving rise to a mind of indolent latent tendencies or conceiving views of self and others and arrogance."
Every morning, from the Tathāgata above down to the great assembly below, they all carry their alms bowls into the city to beg for food.
Without discriminating between the noble and the humble—from the Son of Heaven above to the common people below—they practice impartial compassion and extensively transform all beings.
As for those who cause merit to arise, it is to be distributed equally and universally throughout the world. Why is it called "permanently abiding" (*nitya*)?
It was originally established for elderly and infirm bhikṣus who were unable to go out on almsrounds.
It was not intended for those of young age or in the prime of life to sit at ease and eat in leisure. This was the case until after the Buddha entered the Great Nirvāṇa. Now...
During the era when the True Dharma (Saddharma) prevails, the monastic community continues to practice according to ancient traditions.
However, by the time of the Semblance Dharma (Pratirūpaka-dharma), even in this present age, they still do not abandon the practice of wandering for alms with their bowls (*pātra*).
Rather, they select those who are upright and capable to carry out these practices, while the wealth and offerings thus obtained are collected and brought into the monastery.
To bring peace to the great assembly, he consequently abolished the daily rule of collecting alms with the *patra*.

Now, I hear that the leaders of monastic communities in various regions do not understand causes and their resulting effects; they loathe the sick and abandon the elderly, refusing to provide for them.
This violates and contradicts the intent of the World-Honored One and subverts the disciplinary statutes of the Great Wisdom. If the residence of the elderly and the infirm is not permitted...
Dwelling in a temple, one’s body is already old; to whom should one wish to return? Do not fail to reflect upon this again and again.
Consider for whose sake the wealth and profits accumulated within the *caitya* were originally intended; you should cast away such a mind and align yourself with the mind of the Buddha.
Furthermore, consider what kind of conduct should be practiced; you should cast it away and align yourself with the conduct of the Buddha. Formerly, when the Buddha was at Jetavana...
During the time of the *dhūta* forest retreat, he would sometimes decline invitations from donors and remain within the monastery.
He would tour every single residence in succession to look after the elderly and the infirm, personally inquiring after each one regarding their health, cold, heat, hunger, and thirst.
He attended to each person’s needs by providing bedding, medicines, and decoctions, while further exhorting his fellow monks to look after one another and to treat each other with mutual respect.
To comply with the inclinations of others and employ various skillful means to eliminate feelings of anger and resentment—
this is the standard model for a Master of Discipline (Vinayadhara) presiding over and managing a great assembly. Yet, those who currently serve as abbots act with reckless self-indulgence,
using resources solely to provide for their own persons and nourish their physical appetites, or else to curry favor with others.

These officials bind themselves with worldly attachments and cling tenaciously to their positions. They cast aside and ignore the elderly and the infirm, and they conceal communal property to make it their own.
They possess not even a fraction of the Buddha’s heart or the Buddha’s virtuous conduct—is this not to be lamented?
Is this not to be lamented? An ancient worthy once said: "An old monk is by no means dispensable; he is the banner and model of the mountain gate.
Yet within the Dharma seats of today, one does not see a single old monk among a hundred monks. People loathe the elderly and do not accept them;
the old have nowhere to rely. What benefit is there in such long life? It is actually no better than—
It would be better to die young. I hope that the abbots of the present age will revere the words of the Buddha and continue to promote the ancestral Way.

They should provide for and care for the elderly and the infirm residing at the monastery, whether the funds and grain of the permanent endowment are abundant or scarce, according to the family’s means.
Let them not allow themselves to be deluded by ignorance regarding cause and effect, nor shall they arrogantly monopolize power and authority. [End]
This violates established models and will bring about the retribution of a short life and a premature death in future lives; one must take care to reflect upon this with earnest attention.
Zen Master Juefan inscribed a notice on the gate of Lingyuan, saying: "Lingyuan originally had no desire to appear in the world; he was like a dyke."
Lao. When Zhang Wujin was sent as an envoy to Jiangxi, he repeatedly invited him [to come to court], but [Lao] would not comply.
After some time, he suddenly changed his mind and said: "The Zen groves are in decline; those who propagate the Dharma mostly feign it to seek security and ease.
If we do not support them urgently, their collapse will occur in the blink of an eye. Thereupon, he began teaching at Taiping in Huaiyang. At that time, I traveled east and entered his gate.
The orderliness of the monastic community and the great flourishing of the ancestral tradition were no less than they had been when Baizhang was still hale and hearty.
Thirteen years later, I saw this notice in the room of Fengyuan; reading it, I felt a chilling awe, as if I were beholding his very skeletal essence of the Way.
Shan谷 (Shangu) carved these characters into deep grooves for large-scale calligraphy. With great urgency, he exclaimed: "Alas!

If all those who provide the Dharma as a gift throughout the world were to abide by Lingyuan’s words in their tenure as abbots, then what need would there be to worry that the ancestral Way would not flourish?"
The *Zhuan* says: "It is man who can broaden the Way; it is not the Way that broadens man. Lingyuan acted accordingly (*Shimen ji*).

For the detailed phonology and meaning of the inscription on Lingyuan’s gate, see the *Shimen ji*. Chancellor Zhang Wujin, whose name was Shangying and courtesy name Tianjue, received the Dharma from Chan Master Doushuai Yue.
He repeatedly dispatched messengers with letters to invite [Lingyuan], and thus [the invitation] was granted.
It is also a sudden transformation; it is collapse and ruin. A "tumbling wind" blows from above downward. One single step is called a *qiū* (a half-step). It means "to wait. *Qiū kě xū*:
this speaks of the speed with which the Dharma is destroyed; in the time of a single step, one may wait and witness it. *Wú yàng* means "no affliction" or "no sorrow.
*Féng Yuán* refers to Master Cèng. *Bò fēn* means to divide apart. *Kō* refers to a bird's nest. This speaks of...
The eight-part script (bāfēnshū) is square and round, its calligraphy precisely resembling the form of a bird’s nest (*niǎokō*). "Jī" means to stimulate;
it is to broaden and magnify [the teaching]. This is the inscription for the gate banner of Lingyuan, composed by Master Juefan.

Initially, Lingyuan had no intention of responding to the world, and his resolve was extremely firm. When Zhang Tianjue was serving as an envoy to Jiangxi, he repeatedly sent written invitations requesting his emergence [from seclusion].
The world did not approve of him at all. After a long time, seeing that the world was declining and the Way was fading, he stirred his compassionate resolve and turned over a new leaf, saying:
"The Zen groves have fallen into decay; the Buddha-dharma has overflowed, branching out and spreading like surging currents."
The whole world is thus. Suppose I were to steal moments of leisure for my own comfort and fail to rise quickly to uphold and support the Way;

its collapse would not require even a single step to await. For this reason, I consequently appeared in the world to propagate the Way at Taiping Chan Monastery in Huai'an Prefecture. At that time, I was traveling eastward.
Its gates are flanked by orderly groves of trees; the six excellences are once again complete. The ancestral style is greatly revitalized, and the Three Barriers flourish anew.
It is as if there were no difference between this and the time when the Great Wisdom Gate was free from affliction—not diminished by even a hair’s breadth.
Fifteen years later, I saw this notice in the quarters of Master Fenyuan. Upon reading its text, it inspires a sense of solemn awe in one.
One feels awe and reverence, as if facing the venerable countenance of Master Lingyuan in person.
Layman Shan-gu has specially composed this in the eight-part formal script (kaishu) to inspire and exhort people. Alas!
If the masters of monasteries throughout the land who practice the Dharma and bestow their gifts were all to follow the words of Lingyuan and put them into practice as abbots, then furthermore—
Why should one worry that the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs will not be practiced, or that it cannot be greatly propagated? The *Analects* says:
"The human mind possesses awareness, while the essence of the Way is non-action. Therefore, it is the person who can fully unfold this Way;
it is not the Way that unfolds the person. When Lingyuan appeared in the world, he expanded this Great Way to benefit humanity, precisely in accordance with this principle.
These two statements are similar; therefore, I accept this on that basis.
Regarding Master Guyun Ben, the "Chapter on Distinguishing the Flatterer" states: In our dynasty, the Duke Zhongshu Fu Bi sought the Way from Chan Master Touzi Yongyong.
Their correspondence, including letters and gāthās, totaled fourteen sheets, which were inscribed upon the two corridors of Hongfu Temple in Tai.
On the walls, one clearly perceives the strictness with which former masters upheld the Dharma and the profound sincerity with which princes and nobles believed in the Way.

Zheng Guo Gong was a high minister of state; in his later years, he came to realize that the direction of the path was such as this, and he felt that Yuan Yong must possess qualities far surpassing ordinary men.
He considered himself inspired by Yuan Yong’s example, and among the scholar-officials, those who truly believe in this Way are able to set aside their age and humble themselves before him.
Their momentum was vigorous and fierce, vowing to achieve thorough realization before they would cease.

For instance, the Vice Minister Yang Dainian and the Commandery Marshal Li Hewen encountered the great masters Guanghui Lian, Shimen Cong, and Ciming, with whom they engaged in spirited exchanges and poetic duels.

This can be seen clearly in various Chan texts. Yang Wuweis [studying] under Baizhen Wuben, and Zhang Wujin [studying] under Doushuai Daoyue—both knocked at the gate and struck the joints, penetrating to the very source and bottom; they were by no means superficial.
In recent times, Minister Zhang Wugou, Councilor Li Hanlao, and Scholar Lü Jurén all met with the Elder Miaoxi and ascended [to his level].

He entered the inner sanctum of the Hall and was called a spiritual friend beyond the mundane world. Whether faced with love or hatred, favor or opposition, he acted with the force of a thunderclap and the swiftness of a flash of lightning.
He cast aside worldly constraints and inhibitions, such that onlookers stood with bated breath, recoiling in awe, unable to fathom his limits.
Yet, these gentlemen sought him out on the shores of empty stillness and profound solitude, intending only to settle their minds in meditative silence and manifest their innate nature.
Guiyun’s name was Ruyuan; he was a successor of Huilin and Huiyuan. The Prime Minister of the Song Dynasty, Duke of Fuzhou, was surnamed Fu, named Bi, with the courtesy name Yanguo.
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Zheng and posthumously honored with the title Wenzhongding Gong.
He received the Dharma from Touzi Yong, whose style name was Wuzheng and whose given name was Xiuyong; he was a successor of Zongben of Huelin. This is recorded in the inscription.

"Merit" (*gōng*) refers to stone. "Resplendent" (*zháo*) means manifest. "Sincere" (*dū*) means earnest; it also means profound. "She" (*shè*) is the deity of the soil; "Ji" (*jì*) is the deity of the grains.
Speaking in terms of the state, Yang Dainian of the Song dynasty was named Yi; his posthumous title was Wenzheng, and he served as a Hanlin Academician. Li Hewen was a son-in-law to the Emperor.
Mingzun was named Xumu; both received the Dharma from Guyin Cong. Guanghui was named Yuanlian; he was the successor to Shoushan Nianzu.
"Jife" means to stimulate and exalt. "Babban" is synonymous with "tiaotiao" (line by line). Toushuai was named Congyue; he was the successor to Zhenjing Wen.
"Kouguan jikai" means to strike at the barrier and open it; to strike at the obstruction and break through the blockage. Zhang Wugou.
His style name was Jiucheng, and his courtesy name was Zishao. Li Hanlao’s name was Binglü; Ju Ren’s name was Benzhong, and he served as a Hanlin scholar.
All three were Dharma heirs of Miaoxi Zonggao and were spiritual friends beyond the mundane world—friends who met and interacted on the path.
"Thunder-sweep" refers to a shout like a thunderclap; "lightning-sweep" refers to the swift movement of one's spiritual mechanism.
"Like a flash of lightning": *rèn* refers to the lapel of a garment. "Bìyì" (辟易) describes a state of being terrified and losing one's composure.

"Yáysǐ" (涯涘) refers to the boundaries or shores of water. "Nǐ" (擬) means to wait for or intend to do something. In the "Discriminating Between the Sycophantic and the Honest" (*Biànnìng piān*) by Master Guīyún, it is said:

"The good may be emulated and the evil may be avoided. The first section provides a general overview of men of the Way who moved and won over kings and ministers, leading them to come [to seek instruction].

This concludes [the section]. It is said that one cannot hope for the branches while neglecting the root. During our own dynasty, the Duke of Zheng, Fu Yanguo, sought the Way from Master Yongyong of Touzi.

He composed a series of verses and eulogies spanning fourteen sheets of paper, which were carved onto stone tablets and installed upon the walls of the two corridors within Hongfu Temple in Taizhou. Thus, the achievements of the former sages are clearly visible before us.
Those who uphold the Way of the Dharma are thus respectful; those kings, ministers, and officials who believe in the Way are thus sincere and steadfast.
Lord Zheng, who went to the alliance at Danyuan, was a minister who bore the heavy responsibilities of the state.

By his old age, he knew that such was the direction one must take; yet even Touzi must have possessed a path of profound virtue and great excellence beyond ordinary men before Yu Yongyong could say of himself that he had been inspired by him.
When speaking to Yuanzhao, he remarked, "I once saw Master Yongyong’s realization was deep. Among the scholar-officials, there were those who truly believed in this Way. Furthermore...
They were able to forget their age, being unconstrained by years; they could humble their status, being unconstrained by rank.
They roused their great resolve and sought the Way with fierce intensity, determined to penetrate and realize it before they would cease.
This was like the cases of Minister Yang Dainian and General Li Hewen of the Song dynasty, who both encountered the great masters Guanghui Lian, Shimen Cong, and Ciming. All...

Within a single phrase, there was a moment of realization; they were inspired and uplifted, responding one to another in a call-and-response dialogue that has been ranked among the *Chuan-deng lu* (Records of the Transmission of the Lamp).

Yang Wuweizhi’s encounter with the ancestral master Baiyun Yuan, and Zhang Tianjue’s meeting with Doushuai Yue, both struck at the most critical and essential points—passing where it is difficult to pass, and striking through the most obstructed barriers.
To be able to penetrate where there was no penetration requires, in truth, a thorough awakening and entry into the fundamental source;

it is not a matter of mere expediency or superficiality. In recent times, the Minister Zhang Wugou, the Vice-Minister Li Hanlao, and the Academician Lü Juren all personally encountered the Elder Miaoxi; they ascended his hall and entered his chamber, and thus were called "Fang."
This was the seal of the heterodox practitioners. Some were filled with affection and joy; others were consumed by hatred and loathing.
Whether blowing against the wind or with the wind, his roar was like the crashing of thunder and his swift movements like a flash of lightning.

All were made to attain sudden enlightenment beneath his words, transcending worldly conventions, the toils of affliction, and all restrictive taboos. Those who observed him drew back their robes in reverence, recoiling in astonishment, unable to fathom him.
This is the ultimate limit. Yet, why do gentlemen and scholars seek this Way on the shores of empty, secluded, and tranquil places?

It is because they intend to let rest this mind of worldly toil, to enter into meditative stillness and concentration, and to extract from and manifest the great matter that is inherently possessed by themselves.
If the aforementioned great masters had not attained actual realization, they would have no true...
How could Cao possibly have moved such kings, ministers, and officials to set aside their status and forget their seniority to place their faith and devotion in him?
This is something the virtuous may take as a model.
In later generations, people no longer observed the models set by the virtuous predecessors; they devoted themselves solely to flattery and sought advancement through crooked means.

Generally, those who were recommended for the position of abbot and given the title of "Elder" (Changlao) often wrote formal notes (shaci) addressing their former patrons as "Gate Monks" (menseng) and "Lord of Grace" (Enfu).
They seize the property of the world and present wrapped gifts as flattery; those with discernment pity and laugh at them, yet these men remain complacent and feel no shame. Alas!
We, the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya, carry but a single water jar and a single alms bowl, traveling like clouds or birds;

we are not pressed by the urgency of cold or hunger, nor do we harbor attachments to children, jade, or silks. Yet we wish to bow our waists and sweep the floors, shrinking with a shivering coldness and taking upon ourselves this humiliation and baseness.
Is it truly so? To address someone as "Enfu" (Lord of Grace) is a private invention of one's own self, lacking any basis in authority.
When a single frivolous and ignorant person initiates this before others, hundreds of frivolous and ignorant people harmonize with it thereafter, vying to offer their service;

it is truly nothing more than a mark of base and petty character. No practice has done more to weaken moral instruction than flattery; it is indeed the gradual emergence of treachery, wickedness, and deceit. Even for upright men...
O noble beings! To be skillful in the ways one enters [the path] yet cause oneself to fall into unrighteousness and lose virtue beyond redemption—is this not to be lamented?

These bhikṣus who destroy the Dharma are vessels for the influence of Māra; they are self-assured in their deceit and hypocrisy, falsely manifesting the physical appearance and demeanor of those who possess true knowledge.
They take the great elders of the Chan forests as their spiritual lineage and curry favor with powerful officials of the day as their kinsmen.

They proffer unsolicited reverence and initiate the ruinous precedent of the Dharma: laypeople ascend the meditation platform and prostrate themselves before them, thus willfully contravening the sacred regulations.

This is a great disgrace to our ancestral tradition; the decline of my Way has reached this extreme. Alas! To be struck by Heaven’s punishment or entered into the registers of the ghosts—how could ten thousand deaths atone for this?
Is this not the act of a sycophant? (Mù [pronounced jū], Suì [pronounced suì], Mó [pronounced mó]).

To write one's name on a petition or memorial is called a *cì* (刺). "Tián" (恬) means tranquility and stillness. "Nǎi" (餒) means hunger. "Zhé yāo" (折腰) and "qū yāo" (屈腰) mean to bend the body and lower the torso.
To "hold the broom" (*yǒng sì*) means to cover the dustpan with the broom, so that the dust does not reach the elder; this expresses the intention of showing respect.

"Hán sūn" (寒酸) and "jú jí" (跼蹐) collectively describe the state of humbling one’s body, being unable to act with unrestrained ease, and the appearance of fearing others. "Zhōng" (鐘) means to gather together.

This is a formal petition. "Prostrating with palms joined" refers to bowing in reverence. "Heavenly execution and thunderous strikes," "fires burning and the registers of ghosts," and "secretly robbing away one's life-span" refer to divine retribution.
"Redemption through the payment of gold" means being exempted from punishment by offering a ransom. The subsequent section describes the character of sycophants:
they fawn upon those in power, bring ruin to the Dharma-gate, and abandon morality for the sake of fame and profit. Those of later generations do not see this...
He exclusively devoted himself to emulating the models and standards set by former masters such as Touzi Guanghui, Shimen Ziming, and other holy ones;
he strove to flatter famous officials and went to great lengths to solicit the powerful in order to achieve prominence.

Whenever he served as an abbot and submitted his name to serve as the Elder of a certain temple, he would repeatedly write letters on slips of paper to claim the status of a "gate-monk" (men-seng) in order to curry favor with his predecessors.
For the sake of the Lord of Grace, he took communal property belonging to the monastery to wrap and present as offerings. Those who understand see that he is ignorant of cause and effect;
such a person is both pitiable and laughable. Yet the sycophants, on the contrary, find peace in this and do not consider it shameful.
Alas! We, the śramaṇas and disciples of Śākyamuni, carry a single water jar at our side and hang a single alms bowl from our bodies.
Moving like clouds and flying like birds, we are free from the oppression of hunger and cold, and devoid of attachment to children, jade, or silks.
Yet, we adopt all manner of demeaning postures—bending our bodies to hide in the dust, shivering with cold, and crouching in cramped spaces—to seek out our own humiliation. How deplorable!
To be so humiliated, loathed, and despised! As for the title "Enfu" (Lord of Grace) used by those who serve you, it originates from the private views of a single sycophant;
it lacks any basis in fact. When one fool leads the way, a hundred fools follow in harmony.
Those who wish to vie with one another in flattery toward government officials are truly base and self-degrading petty men. They bring about decline.

Regarding the traditions of Chan and Teachings, none surpass those of the sycophants; these are truly the gradual advances of the wicked, the depraved, and the deceitful who have promoted and established this trend.

Even those who are dignified and upright, or scholars of integrity, may skillfully allow themselves to be drawn into it in order to propagate their religious teachings, yet they instead find themselves ensnared in fields of unrighteousness and fall into grounds of irredeemable moral failure. This is lamentable.
Do you not feel sorrow for such monks who destroy the Dharma? They are mere gathering places for demonic influences, practicing deception and falsehood;
not only do they feel no shame, but they remain self-composed, feigning the appearance of Chan masters.
They point to men of renowned virtue as their own lineage masters, and they curry favor with high-ranking officials of the day, treating them as their own kinsmen and relatives.
To persistently refuse requests out of a misplaced sense of reverence is entirely to deceive others; it initiates the ruin of the Dharma, yet one remains unaware of self-deception.
Laypeople who possess no precepts ought not to ascend the platform to receive prostrations, yet they do so;

monastics should not prostrate themselves before laypeople, yet they do so. Thus, they willfully contravene the regulations established by the sages of antiquity and bring great disgrace upon their ancestors.
The tradition of our house and the Way we follow have declined to such an extreme. Alas! There are the forces of yin and yang that hasten your life’s end;
there are the ghosts and spirits who envy your blessings. A sycophant such as this—amidst ten thousand deaths, there is not one instance where their crimes can be redeemed.
Reaching such a state, is this not indeed the work of a sycophant? Let those who are evil take this as a warning.
Furthermore, Chan Master Yuansong’s *Yuanciao* states: "Among the eminent monks of antiquity, when they met the Son of Heaven, they did not act as subjects.

When receiving official decrees, they were addressed as 'Duke' or 'Master. When the imperial carriage arrived at the gate of Sengyuan of Mount Zhong, he did not rise from his seat to welcome it. At Tiger Creek—
Huiyuan. When the Son of Heaven visited Xunyang, he issued an edict [inviting him], yet Huiyuan did not leave the mountain. The world of that time esteemed his person and revered his virtue;

thus, the Way of the Sages was revitalized. As for those of later generations who admire such eminent monks, even when they associate with high officials and ministers, they do not receive the same courtesy accorded to a common scholar.
Whether in public or in seclusion, their state of self-contentment does not even equal that of an ordinary man—how much less so, then, [the case of Huiyuan]?
If even Sengyuan could not see the Son of Heaven, how much less could Huiyuan maintain his composure? I look toward the flourishing of our Way;
can the cultivation of those like us truly achieve this? To preserve the teaching without the person who embodies it—what benefit is there in such preservation?
Thinking of this alone, tears have never failed to fall. In the Dingyou year of the Chunxi era, I retired from my duties at Xian'en and took up residence here.

The small valley of Mount Seizan by Hirata is a place where, based on my recent observations and hearing, affairs are often characterized by hypocrisy and pretension, and the ancient traditions have fallen into decay.
My words are insufficient to weigh such matters, yet I have recorded this briefly as a reminder to myself. (A Flourishing Matter of the Forests; *Xun* is pronounced like *xún*).

Sengyuan: Emperor Gaozu of the Qi dynasty personally visited Mount Zhong to seek him out. Sengyuan was seated on his bed; declining on account of old age and illness, he did not go out to welcome him.
Emperor Gaozu went to his bedside to see him, inquired after him with great courtesy, and then departed. Huiyuan resided at Donglin Temple on Mount Lu.
When Emperor An of the Eastern Jin dynasty visited Xunyang, he issued an edict for Huiyuan to come forth once, but the Master declined on account of his old age.
He did not venture out for long periods. The Emperor’s reverence for him increased all the more, and he issued an edict to the Governor of Jiuyang to provide annual supplies for his travel needs.
He resided there for thirty years, his shadow never leaving the mountains. He established the Tiger Creek as the boundary beyond which no guests were permitted to enter;

even when the three seasonal festivals arrived, he would only receive them by leading them back beyond the creek. The eminent monk Hongjing used this to serve as a warning. As Master Huihong of Mount Song said in his *Original Teaching Treatise*: [text follows].
In antiquity, eminent monks did not perform the rites of a subject when they met the Son of Heaven.
When the Son of Heaven admired such eminent monks, he would first draft an edict to address them with honorific titles such as "Duke" (Gong) or "Master" (Shi).

When Emperor Wu of Liang’s imperial carriage arrived at the gate of Sengyuan of Mount Zhong, Sengyuan declined on the grounds of illness; seated upon his couch, he did not go out to welcome him. When the Son of Heaven visited Huìyuǎn of Húcǐ...

The imperial decree was issued at Xunyang, yet [the Master] did not leave the mountains. Nevertheless, at that time, had it not been for the Son of Heaven with a Buddha-mind, he could not have honored the eminent monk;
and had it not been for the eminent monk, he could not have moved the Son of Heaven.
Because there was such a person and such virtue, the Way of the Sage was revitalized. Those in later generations who admire eminent monks do so because both parties were merely empty names.
Furthermore, when meeting with high officials and great officers, they were still not permitted to receive the ritual courtesies accorded even to the lowest-ranking scholar-officials.

Looking at it this way, whether in public or in private, their conduct was truly not as self-assured as that of ordinary people. How much less could one expect a monk like Sengyuan to rise from his seat upon seeing the Emperor?
And how much less could one expect a monk like Huiyuan to remain composed when the imperial edict did not [command him to rise]?
It has emerged from beyond expectation that my Way shall flourish. Can the true cultivation of those among us be achieved?
If one preserves its teachings without needing to wait for those who yearn for the Way, it would be better not to preserve them at all; even if preserved, what benefit would there be?

Reflecting upon this, there have been times when my tears could not help but flow. In the *dingyou* year of the Chongxi era of the Song dynasty, I resigned from my duties at Xian'en Temple and took up residence in a small valley on the western mountains of Pingtian.

There, based on what I had recently seen and heard, I observed that many matters were false rather than real, and that the traditions of antiquity had almost entirely withered away; thus, I wrote this.
[The author] says: "My words are not sufficient to weigh the matter; yet, fearing that my beginning and end may lack care, I have written this briefly as a self-reproach.
Master Yuanji Cen’s colophon states: "The Buddha’s era is far distant; the True Dharma has grown faint, and a spirit of decadence prevails."

It has reached a point where those who preceded us have passed away and the younger generation lacks understanding; the standards and discipline of the monastic community are nearly swept away from the ground.
Even if there are those who attempt to support and rescue them, they are instead treated as "barbarians" (like Wang Manzi).

Now, observing Master Shushan Ben’s *Discerning the Sycophant*, its phrasing is profound and its meaning vast, penetrating and illuminating. It is most capable of diagnosing their ailments; yet how can ordinary people like myself [fully grasp it]?
Their consciousness is dark and shallow; intoxicated by the realm of the wicked and sycophantic, they will surely regard the finest clarified butter (*tīrtha*) as a poisonous drug.
Yuanji (圓極) is the eminent master Cenming Yan (岑名彥岑), the successor of Yunju Faru (雲居法如). Ritual codes (*dianxing*) are the instruments for eliminating evil and preventing transgression.
"Nearly" (*ji*) means close to it. "Sweeping the ground" (*sao di*) is like using a sharp pole to strike the earth. This is the Dharma-gate of Wang Manzi (王蠻子).
"Zhong" (中) means a servant. "Zhen" (箴) means admonition; it is also the same as "zhen" (鍼), meaning one can remove poisonous diseases. "Zui" (醉) means being deeply intoxicated.

In the postscript to the "Pian on Distinguishing Flattery from Returning Clouds" by Master Yuanji Cen, it says: "The Buddha passed away long ago; until now, a very great distance of time has elapsed."
The True Dharma has grown faint and thin; a spirit of decadence prevails, and there is nothing that does not exist.

Virtuous men of former generations have withered and passed away, leaving those who follow them with no standard upon which to model themselves. The regulations of the monastic community (*saṃghārāma*) have recently reached the point of extinction.
Even those who attempt to support and rescue it are, conversely, treated as mere slaves within the Dharma-gate. Now, Zen Master Shushan Ben has distinguished [the truth].

The words and meanings are profound and far-reaching, while the underlying intent is vast. Furthermore, they penetrate deeply into the principles of ultimate truth and clearly elucidate the Buddha’s intention.
They are uniquely capable of curing the incurable diseases of the heart and diaphragm.

However, those who are deceitful, false, and vulgar—fearing that their karmic consciousness is deep-seated and rigid, their wisdom is obscure and shallow, and that they are steeped in the realm of perverse flattery—will likely not be willing to believe them.
"The supreme flavor of *amṛta* (ghee) is prized by the world; yet when encountered by such persons as these, it turns instead into a poisonous drug.
Master Kū of Tōzan replied in a letter to Yō Saimō, who had borrowed porters, saying: "I was honored by your visit and deeply grateful for your profound affection.

Since our parting, I have further received your gracious letter, which only increases my sense of gratitude and shame. I am originally but a man of the mountain caves, one who has no concern with the world..."

Indifferent. Taemo (Caimao) seems to understand this. Although he now serves as an elder residing in the abbot’s quarters, he remains essentially the same person he was as the "Empty" (Kong) Upadhyaya of the previous day.

Matters concerning the existence or lack of property in the monastery are entirely entrusted to the administrative officers; he does not look over the accounts of income and expenditure. He does not keep robes or bowls, nor does he use the monastery's resources.
He does not accept invitations from outside, nor does he seek external support. He dwells according to conditions, never having [previously]...
I am making plans for tomorrow. Since Cai Mao has already been praised for his familiarity with the Way, we ought to forget ourselves within that Way.
Now, in this letter, you seek several porters; I do not know whether these porters come from the monastery’s permanent endowment (*sangha-rāma*) or from Master Kong?
If they come from Master Kong, what does he possess? If they come from the permanent endowment, that is the private use of the monastery’s property. Once it involves the private, then—
This is theft. How could a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) misappropriate permanent property?

Since you have entered the imperial capital to seek good fortune, it is inappropriate for you to engage in such matters at a monastery. You are a man from Min; everything you see and know is that of the elders of Min.
Once you settle in a monastery, you will exhaustively steal the permanent property to make it your own, or you will use it to cultivate relationships with the nobility.

Or they use it to provide for lay households, or to entertain their own acquaintances; they fail to consider that these are the goods of the Sangha of the ten directions, belonging to the *caitika* (monasteries) and the *sāmghika* (the community).
Many of those who now wear horns and clothe themselves in fur to repay their debts are people of this sort.

The former Buddhas spoke clearly; how can one not stand in awe? In recent years, temple buildings have fallen into ruin and the monastic community has become sparse—all because of such faults as these. I pray that you will not place me among such as them.
If you truly trust me, then I shall decline all that is offered by other temples and accept nothing from them; thus, your future prospects will be immeasurable. These words may be harsh to the ear.
These words—I do not know what he meant by them. It was cold at the time; take care on your journey (from the *Yulu*).
Dongshan’s name was Huikong; he was a successor of Letan Shanqing. "Ruru" (辱) means shame or disgrace; it signifies being so humble as to feel one does not dare accept [the honor].
"Mohan" (漠然) and "danyan" (澹然) mean detached and tranquil. Min refers to Fujian. "Peizhu" (陪助) means to assist or accompany. This is a record of Dongshan.
The Master’s reply to the candidate Yu Caimao, in a letter regarding the loan of porters, states:

"In the past, when you deigned to visit me, I was deeply moved by the sincerity of your affection. Since our parting, I have received your letter once more, which only increases my sense of gratitude and shame.
However, I, Huikai, am but a common man who dwells among the empty mountains and caves; I am indifferent to the world and have no worldly desires. Caimao—"
It seems you understand this. Although Hui-kong now serves as the Elder and occupies the Abbot’s quarters, he remains essentially the same person as the Venerable Kong of former days;
he merely presides over the Dharma duties and transforms those who come after him.
As for the monastery’s assets and profits—whether they exist or not—they are all managed by the Chief Steward (Jiansi). He does not even review the ledgers of expenditures and income.
How much less, then, would I dare to use the property of the Sangha when even my own robes and alms-bowl are not accumulated?

Furthermore, I do not attend invitations for meals nor do I perform ritual recitations; I do not seek support from outside or engage in soliciting donations. I dwell wherever I happen to be, making each day that passes simply another day.
Do not plan for tomorrow what cannot be done today. Since Cai Mao has already been praised for his familiarity with the Way, he is one who walks that path;
we should all forget ourselves within the Way. Yet in your recent letter, you seek out several porters.
Thus, the sentiments of those who adhere to tradition seem to be at odds with this. I simply do not know from where this [practice] originates:

does it come from the permanent endowment of the monastic community (*saṃgha*), or does it originate from the single person, the Venerable Huikong? If it were to originate entirely from Huikong, what would he have to offer?

If it were to originate from within the permanent endowment of the community, who would dare to privately misappropriate such property? Should he indeed act with private favoritism, it would constitute a transgression.
This would be to misappropriate the permanent property of the Sangha.

How could one who acts as an Elder and a teacher and model for humans and devas steal from the Sangha’s assets merely to curry favor? For you, sir, to enter the capital and seek advancement is the most excellent of pursuits;
you must not engage in such matters within the temples of the Triple Gem. You are a man from Min; look upon this with your own eyes.
What I have seen and what I have heard from the elders of Min Province is this:

as soon as someone takes up residence in a monastery, they plunder all the assets and profits of the monastic community for their own use, or else they employ them to cultivate relationships with influential men.
Or they may use it to support and provide for their lay relatives, or to welcome and assist their spiritual friends and companions;

yet they never consider that these are the goods of the Sangha of the ten directions, permanently maintained at monasteries, which belong to all in common and are not the private property of a single individual.
It is because of this that they now wear iron bits and carry saddles, or pull plows and drag harrows, repaying their debts and deficiencies.

They are all such as these. The Buddha’s eye of wisdom illuminates the three periods of time and the ten directions, clearly discerning prior causes and subsequent effects without the slightest error;
yet he uttered these words—how can one not stand in awe? In recent years, the Dharma community has withered and the assembly of monastics has become sparse;
this is entirely due to those who misappropriate the property of the Sangha for the sake of personal favors.
This is a fault. I pray that you do not cast me into the same category as those who misappropriate the monastery's property and the like.

If you truly and sincerely believe my present words, then should there be porters available for borrowing at another temple who grant their consent, you must decline them all and not take them by force;
in this way, your pursuit of superior and virtuous deeds will surely be established.
This is indeed so. Were it otherwise, it would not necessarily be the case. Regarding these words that are harsh to the ear, I do not know how you, Master Yu, would regard them.
It is now winter; the weather is bitterly cold. On your journey to the capital, take good care of yourself and eat well for your own preservation.
The Venerable Master Zhe-weng Yan said: "This book is truly a copy of the imperial pardon issued before the Hall of King Yama.

As for the spiritual vision of those in various quarters today, one knows not what it is like; yet if one can truly receive and uphold this book, there will be great benefit to be gained in the future.
Zhe-weng frequently used this to illustrate his point to others. Chan-yishan also said: "The permanent property of the monastery..."

Grain, apart from that which is provided for the assembly, is much like a lethal poison; as for those who hold office or manage its distribution, even a slight touch causes their entire bodies to rot away.

This is recorded in detail in the Vinaya texts. We can see this in the fact that in ancient times, when one needed money, they would go to the storehouse to exchange it for fresh ginger to decoct into medicine.
Nowadays, those who occupy the abbot’s quarters do not merely scrape the alms bowls of the multitude.
The contents of the alms bowl are used merely to satisfy one’s own palate; it is done only to accompany oneself and not out of genuine human sentiment.
What is worse, they even gouge out [the flesh of others] to seek and purchase rare delicacies, lavishly cultivating social favors in the hope of being transferred to a great monastery.
One can only fear that in days to come, the Iron-Faced Old Man Yan (Yama) will settle the accounts with them. (From the *Nianya Manlu*)
Zhe-weng’s name was Ruyan. His lineage of Dharma succession is not clearly recorded. He resided at Zhongshan in Jinling; "shèyòu" (赦宥) means to pardon or remit;
"shì" (釋) means to release or liberate. Chan-yishan’s Dharma succession is also not clearly recorded; "gǔrén" (古人) refers to Wuzu Jie. "Jùjùwù" (踞據物) means to sit upon an object;
"fàn" (泛) means to float or drift. "Chà" (刹) is a Sanskrit term for *khaṣṭhā*, which here means a pole—that is, a banner staff. Zhe-weng’s verse:
Furthermore, this letter from Dongshan responding to Yu Caimao is truly a decree of amnesty for the release of a sinner before the Hall of King Yama.
In the various quarters today, it remains uncertain whether one’s Dharma-eye is complete or not. If it is indeed complete, you should look upon and read this book;
having read it, recite it; and having recited it, uphold it. Only then will you be fit to serve as the abbot of a monastic community.
As for "The Forest," there will be a time in the future when it proves to be of great utility; one must certainly not mistake the cause for the effect.
Master Zhe-weng frequently used this phrase to instruct others, desiring that everyone should know it—how earnest was his compassionate heart! Furthermore, do you not see what Chan-yishan said:
"Within the monastery’s permanent assets, such as grain, gold, and wealth, these should only be used to provide for the assembly and should not be diverted for other purposes. Aside from this...
Beyond this, even a single hair’s breadth or a single grain of rice is like the poison of a *zhen* bird.

Those who serve as the administrators and stewards, specifically managing all expenditures and revenues, must exercise the utmost care; for were they to be tainted by even a single speck of it, [the consequences would be grave].
It is recorded in the Vinaya-piṭaka that the flesh and bones of one's entire body will disintegrate and rot away; this has been explained therein with great clarity and detail.
When the Fifth Patriarch was ill, he required a piece of fresh ginger for his medicine, so he took money and went directly to the storehouse to purchase it.
This can clearly be seen. Those who currently occupy the position of abbot do not merely scrape the bowls of the assembly and diminish their food and drink for their own indulgence;
they seek only their own fatness, regardless of others' emaciation, using the resources solely for their own private enjoyment.
To engage in illegal and wasteful expenditures merely to cultivate personal favors is yet another extreme.

They even go so far as to gouge out and search for rare and precious objects to wrap up and present as flattery, spreading such favors far and wide. Hoping to be promoted, they seek out fine, large monasteries and ancient shrines, waiting to peddle them for sale;
thus they purchase fame and ensnare profit. As for people such as these, one can only fear that the day will come when the iron [of punishment] falls upon them.
The expressionless Old Man Yama calculates and reckons with each and every one;
how can one not stand in awe? How can one not stand in awe?
*Chanlin Baoxun Shunzhu*, Fascicle Two.
