Compiled by Ji’er Guanshengke of Huayan, Yucheng, Shu; Deyu; Shunzhu.
Master Xuedang Xing was residing at Jianfu Monastery. One day he asked a monk who had arrived for a short visit, "Where have you come from?
The monk replied, "From Fuzhou. Xuedang asked, "Along the way, did you see any fine elder masters? The monk said, "Recently I passed by Master Ben, the abbot of Boshan in Xinzhou;
although I did not pay my respects, I recognize him as a fine elder master. Xuedang said, "How do you know that?"
"It is excellent," the monk said. "The paths to the monastery are cleared and open; the corridors and eaves are well-maintained; incense and lamps are lit without ceasing in the halls;

the bells and drums are distinct at dawn and dusk; the morning and evening gruel and rice are pure and refined; and when the monks see people, they show them courtesy. By these things, one knows this is an excellent elder.
Xuedang laughed and said, "Fundamentally, he is indeed worthy. However, you too must possess the eye [of discernment]."
He then conveyed these words to the Prefectural Governor, Lord Wu Fupeng, saying: "This monk’s argumentation bears a strong resemblance to the matter of Fan Yanling’s recommendation of Zhang Xiyan.
Yet, Your Excellency’s virtue does not fall short of that of Lord Zhang Zhongding.

As this old monk is advanced in years, I pray that you will appoint the current Abbot [Ben] to the position; this would surely be a great achievement for our community. Lord Wu was greatly pleased, and Ben—
On that very day, [he] was transferred to Jianfu Temple (*Donghu ji*; the account of Fan Yanling is found in the *Huangchao lüyuan*).
Xuetang’s name was Daoxing; he was a successor of Foyan Yuan. "Yanxun" means to follow in succession. Boshan’s original name was Wuben.
He was the successor of Dàhuì. He was from Guǎngxìn Prefecture in Xīnzhōu. It is appropriate to address him as "Géxià" (Your Excellency).
The title "Géxià" is used by both high ministers, the Three Ducal Princes, and provincial governors.
When the Venerable Xuētáng resided at Jiànfú Monastery in Ráozhōu, he was about to resign his post and wished to select a worthy successor. One day, he questioned a newly arrived monk. From...
"Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Fuzhou. The Hall Master asked again, "As you traveled along the way, did you encounter any fine elder masters?
The monk stepped forward and said, "Recently I passed through Boshan in Xinzhou;
although I did not pay my respects to Master Wuben, I know he is a fine elder master. Xuedang questioned him further, saying, "In what way..."
For these reasons, one knows that he is a good elder. Monk Jin said: "There are six matters of excellence by which one knows him to be good.
First, the path leading to the temple is cleared and the dwelling place is excellent. Second, the corridors and galleries are well-maintained and the buildings are well-established.
Third, the incense and lamps in the halls are never extinguished, showing excellence in repaying kindness. Fourth...
"Fourth, the sounding of the bells and drums is distinct; this is good for the Dharma regulations. Fifth, the porridge and rice are pure and refined;
this is good for the kindness shown to the assembly. Sixth, the conduct of the monks is respectful toward others; this is good for their decorum.
By these six matters of excellence, one knows him to be a virtuous elder. Xuetang smiled with joy and said, "The Elder is indeed possessed of virtue, yet you—"
He also possessed the discerning eye of a connoisseur. Consequently, he focused exclusively on this opportunity to select worthy individuals.
He informed Public Official Wu Gong Fupeng, the Governor of Ruzhou, saying: "This monk’s manner of responding and his arguments are roughly similar to those of Fan Yanling.
When he was commissioned to lead troops through Jinling, Zhang Yong, the Governor of Jinling, asked Yanling: 'Did you see any good officials along the way?'"
Ling said, "Yesterday I passed through Pingxiang County; Zhang Xiyan is a good official. Yong asked, "How do you know he is good?

Ling replied, "Upon entering the jurisdiction, I saw that the bridges and roads were in excellent condition and the fields and gardens were well-cultivated. There were no idle farmers in the countryside and no gambling in the market.
At night, the sound of the watch-drums was distinct. These must surely be signs of fine governance. Yong said, "Xiyan is indeed..."
"Virtuous one! You are a celestial messenger and an excellent official. Today you have jointly recommended [this man] to the court; this is precisely like the story of that very episode.
Your virtue does not fall short of that of Minister Zhang Zhongding. This old monk is advanced in years;
I pray that Lord Wu will request the imperial edict for him to succeed me as abbot. Only then would it truly be a fine matter for the monastic community. Lord Wu—

I was deeply pleased. That very day, I dispatched an invitation. On that same day, I moved [the Master] to Jianfu Temple. This is indeed the essential method of monastic communities for selecting worthy individuals to succeed as abbots.
Xuedang said: "A golden embankment spanning a thousand *li* can be breached by an anthill; the beauty of a white jade disc is marred by a single flaw. How much more so in this case!"
The unsurpassed, wondrous Way is not merely a matter of golden embankments and white jade; likewise, greed, desire, anger, and hatred are not merely matters of ant-hills and blemishes.
The essential point lies in being upright and prudent in one's resolve, diligent in one's practice, steadfast in one's maintenance, and perfect in one's cultivation.
Only then can one benefit oneself and benefit others.
"Jin" (金) should be viewed simply as the character for "iron" (鐵), taking the sense of solidity. "Di" (堤) refers to a riverbank; "hui" (潰) means to breach or leak.
"Rang" (壤) refers to the *shang* insect (a type of earth cricket); it also refers to the *shang-xi* species, which, though small, are most numerous—this serves as a metaphor for the three poisons.
Xuedang showed this to students as the essential point for fixing one's will, exerting effort in conduct, maintaining firmness, and cultivating beauty.
It is said: A student of the Way must have an extremely firm resolve and conduct, like an embankment cast from raw iron;

even ants and insects can do nothing to it. If it were made of earth or sand—substances of the same kind—and many people did not attend to its repair and sealing, it might at times be perforated by them; how then could one maintain such firmness in cultivation?
Furthermore, it must be unstained, like a beautiful, clear, and lustrous white jade. Not even a hair’s breadth of flaw should exist;
for if there were so much as a single hair’s breadth, people would abandon it and no longer cherish it—how then could it be considered unstained?
This incantation of the unsurpassed, wondrous Way is not merely comparable to a golden embankment or white jade.
This is the case. Furthermore, greed, desire, hatred, and anger are not merely comparable to the flaws of an ant or a wasp.

For one who studies the Way, what is most precious is to establish a correct resolve, to practice with reverence and diligence, to be courageous and energetic, to maintain steadfastness, and to cultivate with sincerity and integrity until one is fully perfected. Only by doing so can one truly subdue one's own emotions.
"And thus he guarded the minds of others.
Xuetang said, "When I was at Longmen, Chuanbing 'Iron Face' was residing at Taiping.

Someone mentioned that not long after Chuanbing had left his hometown on pilgrimage, he heard that his home temple had been destroyed by fire overnight, reduced entirely to ashes. Upon receiving this letter, Chuanbing threw it away..."
Dì remarked, "It merely disturbs people's minds" (*Dōnghú jí*).

*Xuěyìn* (burnt embers) refers to the state where burning has ceased and nothing remains. Xuētáng borrowed past events to encourage students, saying they should resolutely apply themselves to the practice of *chán*.
When I was at Lóngmén in Shūzhōu, Tièmiàn Bǐng was residing at Tà...
Ping. Some say that Huibing was a man who loved the Way with sincere earnestness.

Not long after he first set out on his travels away from home, he heard that the monastery where he had received his formal training had been destroyed by fire, leaving not even a hair’s breadth of anything behind.
When someone brought a letter to him, Huibing took it but did not look at it; he threw it to the ground and said, "This merely disturbs the mind."
[He] listened. Such earnest devotion is truly rare. Xuetang said to Master Huichan:
"In my early twenties, I heard the words of the 'Dwelling Alone' gentleman: 'If there is no master within, one cannot stand;
if that which is outside is not correct, one cannot act. These words should be practiced throughout one's life; they are the undertaking of the sages and worthies."

This is complete. I have treasured these words. Whether dwelling at home to cultivate the self or leaving the household to study the Way, even down to leading oneself and presiding over the multitude, one must be like a scale or a steelyard in determining weight, or like a compass and square in forming squares and circles. To depart from this is to lose the standard in every matter.
Huicān’s name was Huiguang. He resided at Guīfēng in Xìnzhōu. He was a successor of Xuētáng Xíngjī.
At the age of twenty-something, barely past his teens, he alone compiled the *Jūshì Guǎnglù*. It is said that this was the girdle of Xuētáng himself;
it served as a standard for the Dharma rules. Xuētáng stated that the undertakings of sages and worthies value the principle of centrality and correctness. I am twenty...
In my early twenties, I once heard the words of Master Du: "Regarding matters for which there is no sovereign within the breast, one must by all means not establish them;
regarding matters that are not upright on the outside, one must by all means not practice them."
These two phrases should be practiced throughout one's entire life. The deeds of the sages and the worthy are fully contained within them.
I have always worn these words upon my person: while at home, I used them to cultivate my own character;
when I left the household life, I used them to advance in this Way; and upon entering the monastic order, I applied them to guide my conduct as I faced the world at large.
Assembly, it is like comparing lightness and heaviness with a set of scales, or determining squareness and roundness with a carpenter’s square and compasses.
If one discards these two methods of expression, then every single phenomenon and every principle will go astray, and there will be no standard for the Dharma.
Xuetang said, "Whenever Gao'an presided over the assembly, he would invariably say, 'Among you, there must be those who possess true understanding.
I asked him the reason for this, and Gao'an replied, 'Have you not seen how Guishan said: "In your conduct, look to the superior; do not vainly follow the mediocre and base"?
Throughout my life in the monastic community, those who did not sink into the ranks of the ignorant were all guided by these words, even amidst vast crowds."
The base are many; those with discernment are few. The base are easy to associate with; those with discernment are difficult to approach.

If one can truly exert one’s own will amidst this, it is like a single person facing ten thousand enemies. When the power of vulgar habits is exhausted, one becomes a truly outstanding man of immeasurable capacity.
I have followed these words throughout my life, and only then was I able to remain true to my vow of leaving the household life (*pravrajyā*). (From the *Guanglu*)
"Manqie" (謾且) means "to be arrogant. "Tingchaoba" (挺超拔) means "to stand out preeminently"; "tingli" (挺立) means "to stand upright and distinct.
"Molianghan" (沒量漢) is a term for a "great man" (dazhangfu). Xuedang exhorted students, saying they should emulate those good people who possess true insight.
Gaofeng, when presiding over the assembly, would invariably say, "In this vast multitude, there must certainly be good people. Because of this, I once asked him about it.
"How do you know this? Gao'an replied to me, "Have you not seen what Guishan said:
'In your conduct and movements, look to those who are superior and good; do not merely follow those who are base, foolish, and vulgar.

Throughout my life among the great assembly, that I did not fall into the ranks of the base and foolish was entirely due to the power of these two phrases. [He continued: "In a crowd of many people..."

As for "dwelling": it refers to living amidst a vast multitude of diverse people. Among them, there are many base individuals who do not study what is good, while those with lofty and subtle insight are few.
It is easy to associate with and learn from the base, yet it is difficult to find and draw near to the virtuous.
One must each have one's own independent resolve; indeed, one must be able to exert oneself through one's own efforts.
One must maintain great resolve amidst these conditions. It is like a single person who, summoning heroic courage, enters the midst of nine armies and confronts ten thousand men as one.
One must exert all strength to sever the habitual defilements of the ignorant, cutting them away completely until nothing remains.
Only then can one be called a true, upright, peerless, and extraordinary Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa). High!

Ananda answered me with these words. Throughout my life, I have relied upon them for practice; only then was I able to cultivate according to the Dharma, not failing the aspiration that led me to leave the household life once and for all.

Xuetang said to Qi'an: "In your official duties, you must weigh matters according to their relative importance. Before speaking, you must first reflect; ensure that your words accord with the Middle Way and do not lean toward partiality.
If you act impulsively or with haste, it is rare for such efforts to succeed. Even if they were to succeed, they could never be entirely secure.
While among the assembly, I have fully observed both its benefits and its ailments; only those of virtue can win others over through broad-mindedness."

I constantly hope that those of future generations who possess the will and strength to practice will examine this carefully and put it into action; only then will it become a source of sublime benefit.

Lingyuan once said: "Ordinary people, when reflecting inwardly in their daily lives, are often able to understand clearly; yet when they engage with external affairs and their minds run outward, they immediately lose their harmonious integration."

Having lost the integrity of the Dharma-body, if you truly desire to succeed to the task of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and to enlighten future generations, you must constantly examine and reproach yourself.

Furthermore, the name of your hermitage is "Shouren" (Maintaining Humanity), and you are a successor of Xuedang Xingxiu; yet your conduct is biased and not upright. To enlighten others, one must first rectify oneself.

"Fa" means to initiate. "Jian" means to restrain and bind. "Ze" means to reprimand and exact. Xuedang said that Chan'an was examining his words and scrutinizing his conduct, asserting that they should accord with the Middle Way.
One who bears the Dharma and employs administrative officials must weigh matters appropriately, giving weight to what is truly weighty.

When dealing with matters that are light, one must first reflect and reflect again, contemplate and contemplate once more when speaking, striving solely to accord with the middle way and ensuring nothing is improper.
If one acts with haste and excessive force, there will rarely be any success;
even if something is briefly accomplished, in the end one will certainly be unable to ensure that every detail is perfectly complete. I, [the author], while among the multitude...

Among men, having personally witnessed these perils and fully understood this corrupting malady, there are only virtuous and worthy persons who, through the virtue of their magnanimity, inspire others to submit.
They constantly pray that those of future generations may possess great resolve, talent, and strength.
Examine and deliberate thoroughly before acting; only then will it be excellent and beneficial to others. Lingyuan once said:
"When ordinary people dwell in leisure or remain alone, they gather their minds to illuminate within, and for a moment everything is clear and lucid.
However, when they encounter and engage with worldly affairs, their minds scatter outward in response, and they can no longer maintain integration and harmony, thereby losing their purity."

Regarding the essence of the Dharma: if one possesses the capacity for the Mahāyāna and truly desires to take up the responsibility of carrying the ancestral Buddhas' and patriarchs' wisdom-life, and to manifest the principle inherent within both the monastic and lay communities, one must constantly examine and restrain one's own body.
This was to reproach his own mind.
When Master Huaguang Ying’an resided at Mingguo, Xuetao never failed to visit him for even a single day.
Whenever there were those who spoke of him privately with criticism, Xuetao would say: "My nephew Huaguang does not delight in profit or seek fame; he does not praise first and later disparage."

"Arong’s union was merely a superficial fit; he was not lacking in flattery and artful speech. Furthermore, his realization of the Way was clear and lucid, and he moved with effortless ease whether departing or staying.
Such a patch-robed monk is hard to find; I certainly hold him in high esteem" (from *The Anecdotes of Qian’an*).
Ying’an, whose name was Tanhua, was the dharma heir of the patriarch Xueqiu Long. While Ying’an resided at Mingguo, Xuetang visited him daily.
Among the monastics, some privately discussed the matter, saying that since Xuetang was the elder brother of his uncle, it would be inappropriate for him to humble himself by visiting.
Xuetang then explained to them: "This nephew Huazhi is a man of upright conduct; he does not delight in wealth."
He was not interested in profit, nor did he crave fame or reputation. He did not boast of his excellence beforehand only to disparage it later;
he did not flatter others to gain favor or seek inclusion through expedient conciliation. He did not affect artful expressions or employ clever, pleasing speech.
Furthermore, his insight into the principles of reality was penetrating and clear; his conduct regarding entry and exit, or staying and leaving, was洒脱 (suōshuǎ) and unencumbered. Such was the monk.
"Among those who are not easily found, I therefore visit him daily and hold him in high esteem.
Xuetang said, "When a student’s temperament (qi) overcomes their resolve (zhi), they become a petty person; when resolve overcomes temperament, they become an upright and virtuous gentleman;

when temperament and resolve are in balance, they become worthy sages who have attained the Way. There are those who are stubborn and headstrong, refusing counsel and admonition; this is driven by temperament."
It is so. A man of upright character, even if forced to do what is not good, would rather die than act otherwise;
it is his will (*zhi*) that causes this. His temperament (*qi*) is what he is endowed with. Will is where the mind is directed. Ji said: "Temperament is the functional power (*li-yong*);
will is the essential substance (*dao-ti*) of the Way. Xuetang showed that one must not speak of temperament and will in isolation. A student possesses functional power.

To lack the substance of the Way while possessing its function is to have utility without substance; such a person who exclusively displays their talent and strength will inevitably become a petty individual who brings about ruin.
To possess the substance of the Way while lacking its functional power is to have substance without utility;

although such a person cannot manage affairs or benefit others, they may still serve as an upright and honorable gentleman. Regarding these two—functional power and the substance of the Way—[the former]...
When these qualities are fully perfected, one becomes a virtuous sage who has attained the Way.

As for those whose nature and temperament are rigid, stubborn, and perverse—refusing to accept the instruction of the *ghanṭā* (the wooden gong)—it is the force of their innate energy that causes this.
A person of upright character, even if coerced into committing evil until they reach the brink of death, will not shift or change.
That their minds are not divided is due to the influence of their resolve toward the essence of the Way. Those who wish to become sages or worthies—how could their will and spirit be partial?

Xuetang said: "When Gao'an resided at Yunju, Puyun Yuan was the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera), Yicai was the Secretary (Upādhyāya), Baiyang Shun was the Librarian (Bhāṇaka), Tōngwu-tou was the Guest Master (Karmadāna), Xianzhenmu was the Rector (Vaiyāvṛtyakara), Huarui was the Assistant Steward (Vaiyāvṛtyakara), and Yongrui was the Chief Administrator (Karmadāna).
All of them were men of virtue and accomplishment. Yongrui, in particular, was always frugal and austere."
He did not light the lamp oil for the permanent residence. His nephew Hua teased him, saying, "If you are to become an elder in the future, your nostrils must be upright;
how can you consider this sufficient? Fayong’s nephew did not respond. Although Fayong was frugal in his own conduct, he was exceedingly generous toward others.
He received those coming from the four quarters without the slightest sign of weariness. One day, Gao’an saw him and said:
"It is truly difficult to find an attentive head monk (jian-si). Furthermore, you must oversee the monastery’s permanent assets (chang-zhu) and ensure they are not neglected or lost.

The Head Monk replied, "Any failure on my part is but a minor transgression. For the Master to honor the worthy and treat scholars with such magnanimity—welcoming all like the ocean and accommodating all like a mountain, disregarding even the most minute details—is truly the mark of a Great Virtue.
Gao-an simply smiled. Thus, there arose the colloquial expression within the monastic community (cong-lin) for him as the "One Who Uses the Large Bowl" (an anecdote).
Puyun Yuanming was a successor of Gao’an Shangu. Yicai Sengshui was a successor of An Zhiyan.
Baiyang Mingfashun was a successor of Foyan Qingyuan. Wutou Mingfatong was a successor of Changlu Liaoching.
Zhenmu Mingzhengxue was a successor of Foyan Qingyuan. Yongzhi was a successor of Shuanglin Degong, who was himself a successor of Gao’an Shangu.
As for his successor, Xuetang recommended Gao’an. This abundance of finding worthy successors serves as an explanation for those who follow the Dharma after him;

indeed, Gao’an’s success in finding such people can be called magnificent. During his tenure at Yunju, he served as a model for the monastic community and inspired the junior students through the presence of the Head Seat Yuan Puyun.
Furthermore, for the management of literary correspondence and the drafting of official communications for the mountain gate, [he relied upon...]
There was a monk named Cai who served as the secretary. There was the storekeeper Baiyang Shun, who took charge of the scriptures, repairing and mending those that were damaged or moth-eaten.
There was the guest prefect Tong Wutou, who was responsible for receiving guests and providing incense and tea.
There was the rector Xianzhenmu, who oversaw the assembly and exhaustively attended to their needs. He [the abbot] took charge of...
Regarding the distribution of money and rice for daily use, there is the Vice-Abbot Hua-zhi;

regarding the diligent tending of incense and lamps and the reception of officials, there is the Supervising Abbot Yong-zhi. Monks with such titles are all of Mahayana capacity and possess virtuous conduct.
Yong-zhi, in his ordinary dealings, is upright and frugal, never wasting the monastery’s regular provisions.

While he was staying at the oil lamp, his nephew Hua-zhi teased him, saying, "If you are to become an elder in the future, your nostrils must be upright and straight; only then can you perform such duties.
How could you possibly do so now simply because you did not light the communal oil lamp today? I fear that by then, you will not have reached the level you have today."
Furthermore, Yongzhi never failed to respond to others. As for Yongzhi’s character, although he was personally frugal and austere, he was nonetheless exceedingly generous toward others.
He received those coming from all quarters without showing even a trace of weariness or fatigue.
One day, Gao’an saw him and remarked, "It is not easy to find a *jian-si* (superintendent) who exerts such dedication as this."
"You must further examine and understand this. You are to oversee all matters, both great and small, pertaining to the monastery's permanent assets, ensuring nothing is neglected or lost.
Da-yong replied to him, saying: "As for Da-yong, even if there were errors or misunderstandings, the fault would still be minor.
It lies with you, Master, to be able to honor those of virtue and treat those of the Way with distinction, like the ocean that receives all things, like a mountain..."
Yong did not inquire after trivial or minor matters; he was truly a person of great virtue. When Gao’an heard others say this was quite appropriate, he merely smiled.
Thus, within the monastic community, there was the nickname "The One Who Uses the Large Bowl," which was indeed a fitting title for him.
Xuetang said: "When a student does not know where the Way is directed, they seek out teachers and friends to inquire and investigate it.
Since a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) cannot transform others through the Way alone, they rely on students to assist and support them.

Therefore, when one who possesses virtue and the Way presides over a monastery (zhao ti), a Dharma community is established; there must necessarily be worthy and wise monastics (shami) present—these are the 'tigers'."
The whistling wind is piercingly cold; dragons gallop and clouds arise. In the past, Mazu of Jiangxi manifested his great capacity and great function through Baizhang and Nanquan;
Shitou of Nanyue established his great wisdom and great capability through Yaoshan and Tianhuang.

Therefore, that we have met once in a thousand years is beyond doubt according to the treatises. It is as buoyant as a swan’s down encountering the wind, and as powerful as a great fish leaping through a valley;
all are manifestations of natural momentum. Thus, it has led to the establishment of monastic groves and the enhancement of the glory of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
When my late teacher resided at Longmen, one night he said to me: "I possess no virtuous achievements and am unable..."

"Hao has returned to the lakes and seas as a patch-robed monk; in the end, he brings shame upon the Elder of the Eastern Mountain. Having finished speaking, he wept bitterly. I have often reflected on this:
those who act as teachers of the Dharma today are separated from the ancients by a factor of ten thousandfold (Letter to Zhuanan).
"Zan" (贊) means to assist and support. "Xiao" (嘯) refers to making a sound by pursing the mouth. "Lie" (冽) describes the appearance of severe, biting cold.
"Xiang" (驤) refers to horses prancing, rising and falling as they leap. "The tiger roars and the dragon soars" is entirely a metaphor for the meaning of a person practicing the Way.
The name of Yaoshan was Weiyen; the name of Tianhuang was Daowu; both were successors of Shitou Xiqian. "Yi" (翼) means wings.
However, when the wings are fully extended, even the great geese and swans are drenched by the same downpour;
this refers to the giant fish spouting foam that forms rain. "Panshan" (潸然) describes the flowing of tears.
Xuetang held fast to antiquity while governing the present, explaining to those who serve as teachers that they must prioritize finding true disciples. Students do not understand this.

As for the direction toward which this principle tends: one must brush aside the grass and gaze upon the wind, seeking out an enlightened master and questioning virtuous friends through diligent inquiry.

The royal law cannot allow this principle to be monopolized by a single individual; therefore, it promotes the worthy, nurtures virtue, and evaluates talent, commissioning capable officials to provide assistance and support.
Thus, those who preside over monasteries (*caityas*) possess a profound understanding of principle and a broad capacity for inclusion.
As a patriarch of virtue who establishes the Dharma seat, there must be worthy, sagacious, and wise monastics;
when the master of the Dharma finds the right person and the student finds the right teacher, they harmonize with one another.

This is like "like sounds responding to like sounds," where the tiger’s roar brings forth the wind, and "like energies seeking one another," where the dragon’s ascent causes the clouds to rise. The harmony between teacher and disciple is much like this.
This is it. In the past, the "Horse Colt" of Jiangxi trampled the people of the world;
through Baizhang, Hai, and Nanyuan Yuan, his great capacity and great function were revealed. The path at Shitou on Mount Nanyue was slippery;
through Yaoshan Yan and Tianhuang Daowu, his great wisdom and great capability were made manifest. Thus, this rare encounter of a thousand years has dawned all at once.
In perfect accord. In discussion and discourse, there is no doubt beneath a single word. It is like the great garuḍa spreading its wings upon encountering a typhoon;
it is also like the kun-yin and jing fish leaping from the valley to meet a torrential rain.
These are all matters of natural momentum; they are not the result of forced effort. In Nan Yue of Jiangxi, the flourishing of realized persons is of this very caliber.
Thus, the merit of establishing this monastic community is not small, and the enhancement of the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' radiance is likewise great;
how could this be a mere coincidence? When my late teacher resided at Longmen in Shuzhou, one night he said to me:
"I possess no virtue, conduct, or spiritual accomplishments such that I might flow forth majestically like water seeking its course downward, reaching the Five Lakes and the Four Seas."
"Monks, you ultimately feel shame and remorse; you do not equal Old Dongshan Yanzu. Having finished speaking, he shed tears.
I have often reflected upon these predecessors to observe those who today serve as teachers for devas and humans and provide models for the Dharma.
Compared to the ancients, how could the difference be merely a thousand li? It is ten thousand times further.
Xuetang said, "When I was serving at Longmen, Lingyuan was residing at Taiping. The local authorities disturbed him with ill-intentioned interference."
Lingyuan wrote in a letter to his former teacher: "To be straightforward is what allows one to practice the Way; it is truly impossible to be crooked.

While one might be able to serve as an abbot, this is certainly not my aspiration. It would be better to let my mind roam freely among a thousand crags and ten thousand gullies, daily satiated with fodder and grain."
To fulfill the remainder of his life, why should he be so weary? Within less than ten days, there came a summons from the Yellow Dragon;
thus, following his inspiration, he returned to Jiangxi (as recorded by the Head Seat Cóng).
"Chu-su" refers to grass seeds and rice. "Juan" (pronounced with the *yuan* rhyme) means to look back with concern. "Xun" and "jia": one full cycle of ten days is called a *xun*;

one full cycle of twelve hours (*chen*) is called *jia*. This is the discourse by Xue Tang Xiao, the abbot, intended for those who wish to understand the mechanism of the pivot and recognize when to withdraw or advance.
In the past, when I was at Longmen in Shuzhou, Lingyuan was the abbot of Taiping Temple. Local officials disturbed him with improper conduct.
Lingyuan wrote to my late teacher, saying: "Only by being straightforward in heart and straightforward in action can one practice the Way.
However, one must not act with a crooked body or adopt a crooked stance; yet, it is precisely through this that one can serve as an abbot. Furthermore—

"This is not my aspiration. It would be better to let my body and mind roam free in a place of supreme height and depth, eating grass seeds daily and enjoying the remainder of my years. Why then do you look back with such longing toward this place, refusing to let it go?
Within eleven or twelve days, there was an invitation from the ancestral seat of Huanglong; I then accepted it."
Taking this opportunity, he crossed at Xunyang and returned to Jiangxi.
Xuetao said, "Lingyuan is like a fellow monk who once remarked: 'The ancients have said that it is like making a wooden or earthen figure.
When making a wooden figure, one first desires the ears and nose to be large, and the mouth and eyes to be small. If people were to criticize this...'"
The ears and nose, which are large, can be made small; the mouth and eyes, which are small, can be made large. Suppose one were to fashion an earthen figure;

if its ears and nose were initially intended to be small, and its mouth and eyes initially intended to be large, people might criticize it. Yet, those same ears and noses that were small can be made large, and those mouths and eyes that were large can be made small.

Although these words concern a minor matter, they may serve as a metaphor for matters of great importance. When scholars face practical affairs, they must exercise discernment in what to adopt and what to reject.
"Disgusted by the three [worlds], he contemplated them; he may be called a person of loyalty and integrity" (*Jiwen*).
An idol is a statue. A wooden image is called a "wooden puppet" (*mumu*); an earthen image is called an "earthen puppet" (*tumu*).
Master Xuetang said that Lingyuan liked to compare people to objects, weighing their merits and demerits, and remarked: "The ancients had a saying: 'For example, it is like making...'"
They are like earthen or wooden puppets. When making a puppet, the ears and the bridge of the nose must initially be made extremely large;
the lips and the eye sockets must initially be made extremely small.
People may criticize this, thinking it is incorrect, because they do not understand why the ears and the bridge of the nose should be large so that they can later be pared down to make them smaller.
Furthermore, as for why the lips and eye-sockets are small: they can be carved open and made larger.
When fashioning an earthen figure, the ears—including the lobes—and the bridge of the nose must initially be made small; whereas the lips and eye-sockets must initially be made large.
If people criticize this, considering it incorrect, it is likely because they do not understand that the ears and the bridge of the nose should first be small.
What can be used to fill that which is large and make it great? What can be used to fill that which is large in the mouth, lips, eyes, and nostrils and make them small?
Although these words concern a minor matter, they can truly serve as a metaphor for the great matters within the monastic community (saṃgha).
When a practitioner of the Way faces a situation, whether taking or rejecting, they do not decline to reflect deeply or savor the significance of their actions.
"He can be considered a person of loyalty and profound sincerity. [The character for "ear" (耳) with a "droop" (垂) below it is pronounced "duo.
Xuetao said: "When Wanan sent Gaowan to visit Tiantai and returned, he told me: 'There is a head seat named Deguan.'"

For thirty years, he had hidden his form within the Star Rock, his shadow never leaving the mountains. When Lord Geng of Longxue served as the regional governor, he specifically sent for him from Ruiyan.
Zhi-guan declined the invitation with a verse, saying: "For thirty years I have kept my door closed alone; How could an official summons reach these green mountains?
Do not trade my lifelong leisure beneath the forest trees For the trivial affairs of the human world. The imperial mission arrived once more.
In the end, he did not comply. Master Geng sighed and said, "Today’s Yinshan is like this.
Wan’an said, "There was an elder who could remember his words; he said: 'Not embodying the root of the Way, one sinks into birth and death; encountering objects, the mind arises.'"

To act according to fleeting emotions and thoughts, with a cruel heart and fox-like cunning, practicing flattery to deceive others, fawning upon those in power for acceptance, pursuing fame and profit, deviating from the truth to follow delusions, and turning one's back on awakening to unite with the dust of the world—such things a man of the Way beneath the forest trees would never do. I said:
"Guan was also one of the middle-ranking spirits among the monastics" (anecdote).
Wan’an’s name was Doyan; he was a successor of Dahui Zonggao. It is not clearly known who the Head Seat Guan succeeded in the Dharma.
A "shifu" (official tally) refers to a bamboo tally held by an envoy, upon which a letter of invitation is written. Regarding "Yishan," this refers to what was said when Dongshan Cui visited Yishan.
A "wolf" (*lang*) is so called because it is greedy and harms living things. An "intermediate spirit" (*jiangqi*) refers to a person of exceptional character. Xuetang cited [this].
This shall serve as a warning to those who lack virtue yet seek fame. When Wàn’ān sent Gāo’ān on his way past Tiantái and returned, he said to me:
"The Head Seat Déguàn has lived in seclusion at Jǐngxīng Rock for thirty years, never venturing beyond the borders of Mount Tiantái. The Imperial Scholar Gěng served as the Prefect of Tāizhōu."
The Abbot (Shou) specifically invited him to emerge from seclusion at the ancient monastery of Suiryak (Suiryan). Although Guàn held his aspirations in high esteem, he declined with a verse, saying:
"For thirty years I have kept my door closed alone, Manifesting that for long I have been estranged from the world.

How could a tally of such a nature reach the green mountains? This statement implies that the green mountains are extremely remote from the dusty marketplace; for what reason, then, would one go there?
A letter of communication: Do not trade my lifelong leisure beneath the forest for the trivial affairs of the human world.
To a recluse of the forest, leisure is what is most precious. As the ancients said, "Thirty-six thousand [moments] cannot be exchanged for half a day"—the value of this can be known.
How could the trivialities of Ruigan possibly be traded for it? Seeing that the verse he composed was solitary and wondrous, Lord Geng [responded].

Later, messengers were sent again to invite him, but he ultimately refused to comply. Master Geng sighed in admiration and said, "Was there only a high-minded recluse dwelling in the mountains in days of yore?
Today, too, there is such a high-minded recluse dwelling in the mountains; he is a peer of the likes of those great men.
Wan’an also told me, "At that time, fortunately there was an elder who was able to record these events."
As for those who speak of "pervading" [the truth], it is said that they refuse to fully realize the root of this Way. They wallow and drown in the ocean of birth and death;
encountering objects, they give rise to a mind of grasping and rejecting; following their emotions, they give rise to views of self and others.
Their seductive charm is like that of a fox, while their greed and malice resemble the heart of a wolf. They deceive others with crooked conduct and rely upon power and influence.

To occupy a position for the sake of reputation, to follow worldly trends in pursuit of fame, or to schemingly seek profit while deviating from the truth—these involve chasing after delusions, turning one's back on awakening, and uniting with the sensory dust.
A person who aspires to the Way beneath the forest trees would ultimately refuse to do such things.
I also remarked that the Head Seat Deguan was likewise an extraordinary man among the monastics.
Xuetang was born into a family of wealth and nobility, yet he never displayed an air of arrogance. He lived a life of frugality and simplicity, remaining naturally detached from worldly affairs.
While residing at Mount Wugu, a monk offered him an iron mirror. Xuetang said, "The mountain stream is clear and limpid;
even a hair can be reflected therein. What need is there to keep this? He ultimately declined the gift. (From his *Xingshi*)

The water of the Cizi River is clear. This record concerns the lifelong dwelling place of Xuetang, who, though born into a family of great wealth and high status, never displayed any air of arrogance, extravagance, or haughtiness.
He remained composed in his own station, practicing moderation and frugality;
his mind was refined and upright, yet he had no attachment to material things. While serving as the abbot of Wujishan, a newly arrived monk presented him with an iron mirror.
Yuan said, "The mountain stream is crystal clear, limpid and pure; even a single hair or a single strand of fur can be seen therein without exception.
What would you do with this? In the end, he simply refused it and declined it;
this may be called integrity.
Xuetang was compassionate and benevolent, practicing loyalty and reciprocity. He honored the worthy and respected the capable. He rarely uttered frivolous laughter or vulgar speech from his mouth;

he was free of haughty obstructions and never displayed violent anger. Yet, regarding matters of departure and adherence [to principles], he was extremely upright and pure. He once said: "The ancients studied the Way..."
He was indifferent toward external things and had no personal preferences; he even forgot about rank and position and abandoned fame and sensory pleasures as if it were effortless.
Yet, when scholars of today exhaust all their clever efforts, they ultimately cannot achieve this. Why is this? Their resolve is not firm and their focus is not singular;
they treat the matter as something merely ordinary. (From the *Xingshi*)
Loyalty (*zhōng*) and reciprocity (*shù*). Loyalty means exhausting one’s own potential; reciprocity means yielding to others. "Vulgar speech" refers to coarse and lowly language.
"Principles" refers to the integrity of what one maintains. "Artifice" means cleverness. "A mere likeness" is a colloquialism meaning it does not matter.

[The Master] recorded that Master Xuetang possessed benevolence through principle and compassion through virtue. Through loyalty he exhausted his own potential; through reciprocity he yielded to others. He was a worthy man.
He honors those worthy of honor and respects those who are capable. Rarely does his mouth utter jests, mockery, or vulgar speech. He is neither aloof and haughty nor harsh and obstructive;
he is never arrogant, violent, or prone to anger. Thus, whenever he leaves one monastic grove or enters another community, [he is received with respect].
During that interval, he was exceedingly upright, dispassionate, and pure. He once said: "The sages of antiquity devoted themselves to studying this Way;
regarding all worldly affairs, they did not interfere at all. They were tranquil and free from desire, entirely without greed or attachment.
Thus, even those who possessed power and rank forgot their status, and those who had a fine reputation and prestige abandoned it."
Regarding sounds and forms, it seems as though one need not exert effort to be able to forget them and cast them aside.
Yet, the practitioners of today exhaust so much mental energy and employ every conceivable artifice, yet in the end they cannot achieve success;
they ultimately remain helpless before this very matter. Why is this so? It is because they lack that which is forged from raw iron.
Their aspirations and actions are firm and resolute, yet they lack earnestness and single-minded focus; they treat their practice as something trivial.
This is why they fall short of the ancients.
Xuetao said: "When Sijian resided at Yunyan, he was prone to anger and abuse within his quarters, such that the monks all retreated as if facing a precipice.

Attendant Fang said: 'One who acts as a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) practicing the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to command the humans and devas ought to regard students as their own infants.
Yet now, you are unable to bestow the compassion of sorrow upon them or grant the grace of consolation; to employ the Middle Way [in this manner]—'"
"The teachings of the Buddha—how can you treat them like enemies? To see them and revile them—is this the way a *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend) applies his mind?

Sī-mind (Si-xin) dragged his staff and pursued him, saying: "With such a view as yours, it is certain that one day you will sycophantically serve those of power and position, fawning upon the influential and wealthy, and baselessly selling out the Buddha-dharma to deceive the ignorant masses. I cannot bear this, and therefore I have used these harsh words to stir you."
What else could there be? It is simply a desire for them to know shame, reform their faults, cherish this aspiration without forgetting it, and become good people in the future.
(Recorded by Chan Master Cong)
The attendant at that time was named Huifang, styled Chaozong; he was a successor of Huanglong Nan. "Cāndatā" refers to a compassionate mind and a heart of profound regret.
"Fǔ'ān" means to soothe and bring peace through compliance. "Zhōnghé" refers to matters of principle that are impartial and free from bias.

"Bǐ" (苾) means urgent or pressing. "Qiúchóu" (仇讎) refers to those who cause harm like bandits. "Gòu" (詬) means to revile. "Chèn" (趂) means to pursue. "Jī" (激) means to stir up or inspire one's resolve.
Xuetang showed this to people so they would recognize the reason for the master’s sternness; he wished for them to reform their errors.
This was not a matter of treating others as enemies or bandits. When Sīxīn was serving as abbot at Yún'ān, during the occasion of entering the inner quarters for private instruction—
Sometimes he mounts a lion and displays the majesty of its prowess, appearing as if angry; sometimes he unleashes the mechanism of swift thunder and flashing lightning, appearing as if scolding.

Disciples who do not understand the master’s compassionate intent behind these "discourses that descend into the weeds" instead mistake the finest nectar for poisonous medicine, perceiving it as anger and abuse. All who encounter him regard him as if he were a precipitous cliff.
And thus [the student] gives rise to despondency and ceases [his practice]. Does the attendant not understand this expedient means?

It is because he wishes to make the student know that the master’s counter-movement and conformative movement are unfathomable even to Heaven, and so he deliberately poses a dialectical question, saying:

"Now, as for one who acts as a Good Knowledge (Kalyāṇamitra), practicing the path of the transmission between Buddhas and Patriarchs, issuing world-transcending commands, and serving as a teacher for humans and devas—"
The Master should have regarded himself as a nursemaid and viewed his students as if they were infants.
Now, on the contrary, he is unable to bestow a heart of compassion and empathy, nor to exercise the virtue of constant, nurturing care.
Instead of using the principle of the Middle Way to harmonize and benefit all sentient beings, how can he act like an enemy or a foe?
"An enemy! Upon seeing you, he reviles, rages, and scolds you; how can such conduct be considered the proper way?
Is this the way a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) applies his mind? At this, Sīxin manifested his great functional power directly, revealing his entire being.
He seized his staff and drove [the monk] away, saying: "Do you still harbor such views? In the future, you will flatter officials and bend your back to serve them with sycophancy."
The powerful and the wealthy exploit the Great Dharma of the Tathāgata to delude the deaf and the mute among the common folk.
Because I cannot bear such things, I have used harsh words to shake them against the wind. How could there be any principle of enmity here?

It is my desire that they come to know the Way and feel shame, that they reform their faults and turn toward goodness, and that longing for it enters their hearts so that they may never again [fall into error] throughout eternal kalpas.

As a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), if one loses virtue and transgresses propriety, how can one serve as a model for future generations?
(This was written to Lingyuan. Xiu Yuan-tong, whose name is Fa-xiu, is the successor of Tian-yi Huai.
Master Si-xin said that those who preside over the Dharma should personally practice it to set an example for later students. Xiu Yuan-tong once said: "If one's own body and mind..."
To be upright oneself while wishing to make the bodies and minds of others upright is what is called losing one's virtue.
To have one’s own body and mind lacking in reverence while wishing to make the bodies and minds of others reverent is what is called violating propriety.
Now, as one who serves as a teacher and model, claiming to be a "good spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*), if one has already lost their virtue and thrown propriety into disorder, how can they be so?
I do not know what you intend to take as the standard by which to provide a model for future students.
Sishi said to Chen Yingzhong: "If one wishes to seek the Great Way, one must first rectify the mind. If there is even a slight degree of anger or resentment, the mind will not be rectified;
if there is even a slight degree of craving or desire, the mind likewise will not be rectified. However, unless one is a sage or a worthy who appears in the world,"
How can one be without love and hate, joy and anger? One must simply not place them before oneself so that they harm one's rectitude;
this is what constitutes success (from the *Guǎnglù*).
*Fen* (wrath) is the intensification of anger; *chi* (resentment) is the stagnation of anger. Chen Yingzhong was called "Dead Heart.
He taught that in seeking the Way, one must take rectifying the mind as the primary focus. If you wish to seek the Unsurpassed Great Way, you must first make your mind upright.
Do not allow even a hair’s breadth of thoughts regarding likes and dislikes to arise. If even a hair’s breadth of wrath arises—
If one harbors thoughts of resentment, one has already lost their rectitude. Even if there is but a hair’s breadth of desire or craving, one has likewise already lost their rectitude.

Unless one is a sage born with innate knowledge or a worthy one who practices with vigor, how could one avoid the seven emotions and six desires while engaging with the world? One must exert all effort to eliminate them. Not...
If one can set aside even a hair’s breadth [of bias] before oneself, thereby eliminating what harms one's rectitude, only then can one be said to have attained rectitude and be able to seek the Way.
How can one who seeks the Way fail to rectify the mind?
Sishin said: "Frugality and letting go are the most direct paths for entering the Way. I see many students whose minds are full of resentment and whose mouths are filled with complaints;
who among them does not wish to follow in the footsteps of the ancients? Yet when one observes their practice of letting go and frugality, not even one in ten thousand succeeds.
They are just like the sons of common families who refuse to study but wish to become officials. Though they may be three feet [tall]..."
"Child," he said, "you know that you certainly cannot do it. (From the *Guǎnglù*). "Jié" (節) means to exercise restraint, moderation, and frugality.
"Fèn" (憤) is the state of mind when one seeks to penetrate a principle but has not yet attained it; "fěi" (悱) is the expression of one who wishes to speak with the mouth but is unable to do so.
These terms describe the earnest resolve with which one shows others the essential method for entering the Way and the principles of frugal economy.
This is the root of both the mundane and the supramundane. Why is this? Because one must let go of speech and practice frugality;
if one must let go even of these, how much more so of that which is neither frugal nor parsimonious? If one cannot let go, then even what is a good thing becomes a hindrance.
This too constitutes an obstacle to the Way; how, then, can there be a path of entry? Therefore it is said: "Frugality and letting go are the most direct shortcuts for entering the Way.
I often observe students whose minds are filled with agitation as they seek penetration, yet whose mouths are full of hesitating and struggling words.
However, I wish to speak of those who do not love to follow in the footsteps of the ancients.
When you observe those who wish to succeed the ancients yet fail to let go of parsimony, it is difficult to find even one in ten thousand.
Once they cannot let go of parsimony, how could there be any principle in their desire to succeed the ancients? Tell me, what kind of person is this?
What is it like? It is like a householder’s son who, without having read a single word of a book, wishes to become an official;

even a three-year-old child knows this is impossible. One who enters the Way without relinquishing worldly attachments, or one who seeks office without reading books—by this analogy, it can be understood.
Sishin said to Zhantang, "Among students, those who possess talent and discernment, as well as loyalty, integrity, and a sense of honor, are the highest type.

Those whose talent may not be great but who are conscientious and possess a broad capacity are the next best. As for those who harbor depravity and wait for opportunities, changing their ways according to circumstances—"
"This is truly a petty person. If he were placed before others, he would surely destroy the monastic community and defile the Dharma-gate" (Shilu).
Sishin said that Tanzhang should know how to discern people's worth; the temperaments of students are of many kinds, and [this] is but a brief [account].
To speak of this, there are three types. First, those who possess talent, learning, and insight;
who are loyal and not deceitful, trustworthy and grounded in reality, principled and steadfast in their conduct, and righteous and appropriate in their actions—such individuals are the superior type.

Second, those whose talent and insight, though not particularly sublime, are respectful, prudent, and possessed of great capacity for judgment—such individuals are the intermediate type. Third, those who...
Or perhaps harboring private and deviant thoughts within their chests, they observe from the sidelines and watch with longing;
according to the shifting tides of victory and defeat, they alter their minds without any sense of regard or consideration. Such individuals are truly petty men.
One must strictly avoid employing such people. If they are brought forward in the future, they will surely destroy the *caityas* and bring defilement upon them.
This is the gateway through which the Dharma transforms others;
one must not fail to be cautious. Sīxin said to Caotang: "In the duties of a *zhuchi* (abbot), the essential point in speech and action lies in sincerity and trustworthiness.
If words are sincere and trustworthy, what they evoke will necessarily be profound. If words are not sincere and trustworthy, what they evoke will necessarily be shallow. Words lacking sincerity—"
Regarding the matter of faith: even among the common people in their daily lives, they are still unwilling to act with deceit for fear of being cheated by their neighbors and fellow villagers;
how much more so for one who is the master of a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*), acting as a successor to the Buddhas and Patriarchs to propagate the Dharma?
If one’s speech and conduct lack sincerity and trustworthiness, then what forest-dwelling monks from the lakes and seas would follow them? (From the *Huanglong Shilu*)

"Sincerity" (cheng) is the true principle within the mind; "faith" (xin) is the noble speech that accords with righteousness. Twelve thousand households constitute a district (xiang), and five hundred households constitute a clan (dang).
Sishin addressed the abbot of Caotang, stating that one must take sincerity and faith as the primary tenets of discourse.
In all matters pertaining to the office of an abbot, every word spoken and every action performed must ultimately be sincere and must ultimately be trustworthy.
When one speaks with genuine sincerity and without falsehood, that which moves others will surely penetrate to the very bone and marrow.
If one speaks with falsehood and lacks sincerity, that which is intended to move others...
Such people are ultimately superficial and frivolous; their words are unsubstantial and their deeds are false.
Even ordinary commoners would not dare to act in such a way, fearing they would not be trusted by their neighbors and would lose face.

How much more so for one who is the master of a temple (saṅghārāma), acting as a successor to the Buddhas and Patriarchs to proclaim the Dharma and transform others—how could one utter a single word or carry out a single deed [without integrity]?
If one’s mind lacks true principle and one’s words do not reach the meaning, with what can one move and serve others,
such that the monks of the four seas and five lakes would come of their own accord to follow them?
Sishin said: "Those who seek profit cannot be given the Way; those who seek the Way cannot be given profit.
It is not that the ancients were unable to practice both together; rather, it was because their circumstances made it impossible.

If profit and the Way could be practiced simultaneously, then merchants, butchers, wine-sellers, and common folk peddling their wares would all be able to pursue them. Why then would one need the ancients? [They] abandoned wealth and honor and forgot..."

Regarding fame and achievement: would one not rather extinguish the will for glory and dissolve all wisdom amidst the vast mountains and great marshes, drinking from mountain streams and eating from the trees for the rest of one’s life?
It must be said that if profit and the Way are practiced together, they cannot coexist without conflict;
it would be like pouring water from a leaking cup into a scorching cauldron—it can never suffice. (This was written in response to a letter from Han Zicang.)
To travel about selling is called *shāng* (merchant); to sit and sell is called *jiǎ* (peddler). To slaughter living beings is called *tú* (butcher); to sell wine is called *gū* (liquor-seller).
*Lǚ* refers to the gates of a neighborhood; *fù* means to carry a load on one's back. To buy cheaply and sell dear is called *fàn* (trading); a *lóu zhī* is a leaking wine vessel.
A "scorching cauldron" refers to a boiling pot. One who has realized the death of the deluded mind understands that the Way and worldly profit cannot proceed together.
Those who seek wealth and profit understand only profit; how could they understand the Way? Those who seek the wondrous Way understand only the Way.
How could one possibly pursue profit? It is not that the ancients were unable to practice the Way and pursue profit simultaneously;

rather, it is because the forces of these two cannot coexist. If wealth and profit and the Great Way could be practiced together, then merchants who travel and shopkeepers who sit, butchers, tavern-keepers, commoners of the villages, and even porters and servants—all would be capable [of practicing the Way].

One exchanges material gain for the Great Way. Furthermore, why must one follow the ancients who renounced the wealth of the four seas and the nobility of the Son of Heaven, forgetting their vast achievements and widespread fame, extinguishing the fire of their hearts and annihilating their intellects?
One would end one's life in a desolate, vast marsh, in a place remote from the world, drinking from mountain streams when thirsty and eating the fruits of trees when hungry.

To insist that the wondrous Way and worldly profit can proceed side by side without contradicting one another is like taking a broken, leaking wine cup and using it to pour water onto a blazing cauldron.
The source of a leaking cup pours its contents into rivers and streams, yet it cannot fill them; how much less could it fill the Voca (沃焦) cauldron?
It is certain that such a vessel can never relieve this urgent need. [The character for "flame" (火) with the radical "mouth" (口) below has the pronunciation *là*.]
Sishin said: "In the past, when our late master Huìtáng was traveling through Eastern Wu, he saw Yuánzhào being invited to Jìngcí Monastery.
The monastics and laypeople of Suzhou and Hangzhou vied for him without ceasing. One said, 'This is my teacher; why do you seize him?
The other said, 'He is now my teacher; what right do you have over him? (According to one version in the *Línjiān lù*)."
Yuanzhao was the founder of the school; Tianyi was his successor. Sixin expressed that he possessed virtue, and moved the hearts of others with such longing that they would not cease speaking of him.
My late teacher, Huichang, once traveled to Gusu in Eastern Wu and saw Master Yuanzhao accepting an invitation to Jingci Temple in Lin’an, Hangzhou.
Monastics and laypeople from both Suzhou and Hangzhou vied for his presence.
They would not let him go. The people of Su clung to him with deep affection, like a child longing for its mother, saying, "This is our teacher, the people of Su.
How can you people of Hangzhou act so improperly as to seize him away from us?
The people of Hangzhou, however, were eager to have him, like those who encounter nectar when thirsty, saying, "Now he is our teacher, the people of Hangzhou. You..."

How could it be that [the practice] was restricted solely to the people of Sō (Silla), such that it has persisted for so long? That the virtue of its perfect illumination moves people to feel such deep admiration is precisely why this is so.
Sixin was residing at Cuoyan when he heard that Juefan had been exiled to the overseas regions.

As Juefan’s route passed through Nanchang, Sixin invited him to return to the mountains, where he hosted him for several days and saw him off with generous gifts. Some remarked that Sixin’s moods were inconsistent, to which Sixin replied, "Juefan is a virtuous monk.
Previously, I spoke of him with great intensity to blunt his sharp edges; now that he has suffered such injustice, this is simply his true nature."

[The matter] was divided; I handled it according to the principles of monastic propriety. Those who understand the matter remarked that because Sishin was selfless toward others, he acted in this manner (from the *Xishan Jiwen*).
"‘Cuan’ (竄) means to drive away. ‘Dao’ (道) refers to the road. ‘Nanchang’ is Hongzhou. ‘Qing’ (卿) is an honorific for ‘you’ in the past. ‘Li’ (罹) means to encounter or suffer.

This records how Sishi (死心) was residing at Cuoyan (翠巖). Hearing that Juefan (覺範) had been banished overseas, he traveled through Hongzhou on his way and sent a messenger to invite him into the mountains.
He welcomed and entertained him for several days, presented him with generous gifts as parting fare, and saw him off."
Someone said, "In the past, Sishin did not take pleasure in Juefan; why does he now take pleasure in him?
Such instability in his changes is like this. Sishin replied, "Juefan is a patch-robed monk who possesses both the Way and virtue.
My anger in the past was to suppress him with extreme words, so that he would not allow his sharp edges to be revealed to the outside."
This was to avoid calamity. Now that I have encountered this innocent and unjust adversity, it is due to my own past unwholesome karma.
By concealing my brilliance and remaining obscure, I have led myself to this state; such is my natural lot.

As for me, I have always conducted myself according to the principles of the great tradition of the monastic community and acted with what is appropriate. How could I harbor feelings of joy or anger? Only those with true discernment would understand this.
"Both" refers to the state of mind at the moment of death. Being public-spirited rather than private, one manifests this quality toward others. Deshi Xin said to Caotang:
"The late Master Huaitang said, 'A person's magnanimity and kindness are derived from their innate nature.
If one forces them to be fierce, it will certainly not endure. If fierceness does not endure, one will instead become an object of contempt and arrogance for petty people. However...
The natures of the heterodox and the orthodox, the good and the evil, are likewise innate; none of these can be altered.
Only the nature of the "mean person" is susceptible to moving upward or downward, and can thus be transformed through instruction (Shilu).
Sishin said, "The innate dispositions of people, as held by Cudang, include those who can be taught and those who cannot be taught.
My late master, Huichang, spoke of human endowment: there are those who are relaxed and easygoing, and those who are grave and substantial;
all are naturally so by their heavenly nature, and there is nothing that can be forced. If one attempts to teach them through compulsion, how could they ever become courageous?"
How can one’s diligence be sustained over a long period? If it is vigorous yet not enduring, one will instead be treated with contempt and disdain by petty people.
This applies equally to the perverse and the upright, as well as the good and the evil;
all are driven by their innate nature and none can be altered. It lies solely in being neither perverse nor...
Regarding that which lies precisely between the non-virtuous and the non-evil, those whose natures are fixed in the middle can be led upward and can be led downward;
they may be approached and transformed through teaching. As Ji said: "This, too, is a doctrine applied according to the individual."
Except for those with the icchantika disposition, how could there be anyone who cannot be transformed?

In the past, when the celestial Māra used a hundred stratagems to harass and disturb the World-Honored One, the World-Honored One transformed him using both gentle and harsh speech until he was completely subdued.
What more need be said of this?
Master Qing of Caotang said: "The fire that consumes the plains arises from a tiny spark; the flood that destroys the mountains originates from a single drop.
When water is minute, a handful of earth can block it; yet when it becomes vast, it drifts away timber and stones and submerges hills and mounds.
When fire is minute, a ladle of water can extinguish it; yet when it becomes vast, it scorches cities and towns and incinerates forests and mountains."
Now, as for the waters of attachment and the fires of hatred, how could they ever be different?

When the ancients cultivated their minds, they guarded against thoughts before they were born and emotions before they arose; thus, the effort they exerted was extremely subtle, yet the achievement they reaped was exceedingly great.
When their emotions and natures become disordered and love and hatred attack one another, they harm their own lives and harm others;
this is perilous and dangerous, beyond the possibility of rescue.
Cao Tang’s name was Shanqing; he was a successor of Huanglong Zuoxin. *Liao* means a blazing fire. *Yíngyíng* (fireflies) refers to shining together;
it signifies something smaller than a fire. *Fánshāo* means to burn. In a letter from Master Cao Tang Qing to Han Zicang, he showed people the method for cultivating the mind.
Generally speaking, human beings love water and resent fire; this is most difficult [to overcome].
The embankment is the most difficult to construct. All those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables, and only then are they able to construct the embankment and achieve subjugation.
This fire of anger is like a great conflagration that spreads across the wilderness.
This water of craving arises from what is like a single flickering spark; it is like a great flood that has breached a mountain embankment, yet it begins as a mere trickle.
When the water is but a single drop leaking through, one can block it with a handful of earth held in both hands;
little effort is required. However, once the force of the water becomes vast and surging—
It drifts along large timbers and small stones, submerging hills, valleys, and mounds.
When the fire has only just begun as a single spark, a single ladle of water can extinguish it; the effort required is slight.
Yet when the fire's power becomes full-blown, it scorching the prefectures, capitals, and counties, and burning down vast mountain forests. Compare this to [the fire of] craving—
The water of drowning and the fire of anger—how could there ever be any difference between them? Those who study the Way in antiquity cultivated their minds;
this was their embankment. When a single thought had not yet arisen and the seven emotions had not yet been stirred, they held fast and remained steadfast.
Thus, they exerted the least effort while reaping the greatest reward. Once a single thought...
Once born, one’s nature and emotions become entangled. When the seven emotions arise, love and hatred attack one another within oneself;
they destroy one’s life-force, and others may injure one’s physical form. If things reach this state, is one not in peril?
Its peril will surely come; it is certain that this cannot be saved. One who governs the mind—should they not guard their thoughts before they have even arisen?
Caotang said: "The abbot has no other task than to scrutinize human affairs and to have a thorough knowledge of those above and below. For human affairs..."
When one is discerning, there is harmony between the internal and external; when the upper and lower levels communicate, all affairs are orderly. This is why an abbot’s tenure is secure.
When human relations cannot be scrutinized and the conditions of those below cannot be communicated upward, the upper and lower levels become discordant and all affairs fall into contradiction.
This is why an abbot’s tenure fails. Furthermore, if the leader relies on his own cleverness and is fond of adhering to biased views—
Failing to understand human nature, they discard universal consensus to prioritize their own authority and abolish public discourse to exercise private favoritism.

Consequently, the path for promoting the virtuous gradually narrows, and the way of entrusting matters to the multitude becomes increasingly obscure. They disparage what has not yet been seen or heard, while remaining complacent in their habitual prejudices and delusions.
To wish that such a person maintain the teachings so they may be transmitted far into the future is like walking backward while seeking to move forward; it will ultimately lead nowhere.
"Unreachable" (from a letter to Shantang).
"Qian" means the multitude. To retreat is out of fear of running; to seek what lies ahead is to strive to catch up with one's journey. Regarding the abbot of Caotang at dawn:
wishing to transmit the Great Tradition far and wide, he ought to understand human relations and penetrate the principles of things. The abbot has passed away.
There is a distinct method. Its essential point lies in careful scrutiny and detailed examination of human nature, so as to fully comprehend those above and below.

If one thoroughly investigates and verifies each person’s disposition until it is clearly understood within the mind, then internally, when assigning duties, and externally, when addressing the assembly, the spirit and will will naturally harmonize. This applies from the abbot above down to all [the subordinates] below.
The quarters will naturally have their vital energies flowing smoothly and harmoniously, such that all affairs will flourish together and everything will be orderly.

If one dwells as an abbot in this manner, things will certainly be settled. However, if one fails to examine human relations one by one and does not bring them to clarity within one's own mind, then the sentiments of the community will not reach upward, and the intentions of those above will not extend downward. Consequently, the vital energies will not circulate; once the higher [energies]...
To act in opposition and, furthermore, to be perverse and contrary, yet for one’s spirit and energy not to falter—then all affairs will fall into neglect as they contradict one another.

An abbot who conducts himself in this manner will surely bring ruin. Moreover, if the presiding master lacks the virtue of humility and self-effacement, relying instead on his own cleverness and natural talent, he will delight in stubbornly adhering to one-sided views and fail to understand the nature of all things.
Regarding principle and emotion: they discard public opinion to exalt their own arbitrary authority; they abolish public discourse to pursue private favors and petty benefits.
For this reason, the path for advancing the virtuous gradually becomes narrow and constricted, while the way of bearing the multitude grows ever more obscure until it is unheard of.
Though they have never actually seen or heard of these things, they disparage them and refuse to listen.
One who remains settled in their own habitual defilements and self-imposed obscurations, refusing to change them—
yet who desires to uphold the Way of the Dharma so that it spreads throughout the four seas and its fragrance flows for a hundred generations— is like a traveler who, despite being on the road,
greedily seeks a destination that can never be reached. This applies to one who leads the great assembly and desires [to achieve such a goal].
If one wishes for the life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs not to be severed, can one afford not to apply one’s mind to this?
Caotang said: "When a student establishes themselves, they must do so with integrity; do not allow others to harbor private criticisms. Should one fall into heterodox views,"
Then one will be unable to establish oneself for the rest of one's life. Formerly, the attendant Dàyáng Píng was highly esteemed by the monastic community for his mastery of the Way;
yet because his inner heart was not upright, those who discerned the truth condemned him, resulting in a lifetime of misfortune and leaving him with nowhere to turn at the time of death.
How much more so, then, must those who serve as masters of a particular region stand in reverent awe? (A letter to a Secretariat Official)
Attendant Píng. The details of his life are found in the *Yìnyì Hézhù* (Combined Commentary on Phonology and Meaning). Tàiyáng Míng’ān, whose name was Jǐngxuán, was a successor of Liángshān Guàn.
His appearance was rugged and unconventional. In the *Cǎotáng Jǐngxuézhě Chùxīnyào Dànduànshuō* (Caotang’s Essential Instructions for Students on Rectifying the Mind), he states:
"When a student establishes themselves, this very body must have a mind that is fundamentally upright; one's conduct must be firm."

Be careful not to allow others to harbor secret criticisms or judgments. Once you are exposed by such heterodox arguments and accusations, this very body will ultimately be unable to establish itself.
In the past, Attendant Taiyangping had long been within the quarters of Ming’an;
his mastery of the Way was highly esteemed and respected by the vast assembly of the monastic community, yet it was because the state of mind within his breast was not upright and clear.
Anan had a prophecy concerning "hand-crossing. Those with wisdom and discernment all disparaged it, causing him to be unable to establish himself throughout his life.
He suffered through hardships until old age and died in the jaws of a tiger; in the end, he could not avoid Ming’an’s prediction and had no place of refuge upon death.
Yet, how much more so must those who study ensure their mental conduct is upright if they are to become leaders of a region?
As a teacher of the fourfold assembly, you must ensure that your mind remains upright; you should especially be reverent and cautious in this regard.
Caotang said to Master Ru: "The late Master Huītáng remarked that among the vast crowds of people, the worthy and the unworthy follow one another.
Since the gate of transformation is so expansive, it is inevitable that there will be distinctions of intimacy and distance among them. It simply requires a slight effort..."
In selecting [talent], if one’s talent and virtue accord with public expectation, one must not distance them because of personal resentment;
if one’s insight is mediocre and common, detested by the masses, one must likewise not favor them because of personal affection.
In this way, the worthy will advance of their own accord and the unworthy will withdraw of their own accord; thus the monastic community (saṅgha) will be at peace.

However, if the abbot delights in indulging his private whims and exercises authority over others solely according to his own likes and dislikes, then the worthy will remain silent while the unworthy vie with one another to advance;
consequently, the regulations will fall into disorder and the monastic community will come to ruin. These two points constitute the essential principles for maintaining the leadership of a monastery.
If one can truly examine and practice this, then those nearby will be delighted and those far away will spread the word.
What cause for concern would there be that the Way would not prevail, or that practitioners would not come to admire it? (From the Shushan Stone Inscription)
To love and draw near to; to distance oneself from what is alien and evil. *Jianfeng*: to seal up; to remain silent and not speak. "Cao Tang" refers to the Master (the Abbot).
A person who presides over a monastery should draw near to the worthy and distance themselves from the treacherous. This is spoken from the perspective of recognizing the great principle.
My late teacher, Huìtáng, once said: "Within the midst of the throng, in the center of the vast multitude, dragons and snakes are intermingled, and ordinary people and sages are mixed together."
Living together, gentlemen and commoners follow one another in succession. The gate of transformation through the Dharma is the broadest and greatest;
within it, the worthy cannot help but draw near, and the ignorant cannot help but remain distant.
It rests solely with the presiding authority to exercise a degree of refined discernment: those who truly possess talent and virtue, and who accord with the hearts of others, [should be appointed].
Regarding those whom others look up to, one must not, because of what one personally dislikes, treat them with anger or distance;
for if one does so, they will indeed appear ordinary and commonplace, failing to accord with the hearts of men and becoming objects of aversion.
Likewise, regarding those whom one personally desires to love, one must not treat them with intimacy and affection; if one acts thus, the Way of the superior man will flourish and grow day by day.
When they advance, the way of the petty person wanes and they withdraw of their own accord; thus, the monastic community will certainly be peaceful and secure.
