However, if the leaders are prone to loftiness and self-importance, indulging their private whims and adhering solely to their own biased views—advancing when their hearts are pleased and withdrawing when their hearts are angered—then the way of the superior person wanes among men while they remain silent and mute, and the way of the petty person flourishes.
Yet, as they compete with one another for advancement, the primary cords are not maintained and the secondary threads are not held;

every matter is erroneous and chaotic, and the monastic communities will certainly fall into ruin. These two matters are truly no minor details, but rather the fundamental principles of a *zhuchi* (abbot).
If one can indeed examine them with discernment and put them into practice, then nearby, the fourfold assembly will rejoice, and far away, the monks will proclaim them.
"In that case, what cause for concern is there that the Way of the Dharma will not be widely practiced? Why would the monastics of all quarters not come to admire it?
Caotang said to the Head Seat Kung: "Since the beginning of the monastic communities, none have achieved such a flourishing success in gathering disciples as Shitou, Mazu, Xuefeng, and Yunmen.
In recent times, only the two elders Huanglong and Wuzu have truly been able to gather them in."
The eminent monks from the four quarters, according to the depth or shallowness of their capacity and the presence or absence of their talent, were brought forth and employed.

It was as if riding a light carriage yoked to fine steeds: by gathering the six reins and exerting the whip and goad, with the ability to restrain or urge them at a mere glance, what destination could one not reach? (From the *Guanglu*).
The first seat-holder was named Xingkong; he was a successor of Huanglong Wuxin. Xuefeng was named Yicun;
he was a successor of Deshan Xuanjian. Yunmen was named Wenyan; he was a successor of Xuefeng. One whose talent surpasses ten thousand men is called "Ying" (Heroic);

one whose wisdom exceeds a thousand people is called "Quan" (Reformed). That which is equipped with chariots and horses is called a "Jia" (Carriage); the finest among excellent steeds is the "Si Yi" (Quadriga).
This refers to riding in a carriage drawn by four horses. There are six reins. In a single carriage with four horses, each horse has two reins, totaling eight;

however, the two inner reins of the two outer (cān) horses are fastened to the front crossbar (shè), leaving the two outer reins of the cān horses and the two reins of the two inner (fú) horses that flank the axle. Thus, there are four reins for the two fú horses.
Distributing [the reins] between both hands constitutes the six bridles; "whip" refers to the horse-whip. "Gu" means to look back; "pan" (also written as "yan") likewise means to gaze.
Caotang [Dongshan Liangjie] addressed the Abbot Kong, saying: "One who is skilled at winning over people must be skilled at employing them.

He further stated that since the inception of the monastic communities (*sōlin*), it has been through masters who have found those with the Way that the tradition has flourished greatly; it is not otherwise.
From Shitou Xiqian, Mazu Daoyi, Xuefeng Yicun, and Yunmen Wenyan— these four sages of recent times—
down to the two great elders Huanglong Qing and Wuzu Faian alone, have truly been able to gather and assemble the talented and eminent monks from the four directions,
East, West, South, and North, according to their respective capacities and measures, whether shallow or deep. And...
Regarding talent, ability, temperament, and character—whether they possess capacity or lack it—one should cultivate and employ them accordingly.
It is like a person riding a light carriage: seated upon it, with excellent and spirited horses harnessed before him, he holds the six reins in his hands and vigorously applies the whip.
In the mere space of looking left and right, as he alternates between tightening and loosening the reins, [the carriage moves forward].
There is nowhere it does not reach; it is like entering a land of nothingness, where there is no obstruction whatsoever.
The practice of the Way by the Fifth Patriarch of Huanglong was also similar to this.
Cao Tang said: "For a monastic administrator, there is nothing else required but to be cautious regarding the faults of partiality and autocracy.
If one does not allow oneself to be dominated by the words of those who have first entered [one's ear], then the slanderous flattery and sycophancy of petty men will be unable to cause confusion."

For the dispositions of the multitude are not uniform, and impartial discourse is difficult to perceive. One must examine their benefits and harms and deliberate upon what is acceptable and what is not;
only then may one proceed to act (from the *Shushan Shilu*).
A warning to the abbot of a grass-thatched hall: do not listen to one-sided accounts or allow yourself to speak with self-will.
For an abbot, there is no other essential method than to be cautious regarding partiality in listening and prudent regarding self-centeredness.

Regarding these two faults, one must further refuse to accept what has been said first; then, the petty men who are slanderous, sycophantic, and flatterous will find no opening through which to enter.
Riding [this vehicle], the master himself will no longer be deluded by others. For when people are gathered in great numbers, their dispositions differ;

thus, the principles of ultimate impartiality and correctness are difficult to manifest. One must possess a sharp and brilliant mirror of wisdom to scrutinize their benefits and harms, and a penetrating eye of insight to discern what is acceptable and what is not.
Only then may one, with a free hand, pick up [the appropriate response]. With a free hand...
Use [it]. Walk with confidence; in this way, you may perhaps succeed. Caotang said to Shantang:
"In the affairs of the world, as long as right and wrong are not yet clear, one must be cautious.

Once right and wrong are clear, decide them according to principle. Let only the Way be the standard; resolve matters without hesitation. If you act thus, the treacherous and sycophantic will not [prevail]."
He was able to confound them; even those with forceful eloquence could not shift his position (according to the *Qingquan Jiwen*).
Sandang’s name was Daozhen, a successor of Letan. Caotang said that Sandang could discern and adjudicate between right and wrong.
One must speak in accordance with reason. Regarding all matters, there is right and wrong; until these are clearly understood, one must not fail to exercise caution.
Once right and wrong are distinct, one should resolve them through correct principle (*samyak-nyāya*). What is correct principle? It is the ultimate consummation of the Way (*dharma*).
Having attained the ultimate consummation of the Way, one resolves all matters—what further doubt could there be? If one can truly act thus...
Thus, those who are treacherous, depraved, or sycophantic shall be unable to cause confusion; those with glib tongues and sophistry shall be unable to seize the truth.
For one who wishes to determine right from wrong, how could they possibly overlook this principle?
When Master Zhèn of Shāntáng initially declined the summons from Cáo-shān, the Prefectural Governor sent an official letter urging him to accept. Shāntáng declined it, saying:
"If I were to eat fine rice and chew fatty meats, becoming a monk who covets fame, it would be better to wear clothes of grass and subsist on wood."
[This was] by the rustic of Mount Yin (recorded as heard from Master Cailian of Qingquan).
It is a species of millet; it resembles millet but is larger, and its flavor is exquisite. "Nibbling" refers to eating; "fat and abundant" refers to rich flavors.
This records the story of Master Zhen of Shantang, who initially did not accept the invitation from Cao Shan. The Prefect of the local commandery...
The Magistrate sent a formal letter urging him to leave the secular world for the monastic life. Shantang declined with a letter, saying:

"If I were to follow my worldly impulses, fattening my mouth and filling my belly with fine grain and delicacies to become a monk who covets fame, it would be better to exalt my aspirations, wear white rushes for clothing, and eat only large fruits as a hermit of the mountain wilds. The Magistrate... [omitted].
"You must surely grant me your understanding and forgiveness.
Shantang said, "Snakes and tigers are not the natural enemies of hawks and vultures; why then do hawks and vultures shriek after them?
It is because they harbor different intentions. Oxen and pigs are not the mounts for magpies; why then do magpies flock together and perch upon them? It is because..."
Because there is no dualistic mind. Long ago, Zhaozhou visited a hermitage master. It happened that the master was serving rice.
Zhaozhou said, "When a crow sees a person, why does it fly away? The master was at a loss for an answer. He then repeated Zhaozhou’s previous words and asked him about them.

Zhaozhou replied, "It is because I harbor a murderous intent; therefore, those who harbor suspicion toward others are themselves suspected by others. Those who forget about external objects are likewise forgotten by objects."
Forget it. Those ancients who kept company with snakes and tigers were those who skillfully realized this principle. Master Pang said, "The iron ox fears not the lion’s roar;
it is like a wooden man beholding flowers and birds. These words encompass it all (from his letter to Layman Zhou).

The "chī" and "yuán" are malevolent birds that seize and eat fledglings; they are the *qúyú*, commonly called "bāgē" (magpies). The "què" is the *xǐquè* (joyful magpie). "Yù" means to drive or employ as a horse.
"Wǎng" means to be bewildered and unable to fathom. "Niè" means to tread upon. "Wǔ" means to gather together; it carries the sense of companionship.
"Lǎo Páng" refers to Páng Yùn of Xiāngzhōu, whose courtesy name was Dàoxuán and who was a native of Héngyáng County. He attained the Dharma from...
Mazu also, in his "Discourse on the Way of Forgetting Artifice" given at Mount Tang, established a parable and posed a question and answer to himself, saying:
"A venomous snake or a ferocious tiger are not the natural enemies of hawks and crows; yet upon seeing them, the latter immediately shriek and clamor."
What is the reason for this? It is because both parties harbor hearts of mutual alienation and aversion.
When taming oxen or breeding pigs, one does not have a magpie drive them; yet when a magpie perches upon their backs, they mount and ride it. What is the reason for this?
It is because both parties lack any heart of alienation or aversion. Formerly, Zhaozhou went to visit...
There was once a head monk of a hermitage who happened upon the serving of rice. Zhaozhou asked, "When a crow sees a person, why does it fly away?
The head monk was at a loss for words. Zhaozhou then repeated his previous question to him. The head monk replied, "It is because I harbor a murderous intent.
Judging by this karmic occasion, one can see that for this reason I cause doubt in others, and others will certainly cause doubt in me as well.
I have forgotten external things, and since those things are likewise constant, they also forget me.
This is precisely why the Venerable Yan-yang of antiquity could have snakes and tigers come into his hands to eat from him and constantly keep them as companions;
he was truly adept at this principle of forgetting things through non-doubting. Master Pang said: "Simply be without mind toward the myriad things, and there will be no person and no self."
What prevents the myriad things from constantly surrounding one? The Dharma is without self. An iron ox has no fear of the lion’s roar;
it is just like a wooden man beholding flowers and birds. Sentient and insentient beings are all of one essence.
These words fully express the principle of attaining this state without doubt and forgetting external objects. Later, it was said that Shantang [referred to] Zhaozhou visiting the hermitage.
The Master spoke. "The preceding and succeeding seals correspond; there is no difference in the mind.
One may say it is like filling a perfect vessel with water—it does not leak so much as a single drop. If one understands it in this way, what excellence is there in this koan? I once wrote:
"For the sake of another's grain of rice, one loses one’s provisions for ten thousand years. And I wrote: "Why do you fly away?"
[The Master] said, "I have saved half of it. The host looked bewildered and said, "That still leaves something to be desired.

Stepping back on his previous point, he asked, "In this double case, there is a mind of killing; it is said to corrupt the men and women of a household—do you maintain both [of these views] together?"
"To provide for the worthy is to invite broad laughter.

Mount Tang said, "In the method of governing subordinates, favor must not be excessive; if it is excessive, they become arrogant. Authority must not be too severe; if it is severe, they harbor resentment.

If you wish to bestow favor without inciting arrogance, and to exercise authority without causing resentment, that favor must necessarily be bestowed upon those who have performed meritorious service; it must not be otherwise."
To falsely attribute [fault] to others is improper; majesty must be exercised only toward those who have committed offenses, and must not be indiscriminately extended to the innocent.

Therefore, though grace may be profound, people feel no arrogance; though majesty may be stern, people harbor no resentment. Even when merit is insufficient to be praised, the reward is already generous;
even when a crime is insufficient to be censured, the punishment is exceedingly severe. Consequently, petty men will deliberately give rise to arrogance.
"Enmity," "to govern and lead," "to manage," "arrogance," "self-conceit," "guilt," and "transgression. In this letter from Shantang to Minister Zhang,
he sets forth the principles for one who occupies the position of superior to govern and lead those below, and to harmonize and control them.
Regarding the laws for people: when bestowing favors and grace, one must not exceed the bounds of what is appropriate for others.
If they are excessive, they will not serve to benefit the people, but will instead cause them to develop a nature of arrogance. When using authority to restrain people, one must not be overly severe.
If it is too severe, it will not serve as a warning to the people, but will instead cause them to give rise to resentment.
This is what causes one to feel regret in one's heart. One desires to bestow much grace so that people do not become arrogant, and to exercise fierce majesty so that people do not harbor resentment.
Grace must necessarily be bestowed upon those who have rendered meritorious service; it must not be wantonly conferred upon those who have performed no service.
Majestic authority must necessarily be applied to those who have committed transgressions; it must not be indiscriminately extended to those who are innocent.
As for those who are guilty, how could imperial favor hinder thorough investigation? Yet people will not become arrogant. How could majestic authority hinder stern commands?
Yet people will not harbor resentment. Even if one’s meritorious service were not great and thus insufficient to merit reward, [the principle remains].
The favors bestowed have already been extensive, while the offenses were originally minor; it is not fitting to impose heavy reprimands or punishments that are excessive.
This will surely allow petty people to find opportunities for exploitation and grounds for criticism, thereby giving rise to hearts of arrogance and resentment.
Shantang said: "The Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs does not go beyond attaining the Middle. To exceed the Middle is to fall into partiality and deviation.
Among the affairs of the world, one must not push to the extreme; to push to the extreme leads to calamity and chaos.

Throughout antiquity and today, there have been many who, failing to exercise moderation and caution, have nearly met with ruin and destruction. Thus, who is without transgression? Only the worthy and enlightened should reform themselves without stinginess."
This is what is called "beauty.
In a letter to Zhao Chaoran from Shantang, he shows that people should be careful regarding the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). He says that one must not be stingy about correcting one's errors;
the way in which the Buddhas of the three periods and the patriarchs of successive generations transmitted the Dharma did nothing more than attain this Middle Way.
The ultimate truth (paramārtha) is the master. If one does not attain the Middle Way, then there will be no master within the breast, and one will fall into partiality and heterodoxy.
Regarding all matters of the mundane and supramundane worlds, one must never seek their absolute fulfillment according to one's own heart’s desire.
If one must indulge every whim, greed will increase and lead to many affairs, giving rise to calamity and disorder.

Among both ancients and moderns, there have been few who were not extravagant and lacked frugality, or who were unrestrained and lacked caution, such that they reached a state of peril where they lost their very lives.
Yet, since humans are not sages, who among them is entirely perfect and free from fault? It is only...
The worthy who preserve the Way and the scholars who have mastered principle do not begrudge changing their faults; it was only recently that they were taught how to become good people.
At Mount Shantang, together with Minister Han Zicang and Chief Seat Wannan Yan Xianzhimu, they took refuge at Yunmen Hermitage.
Minister Han then asked Wannan: "I have recently heard that you were captured by the soldiers of Li Cheng; what plan did you use to escape?"
Tuo said, "Yesterday I was bound and shackled; for days I suffered from hunger and cold, and I thought I would surely die.
By chance, a great snowfall buried the house, and the wall of the room where I was tied collapsed without cause. That night, by good fortune, over a hundred people were liberated.
The Official asked, "When you were under arrest, how did you manage to dispel [the suffering]? Wan’an did not answer. The Official questioned him again, and Wan’an—
He said, "What is there to say of this? We who study the Way take righteousness as our substance; there is only death. What is there to fear?
The official nodded in agreement. From this, one knows that when the seniors of old encountered worldly calamities or faced life and death, they all possessed a clear resolution.
Han Zicang’s famous steed sought instruction from Master Shantang; it served until it reached the rank of Minister.
Li Cheng, in the first year of the Shaoxing era of Emperor Gaozong of the Song dynasty, incited rebellion in Jianghuai and plundered Xiang and Mian, styling himself the Heavenly King Li.
Recorded at Shantang by Han Shangshu Zicang, Wannan Yan Chanshi, Xian, and Zhumucheng.
When several of us were together avoiding the chaos at Yunmen Hermitage, we sat idly.
At that time, Master Han asked Wannan, "I have heard that in the past you were captured by the soldiers of Li Cheng; I wonder what skillful means you employed?"
"Could you have devised a plan to escape? Wan'an replied, "Yesterday I was taken away and bound at all times.
With little food I suffered from hunger; lacking clothing, I froze. This continued for several days in succession, and I calculated that my death was certain beyond doubt.
Unexpectedly, it snowed heavily with sleet, piling high upon the ridges of the roofs. I did not realize that the walls of the cell where I was imprisoned had completely collapsed."
The building collapsed on its own. During that night, by good fortune, more than a hundred people managed to escape this disaster.
The Official questioned him again, saying, "When you were actually being seized by them, how did you manage to deal with the situation?
Wanan perceived that his question was somewhat pedantic, so he remained silent and did not answer. The Official, too, possessed a sincere heart and wished—
This was merely to seek a means to resolve the matter of life and death; therefore, he questioned him again.
Wan’an also truly said to him: "What is there to say about this? We who practice Chan and study the Way do so for the sake of resolving life and escaping death.

For one who has resolved the matter of life and death, how could there be no sense of righteousness? One must not evade when facing peril; it is that which one ought to do according to righteousness."
Therefore, the gentleman takes righteousness as his substance; he does not recklessly covet life—how could he have any fear or cowardice?

The Duke also nodded silently, granting it in his heart. From this, one may know that when the predecessors of old encountered the world’s vicissitudes, especially at moments of calamity, harm, death, or life, they invariably possessed a guiding principle with which to resolve them. [End of preceding section]
When Shangsheng (Shangsheng was present).
Shantang withdrew from Baizhang and said to Han Zicang: "In antiquity, those who advanced possessed both virtue and destiny;
thus they would proceed after three invitations and withdraw after one refusal. Those who advance today rely only on power and force; though they know how to advance and withdraw—"
"One who loses their correctness may yet be called a worthy and enlightened person" (*Jiwen*).
Regarding the record of Bai Zhang’s retirement to Shantang, it was said that Han Zicang explained:

"When people of antiquity saw someone advancing in the world, they invariably possessed within themselves the virtue of modesty to guide others, while outwardly protecting those who admired the worthy and sought [their instruction]."
Regarding the request for the Way: thus, after one, two, and even up to three invitations, he was compelled to comply and enter the world.
Yet, once his karmic conditions were fulfilled and it was logically appropriate to withdraw, he would decline with a single word and depart.

He never acted with even the slightest trace of attachment or lingering delay. Those who seek advancement in the present age rely solely upon power and influence, as well as their own talents and strength.
The ear can discern when one should advance and when one should retreat, thereby never losing the correct path;
such a person may be called a virtuous and worthy man, a high scholar who has attained the Way.

Shantang said to Yuan'an, "When serving as abbot, one must maintain a mind of impartiality. In conducting affairs, it is not necessary to consider what originates from oneself as right and what comes from others as wrong;
in this way, likes and dislikes, or differences in opinion, will not arise in the heart, nor will the airs of violence, arrogance, or depravity."
"One enters through non-self" (*Huàn'ān jí*).
Yǎn-ān, whose name was Zǔxuán, was a successor of Dàhuì Gǎo. Shāntáng addressed Yǎn-ān, saying:
"When presiding over the essentials of the Dharma, one must maintain a mind of public integrity. Whatever the abbot harbors in his breast, it must be impartial rather than partial. In all actions..."
Regarding all matters, it is not necessarily the case that only what originates from oneself can be considered correct.
When the words or actions of another are appropriate, how could one not regard them as correct? One need not be dogmatic in deeming others wrong.
Likewise, if one’s own words or actions are inappropriate, how could one not regard them as wrong?

If one is willing to maintain the mind in this way, then partiality toward the liked and aversion toward the disliked, whether in difference or similarity, and all manner of private corruptions will not arise within the breast;
likewise, various habitual tendencies such as violence, arrogance, perversity, and sectarianism will not emerge.
"Since there are no seams or gaps, one may enter.

Shantang said, "Li Shanglao remarked that Miaoxi’s character and capacity were profound and far-reaching, his integrity and righteousness surpassed those of others, and he was tireless in his pursuit of learning.
He followed me at Baofeng for only four or five years; if ten days passed without seeing him, I would invariably send someone to inquire after him."

Question: "The old man’s entire family was suffering from dropsy. When Miaoxi visited their home, he personally prepared the broth and cooked for them, observing the etiquette due to a younger son toward his father and elder brother.
Upon returning, the Head Seat (Yuanshou) rebuked him. Miaoxi simply responded with 'yes, yes' and accepted the instruction. Those who recognized him knew he was a man of great capacity.
Zantang once said: 'Attendant Gao is a person of a second birth; I regret that I did not live to see him. Zantang.
Upon his passing, Miaoxi traveled over a thousand li to the capital city of Zhugong to seek from the layman Wujin a stele inscription for the pagoda.
That Zantang’s final radiance was preserved was due to the power of Miaoxi (Record of Daily Excursions).
The name of the Founder’s seat is Dōgen. He was the successor of the Patriarch Enō (Yuanwu). He was simply responsive and straightforward.
His feet were marked with calluses from his sandals. Zhugong refers to Jingzhou Prefecture. Both the stupa inscription and the commentary on the phonetics provide detailed accounts.
In the Mountain Hall, [Dōgen] expressed the essential character of Miaoxi (Huiran) to encourage others in their discourse. Li Shanglao of Mount Lu once remarked that as for Miaoxi—
As for this man, his talent, capacity, and breadth of character are serene, clear, and far-reaching; his integrity and sense of righteousness surpass those of ordinary men.
He has taken a delight in academic pursuits, practicing them with diligence and never retreating. He once accompanied me at Baofeng Peak for four or five years.
Human nature is thoroughgoing and meticulous; if one is not seen for ten days, people will surely send others to inquire after them.

Because I, an old man, had disturbed the local earth deity during construction, my entire family fell ill with swelling. Miaoxi personally visited our home, attending to us in person by decocting medicine and boiling congee.
It was like the etiquette observed between a son serving his father or a younger brother serving his elder brother.
Upon returning to Bao Feng, the Abbot reprimanded the monk for serving a layperson; Miaoxi responded with repeated "yes, yes," bowing low to receive his instruction.
There was one who possessed discerning insight and knew that his capacity was extraordinary; he was certainly a man of great potential.
Zantang often praised him with joy, saying, "Attendant Gaomo is a person who has returned to the world for a second time. I am old now;
it is a pity I shall not live to see his future excellence. When Zantang passed away and his body was cremated, [Gaomo recovered] his eyes, teeth, and prayer beads.
Without damaging [the remains] and including the śarīra, Miaoxi did not shrink from the distance of a thousand li.
He set out on foot with his heavy seals, traveling without rest to visit the layman Zhang Wujin at Jingzhou Prefecture in Huguang, in order to seek a stele inscription for the stupa.
Thus, at the end of Zhantang’s life, his "root-bead" remained unimpaired.
This segment of radiance—if it were not for the power of Miaoxi visiting Wujin—who else could have made it manifest?
Master Miaoxi Gaoruo said: "Whenever Tanzhang obtained calligraphic works by former sages, he would invariably burn incense to read them.
He would sometimes have them engraved on stone, saying, 'How could I bear to cast aside the sublime virtue and excellent names of the former saints? Such was his refined appreciation.

Thus, at the time of his death, he had no savings of even ten gold pieces; he possessed nothing but the ink-traces of various worthies from the Tang and Song dynasties, which filled barely two bamboo baskets."
The disciples vied with one another in composing verses in response and received over eighty thousand coins to assist in the rite of *caubi* (Kekan Ji).

This refers to the acquisition [of the relics]. The "calligraphic manuscript" (*moji*) refers to the book of calligraphic inscriptions (*fotie*). *Caubi* is a Sanskrit term; here it means "cremation."
Miaoxi exemplified the integrity of Zantang and was also fond of antiquity, providing an example for later students.
Whenever Zantang obtained ancient books or calligraphic inscriptions by former sages and worthies, he would invariably wash his hands, burn incense, and read them with reverence.
He would sometimes carve them onto stone to ensure their endurance for all time, saying: "How could one bear to neglect the noble names and great virtues of the former sages?"
Was it cast aside? Master Zhantang’s natural disposition was one that prized ancient relics; such was his character.

Thus, on the day of his passing, he had not even ten *liang* of accumulated wealth. All that he possessed were two bamboo cases containing ink-carved calligraphic rubbings of various worthies from the Tang and Song dynasties.
From this, his integrity can be known. Disciples vied with one another to advance [to serve him].
They took the lead and sang verses back and forth to one another, collectively obtaining over eighty strings of cash to assist with the expenses of the cremation and complete the funeral rites.
Miaoxi said, "The Buddha-nature resides at Dayue; the practitioner was scuffling with the local laborers, and the Buddha-nature wished to discipline the practitioner."

Master Zuchao remarked, "If you allow the estate tenants to humiliate and insult the practitioners, it will not only result in the loss of the proper distinction between superior and subordinate, but I fear that petty people will take advantage of the occasion to act with arrogance, and the matter will not proceed. Foxing did not listen.
Before long, a tenant indeed murdered the administrative official (from the *Kaan ji*).
Fóxìng (Buddha-nature) was named Fǎtài; he was a successor of Master Qín. Dìkè was a tenant farmer.
Ōuchuí means to beat with a stick. Zǔchāorán was named Wénzǔ; he was a successor of Tiānyī Huái. To kill one’s superior is called *shì*. Miàoxǐ said:
One who presides over a monastic community must understand the distinctions between superior and inferior ranks.

When Foxing was staying at Dayue, he was fighting with the son of a tenant farmer; Foxing intended to punish the practitioner. Chan Master Chaoran, because of the pure laws of the Sangha, admonished him, saying:
"The laws of the Sangha are fundamentally pure. If you allow a tenant farmer to reprimand and discipline a practitioner..."

This is not merely a matter of losing the distinction between superior and subordinate; I fear that the hearts and minds of those with inferior character will follow from this point, their courage emboldened as they seek large-scale opportunities for mischief, thereby deceiving their masters and showing contempt.
Thus, the affairs of the great assembly will not proceed. If the Buddha-nature does not permit this and one fails to govern the practitioners, it will not be long before the result occurs:
indeed, there was the incident where the son of a tenant murdered the administrative official (jishi). This burdened the monastic community (conglin).
"Those who hold such responsibilities—should they not be cautious?
Miaoxi said, "When Chan Master Chaoran was abbot at Mount Yang, a tenant stole the monastery's grain. Chaoran had long resented the tenant and intended to dismiss him.
He ordered the storekeeper and the attendant to provide a formal statement on his behalf. The attendant wished to protect the tenant..."

The guest observed Chao Ran’s haughty demeanor and attempted to suppress it by forcing him to rise from his seat and leave; however, he instead returned to shouting and refused to comply with the reprimand.
Chao Ran grew angry that the practitioner had usurped his authority and struck both men with a bamboo switch.
It appears Chao Ran was unaware that he had been secretly plotted against by the practitioner. Alas! Such is the craftiness of petty men (from the *Ke’an ji*).
"Suppression" means to constrain and oppress. "Cunning, crafty, and obstinate" refers to those who are full of deceit.

Miaoxi, you who understand the masters of the monastic groves, must know this discourse on the cunning of petty people. When Chaoran was residing at Mount Yang, a tenant stole the monastery’s stored grain.
By his very nature, Chaoran had long disliked the tenant’s disposition and intended to dismiss him, yet he had not yet found the opportunity.
Taking advantage of this opportunity, he ordered the storehouse keeper and the messenger to quickly prepare a formal statement of provisions for him and then drive him away.
The messengers were all among the ranks of the lowly; not only did they fail to provide the statement, but they instead sought to protect him.

Upon investigation, it was found that they possessed a transcendent intent to forcibly compel the preparation of a statement of departure; furthermore, they even went so far as to have local clients shout and clamor on his behalf.
They refused to submit and were unwilling to accept their reprimands. Chao Ran grew enraged, as the practitioners had usurped authority and acted as masters over the local laypeople;
both parties were then brought to order with bamboo rattles. It appears that Chao Ran did not understand the factions of these petty men;
they had been secretly conspiring and were already prepared for rebellion, yet he devised a plan merely to expel them. Alas! These petty men are treacherous, stubborn, and cunning. This is...
Miaoxi said, "Liking and disliking, difference and sameness—these are the common sentiments of humanity. Only the wise and the enlightened are not turned by them.
Formerly, when Yuanwu resided at Yunju and Gao'an retired from the East Hall, [the former] loved Yuanwu and hated Gao'an."
Gaofeng was at odds with Yuanwu; consequently, the monastic communities were thrown into a state of confusion. There arose factions of Yuanwu’s followers and Gaofeng’s partisans.
Observing these two great beings, one sees that they spread their illustrious reputations throughout the land, far beyond what ordinary people can emulate.

It is a pity that they were clouded by the light-minded trust placed in the sycophantic words of petty men, which deluded their intelligence and led them to become objects of ridicule for the wise. Therefore, it is appropriate that they be held accountable.
The Master of the Seat (Zuozhu) Yinzhan and his lineage were men of lofty character (Zhilin ji). "Great Being" (Dashi) is a title for one of virtuous merit.
Master Liang was a native of Shu; he lectured extensively on the sutras and śāstras, and subsequently went to attend upon Mazu.
Having clarified this great matter, he went into seclusion on Mount Xi (West Mountain) in Hongzhou, where no further news was heard for a long time. Mount Yin refers to Longshan in Tanzhou;

it was there that, through attending upon Mazu, he realized the essential point of the mind and subsequently went into seclusion at Longshan. Both of these matters are detailed in the *Yinyi* (Explanations of Pronunciations and Meanings).
When Miaoxi instructs people, he says: "Each of you should maintain right view and refrain from partiality or preferences regarding what is said. As you wish.

Affection arises from what accords with one's feelings and aversion from what opposes them; they differ according to distinctions and coincide through harmony. These are all the fixed and constant emotions of humanity.

Only those who are virtuous and have attained the Way, scholars who have mastered principle, whose insight is lofty and far-reaching, and whose minds are clear and bright, are not turned by affection, aversion, difference, or sameness.
Formerly, when Yuanwu first resided at Yunju, he was—high... [text fragment ends]
When An retired to the Eastern Hall, those who loved Yuanwu came to detest Gaofeng, while those who aligned with Gaofeng were struck with wonder at Yuanwu.

For this reason, within a single monastic community, there arose a tumultuous proliferation of two competing schools, each adhering to its own faction. Observing the conduct of these two great masters, I see...
This man, responding to the capacities of others and engaging with all beings, guided his children and spread his great fame throughout the world;

he was not comparable to ordinary run-of-the-mill people. Alas! Those with clear vision are blind for the three feet before them, and thus they fail to perceive that they have been deluded by the sycophantic words of petty men.
These words confuse the intelligence of the wise, and consequently, they are led astray by those who possess true discernment.
This is regarded as a joke. Judging from all these points, it is truly difficult for one to transcend the world while remaining among men; it is better to withdraw from the world.
This is why Master Liang of the Western Mountain and Yinyan of Tanzhou were men of their generation who held themselves in high esteem—their aspirations were those of noble scholars.

Miaoxi said: "The ancients would shift toward the good upon seeing it and reform upon finding fault in themselves; they led themselves by virtue and followed righteous conduct, intending to avoid blame.
Nothing was more grievous than not knowing one's own evils, and nothing was more admirable than delighting in hearing of one's faults.

Yet, was it truly because the talent, wisdom, and insight of the ancients were insufficient or their discernment unclear that they acted thus? It was surely because they wished to cause those who come after them..."
The world is vast, yet it is narrowed for man by means of the precepts (*śīla*). Now, the breadth of the monastic groves and the multitude of the four seas cannot be known by one person alone;
it is only by relying on the ears, eyes, thoughts, and deliberations of those around him that one can fully grasp their principles and master human affairs.
If one dwells in honor and self-importance, attending only to trivial matters while neglecting the great principles, even a worthy person will not [be able to fulfill his duty].
I understand. The unworthy do not examine things; they do not reform their errors, and when matters are improper, they do not comply.
They act recklessly according to their own whims, showing no restraint or fear. This is truly the foundation of calamity; how can one not be afraid?

Even if there are indeed no people by your side with whom you may consult, you should still take the former sages as your model. How could you allow yourself to be like a fortified city with strong defenses, having no way out?
This is not it. This is hardly what is meant by "receiving the hundred rivers to form the great ocean.
A letter from Miaoxi to Preceptor Bao, concerning the principle that one should emulate the ancients, honor the worthy, and reform one's faults while embracing goodness.
The sages of antiquity, upon seeing the goodness in others, would emulate it and practice that same goodness themselves. When they committed a transgression, they would immediately repent and reform.
They cultivated and perfected their virtues, adhering to upright conduct and practical integrity. They constantly maintained right reflection, purifying their body, speech, and mind.

Among all things that cause anxiety and concern, none surpasses failing to recognize one's own evils. Among all things that are considered excellent, none surpasses delighting in hearing of one's own transgressions.
But could it be that the ancient sages lacked the capacity, wisdom, discernment, or insight, and failed to perceive the principles clearly, such that they required this [to be done]?
Truly, it was intended to ensure that for those of future generations, [the Way] would be established...
The human self is our crimson banner. To tilt the balance toward the vast and expansive while narrowing oneself for others is to serve as a model of dignified conduct.
Indeed, the density of monastic communities and the multitude of people gathered from across the four seas cannot be understood by the solitary insight or vision of a single individual;
ultimately, one must rely upon the ears and eyes of those around them.
I contemplate myriad concerns, hoping to exhaustively fathom the principles of what is appropriate and skillfully encompass the sentiments of the multitude.

Yet, should the ruler dwell in majesty and maintain a sense of self-importance, regarding trivial matters as too small to pass through the gate of the great body politic, neglecting them without regard—then the gentleman will not know of it, and the commoner will not perceive it. From this point on...
Having already committed errors in one's conduct, one refuses to repent and reform. When others all practice good deeds, one again refuses to follow suit.
Acting according to one's own whims without restraint, wild and unrestrained, there is nothing one will not do; one shows no fear or caution whatsoever.
Such a course of action is truly the very foundation for nurturing and growing calamity. How could one not stand in awe? Should it happen that those around you...
It is perfectly clear; there is nothing to be negotiated or inquired about. One should take as one's model the ancient sages of antiquity.
How could it be that one is like a hundred-foot high fortress with ten thousand armored horses and sturdy soldiers—having no gate or path by which to enter?
If it is of such a nature, it certainly does not possess the magnanimity that "contains the hundred rivers to become the great ocean.
It would be well for you to reform your errors and turn toward goodness, seeking virtue to broaden yourself. This is what must be done.
Miaoxi said: "When various quarters nominate an Elder, they must nominate one who maintains the Way and has withdrawn in tranquility.

If such a person is nominated, their will and integrity will become even firmer; wherever they go, they will not destroy the permanent property of the monastery but will instead bring the monastic community (saṃghārāma) to fruition.

This is also how those who preside over the Dharma may remedy the current弊 (shortcomings). Furthermore, as for those who are deceitful, sycophantic, and crafty, they know no shame and naturally flatter those in power."
Regarding the position: if one is already entangled with the gates of the powerful and noble, what further need is there for recommendation?
Miaoxi wrote a letter to Zhuanan discussing the value of recommending the worthy;

he stated that when various quarters recommend elders to serve as abbots, they must certainly recommend those who possess integrity and spiritual practice, yet prefer tranquility and maintain a retiring disposition. Such individuals should be recommended.

Upon entering the world, his aspirations and moral integrity became even more firm and steadfast. Wherever he went, he ensured that what was lacking remained constant and provided what was incomplete;
how could there be any principle of destruction? He supplemented what had not been augmented, and thus every undertaking was surely brought to fruition.
This was also because the presiding Dharma-master possessed the discerning eye of a sage, thereby rescuing the maladies of the present age.
Furthermore, those who are deceitful, sycophantic, wicked, and unprincipled— lacking shame and conscience, and ignorant of modesty—
who naturally resort to flattery and fawning to serve those in power, seeking profit by forming alliances and seeking fame by entrusting themselves to the gates of the influential and noble,
must by no means be recommended. If you wish to recommend worthy talent to succeed the abbot, exercise great caution.
Do not be negligent regarding this matter.
Miaoxi said to the Layman Chaoran: "In the world, only public opinion cannot be abolished. Even if one suppresses it so that it does not prevail, what can be done about public opinion?
This is why when a forest monastery promotes a man of the Way, everyone who hears of or sees him will surely rejoice."
Nevertheless, when congratulations are offered, if even one person among them speaks without sincerity, the multitude will surely sigh with sorrow.
This is truly due to nothing other than whether public opinion is being followed or not. Alas! By this, one may divine the flourishing or decline of the monastic community (from the *Ke'an ji*).
The Layman Chaoran was Zhao Lingjin, Prince of Jun, whose courtesy name was Biaozhi; he was a successor to the Patriarch Yuanwu Keqin.
"Yi" means to suppress, and "e" means grief and sorrow. Miaoxi said that when Chaoran spoke of recommending worthy men, it was ultimately essential to accord with public opinion.
Public opinion is the correct principle of the world and the upright judgment of all time; it is determined that this must not be discarded.
Even if one were to attempt to forcibly suppress it, how could it be done when it has already become public opinion? What can be done about it?
Therefore, within the monastic community, if there is a lack of an abbot or a shortage of administrative officers, if one is to propose...
When anyone hears of or sees a person of right view who has realized the Truth, everyone will surely rejoice and offer congratulations, and the entire monastery will be filled with joy.

Conversely, if one mentions a person of wrong view who has not realized the Truth, everyone will surely be sorrowful and sigh in lamentation, and the whole community will whisper in private discussion. Why is this so? In reality, there is no difference.
This is brought about by whether public opinion is upheld or disregarded. Alas!
By inferring from this, one can know the good or ill fortune, the calamities or blessings within the monastic communities, without even divining them.
Miaoxi said: "Frugality and letting go are the foundation for cultivating one's person and the essential requirement for entering the Way.

Looking back through history at the ancients, there were few who did not practice frugality and letting go. In recent years, however, monks have traveled to the Jing and Chu regions to purchase woolen mats and gone beyond the Zhejiang area to seek spun silk; are they not ashamed before the ancients?"
This is the essential teaching on cultivating the person and entering the Way as revealed by Miaoxi. Generally, habitual defilements are difficult to eliminate;
none is more severe than greed, which is the foremost and most primary of the three poisons.

There is no other method that can serve as its antidote except for the practice of moderation and frugality—this is the sole method capable of counteracting it. Do not be extravagant. This is the method that can serve as the antidote.
The mind of frugality manifests before one, and the mind of greedy seeking naturally falls away.
This is truly the fundamental basis for cultivating oneself and the essential point for entering the Right Path. Observe those ancients of the past:
who among them was not frugal and renunciant? In recent years, Zen practitioners have traveled through the regions of Jing and Chu.

When he went up to Dongshan, did he ask about the "three pounds of flax"? He merely bought a woolen mat. When he passed through the region south of Zhejiang and crossed over Luojia, did he pay homage to Yuantong?
He merely sought spun silk. Is he not truly ashamed before the ancients? How greedy he is!
Miaoxi said: "In ancient times, the virtuous abbots did not personally manage the monastery's assets; they entrusted everything entirely to the administrative officers (zhishi) for management.

In recent times, however, those in charge, relying on their own superior talents and strength, have seen that no matter how great or small a matter may be, it all reverts to the Abbot’s quarters (fangzhang), while the administrative officers possess nothing more than their empty titles.
Alas! If one merely seeks to consolidate a single monastery for the sake of one's own person—"

To ensure that base people are not deceived, that the fundamental principles of governance are not thrown into disorder, and that the discourse of ultimate public righteousness is achieved—is this not difficult? (Letter to Shantang)

Wondrous Joy, you who preside over this monastery, must maintain the great principle and speak accordingly. Since ancient times, when virtuous predecessors presided over monastic communities (*saṃghārāma*), they focused solely on upholding the Great Dharma and uplifting their disciples;
they did not personally attend to all matters themselves, nor did they manage the various secular affairs of the monastery’s permanent property.

They entrusted everything entirely to the administrative officers (*karmadāna*) and the heads of departments, each of whom was responsible for their own specific jurisdiction. In recent times, those in charge have not been so. They themselves—
Relying on their own talent and strength, they consider themselves sufficient;

whether it be a great matter or a small one, they enter the abbot’s quarters and assume concurrent duties, while the administrative officers are merely established as a formal sequence, their titles being held in vain. Alas! It is truly a pity.
If you, with your own physical constitution and firm resolve, do not abandon diligent effort, but take control in your hands and preside over the community—

Regarding the affairs of the monastery, one must certainly ensure that base individuals do not remain ignorant or obscured regarding our monastic laws, and that the regulations are applied without deviation in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, one must ensure they are fully in harmony with the assembly and that discussions are conducted with the utmost integrity and fairness—is this not indeed difficult?
The presiding master need only uphold the great principles and essential tenets of the Dharma. This will suffice.
Miaoxi said: "When yang reaches its extreme, yin arises; when yin reaches its extreme, yang arises. Prosperity and decline multiply one another; this is the natural law of heaven and earth.

Only when there is abundance and success is it appropriate for the sun to be at its zenith. Therefore it is said: 'When the sun is at its zenith, it begins to wane; when the moon is full, it begins to diminish.
Since the fullness and depletion of heaven and earth wax and wane with the seasons, how much more so must it be for human beings? Thus, when the ancients..."

When one's vital energy and blood are at their peak, if one considers how the light of time passes so easily, then morning and evening one will reflect and contemplate, becoming ever more cautious and fearful.
One will neither indulge the passions nor give rein to desires, seeking only the Way; thus, one can preserve a good reputation.

But as for those who ruin themselves through dissipation and desire, or bring about their downfall through indulgence in passion—such states are perilous and beyond remedy, leaving one only to beat one’s breast and wring one’s hands in regret.
To pursue it now would be too late. The opportune moment is difficult to obtain and easy to lose (from the *Xianglin Shu*).
"Feng-heng" (Abundance and Prosperity): "Feng" is the name of a hexagram. With Zhen above and Li below—Zhen representing thunder and Li representing fire—it is called "Thunder over Fire:

Feng. "Feng" means great. Because of the brilliance of the fire combined with the movement of the thunder, it is the image of grandeur and abundance. Its divination indicates enjoyment and prosperity.
This is the Way. Therefore, it is said: "Abundance brings success. When the Yin dies, it is called waning; when the Yang dies, it is called ceasing. This is what is meant by goodness.

To have one's name heard and reach far is to be renowned. Wondrous Joy enlightens people in their quest for the Way, emphasizing that one must act in a timely manner and be cautious not to miss the opportune moment.
As for the principle of human birth and death: it is like when pure Yang reaches its limit, a single Yin arises beneath it; so too with pure Yin.

When [the yin] reaches its extreme, one yang arises beneath it. There is waxing and waning; these two interact through multiplication and subtraction, which is the fixed and natural number within heaven and earth.

Only the *Yi* hexagram *Feng* (Abundance), composed of thunder and fire, takes as its image the movement of thunder and the brilliance of fire, embodying the meaning of grandeur and abundance, as well as the way of unimpeded penetration (*heng*). However, one must not exceed this limit. Only...
"It is appropriate that it be midday. This means that abundance is difficult to sustain forever; it serves as a warning. Therefore, the *Huan* hexagram commentary further states:
"When midday reaches its peak, the sun declines toward the west; when the moon is at its full, there is waning.

Observing the natural cycles of Heaven and Earth, such principles of peak and decline, or fullness and depletion, still exist. As for midday— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
At the time of the full moon, even the tides merely subside and recede; how much more so for human beings? Thus, one may also exercise self-restraint in accordance with the seasons.

For this reason, when the ancients were in the prime of their youth and their vital energy was at its peak, they deeply lamented that time passes too easily and that years and months cannot be retained;
consequently, they contemplated the Way in the morning and reflected upon the Way in the evening, remaining ever cautious and vigilant.
With reverent caution, one should increase one’s sense of anxiety and fear;

not indulging the seven emotions, nor being heedless toward the six desires, striving with diligent perseverance to seek only the Way, one can thus achieve perfect beauty and cause one's virtuous reputation to be heard afar.

As for those who ruin it through ease and sensual craving, or destroy it through unrestrained indulgence of their nature and temperament, they bring themselves to a state of peril from which there is no rescue.
"Save me! Only then will one stumble, beat one's breast, and repent; by that time, it will already be too late.
Thus, when the Han general Kuai Che exhorted Han Xin, he said: "Success is difficult to achieve yet easy to ruin; opportunity is difficult to find yet easy to lose.
The moment, the moment—once gone, it does not return. Although these are merely worldly sayings, they can truly serve as a metaphor for life.
When one dies, there should be deep sorrow and regret; at such a time, it is truly difficult to encounter and easy to lose.
Miaoxi said: "In ancient times, people first selected those with virtue and character, and secondly promoted those with talent and learning before advancing them to office.

If one was not a vessel of excellence yet placed themselves before others, many would look down upon them upon seeing or hearing of them. For this reason, monastics reflect upon themselves and strive for self-cultivation."

One establishes oneself through reputation and integrity. Lately, however, I have observed that the monastic communities are withering away; scholars disregard morality and virtue, possessing little sense of principle or righteousness and lacking shame.
They deride those who are pure and simple as being vulgar and crude, while they prize those who are noisy and frivolous as being talented and quick-witted.

Consequently, the younger generation’s discernment is clouded; they merely engage in superficial reading and copying to fuel their verbal eloquence. As days accumulate and months pass, this has ultimately led to a state of moral decay.
When it comes to speaking of the Way of the Sage, one is as bewildered as if facing a wall; this is perhaps beyond salvation.
The intent behind "whetting and polishing" [one's faculties] is like hunting for game upon water—this is a metaphor for the lack of sincerity in studying the Way.
"Bewildered as if facing a wall" means that one sees nothing at all and cannot take even a single step forward.
Furthermore, Miaoxi instructs students that they should establish their reputation and principles through their discourse.
When the ancients selected students, they first sought those whose insight was clear and who possessed the Way, and whose conduct was upright and endowed with virtue;

only then did they promote them based on their talent, capability, and learning for service in the present age. If one were not a person of excellence or a vessel of beauty, how could they be settled among the multitude?
Those who encounter such individuals often treat them with much contempt upon merely seeing them with their eyes or hearing of them with their ears.

Consequently, these monastics reflect privately, rousing themselves to exertion and sharpening their resolve to maintain their integrity and reputation, thereby establishing themselves. Recently, I have observed this within the monastic communities.
They have withered and fallen into ruin. Those who study possess neither genuine realization in their Way nor authentic cultivation of virtue. They lack integrity and steadfastness;
they seldom act in accordance with righteousness. Greedy and lacking modesty, they are defiled and shameless, even going so far as to mock and deride those whose natures are pure and simple.

They regard those who are base, vulgar, simple, and honest as unworthy, while they praise and honor those who are boisterous, stubborn, frivolous, and shallow, regarding them as talented and quick-witted.
For this reason, those of later generations lack clarity of insight; they devote themselves exclusively to copying words and phrases, considering this to be true learning.
They wrap these up in layers upon layers of commentary, taking them to be the profound essence of the teachings. To apply one's mind in such a manner—is this not a great error?
It is just like one who wades through water holding a net to hunt wild beasts; there is a vast disparity between the two.

Having already waded through and hunted down [the texts] by means of transcription, one records and internalizes them, employing them to nourish oral eloquence, which grows and accumulates day by day.
Month by month it has grown deeper; thus, a style of conduct characterized by superficiality, insincerity, and decadence has come into being.

When it comes to inquiring about the Great Way of the Sages, their tongues press against the upper palate, their mouths remain as stiff as foundation stones, and their eyes are like those of the blind.
With walls on all four sides, can such people still be saved? It is hardly possible.
Miaoxi said: "In the past, Huītáng composed the 'Record of the Inscriptions at Hánglóng,' stating: 'In ancient times, scholars lived in mountain caves;
they ate earth and wood; they wore skins and grass. They did not set their minds on fame or profit, nor did they register their names with government offices.
It was only from the Wei, Jin, Qi, Liáng, Sui, and Táng dynasties onward that monasteries were first established to gather students from the four quarters. He then selected...

The worthy provide counsel for the unworthy, and the wise lead the ignorant and deluded; it is through this that the roles of host and guest are established, and the distinction between superior and subordinate arises.
Now, when the multitudes of the four seas gather within a single monastery, the task of presiding over them is indeed difficult to accomplish.

The essential requirement is to grasp the great while relinquishing the trivial, to prioritize the urgent and defer to the slow, and to refrain from private schemes, seeking instead to benefit others. Thus...
Those who are busily preoccupied with schemes for their own bodies alone differ from these by as much as heaven and earth.
Now, Huanglong has had the names of successive abbots inscribed upon this stone, so that those who come in the future may see them and ask: "Who possessed virtue and morality?
Who possessed benevolence and righteousness? Who was impartial toward the community? Who sought only his own benefit? Alas! Is this not something to be feared? (Stone Inscription)
Miaoxi composed a record of the inscriptions on the names [of those who visited] to serve as a warning for later generations, so that others might cherish this knowledge and know what to fear.
Formerly, Huītáng wrote a record of the inscriptions at Huánglóng, stating: "Those who studied the Way in ancient times dwelt in high crags and deep caves;
they ate wild yams and forest fruits; they wore garments of *bōng* bark, lotus leaves, and the like. Fame, profit, and worldly sustenance had no concern with them."
It is registered with the heart. In government offices and administrative bureaus, it does not submit its name to the registers; originally, there were no matters concerning abbots or the like.

It was only after the various dynasties of Wei Cao Cao, Jin Sima Yi, Qi Xiao Daocheng, Liang Xiao Yan, Sui Yang Jian, and Tang Li Yuan that monasteries (*zhao ti*) were first established, gathering vast multitudes from the four quarters and selecting [leaders].
Virtuous and worthy sages rectify those who are unworthy, while those possessed of the Way and wisdom guide and lead the ignorant and deluded masses.
It is by means of this that there exist guests and hosts, superiors and subordinates, and the proper distinction of rank.
Indeed, when the vast multitude of the four seas gather within a single monastery, those who shoulder such a great responsibility are truly...
This is not an easy matter. The essential point lies in grasping the general principles while setting aside minor details; prioritizing what is urgent and postponing what can be deferred.

To seek not even the slightest self-interest, but to focus single-mindedly on benefiting others—when compared to those who are preoccupied with scheming for their own individual benefit—this is truly a difference between the light and pure and the heavy and turbid. It is difficult.
This is now complete. Why has Huanglong had the names of successive abbots inscribed upon stone?
It is so that those who succeed him in residing here may behold them with their own eyes and say: "That elder possessed the wind of the Way; that elder possessed the grace of virtue;
that elder possessed benevolence and compassion; that elder possessed righteousness and integrity. That elder...
For the sake of the multitude, that elder acted for his own sake. Alas! How can one not be struck with fear?
There is no other purpose for this title than to cause those who read it to reflect: let the good take it as a model, and let the evil take it as a warning.
Shallor Zhang, the Vice Minister, said to Miaoxi: "The position of Head Seat (shouzuo) in a Chan monastery is a rank for selecting the worthy.
Yet nowadays, regardless of whether one is worthy or unworthy, all quarters treat this as a shortcut to fortune. This is also the fault of those who preside over the Dharma.
Nevertheless, in this degenerate age, it is indeed difficult to find such a person; however, if one were to select someone whose conduct is somewhat superior—"
Those with a modest measure of talent and virtue, who recognize integrity, shame, and the principles of honor and righteousness, should occupy this position;
they are certainly superior to those who advance through treacherous means (from the *Ke'an ji*).
Director Zhang’s name was Jiucheng; his courtesy name was Zishao. He received the Dharma from Miaoxi. Zishao said to Miaoxi:

"Regarding the discourse on selecting the head officials of the western quarters, within the Zen groves, the position of the Head Seat (Shouzuo) for humans and devas is a rank that must be selected for those of virtuous character;
it is not a station that can be occupied by those of mediocre or common standing. Now, in various quarters...
Regardless of whether one is a gentleman or a petty person, everyone indiscriminately relies on this as a means of seeking advantage.
It lubricates the path of worldly life, serving as a pretext for seeking fame and profit, thereby destroying the established order. This, too, is the fault of those who preside over the Dharma.
Although it is indeed an age of decline, it is inherently difficult to find truly virtuous people; yet, if one were to select those whose conduct and deeds are somewhat superior, and whose talents—

Their power, virtue, and deeds are somewhat established; they recognize integrity, purity, and a sense of shame. Those who possess steadfast character and righteous conduct are selected to dwell there.
Compared to those who rush forward through perilous risks, heedless of the laws of cause and effect, these people are perhaps slightly superior.
Miaoxi said to Zishao, "Among those who preside over the Dharma in recent times, none is like Zhenru Zhe; as for skillfully assisting the monastic communities, none is like Yangqi.
Critics say that Ciming was straightforward and simple, handling affairs with negligence and having no sense of restraint."
Yangqi served him with selfless devotion, fearing only that his service might not be thorough or his tasks unaccomplished.
Though he braved the cold and endured the heat, he never displayed haste for his own sake or a look of indolence. From Nan’uan until his final days at Xinghua, this lasted for nearly thirty years;
he held the reins of discipline throughout the entire lifetime of Ciming before finally passing away. As for Zhenru, from the time he first packed his bundle to begin his travels...
In leading his disciples in accordance with the world, he forgot his own body for the sake of the Dharma as if he were driven by hunger and thirst.

Even in moments of haste or distress, he never showed a sudden change of countenance nor spoke with hurried words. In summer he did not open the windows, and in winter he did not sit near a fire; his single room was serene and solitary, with layers of dust covering his desk.
He once said: "If a monk lacks lofty insight within and is deprived of strict teachers and virtuous friends without, it is rare that he can achieve anything."
Those who were capable vessels—such as Fu Tiejiao, who was stubborn at the time, and Xiu Yuan-tong and others, who were headstrong—all bowed before his reputation.
Alas! These two elders truly serve as a mirror for the monastics of a thousand years to come (from Ke’an’s *Jiwen*).
"Fu" (輔) means to assist and support. "Nanyuan" (南源) refers to the ancient monastery of Yichun. "Zaozai" (造次) and "jiju" (急遽) refer to moments of haste, urgency, or negligence;
"dianpei" (顛沛) and "qingfu" (傾覆) refer to times of distress, overturning, or wandering in exile. "Ju" (遽) means sudden distress; "zu" (卒) means to end.

"Aoyao" (拗拗) and "lilie" (捩) mean to twist and turn, hence to be in opposition. "Futiejiao" (孚鐵脚): his name was Yongfu (永孚), a successor of Hetan Huacheng (泐潭懷澄); the details may be found in the *Yinyi* (音義).
"Yanmi" means to be compliant and yielding. The tortoise knows the auspiciousness or misfortune of the future; the mirror reflects the beauty or ugliness of the present.
Miaoxi said that Zishao’s citation of one who possesses the Way may serve as a model for later students.
Among those who have presided over and upheld the Great Dharma in recent years, none has equaled Zhentrushi; he was excellent at assisting and supporting the monastic community.

Regarding "The Forest": Linmen attained Yangqi. Some have discussed this, saying that Ciming was sincere and straightforward in his character, and his conduct was generally bold and unconcerned with avoiding taboos or prohibitions.
Yangqi, however, served him with total devotion, remaining ever-vigilant and diligent, fearing only that he might not provide full support;
he was cautious and reverent, worrying only that he might not be fully prepared, even during the depths of winter.
In cold weather or the intense heat of midsummer, he never showed haste for his own comfort, maintaining an air of relaxed ease.
Beginning with Chimi (Foyan Qingyuan), he accepted the invitation of Huang Shou-dan, the Governor of Yichun, to the Nan-yuan monastery;

next, he succeeded to the seat of Benyan and Daowu; subsequently, he moved to Shishuang and Foyan, finally concluding his career at the great monasteries of Xinghua—altogether thirty such establishments.
For many years, he held the reins of the monastic groves and maintained the codes of discipline until the end of Ciming’s lifetime.
As for Zhenru, from the time he first packed his bags to travel as a wandering monk and practice the way of a Chan practitioner,

until his emergence in the world to manifest his transformation, guide his disciples, and lead the assembly, he truly devoted himself to the Great Dharma with such diligence that it was as if he were starving.

Regarding those who are driven by craving: they may act with haste, negligence, or recklessness, falling into ruin and wandering in exile. Yet, one sees in them no look of panic nor any words of distress.
When summer reaches its peak heat, they do not open their windows to seek coolness; when winter reaches its extreme cold, they do not huddle by the stove for warmth.
Sitting alone in a single room, they maintain stillness of body and a carefree spirit, never abandoning their practice. They abide in non-action and meditative concentration.

Dust filled his desk. Zeng said, "If a Chan practitioner lacks a penetrating insight that reaches from the top to the bottom, a vision that spans from antiquity to the present, and lacks outside a teacher who administers the 'painful stick' and 'hot shouts,' as well as friends who can strike the joints and penetrate the barriers, it is rare for one to achieve the great vessel of realization.
Therefore, at that time, he was stubborn and perverse, refusing to follow others."
His character was like tempered steel—stubborn, defiant, solitary, firm, and upright. Like Xiu Yuantong, all were swept away by the influence of his Way;
there were none who did not revere and submit to him. Alas! How can one not admire this?
The conduct of these two great elders, Zhen and Yang, serves as a mirror not only for the present day, but truly for the monastics of ten thousand generations.
This is a mirror for reflection. As those who truly study the Way of the Patriarchs, can you not realize this?
Zishao, along with Miaoxi and Wan’an—these three men—went to the quarters of the former Hall Head, Benchou, to inquire after his health.
Miaoxi said, "Only when the body of one in the 'groves below' is at ease can one then study the Way. Wan’an directly disagreed, asserting that it was certainly not so. He insisted that—
"One who studies the Way should not look back at their own body. Miaoxi said, "You fool, you are deluded again!
Although Zishao respected Miaoxi’s words, he ultimately felt that Wan’an’s statement was more appropriate (Recorded Sayings).
The former Head Seat was Bo-shan Wu-ben (Wu-ben of Bo-shan). "Zhong" (Middle) refers to the meaning of being centered in the seasonal rhythms.
It is recorded that Zi-shao, along with three others—Miao-xi, Wan-an, and another—went together to the quarters of Head Seat Ben to inquire after his illness.
Miao-xi then comforted him, saying: "For one who cultivates the Way in the seclusion of the forest, the first requirement is for the body to be peaceful and at ease; only then..."
"One can attain the ultimate Way; yet if there were no physical body, who would cultivate and realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
Wan’an held this view directly, asserting that if one truly wishes to reach the ultimate realization of this Way, one must not further concern oneself with the body;
only by forgetting the body can one study the Way. Miaoxi rebuked him, saying: "You fellow, you are mad again!"
"It is already understood! Why have you come here now with me to speak such words?
Although Zishao values Miaoxi’s words, they are merely appropriate for the occasion; ultimately, Wan’an’s words are more urgent in their exhortation to others and are therefore even more fitting."
Zi Shao asked Miaoxi, "What is the foremost priority for one currently serving as an abbot? Miaoxi replied, "It is nothing more than providing for the Zen practitioners;
it boils down to money and grain. At that time, Wan’an was present in the assembly and disagreed, saying, "That is not so.

If one can skillfully economize on the monastery's income and ensure that expenditures follow the proper path, there will be no shortage of money and grain. Why should this be a cause for concern? However—
For a current abbot, it is essential to prioritize monastics who embrace the Way.

Even if an abbot possesses strategic wisdom and can store ten years' worth of provisions, if there are no monastics under him who embrace the Way, what the former sages called "sitting and consuming offerings while looking up with shame at the dragons and heavens" applies;
what benefit does such an abbot provide? Zishao said, "What the Head Seat has said is extremely appropriate. Miaoxi turned back.
Gu Wan’an said, "Every single one of you is just like you, Wan’an; you must withdraw. (The above is found in the *Kānán jí*).
"Zūnjié" means to restrain and limit. It carries the sense of reducing expenditures, as well as storing and accumulating.
When Minister Zhang asked Miaoxi, "In the present day, what do you consider the primary task for those presiding over monastic communities? Miaoxi replied:
The answer was: "The Chan practitioners residing in the four directions are concerned with nothing more than silver coins, grain, and rice.

At that time, the Head Seat Wan’an was present among those in the assembly; he remarked, "It is not a matter of money and grain; one should calculate what the monastic community (sangha) has obtained."
Whether the resources be great or small, those in charge can skillfully reduce extravagant expenditures and ensure that usage is reasonable;
thus, silver, money, rice, and grain will be more than sufficient. Why, then, should this be a cause for concern?

However, what is currently required of those who preside over these matters is first and foremost to recruit and nurture monastics who possess the Way and virtue, maintaining them with deep provision and generous support. This is the primary task. If—
The abbot must possess great wisdom and grand strategy, capable of accumulating ten years' worth of funds and provisions.
Among those under his command, there shall not be even one or half a person who lacks integrity and righteousness, nor any monk who has realized the mind and seen its nature.
As the former sages cautioned: "To sit idly while consuming offerings is to look up with shame before the dragons and heavens. Regarding such an abbot:
"What benefit is there? Master Zishao then praised and approved him, saying, "It is no mistake for you to be the head seat among gods and men;

what you have said is most appropriate. Miaoxi turned his head back, looked at Wan’an, and said, "In a vast assembly where the foolish are many and the wise few, does every single person harbor such thoughts as yours? Wan’an then...
He remained silent, and without speaking, he withdrew. One who is a true master of the teaching should know that this is the primary duty.
Master Wanan Yan said: "When my late teacher Miaoxi first resided at Mount Jing, during a night discourse he spoke incessantly on the various schools and the tenets of the Caodong tradition.
The following day, Head Seat Yin said to my late teacher, 'As for one who has appeared in the world...'"
Benefiting sentient beings is by no means a trivial matter. If you truly intend to support and revitalize the Buddhist teachings, you must address their deficiencies according to the times;
you should not seek mere immediate gratification. When the Master was formerly a Zen practitioner traveling among various regions, he could not afford to be reckless in his discourse.
How much more so now that you have ascended the Precious Flower King’s Throne and are known as a *kalyāṇamitra*? As our late teacher said: "Last night, for a single moment..."
The head seat spoke thus. The head seat said, "The learning of the sages and worthies is rooted in their innate nature; how can it be undertaken so recklessly?
The former master bowed his head in thanks. Yet the head seat continued to speak at length without ceasing.
The Cao-Dong (Caodong) school: "Cao" refers to Mount Cao in Fuzhou, where Chan Master Benji succeeded the Venerable Liaojia of Dongshan.
Having initially departed from Dongshan, he went to Caoqi to pay homage at the ancestral pagoda; upon his return, he settled in Linchuan, which possessed fine mountains and waters.
He settled there permanently. Because he admired the Sixth Patriarch, he named the mountain Cao (Tiger). The lineage of Dongshan flourished greatly through this master;

thus, it is called the Caodong School. Regarding the sense of being hasty or dismissive—Wan’an Yan Heshang said that those who uphold the Dharma must value themselves and refrain from lightly criticizing the teachings of various quarters. My late teacher Miaoxi [said the same].

In the seventh year of the Shaoxing era of the Song dynasty, when he first resided at Mount Jing, during a night assembly, he discussed the methods and paths of various masters as well as the fundamental tenets of the Cao-Dong school;
what he spoke of was extensive. The following morning, Head Seat Yin said to the Master:
"A true spiritual friend appearing in the world to teach and guide sentient beings is by no means a minor matter; it must certainly..."
One must support and propagate the religious teachings of the five schools; one should address their accumulated defects according to the times.

How could one merely seek immediate convenience? When you, Venerable Sir, were formerly among the traveling monks within the great assemblies, even your casual conversations and discussions were not permitted to be false or deceptive; how much more so now that you have ascended the Buddha’s [throne]?
The Patriarch, seated upon the precious lotus-flower throne, proclaimed the Great Dharma and was hailed as a *kalyāṇamitra*.
The former master then said, "Last night, this was merely a spontaneous remark made at a single moment; how can it be grasped as literal truth?
The head seat replied, "Whether one becomes a sage or a worthy, the foundation of such learning lies in the innate nature of man; how can it be treated with levity? The former master—
He then bowed his head in delay and offered his thanks; yet the Head Seat continued to speak at length and with earnest urgency, not ceasing his exhortations.

Viewed from this perspective, the Head Seat possessed the mouth that speaks forthrightly and dares to remonstrate, while Miaoxi possessed the capacity to receive such counsel with magnanimity. Both are worthy of emulation.
Wan’an said, “When our late Master was exiled to Hengyang, the Venerable Attendant recorded the words of his banishment and displayed them before the Sangha Hall.
