The monks were as if they had lost their parents; they wept and sighed in grief, finding no place to dwell in peace. At that time, Vinaya Master Yin went to the various quarters and informed the assembly:
‘In human life, calamities cannot be evaded at will. If Miaoxi’s entire life had been like that of a woman or a girl—’”
If you had remained submerged like land in water and maintained a vow of silence without speaking, there would have been no such event as today.
Furthermore, what the former sages were called upon to do did not stop at this alone; why do you distress yourselves so? In the past, there were Ciming, Langye, Guquan, and Dayu.
He joined a group to visit Fenyang. As it happened that the northwest was engaged in military operations at the time, he changed his clothes and mingled with the ranks of the army to go there.
Now, Mount Jing and Hengyang are not far apart; the roads are free of obstacles and the mountains and rivers present no difficulties.
If one wishes to see Miaoxi, what could possibly be difficult? Thereupon, the entire assembly became silent. The next day, they departed one after another (from Zhilin of Mount Lu).
Hengyang: This refers to Hengyang County in Hengzhou Prefecture, within the Hunan Circuit. To "unfur and raise" means to display prominently. "Tears and snot":
the fluid from the eyes is called *ti* (tears), and the fluid from the nose is called *si* (snot). "Unable to settle the mind": in such urgency, there is no leisure for composure.
"Lowering the board" means to occupy a subordinate position. "Guquan" is the name of the Great Way; "Dayu" is the name of the Guardian.
Zhi was a successor of Fu-yang Zhaozu; Fu-yang’s name was Shan-zhao. He was a successor of Shou-shan Nian-zi.
"Fire brigade" refers to a unit of fire soldiers within a military camp. Master Wan-an was a man of virtue;
even when disaster threatened his very person, people still clung to him and would not leave. My late teacher once discussed the investigation of things with Minister Zhang.
[The Master] spoke. Upon hearing these words, the Vice Minister attained realization. Later, when the former master ascended the hall, he cited the verse:
"A single shot from a *shenbi* bow pierces through a thousand layers of armor; the old monk picks it up and looks at it—it is not worth even a pair of stinking leather shoes.
The Chancellor Qin Hui, taking this to be a criticism of the state administration, subsequently exiled the former master to Hengyang. Worthy Attendant [name].
The records of the imperial court’s decrees of demotion were displayed prominently before the Sangha Hall. When the monastics saw them, they felt as though they had lost their own biological parents;
they lamented and wept, sighing with their mouths, shedding tears from their eyes, and letting snot flow from their noses.
Their hearts were filled with distress and urgency, leaving them no leisure for composure. From this, one can infer that Miaoxi was...
This is self-evident to all people. Chief Seat Yin went to the communal quarters and informed everyone one by one, saying:
"When a person of realization dwells in the world, righteousness is their fundamental principle. Since we have encountered this hardship, we cannot evade it through expediency.
Even if Miaoxi had spent his entire life as a woman or a girl, never allowing himself to be seen on dry land, he would have remained submerged in lowly positions."
Lower the boards. Seal your mouths with three silences; maintain reticence and do not speak. Had you done so, the events of today in Hengyang would not have occurred.

Furthermore, consider that the ancient sage masters—such as [Bodhidharma] at Jibin and the Second Patriarch at the capital of Ye—all engaged in such actions as manifestations for the sake of the Dharma;
how could it have been limited to this alone? Why do you distress yourselves so, inflicting such bitter pain upon yourselves? In the past...
Fenyang’s reputation for the Way was renowned throughout the world. Ciming Yuan, Langye Jue, Guquan Dao, and Dayu Zhi formed a group of companions, wishing to travel there to seek instruction.
At that time, heavy troops were stationed in both Zhezhou and Luan’an, such that no one dared to go.
The four disciples of Master Ci disregarded all dangers and obstacles; they crossed the Rongze River and ascended Mount Taihang.

Changing their clothes, they mingled among the imperial guards, sleeping in the open air and on the grass, undaunted by toil and hardship as they went to pay their respects to their ancestral master, Fenyang Wude.
Today, Jingshan is not very far from Hengyang; the roads between them are free of marshes.
"Between Lu and Jian-guan, the mountains and rivers present no perilous obstacles for one of honorable conduct. To see Miaoxi again—how could that be difficult?
Because of these words, the assembly finally ceased their weeping and lamentations, falling into a profound silence.
On the following day, they all departed one after another at a leisurely pace. If Miaoxi did not possess true virtue, how could he have moved them so?

People’s yearning for her was indeed such as this. These are the traces of one who responded to the capacities of beings. The Dharma does not arise in isolation; it is born only by relying on conditions.
Her ability to move others was due to her true virtue. Like a child who has lost its mother, tears flow from the pain in their entrails—how could anyone possibly equal this?
"Those who study must not doubt his outward traces while failing to contemplate his virtue.
Wanan said, "When our late master moved to Mei Yang, there were some among the monks who spoke of him privately with criticism. Yun, the Head Seat, said:
'In general, when evaluating a person, one should seek what is faultless within their faults; how could it be right to seek faults within what is already faultless?'"
There is a fault here. To fail to examine the mind and instead doubt the outward traces—how can this truly console the public judgment of the monastic community?
Furthermore, Miaoxi’s moral virtue, talent, and capacity were innate; in establishing his character and conducting his affairs, he followed only what was righteous.
His capacity for discernment certainly surpassed that of others. That the Creator now restrains him must surely have its reason. How could one not know it to be so?
"Is this the merit of a different time for the Dharma-gate? Those who heard it shall henceforth no longer engage in such debate.
(From the *Zhilín jí*). Méiyáng refers to Méiyáng County in Cháo Prefecture, Guangdong. When Miaoxi was exiled to Hénghuáng, he composed the three fascicles of the *Zhèngfǎyǎn zàng*.
After being falsely slandered once more, he was further exiled to Méiyáng. Among the monastics (*nàzǐ*), there were those who privately discussed [the matter].
The one who [criticized him] said, "In general, when criticizing or discussing others, one should seek within their faults a portion of faultless principle;
thus, even faults can be explained away. How could one seek faults within what is faultless?
Would that not be adding frost to snow? Now, as for failing to examine the actions of Miaoxi—
Regarding the mind of the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, one might doubt the traces of its further degradation and offer groundless critiques of others;
how could such things truly comfort the public opinion, reason, and the ears and eyes of those within the monastic community?

Furthermore, as for Miaoxi’s lifelong spiritual influence, moral conduct, talent, and capacity—all emerged spontaneously from his natural disposition. He established himself with distinction and personally practiced for the multitude.
In all matters, one should simply follow what is appropriate. His magnanimity and great breadth of character were originally born of his noble station;
yet now, by the fixed destiny of the Way and the spontaneous workings of creation, he is being constrained and suppressed. There must surely be a certain ultimate principle at work here.
How could one not recognize this as a favorable omen for future blessings within the Dharma-gate? All of you—
Having heard the Head Seat speak in this manner, from now on there will be no further discussion regarding the matter of Miaoxi being demoted to Mei Yang once more.
The Head Seat said to Wan’an, "One who is called a 'good knowledge-holder' (śāstr) ought to cleanse their mind with the utmost impartiality."

Upon reaching the era of Zhizheng, he received disciples from the four quarters. Among them, if there were those who embraced morality, benevolence, and righteousness, he would necessarily admit them even if they harbored resentment or enmity.
Conversely, if there were those who were treacherous, wicked, or base, he would necessarily distance himself from them despite any private favors they might have rendered.
Thus, he ensured that all who came understood what to uphold, so that they might be of one mind and one virtue, and the monastic community remained at peace (from his letter to Miaoxi).

Yin Shouzuo said to Wan’an, “When you purify your mind to receive the assembly and speak of settling the monastic community, you who are called an Elder practicing the Dharma must first cleanse your own heart, liver, and five viscera one by one until they are perfectly pure.
Do not allow even a single hair’s breadth of defiled habituation or impurity to remain; only then may you proceed.”
The law of the Duke is the Way of Ultimate Rectitude. It welcomes those from all quarters;

among them, if there be those who preserve the Dao and cultivate virtue, or who abide in benevolence and act according to righteousness, even if they harbor enmity or a rift with me, I must certainly recommend and promote them.
Conversely, if there be those whose intentions are treacherous and whose hearts are depraved, or who are reckless and frivolous, even if they have had private dealings with me—
Your extraordinary favor must be set aside and distanced from this matter, so that those who come from the four quarters may each recognize for themselves what is upheld by moral virtue,
wisdom, benevolence, and righteousness. When the myriad people are of one mind and share in these same virtues,
the monastic communities will not require further commands and will naturally abide in peace and security.
It is further said: "In general, among those who serve as abbots, who does not desire to establish a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*)? Yet few are able to truly revitalize it.

This is because they neglect the Way and its Virtue (*mōrì*), abandon benevolence and righteousness (*rén-yì*), discard the laws and regulations, and instead indulge their private passions; it is for these reasons that such a state arises.

Truly mindful that the Dharma-gate is in decline, one should rectify oneself and treat others with humility, select the worthy to assist and support, recommend those of long-standing virtue, and distance oneself from the unworthy."
A person of small virtue practices frugality and economy within themselves, while their virtuous kindness extends to others.

Only then, regarding those they employ as attendants, do they retain those who are somewhat mature and experienced, while distancing those who are sycophantic and flattering. This is to avoid the slander of being ugly or wicked, as well as the chaos of partiality and factionalism.
If one acts in this manner, they may be compared to Mazu and Baizhang, and can reach the level of Linji and Deshan (from the *Zhilin ji*).
"Mou" means "to equalize. Linji’s name was Yixuan; he was the successor of Huangbo Xiyun. Deshan’s name was Xuanjian;
he was the successor of Longtan Chongxin. Regarding the statement that the Head Seat (Yinsu) also understands the duties of the Abbot:

one should speak of rectifying oneself, selecting the worthy, being humble, and benefiting others. Among all those who serve as abbots, who does not love to establish and build up the monastic community?

The forest [of the Way] has long been neglected, and few are able to revitalize it. Why is this? It is because their understanding of the Way is not yet genuine, and their cultivation of virtue is insincere and prone to forgetfulness.
They lack compassion in benevolence, and their righteousness fails to accord with what is appropriate, leading to much neglect.

They abandon laws and regulations without practicing them, and indulge in private passions without reforming them; it is these factors that cause such a state of affairs. If one were to contemplate this with sincerity...
The Way of the Dharma is declining; the lineage is falling into ruin. You should rectify your mind and humble yourself in self-restraint.
Select those of virtue to assist you one another; honor the elderly and remain close to them, while distancing yourself from petty people and exercising self-discipline.
Practice moderation and frugality to cultivate yourself, and extend your benevolence and kindness to others. Only then will your attendants...
Regarding those persons employed to serve you at your side: retain those who are somewhat mature, experienced, and adept;

distance yourself from those who are fickle, sycophantic, and flattering. This is intended to ensure that you are not defiled by vulgar and wicked slander, nor disturbed by the partisan intrigues of private factions.
If you can truly act in this way, then you may join Ma Zu and Bai Zhang.
They walk hand in hand; Linji and Deshan breathe through the same nostril. Were it not for such as these, who would there be to match them?
Chief Seat Yin said: "The sages of antiquity took no calamity as a cause for fear, yet they said: 'Does Heaven abandon me, the unworthy?'"
Fan Wenzi said: "Only a sage can be free from anxiety both within and without. For anyone other than a sage, external peace inevitably entails internal worry.
The worthy and enlightened of all ages have known that they cannot avoid this; thus, they have always been careful at the outset and established their own defenses for themselves.

Therefore, if a person’s life involves even a slight degree of anxiety and toil, it may not fail to become a blessing for their entire life. This is because calamities, misfortunes, slander, and disgrace—"
Even Yao and Shun could not have escaped it; how much less others? "Disaster" (*zai*) refers to harm; "grain" (*gu*) refers to goodness. "To escape" (*tāo*) means to avoid.

[This is] a letter from the Head Seat to Miaoxi, instructing him to be naturally cautious and to speak with the fear that no disaster may occur. The perfected beings of antiquity were constantly anxious and apprehensive for this reason.
Fearing that no calamity would ever befall him, he spoke again, saying: "The Way of Heaven is impartial; how could it single out and utterly reject an unwholesome person such as myself?
Lord Wen Zhengfan said: "Only one who is all-pervasive in his understanding—a sage—can be free from affliction both within and without.
If one is not a sage, it is certain that one cannot be entirely free of them, whether externally or internally. Or perhaps externally...
Though one may be secure and at peace, there must surely be hidden anxieties within.

Throughout antiquity and the present, the wise and accomplished have known that they could not escape entirely from suffering and affliction; therefore, they were constantly cautious from the very beginning.

At every moment, they took precept and patience as their ramparts and fences, and concentration and wisdom as their armor, always guarding themselves. Thus, when people dwell in ordinary leisure and repose, they do not—
Those who exert themselves with weary hearts and burning thoughts will surely find that these efforts become the auspicious fortune of their entire lives.
For even regarding calamities and slander, though Yao and Shun were sage rulers, they still faced the calumny of being unkind and the disgrace of being unfilial.
Since neither can be avoided, how much less so for others? You should prudently guard your conduct from the outset, fearing disaster rather than fearing slander or humiliation.
Master Wanan Yan said: "Recently, I have observed that the monastic communities (conglin) are utterly devoid of mature and accomplished men.

Wherever there are three hundred or five hundred people, one person takes the lead as the leader while many others act as his companions. They occupy the throne of the Dharma King, wielding the mallet and raising the whisk, yet they deceive one another.

Even when they engage in discourse, it does not touch upon the canonical teachings. This is precisely why there are no mature men in these communities. As for those who have left the mundane world..."

To benefit sentient beings and act as the Buddha’s representative in propagating the transformation [of the world], one must clarify the mind and penetrate the fundamental source; only when practice and understanding correspond can one dare to undertake such a task.

For example, if someone were to falsely claim the title of Emperor, they would bring about their own destruction; how much more so for the Dharma King—how could one dare to usurp his position through falsehood?
Alas! As we move further from the Sage, those like the cranes in the floodwaters proliferate everywhere, causing the gateway to the teachings of the former Sages to decline day by day.
Having thus fallen into ruin and drowning, how could I wish to remain silent? Taking advantage of my current leisure while dwelling in a mountain hermitage,

I shall set forth one or two matters that are most severely harmful to the wind of the Dharma and the destruction of the teachings, to be circulated throughout the monastic communities so that later generations and junior practitioners may know that their predecessors were ever-vigilant and earnest,
taking the upholding of the Great Dharma as their primary concern— acting as if walking upon sheets of ice or treading upon the edge of a sword— and not acting with mere negligence.
This concerns fame and profit. Whether they know me or blame me, I have no words to offer (from the *Zhilinjí*).
Regarding the "crane in the floodwaters": Ānanda saw a bhikṣu reciting a Dharma verse which said:

"If a person lives for a hundred years, yet does not see the crane in the floodwaters, it would be better to live for but a single day and behold it. Having heard this, Ānanda sighed in admiration and said: [The rest of the passage follows].
"The Eye of the World has been extinguished; how swift was its passing! He spoke to the bhikṣus, saying, "This is not the Buddha’s word; it is not to be practiced.
You should now listen as I recite the Buddha’s verses: 'If a person lives for a hundred years, yet does not understand the essential principles of the Buddhas...'"
"It is not as good as living for a single day and attaining definitive understanding. The bhikṣu took this and reported it to his teacher.
The teacher said, "Ānanda is old and senile; he is not to be trusted. You should consider what you previously recited to be correct.

Later, when Ānanda heard that the bhikṣu was still practicing the former recitation, he asked him the reason. The bhikṣu replied, "My teacher told me that Ānanda is old and senile [and thus unreliable]."
"Xin, you should take me as being right. Seeing that he did not believe him, Ānanda immediately entered samādhi and sought to manifest superior virtues, yet none could save him.
He then sighed and said: "How strange! How strange! This cannot be corrected; it is a matter of karmic affinity."
The subsequent character "shu" (屬) means "to encounter. It means that those who know me, Confucius, understand that I composed the *Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals) to embody the royal law;

its great essentials are all matters pertaining to the Son of Heaven. Those who know Confucius say that the composition of the *Chunqiu* serves to arrest human desires before they have sprouted and to preserve the principles of Heaven (*tianli*) after they have already perished.
His concern for future generations was most profound and far-reaching. "To blame me"—to blame [me].

As for Confucius, it is said that although he lacked the proper station, he relied upon the authority of the sovereign for two hundred and forty-two years, causing rebellious ministers and treacherous sons to fear and refrain from acting recklessly; this was his concern.
Master Wanan cites this to justify his own petitions, meaning he does not fear others’ censure. Master Wanan feared that the Way would decline and the Dharma...
This is the discourse on the masterless chaos within the monastic groves. Recently, I have observed that within these monasteries there are almost no seasoned or realized practitioners.
Wherever one goes, there may be three hundred people in a single hall or five hundred in a single courtyard;

yet a single individual occupies the abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) as the head of the hall, while many others reside together in the common dormitories as mere companions. The leader holds [the position].
At the Dharma seat, the presiding elder strikes the gavel, and the senior monk raises the fly-whisk; these acts appear to be correct yet are actually false, as they deceive one another.
Though there is discourse, it is largely fabricated and lacks connection to the canonical scriptures, being devoid of any authoritative basis.

It is therefore no wonder that there are no seasoned or authentic masters among them. Indeed, those who first emerge from the mundane world to propagate the Way and benefit sentient beings act as the mouthpiece for the Buddha.

To propagate the Dharma-transformation by means of one's vital energy (qi) without truly illuminating one’s own mind and genuinely penetrating the fundamental source—such that practice accords with understanding and understanding accords with practice—is this not to act recklessly? Have you not seen what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"It is like a common person who, lacking any real virtue, claims to be an emperor and steps into the position of a Son of Heaven; he is merely a usurper."

They incur their own guilt and are subsequently executed and slaughtered; how much more so for the King of the Dharma—how could he falsely usurp this position of the Dharma without genuine virtue and morality? Alas! How truly tragic it is!
Since the passing of the Buddha’s world, the decline has become even more remote; those like the cranes in the floodwaters have emerged once again, roaming about in all directions.
I have followed the True Path, yet the gateways of the Dharma-transformation of the former sages have declined day by day, gradually sinking into oblivion.
How could I bear not to speak? Taking advantage of a leisurely day while dwelling in a hermitage, when there was nothing else to do, I have merely categorized and set forth these points.
Now, as for those who wound the customs and ruin the teachings—those who constitute the most extreme poison to the Dharma-gate—I shall cite one or two instances.
This [teaching] is spread throughout the monastic community, so that later generations and those of humble standing may know that their predecessors were of such character:

ever-vigilant and cautious, ever-alarmed and fearful, with hearts set upon shouldering and bearing the Unsurpassed Great Dharma upon their own backs—walking as if treading on thin ice for fear of falling, and stepping as if walking on a sharp blade for fear of injury. This was not done out of mere expediency.

Furthermore, it is merely to seek fame and profit. Those who understand me will consider my words to be right; I have no argument against them. Those who condemn me will consider my words to be wrong;
I likewise have no argument against them. I am simply concerned that the Way may decline and the Dharma fall into disorder.
It is the same with Gong County; I simply cannot bear to remain silent.
Wan’an said: "In the past, when the ancients ascended the hall, they would first present the essential framework of the Great Dharma and examine the assembly.

Students would then come forward to request instruction, resulting in a formal exchange of questions and answers. Nowadays, people compose four-line poems that rhyme at random and call them 'fishing talk' (diao-hua)."
One person stepped forward from the assembly and loudly recited a couplet of ancient poetry, calling it "insulting the ranks. It is vulgar, indeed vulgar; it is tragic and pitiable.

Our predecessors, mindful that the matter of birth and death is of great importance, resolved their doubts before the assembly. Having already brought this forth for illumination, they had not yet given rise to a mind of arising and ceasing.

Master Wanan lamented that the Dharma had long fallen into decline. When the ancients ascended the hall to preach the Dharma, they would first present the fundamental principles and general outline of the Great Dharma.
They strictly required them to examine and question the assembly. If a student attained realization therein, the master would grant him certification;
if a student did not understand it, he would come forward to seek instruction, and thus the process of inquiry and response ensued. This was because...
This is so. People nowadays, however, do not act this way. First, they fabricate four lines of fresh, rhymed verse and call it "bait" to entice them.
Then, one person suddenly steps forward from the crowd and loudly recites a couplet from an ancient poem.

To call this a "battle of insults" and regard it as a "Dharma-battle"—is there any logic in such a thing? How depraved is the world! How diminished has the Dharma become—to this point! It is truly lamentable.
The Way has declined in our time—how painful it is to reflect upon! My predecessors all used to reflect for themselves:
they did not know from where they came when born, nor where they would go when dying; they treated this as one most urgent and vital matter of great importance.

He came forth to resolve the doubts of the assembly. Since this was the manifestation of one’s own great matter, how could he have given rise to even a hair’s breadth of a mind of birth and death, or views of self and other?
Wan’an said: "When a renowned elder arrives at a monastery, the host should ascend the seat and express gratitude with humility and respect. He then invited [the guest] to take his place.

The Venerable One descends from his high seat to a lower one to speak words of increased gravity. The junior monks, together with the Head Seat and the assembly, request him to ascend the seat so that they may hear the essentials of the Dharma.
It is common nowadays for people to emulate the practice of citing ancient kōans and ordering the assembly to provide critical commentary, claiming it is "testing others.
Do not harbor such a mind at all. The former sages forgot their own emotions for the sake of the Dharma; together they established the transformation of the teachings, responding to one another.
I proclaim this so that the Dharma may endure for a long time. How could you allow thoughts of arising and ceasing to give rise to such evil intentions? Reverence takes humility as its core;
you should reflect upon this deeply.
Wan’an Xie was a master of the Dharma who understood the etiquette between host and guest.

When a person of virtue, a respected elder, or one of venerable practice and seniority arrived at the monastery—whether invited specifically by the abbot or otherwise—the abbot should ascend the seat to preach the Dharma with humility, harmony, and reverent compliance, offering words of praise and gratitude.
Even if the visiting guest’s rank is originally higher, the abbot must further humble himself to accord with the lower position.

Furthermore, one should employ even more earnest and respectful language. Upon concluding the discourse and descending from the seat, together with the head seat and the assembly, one should likewise invite the visiting elder to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma, listening reverently to the essential points of the teaching; this is the proper ritual.
Lately, however, I have observed that those with competitive minds vie with one another; whenever an ancient kōan is raised, they compel others to deliver a critique before the assembly.
Cut it off. Observe how their consciousness and views are; to call this "interrogating and discerning others"—is there such a thing as ritual propriety?
As for the royal law of later times, one must by all means refrain from harboring this competitive spirit, for it harms social customs and transformation.

The former sages were so earnest in their dedication to the Dharma that they forgot their personal feelings toward one another; together they established the banner of the Dharma and flourished the teachings, whether by suppressing or by uplifting.
By mutually responding in song, we cause the Buddhadharma to abide long in the world.
How could there be any thoughts of arrogance, the views of self and other, or even a single hair’s breadth of an evil mental state? The etiquette between host and guest takes humility as its core;
you should reflect on this deeply so that the two Gui lineages may flourish and repay the kindness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

Wan’an said: "Recently, I have observed that when officials such as provincial inspectors or prefects enter the mountain, they sometimes instruct their attendants the following day to inform the Elder:
'Today, the seat has been specially raised for such-and-such an official. This single matter is something that still merits threefold reflection."
However, although such matters have been recorded in volumes since antiquity, they were all instances where scholar-officials sought out spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
On such occasions, the abbot, during the course of a formal interview, would briefly mention the meaning of protecting the teachings and illuminating the springs and rocks.
Since these individuals were already "insiders," the abbot would speak two or three simple, intimate words to inspire in them a sense of reverence, much like the cases of Guo Gongfu and Yang Ciji.
When Lord Gong visited Baiyun, and Su Dongpo and Huang Taishi met with Foyin—this was precisely the standard model.
How could it have been a deliberate act of recklessness intended to invite derision from those who understand?
The *jiansi* (censor), the *you-si* (local official), and the local magistrates are the officials of the region; the *junshou* and *taishou* are the prefectural governors.

"Bound volumes" refers to the recorded sayings (*yulu*) and their manuscript editions. Wan’an Xian was one who upheld the Way of the Dharma; he received external protection and spoke of the essential principles of the Great Body.
Recently, I have observed that both unappointed scholars and appointed officials—whether they be provincial inspectors, prefects, or governors—visit monasteries.

Should there be some official business requiring their attention, they delegate the administrative affairs to the *zhishi* (administrative officers) and *toushou* (head monks). On the following day, they inform the *shizhe* (attendant) to report back on the matter.
The abbot (*changlao*) should then dedicate himself exclusively to ascending the hall to preach the Dharma for such government officials. This point, in particular, merits further reflection.
He further reflected: "If it can be practiced, then practice; if it cannot be practiced, then stop.

Although such accounts have been recorded in the *yulu* (recorded sayings) of antiquity, they all concern those lay gentlemen who possessed a sincere longing for the Way and sought out masters to inquire after them in order to have their doubts dispelled.
The abbot, taking advantage of this opportunity, provided guidance according to their individual capacities. If, indeed, there were...
As one whose dharma is truth, you have been respectfully invited to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma; thus, you must not decline.
On this occasion of his inquiry, I shall briefly mention the matters of external protection and those who assist in the teaching gate, with the intent of bringing glory to the springs and rocks.

Since you are already one among those within the family of the Buddha-dharma, I shall simply offer an ordinary provocation: when the pointing is present, one does not arrive; when one arrives, the pointing is absent. I shall speak briefly.
A few simple and straightforward words can inspire reverence in others. For example, when Guo Gongfu crossed the river to visit Baiyun, Yang Cihui met with Furong Kai.
Gongfu asked, "How many years has it been since we parted? Furong replied, "Seven years."
The Duke said, "Have you come to study the Way? Have you come to practice Chan? Rong replied, "I am not playing these drums and flutes.

The Duke said, "If that is so, then you have merely traveled through the mountains and waters, accomplishing nothing at all. Rong said, "It has not been long since we last met, yet you are well able to discern this with your lofty insight.
The Duke laughed heartily. Su Dongpo visited Mount Jin; encountering Foyin, he entered the room. As they were entering, Foyin said, "This..."
There was no place to sit. Su Shi said, "I shall borrow the Master’s four elements to serve as a meditation seat. The Master said, "The old monk has a question. If you can answer it, you may sit;
if you cannot answer it, you must forfeit the jade belt at your waist. Su Shi immediately untied his belt, placed it on a table, and asked for instruction.
The Master said, "The old monk’s four elements are fundamentally empty and the five aggregates do not exist. Where would you turn?"
As they sat, the slope remained silent. Xuedou summoned his attendant and had him take away the jade belt.
When Huang Taishi met Huitang, he requested instruction on the direct and swift path. Huitang said, "Confucius said, 'I have nothing hidden from you. How do you understand this?
As the official was about to respond, Huitang said, "Not so, not so. The official was left in a state of persistent confusion. Suddenly, while attending at the mountain...
As they were walking, the rock-peonies were in full bloom. The Master said, "Do you smell the fragrance of the *mugicha* (wood-grain) flowers?

The official replied, "I do. The Master said, "Is there anything I have hidden from you? The official attained great enlightenment and immediately prostrated himself, saying, "The Master’s compassionate heart is too earnest.
The Master laughed and said, "I only wish for you to reach home. As with these various gentlemen, all were those who took up the Way for their own sake.
I visited Baiyun, Furong, Foyin, and Huitang; they likewise responded according to circumstances and revealed what was concealed.
This is precisely the model and standard for later generations. How could these be the reckless fabrications of ignorant people intended to invite the ridicule of the wise?
Wan’an said: "In the past, when entering the inner quarters [for formal instruction], the master would first have a notice hung up.

Each person, regarding the great matter of life and death, would come with eager anticipation to seek definitive resolution. I have often observed that nowadays, regardless of whether they are old or ill, everyone is ordered to come and submit their surrender.

If one has musk, it naturally has its fragrance; why use public boundaries to drive it away? Because of this, arbitrary regulations are created, leaving both guest and host uneasy. The Master [Wan’an]...
"Dharma" means one should contemplate it;

it means to decide and judge, and to select and discern. Altogether, it signifies the meaning of resolving and breaking through doubts and obstructions, and selecting between the heterodox and the orthodox.
It means to subdue; it means sincerity; it means intimacy and respect. It signifies the meaning of humbling oneself, expressing sincerity, and exhausting one's reverence. Ten thousand...

A master who presides over the Dharma must not rely on the Way to suppress others. When the ancients entered the room for instruction, they first ordered the hanging of the plaque to notify everyone that this was a matter of profound life-and-death urgency;

those who could not yet achieve liberation were expected to exert themselves with vigor and come forward eagerly to seek decisive resolution—this is the correct principle. Yet, I frequently observe that contemporary masters do not inquire [into this].
To instruct the elderly and the infirm to all come and submit their surrender—claiming that if they do not, it is because they refuse to be bound by the "rope and net" of others—is this reasonable?
When a person possesses virtue, morality, and propriety, they naturally exude a pervasive fragrance like that of musk;
why then must one use public authority to compel them to come? To teach such things is delusion.
There have been many instances where the proliferation of branches and sub-sections has caused discord and a lack of harmony between host and guest;
those who preside over the Dharma should reflect deeply on this.

Wan’an said: "The First Patriarch of Shaolin transmitted both robe and Dharma. By the sixth generation, the robe was no longer transmitted, for it was the practice and realization [of the Dharma] that were taken up."
This is appropriate. In the world, their family vocation flourished and the ancestral Way grew ever more radiant; their descendants multiplied.
Among those after Dajian, both Shitou and Mazu were legitimate grandsons, fulfilling the prophetic omen of Prajñātāra that "it must rely upon the feet of the children and grandchildren.
The profound words and wondrous sayings of these two Great Beings have spread throughout the realm, and those who secretly accord with and secretly realize them are found everywhere.
As the methods of the masters became numerous, there was no single school of specialization. The lineage of Caoxi branched into five schools;
though their forms were as diverse as the vessels they filled, the essence of the water remained the same. Each school enjoyed a distinguished reputation and strove diligently in its own mission.

In the course of daily life, a single word or a single command would ensnare scholars, causing the monastic forests to boil with activity—not for trivial reasons. Thus, they exchanged verses and manifesteds [their teachings] to one another.
To slightly elucidate what is obscure: sometimes suppressing, sometimes exalting, they assist and support the transformation of the Dharma.
Their words lack flavor, like a soup boiled from wood shavings or rice steamed from iron nails; yet when chewed by later generations, these are designated as "picking up the ancients" (niangu).

The practice of composing verses (songgu) began with Fenyang and Xuedou, who magnified its sound and revealed its intent, making it vast and boundless. Those who followed strode forth across this field.
Xuedou acted thus, disregarding what his virtue and character might be like, and striving instead for a beauty of brilliant literary flourish.
This caused later generations and those who entered the path late to be unable to perceive the ancient masters' aim of profound purity and complete perfection. Alas!

In my travels through the monastic forests and my encounters with senior practitioners, I have never failed to study the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of the ancients, nor have I ever disregarded the precepts and commands of Baizhang.

This is not merely a fondness for antiquity; rather, it is because those of the present day are insufficient to serve as models. It is enough for men of broad vision and great attainment to understand me beyond these words.
Wan’an Xue said: "If you students wish to know the source of the Great Way, you should emulate the ancients and follow the predecessors.
When the First Patriarch, Bodhidharma, arrived at Shaolin Monastery, he transmitted both the robe and the Dharma. By the time of the Sixth Patriarch, Huineng, the robe became a cause for contention."

The robe was not passed on; only the Dharma was transmitted. Those whose practice accorded with their realization, and whose realization accorded with their practice, succeeded one another from generation to generation to inherit the family legacy.

Thus, the Way of the ancestors became increasingly radiant, and the lineage of descendants grew ever more flourishing. After the Sixth Patriarch, Dajian Huineng, came Shitou Xiqian and Mazu Daoyi of Jiangxi.
All of them received direct instruction and personal transmission from Qingyuan and Nanyue; thus they were the legitimate grandsons.
This precisely accords with the distant prophecy of the twenty-seventh patriarch of the Western Regions, Prajñātāra: "Though China is vast, there is no other path; the Way is one.
It must be traversed by the feet of sons and grandsons. [This refers to] Shitou as well. The golden rooster knows how to snap its beak once—
Liliangzu was a native of Jinji County. He made offerings to the arhat-monks of the ten directions.
Mazu was a monk at Luohan Temple in Qufeng County, Sichuan; it is precisely this that is meant here.
The profound and mysterious words, the refined and wondrous sayings of these two great masters, have circulated and spread throughout the realm, communicating in secret and harmonizing in the unseen.
Secret transmissions and hidden realizations have occurred time and again. Since the methods of the masters were thus so vast and extensive, students did not possess any single, fixed dharma-gate.

The one flower of Caoxi split into five petals; though square or round, large or small, they differed according to the capacity of the vessel, yet the source of the water’s essence remained of one and the same flavor.
Each specialized in spreading the transformation [of others], and all attained fragrant reputations.

Exert yourself in personal practice and take benevolence as your own responsibility. When you casually offer a word of instruction or issue a single decree, you gather scholars from the four quarters;
the monastic communities flourish, resounding with great vigor like boiling water in a cauldron.
This is not a matter of mere expediency or empty pretense. Consequently, students come and go, proclaiming this to others and transmitting it to them. Proclaim!
They penetrate this [truth], responding to one another in song to manifest its subtlety and elucidate its profound depths. At times they suppress and seize;
at other times they exalt and release. They assist and support the Dharma-transformation of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Yet the words they speak are entirely devoid of flavor—like a soup boiled from wood shavings or rice steamed from iron nails. When given to later generations to chew upon...
It is rotten; chewing it yields no flavor. This is what is called "picking up the ancients" (niangu). Herein, the True Dharma still endures and the fundamental tenets still remain.
These verses began with Zhaozu of Prince’s Monastery in Fenzhou and were extensively propagated by Xuedou Chongxian.
They fully manifest the intent of the "Verses on the Ancients," as vast and expansive as the great ocean.

Its depth is unfathomable, beyond the reach of measurement. Subsequent authors have likewise galloped across Xuedou’s verses, imitating them regardless of their own moral character, talent, or learning.
They do nothing but employ flowery language and novel phrasing, carving and embellishing with artifice until later generations and junior disciples can no longer [apprehend the original meaning].

When one examines the public cases (gong'an) of the ancients, they are profound, substantial, and pure, fully embodying the essential purport of the school. Alas! How could one not cherish and preserve them?

As I have wandered through various monasteries, whenever I encounter the institutional precedents of my predecessors, I resolutely refuse to look at anything that is not the recorded sayings (yulu) of the ancients;
I resolutely refuse to practice anything that is not the regulations and commands of Baizhang’s Pure Rules (Qinggui). How could this be otherwise?
It is not that I am intentionally fond of antiquity; rather, the speech of people today does not derive from ancient statutes nor follow classical precepts, and thus it cannot serve as a model.
I hope that those who comprehend principle and scholars who have attained the Way will understand that my intent lies beyond words and symbols.
Ritual has its origins, and law has its transmission; how could there be anything without roots?
“Are there branches that bear fruit without flowers?

Wanan said, “Recently I have observed that some monastics are fond of clinging to biased views and fail to understand the nature of things. They are easily swayed by false beliefs and difficult to turn back;

they flatter others and praise themselves. If one complies with them, they consider it beautiful; if one opposes them, they become distant. Even if they possess a modicum of knowledge or partial understanding, they are instead overcome by these [faults].”
There are many who, obscured by such evil habits, reach their white-haired old age without achieving anything (the above is all seen in the *Zhilin ji*).
Whenever the Chan practitioner Wannan Xiao saw a monk, he would speak with a spirit of perfect integration and vast openness, thoroughly understanding human nature.
Affection is stubbornly attached to one-sided views; it does not penetrate human sentiments or the principles of things.
As soon as they hear a single matter enter their ears, they immediately believe it lightly, making it difficult to turn them back. They delight in others' flattery toward themselves;

when others comply, their hearts are joyful and they regard them as excellent, but when others oppose them, their hearts become resentful and they distance themselves from them. Even if they possess a fragment of knowledge—
I understand. There are many who, being obscured by such evil knowledge and evil views, fail to become accomplished vessels even unto old age.
This is why it is said that in the study of Chan, "perfect integration" (yuanrong) is prized.

Wan’an said: "In every monastery I have visited, false doctrines are rampant. They claim that the precepts need not be observed, meditative concentration and wisdom need not be practiced, the Way and its virtue need not be cultivated, and sensual desires need not be abandoned.

Furthermore, they cite the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Awakening of Faith* as proof, praising greed, anger, ignorance, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct as the 'Brahma-conduct' (*brahmacarya*). Alas! How could such words arise anywhere other than within the monastic communities?"

The harm of today is truly a harm to the Dharma-gate for ten thousand generations. Furthermore, ordinary people of this world are possessed of greed, hatred, craving, and desire, as well as the ignorance of self and others;
their thoughts cling to objects of perception moment by moment like a cauldron boiling over—how could they ever become clear and cool?

The former sages surely considered this great matter and thus established the three trainings of precept, concentration, and wisdom to restrain them, so that one might turn back [from these afflictions].
Furthermore, those born later in these degenerate times do not uphold the precepts, do not practice meditative concentration and wisdom, and do not cultivate the Way and its virtue.

They focus exclusively on extensive learning and eloquent debate to agitate the common world, leading people astray so that they cannot return. This is precisely what I mean when I say such talk is a calamity for ten thousand generations.
Only those gentlemen of right cause who travel as pilgrims should clarify this single point of birth and death, and maintain [the Dharma].
Maintaining sincerity and faith, he was not led astray by such people, but said: "These words are not to be trusted;
they are like the excrement of a venomous *viṣa* bird or water drunk by a snake. One should not even hear or see them, let alone consume them. They will undoubtedly kill a person."
Those who possess discernment naturally distance themselves from him (Letter to Caotang).
Wanan served as a teacher for scholars, destroying heterodoxy and manifesting the orthodox teaching throughout the monastic communities of his time.
Whenever he arrived at a place, erroneous and deluded words were as fiercely blazing as fire; he then proclaimed: "The precepts and regulations bind the body, so one cannot be unrestrained."

There is no need to follow others; when concentration and wisdom restrain the mind, one must not act according to whim. There is no need to practice after others; the Way is fundamentally manifest and complete—whose virtue could be lacking?
There is no need to cultivate after others; since one’s inclinations are constant, what hindrance can private desires pose? There is no need to reject others;
for fear that people might not believe you, [the Buddha] further cites the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, which says: "Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas enter into all..."

He frequented brothels to demonstrate the faults of desire; though he had a wife and children, he constantly practiced the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). Furthermore, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* states:
"All obstacles are themselves ultimate enlightenment," and even that "all precepts, concentrations, and wisdoms, as well as lust, anger, and ignorance, are collectively the pure conduct.
These were used as false evidence to compel people to believe him. Alas! How could such foolish words be anything other than [deceptive]?
The establishment of these monastic groves poses a threat to our very eyes today; within the true Dharma-gate, they pose a threat for ten million generations.
Furthermore, the foolish men and women of this great earth, as well as the fourfold assembly throughout the world, harbor greed, anger, and the defilement of lustful passions.

Driven by the various poisons of ego-clinging and ignorance, their afflictions do not cease for a single moment; like monkeys leaping from branch to branch, they abandon one thing only to grasp another.
Furthermore, it is like a cauldron of boiling water that has no way to become cool and clear on its own.
Based on my examination of the intent of the former sages and Buddha-patriarchs, they must have considered how the three poisons of sentient beings are so difficult to subdue.
Therefore, they established the three untainted studies of precepts, concentration, and wisdom to restrain them, so that one might perhaps turn back [the tide of suffering].
Furthermore, those of later generations and junior disciples who have recently entered this gate have no foundation upon which to rely.
They defile their own bodies while failing to uphold the precepts; their minds sink into dullness or fluctuate with agitation while they do not practice concentration and wisdom.

Neither the principles nor the virtuous deeds are cultivated, as they devote themselves exclusively to the extensive reading of texts and indulge in forceful, impulsive disputation to delude the common folk and deceive the ignorant. Thus they proceed...

They do not turn back. This is why I have said that these citations from the *Vimalakīrti* and the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* constitute a misinterpretation of the Buddha’s words and a fallacious justification for the practice of Brahma-conduct;
they are a poison that harms the world for ten thousand generations. Only by ensuring that the ground of one's practice is upright can one truly engage in the fundamental journey of cultivation.
Those of lofty vision should directly take this "single point" regarding the great matter of birth and death as the standard for discernment and clarity.
He replied: "I shall maintain integrity and sincerity, and harbor a heart of faith and truth. I will not be led astray by such people of evil knowledge and evil views.

Instead, I shall declare for myself: These words regarding the failure to uphold the precepts and the lack of cultivation in concentration and wisdom are like the poisonous excrement dropped by a *viṣakīra* bird or the poisoned water drunk by a snake—these two kinds of poisons."
Regarding objects, it is already impermissible even to hear of or see them, let alone consume them. Their harming of human beings is certain and beyond doubt.
Those of evil views who cite two sūtras to prove that the three poisons constitute the practice of Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*) are likewise in error.
Those with discernment will naturally disbelieve such delusions and distance themselves from them.
Wan’an said, “Among the disciples of Caotang, only Shantang possesses the style of the ancients.

During his tenure at Huanglong, whenever an administrative official had business to attend to, he would invariably approach the abbot’s quarters with full ceremonial decorum to receive instructions on the details;

only then would he prepare the offerings of tea and soup, maintaining this practice from beginning to end without change. There was a senior monk named Zhien who, for the sake of performing merit for his deceased mother, offered two gold coins. Two days later—
Fuxin, the attendant of the Venerable Sengcai, found it while sweeping the floor. A "Lost and Found" sign was posted, and only then did the entire assembly come to know of it.
This is because when those who preside over the Dharma are pure, those above set the example for those below (from the *Qingquan ji*).
Wan’an’s discourse on Mount Shantang being solemn and pure, such that it may serve as a model for future generations, states:
"Among the Dharma-disciples of Caotang Qing, only Shantang’s conduct possessed the style of the ancients.

During his days at Huanglong, whenever he had official business for the monastery or as an administrative officer, he invariably maintained full ceremonial decorum; only upon entering the abbot’s quarters would he accept his assignments."
When this was finished, the tea and soup offerings were prepared again; from the beginning until the conclusion of the rite, nothing was changed.

Among them was the senior monk (Upādhyāya) Jie’en, who was performing meritorious services for the benefit of his deceased mother in the netherworld. He had inadvertently omitted two copper cash from the silver offering.
After two periods of the ritual had passed without anyone noticing, the attendant Saint-Seng (Shèngsēng Cái) happened to be sweeping the floor when he picked them up.
He obtained it and was about to hang it upon the "Miscellaneous Omissions" (Shiyi) board when the assembly only then realized what had happened.
This was because the presiding master did not seek personal gain; being so pure and unattached, those under him likewise did not seek gain.
This is how one attains such purity; those above act first, and those below follow their example.
Wanan was frugal and used his savings from small and general sermons to provide offerings.

Among the monks, some privately criticized this, but when Wanan heard of it, he said, "To enjoy rich delicacies in the morning and grow weary of coarse food by evening is but human nature. Since you all are mindful of life..."

The matter of death is great; yet you seek one another on the shores of desolation. You should reflect that your spiritual practice remains unaccomplished and that the time since the Sage passed away is remote;
how can you continue to devote yourself to greed and gluttony morning and evening? (From the *Zhenmu ji*)
The "Small Assembly" (xiǎocān) is precisely the "Evening Assembly" (wǎncān). Whenever the assembly is gathered for instruction, it is all termed a "cān" (assembly/discussion).

When the ancients guided their disciples, they caused them to inquire and consult morning and evening, never failing to stimulate and exalt this Way at any time; therefore, there was necessarily a cān every evening, held at the hour of *bú* (the late afternoon).
This was also the case when the abbot entered his residence, or when officials and lay patrons (*dānapati*) visited the mountain, or when [receiving...]
When requested by individuals, or to provide instruction for the deceased, or during the four seasonal festivals (*lajie*), the session is moved to the time when the evening bell tolls;
this is called the *xiaocan* (small *can*). There is no fixed location for the *xiaocan*; it depends on the number of people present, being held either in the dormitory hall or the Dharma Hall.
Upon reaching the afternoon, the attendant informs the Abbot, saying, "There will be a *xiaocan* this evening," and instructs the guest-master acolyte.
When the small-seated sermon (xiaocan) plaque is hung to notify the assembly, a single roll of the drum is struck at the hour of the dusk bell.
Those who have been invited gather, and the abbot is welcomed to ascend the seat. He presents the core outline (tigan) and offers words of gratitude in full detail.

He then cites ancient precedents and concludes the session with a general discourse (pushe), which serves as a universal instruction following the offering of incense. Wan’an Zun recorded that this was practiced as a small-seated sermon characterized by frugality and restraint.
He spoke universally: "When providing for a son of Chan, there may be private discussions. Wan’an, having heard of this, warned them, saying:
'It is a common human sentiment that one’s morning meal is good while one’s evening meal is poor. Since you all feel such deep urgency..."
The matter of birth and death is of great importance; we have come to seek definitive resolution. Let us together dwell in a secluded and solitary place, each contemplating the Great Way.
Those who have not yet attained true realization should quickly seek it; those whose virtuous deeds are not yet accomplished should strive to complete them.
Seek swift accomplishment. Since the time until you reach the Buddha is still remote, you should reflect upon the subtlety of the Dharma and diligently maintain mindfulness of the Path.
How could you possibly indulge in gluttonous cravings morning and evening, making the satisfaction of your own belly your sole concern?

Wan’an Tian’s nature was benevolent and generous. He conducted himself with integrity and frugality. In his daily teachings, his phrasing was concise yet his meaning was profound. He was widely learned and possessed a powerful memory;

he investigated principles exhaustively, refusing to settle for superficiality or follow others blindly. When discussing matters of antiquity and the present with others, it was as if he had personally experienced them;
those who listened understood clearly, as if witnessing the events with their own eyes. A monk once remarked that throughout the entire year...
Regarding his studies, it was not as well for him to spend a single day listening to the Master’s discourses (from *Jiwen*).

As recorded, Wan’an’s innate disposition was benevolent, compassionate, loyal, and sincere; he conducted himself with personal integrity, maintaining a life of purity, integrity, frugality, and moderation.
In his ordinary teachings to the great assembly, his language and phrasing were concise and direct, yet the underlying principles were profound and subtle.

Having extensively surveyed the scriptures and diligently committed them to memory, he investigated and scrutinized their meanings until he had thoroughly mastered the correct doctrines; he never acted with negligence.
He did not rest in emptiness or allow himself to follow the common crowd with superficiality or frivolity. When engaging others in critical discussion, he was ever-illuminating throughout the ages.
It is as if one were personally walking within it oneself; those who hear it understand it with perfect clarity, as if seeing it with their own eyes.
A monk once said: "To diligently practice and study for an entire year is not as good as listening to the Master’s discourse on the past and present for a single day, for the latter yields far more."
Wan’an said to Chief Seat Bian, “Master Yuanwu once remarked: ‘The Chan practitioners of today lack integrity and have little sense of shame;

the scholar-officials mostly hold them in low esteem. If, in the future, you cannot avoid becoming one of these vermin, always walk within the boundaries of discipline, do not pursue trends or profit, and do not flatter others with sycophantic expressions, even in the face of life-and-death calamities.’”
"Leave everything as it is; this is precisely not departing from the realm of Māra to enter the realm of the Buddha" (Dharma Words).
Regarding the Head Seat Bian: he was the successor of Daomeng Fatai. If one were to use such words, "having feet" refers to an insect, while "lacking feet" refers to a *zhì* (a type of beast).
This is still intended to convey the meaning of conduct and movement. "Rope and ink-line" refers to the ink in the carpenter’s compass.
It is also a "line. It serves as a metaphor for the meaning of the direct path. Wanan said to Chief Seat Bian:
"At that time, practice the true Way and do not pursue trends or profit. The Elder Master Yuanwu had this to say: "The Chan practitioners of these times..."
There are few who possess integrity and righteousness, and none who maintain a sense of shame.
Consequently, when recluses practice such noble conduct, even high officials who hear of it often treat them with contempt and disdain.

Elder Bian, in the future, should you perhaps find yourself in such a position, you must ensure that your conduct always remains within the path of rectitude; you must not seek after fame or influence for the sake of status.
Benefit others and cultivate a pleasing countenance. Whether life or death, or calamity and misfortune arrive, accept everything as it comes and do not seek to avoid it by any means.
This is precisely turning the Great Dharma Wheel within the boiling cauldron and performing great Buddha-work amidst the dust and toil of worldly afflictions.
Why then would one abandon the realm of Māra to enter the realm of the Buddha? This very direct path is it.
The Head Seat Bian left the monastery to reside at Qixian on Mount Lu. He was constantly carrying a single staff and wearing a pair of sandals as he traveled through Jiuyang.
When Old Man Rongrong of Donglin saw him, he rebuked him, saying, "A teacher is a model for others. Your deportment is like this?"
He did not disparage himself. The host’s hospitality was extremely perfunctory. Bian laughed and said, "In human life, one takes finding contentment as joy;
what fault is there in me? He took up his brush and wrote a verse before departing. The verse said: "Do not say that Qixian is in poverty; Though the body is poor, the Way is not poor.
My straw sandals are as fierce as tigers; My staff is as lively as a dragon. When thirsty, I drink from the waters of Caoxi; When hungry, I swallow the thorny chestnuts."
Péng. "A man with a copper head and an iron forehead—all are within my mountains. When Húnróng read this, he felt ashamed (*Yuèkù jí*). Qīxián belongs to Nánkāng Prefecture;
*qióngzhú* is a bamboo staff, and *jù* is a straw sandal. Dōnglín belongs to Jiǔjiāng Prefecture; Húnróng was the abbot of Dōnglín Temple.
*Miè* means extinction; *jié* means destruction. "Too much extinction and destruction" is what it says.
To utterly destroy propriety is excessive. "Adi" means "just so"; it means "self-attainment. "Ning'e" means "ferocious and evil. Regarding the *liji peng* (the bristly fruit):

Yangqi addressed the assembly, saying, "If you can pass through the diamond circle and swallow the *liji peng*, then you will walk hand-in-hand with the Buddhas of the three periods and breathe from the same nostril as the patriarchs of all generations. If you have not yet..."
However, one must practice true practice and attain true realization.
When the Record-keeper Bian was serving as abbot at Xixian on Mount Lu, he always carried a single bamboo staff with him.
Upon passing through Jiujiang and arriving at Donglin Monastery, Elder Hunrong saw Bian and immediately rebuked him, saying: "A teacher is the model for others and must serve as a safeguard."
His movements and conduct were composed and steady; he was of such a character. Was this not to slight himself? Why did the host’s etiquette fail so utterly, lacking all formal decorum?
Bian laughed and said, "A person's life finds joy in following one's own will. What fault is there in me?
He then took up his brush and wrote a verse, after which he returned to Xixian. The verse says: "Do not say..."
Qixian is destitute. Do not seek to see me through form; though my body is poor, the Way is not poor. I have this here:
my straw sandals are as fierce as tigers, wandering from west to east; my staff is as lively as a dragon, propping up heaven and supporting the earth.
When thirsty, I drink the waters of Caoxi—far superior to Tiger Creek. When hungry, I swallow the thorny chestnut—this is no boast of wealth. Copper heads and iron...
"E Han, there are several people here as well, all within my mountains; they are not easily released.
When Elder Hunrong saw this, his face showed a look of shame. This is what is meant by the saying: "Without undergoing one event, one does not gain one wisdom."
Master Bian said to Hunrong: "A painted dragon cannot bring rain; how can a drawn cake satisfy hunger?
A monk who lacks inner, actual virtue yet relies outwardly on flowery artifice is like a leaking and dilapidated boat coated with vermilion and cinnabar;
if a puppet were made to drive it, it might indeed look impressive while on dry land. But should it venture onto the rivers and lakes and encounter a gale—"
[Tao] asked: "Is it not dangerous to attain [such a state]? (From the *Yueku ji*).
Master Bian said that [the truth] is a harmonious fusion. He told the novice Xiaoxiao that one ought to cultivate actual virtue.
How could an image of a dragon made of clay or carved from wood be expected to bring down rain? How could a painting of a cake made with ink, water, glue, and green pigment ever be eaten?
Is it to satisfy hunger? A patch-robed monk who lacks genuine inner virtue yet relies on flowery speech and clever words on the outside to deceive the ignorant—how is he any different from this?
Furthermore, it is like a ship that has already decayed and is leaking;
one paints many layers of five-colored lacquer upon it, places wooden and earthen figures atop it to steer it, and raises the sails to catch the wind.
A boat, when resting securely on dry land, is indeed beautiful to behold.
Yet, once released to drift across the Three Rivers and Five Lakes, braving thousands of surges and tens of thousands of waves, how perilous it would not be!
A person who lacks inner virtue yet relies outwardly on flowery artifice is just like this.
Master Bian said: "Those called 'Elders' propagate the transformation [of the Dharma] on behalf of the Buddha. The essential requirement is to purify oneself when presiding over the assembly;
in performing one's deeds, one must exhaust all sincerity. How could one choose between benefit and harm to divide one's mind? To act from within oneself, it must certainly be thus.
As for whether success or failure will follow, even the former sages could not guarantee it—how then could I act with mere expediency? (From the *Yueku ji*)
Master Bian informed the abbot: "You must exhaust your sincerity and must not speak with stubborn insistence.

What is called a 'Venerable Elder' acts on behalf of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to proclaim the Dharma and its transformation; this depends on purifying one's own body and mind when presiding over the great assembly.
In speech and action, you should be straightforward and without pretense, striving only to exhaust your own sincerity; you must not engage in discrimination between what is beneficial or—"
Harm has no single master; even if one’s mind is divided, as long as I maintain sincerity, I shall act upon whatever is right according to principle.

This is the proper course of reason. As for whether an undertaking succeeds or fails, even the ancient sages and former worthies could not guarantee it; how then can I seek success through mere expediency?
Master Bian said, "When Fozhi resided at Xichan, the monastics were required to maintain strict discipline.
Only Shuian was by nature simple and unadorned, maintaining the most frugal lifestyle; he stood tall and dignified amidst the crowd, never deigning to give it a thought.
Fozhi, upon seeing him, scolded him, saying, 'How can you be so unkempt? Shuian replied, 'It is not that I do not like fine things to use.'"
"Because I am poor and lack the means to act, even if I had money, I would still wish to perform one or two superficial acts to join the ranks of the assembly.
Since I am poor, there is simply nothing to be done. Fozhi laughed at him, thinking that it was impossible to force such things;
he then let the matter rest (from the *Yueku ji*).
Fozhi was named Duan Yu; he was the successor of the Patriarch Zhaojue Qin. Shu'an was named Duan Yi; he was the successor of Fozhi.
"Chongxu" (profound emptiness) and "dandanbo" (tranquil detachment) describe an appearance of placid stillness and non-action. "Ang" (lofty) means high.
"Āng-āng" means lofty and solitary, remaining as one pleases. "Ruò-jū": the first character is pronounced with the third tone (là), and the second has the sound of "zǎ.
People of the Central Plains say that when people of Shu do not follow established rules and conventions, they are called "ruò-jū"; it likely refers to an appearance that is coarse and unrefined.

"Cāo" and "jū" share the same pronunciation. "Shèhuǒ" is a colloquial term for a gathering or companions; "shè" carries the meaning of assembly. One does not refer to a large assembly as "shè," yet...
It is said: "Fire. To stack firewood and kindle a flame signifies the broad practice of many monks. Master Bian instructed the Zen practitioners:
"You must be upright, pure, frugal, and modest, taking Water Hermitage as your model for the Dharma.

When Fozhi resided at Xichan Temple, the deportment and attire of the monastics were required to be strictly clean and orderly; only Water Hermitage alone possessed a nature that was profound, empty, and humble.
He was serene and aloof; his bearing was exceedingly refined. He stood tall and eminent, remaining self-possessed even amidst great crowds, never casting anxious glances or showing concern.
When the Buddha observed that his appearance and demeanor were so distinct from those of the multitude, he rebuked him, saying:
"Why do you harbor such coarse and biased views? They are neither appropriate for the times nor in accord with human sentiment."
Shui-an replied to him, "It is not that I do not like to enjoy comforts;
it is precisely because I have acted with such intent that I am now bare-handed and empty-fisted, poor and lacking the implements for anything grand.
Had I possessed money and notes, I imagine I could have fashioned a set of respectable clothes to join the festive procession entering his gate. But since I am poor—"
Yet it cannot be said that there was no end to this; what could be done? The Buddha’s wisdom merely smiled at him and did not speak further.
Knowing that his innate disposition could not be forced, he finally desisted.
Cánlín Bǎoxùn Shùnzhū, Scroll Three; Cánlín Bǎoxùn Shùnzhū, Scroll Four.
Compiled by Jì Érguān Shèngkě of Huáyán in Yú, Shǔ. Virtue-Jade (Deyù). Shùnzhū.
Master Fozhi Yu said: "That a swift horse does not dare to run wild is due to the restraint of the bit and reins;
that a petty person does not dare to indulge their passions is due to the constraints of law and punishment;
that the wandering of consciousness does not dare to cling to objects is due to the power of awakening and illumination. Alas! If a student lacks this awakening and illumination, it is like..."
A swift horse has no bit or bridle; a petty person has no laws or punishments. How, then, can one sever greed and desire and govern delusive thoughts?
"Swift" (駿) means rapid. A "bit" (衘) is the iron rein in the horse's mouth. A "bridle" (轡) is the horse's halter. "To restrain" (禦止) means to stop or check. Master Fozhi said:
"To show people that they must control greed and desire, they must rely on awakening and clear observation. This is like the case of a galloping horse that lets its wind escape.
Why is it that a horse runs swiftly yet does not dare to gallop recklessly? It is because its mouth is controlled by the bit and reins.
Why is it that a petty person may be stubborn and violent, yet does not dare to indulge their desires and passions? It is for the same reason.
This is because the state possesses codes and punishments to rectify it.

As for the consciousness that arises from the sense faculties and mental objects of all people—the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations that continue to arise like waves on a rapid current, flowing moment by moment—why is it that they do not dare to grasp at or connect with external conditions?
It is because there exists the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in which all phenomena are quiescent.
First is the power of wisdom corresponding to a single thought; second is the power of precepts, which restrains and tames one.
Alas! How can a student be without the power of meditative concentration and the power of wisdom?

If a student lacks the power of meditative concentration and the power of wisdom, they are like a wild horse without a bridle or rein, or like a petty person without the codes of law. With what handle, then, could one cut them down?
Is this not the severing of the three poisons as they manifest before one, and the elimination of the delusive thoughts that flow through the three periods of time?
This is indeed the true study for cultivating the mind. *Hàn* (pronounced *gàn*) means a horse charging headlong; *jī* (pronounced *jī*) refers to the halter placed in the horse’s mouth.
Buddhiji said to Shui'an: "The essence of abbotship consists of four aspects: first, moral virtue; second, speech and conduct; third, benevolence and righteousness; and fourth, ritual and law.
Moral virtue and speech and conduct are the foundation of the teaching; benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and law are its branches.
Without the foundation, one cannot stand; without the branches, one cannot flourish. When the former sages observed that students were unable..."
To ensure self-governance, monasteries were established to provide stability, and abbots were appointed to exercise authority.

Thus, the dignity of the monastery was not for the sake of the abbot, nor were the four requisites provided in abundance for the sake of the students; rather, it was all for the sake of the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Therefore, one who serves as an abbot must first honor the Way and its virtue, and maintain their words and conduct.

One who is a scholar must first preserve benevolence and righteousness, and follow ritual and law. Thus, an abbot cannot be established without a scholar, and a scholar cannot achieve fulfillment without an abbot.
An abbot and a scholar are like the body and its arms, or the head and its feet; their sizes must be perfectly proportioned.
They do not contradict one another; rather, they proceed in mutual dependence. Thus it is said: "The student relies on the monastic community (*saṃghārāma*);
the monastic community relies on the Way and its Virtue (*moral*). If the abbot lacks the Way and its Virtue, then the monastic community will surely see its decline" (Shilu).

The Buddha-wisdom refers to the Great Substance of Master Shui'an's Dharma. To understand the fundamental discourse on the roots and consciousness, there are four aspects to the substance of abiding and maintaining [the teaching]:
first, the path that should be practiced in daily life, along with the virtues habitually cultivated therein;
second, the words used to inspire and develop those who come after, along with the conduct personally practiced; third, compassion...

Love is the benevolence (*ren*) of compassionate empathy; righteousness (*yi*) is that which accords with proper regulation and suitability. Fourth, ritual (*li*) consists of seasonal festivals and the reduction of assemblies;
law (*fa*) consists of the methods of commands and proclamations. The first two types—benevolence and righteousness—are conduct and speech, and are thus the root of the teaching.
The latter two types—ritual and law—are ritual and law, and are thus the branches and leaves of the teaching. If...
Without a root, upon what could it be established? If there were no branches and leaves, it could not reach completion.
To truly become a great tree that provides shade for all people under heaven, one must understand this root.
Seeing that those who study under them could not cultivate themselves, the former sages established monasteries with lofty halls and vast grounds.
[The monastery] is expanded to provide for their peaceful sustenance. A *zhuchi* (abbot) is established, a person of lofty virtue and great wisdom, to govern and manage it.
Thus, the honor of a temple belonging to a vast multitude of people is not intended solely for the personal abundance of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine for the *zhuchi* alone;
nor is it exclusively for the sake of the students. Since this is not the case, [the merit] is complete.
That he has acted in such a manner is entirely for the sake of the Way of the Buddha’s and Patriarchs’ life-force (*jīvitendriya*).

Therefore, one who is able to shoulder this Way and treat it as his primary task—acting as a *zhuchi* (abbot)—must ultimately prioritize honoring virtue and morality, taking the maintenance of conduct and speech as the foundation. He must diligently seek this Way and treat it as his foremost concern.
For those who study, this must ultimately be their primary task. To cherish benevolence and righteousness and to abide by ritual and law constitutes the branches and leaves;
therefore, if the abbot has no students, from what source could the flowers and fruits of wisdom be produced?
If there were no abbots to maintain the monastery, from what source could the seeds of Bodhi be nurtured and brought to fruition?
Therefore, the relationship between the abbot and the student is like a person having a body and arms, a head and feet;
the four limbs, the hundred bones, the five viscera, and the six bowels all fit together perfectly and accord with one another’s hearts, without any contradiction or opposition. Thus they are...
Those things that must be practiced through mutual dependence—would these not form a great, magnificent tree of humanity?
Radiantly possessing roots and a trunk, branches and leaves, the flowers and fruits of wisdom, and the seeds of Bodhi—all arise from this mutual dependence.
The life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is transmitted in continuous succession; how could it ever come to an end? Therefore, it is said:
Scholars preserve the monastic groves, and the monastic groves preserve morality; these two preserve one another.

If the abbot lacks both the Way and virtue, then it has never happened that the grove could maintain its roots and branches in strength and vigor, or endure forever without decline from beginning to end.
The Monk Shu-an Yi said: "The *I Ching* says, 'The noble person contemplates misfortune and provides for it in advance.
