Therefore, people of antiquity contemplated the great misfortune of birth and death and provided for it through the Way; thus they were able to pass through great trials and transmit their legacy far into the distance.

People of today say that seeking the Way is迂闊 (obscure and impractical), and that it is not as appropriate as seeking profit. Consequently, they compete to practice superficial splendor and calculate matters down to the smallest fraction."
In the end, people hope for immediate results and harbor expedient schemes; thus, they are unwilling to establish plans for even a single year, let alone consider the concerns of life and death.

Consequently, students grow more base by the day, monastic communities fall into ruin, and the disciplinary regulations decline daily, until the tradition is so dilapidated and fallen that it is nearly beyond salvation. Alas! How can we not take this as a warning? (From the *Shuanglin Shilu*)
"Lingyi" means that the Way of the Dharma has declined and fallen into ruin, much like a hill or mound gradually leveling out.
Master Shui'an, the One Monk, taught that regarding the great matter of birth and death, one must prepare in advance; do not speak of it with haste when the moment arrives.

The *Book of Changes*, in the hexagram "Water and Fire in Perfect Order," states that a gentleman who has perfected his virtue constantly contemplates potential calamities in his heart and prepares for them beforehand.
Be cautious regarding the minute; block the gradual [onset of evil] to prevent it. Therefore, people of antiquity constantly reflected:
they did not know from where life comes, nor did they know where death goes. This is the greatest affliction of humanity.
Thus, they prevented it by means of the direct pointing to the human mind—the true Way that should be practiced in daily life—and were thereby able to shoulder the great matter and transmit it.
For a long time, people of today have failed to understand the ultimate goal of the Way;

on the contrary, they claim that seeking the Way is circuitous and remote, unable to alleviate the immediate urgencies of hunger and cold before one's eyes. They argue that it is more practical to seek wealth and profit, which can be immediately enjoyed in the present.
Consequently, they compete for advancement and indulge in their habits, spending lavishly on luxury while calculating every fraction of a cent.
These matters are trivial and petty; they seek only immediate results rather than the vast and profound.
They harbor expedient schemes while lacking constancy; thus, they are unwilling to establish themselves or conduct their affairs according to a plan for a single year.
How could they recognize the wondrous Way that transcends past and present, vast and eternal, neither born nor dying? Therefore,
as the insight of scholars daily becomes more base and vulgar, the laws and regulations of the monastic groves daily fall into ruin,
and the general principles and various codes daily collapse until they reach a state of decay, overturning, and peril so grave that they can no longer be rescued.
To save them from this ground—how can those who cannot bear to see or hear such things fail to take heed? Alas! Is it not fitting that they reflect upon this?

Those with the aspiration for the Way should examine themselves through introspection; by observing with the mirror of wisdom, the distinction between the beautiful and the ugly will naturally become clear.
Shuian said: "In the past, while traveling to Yunju, I attended Gao’an’s night discourse. He stated that the ultimate Way is direct and straightforward, not conforming to worldly sentiments;
one must possess a sincere heart and upright intent, and must not engage in artificiality, pretension, partiality, or deviance.

Artificiality leads to deceit and flattery, while partiality and deviance result in a lack of centrality and rectitude—both of which are incompatible with the ultimate Way. I have reflected privately on these words and find them to be profoundly reasonable. Thereupon, he carved [this record].
He took this to heart. Upon meeting Master Fozhi Xianshi, he finally attained a vast and profound enlightenment (*haorandache*).
Only then was he able to fulfill his lifelong vow of traveling as a pilgrim. "Hao" means vast; "haorandache" signifies the state where there is nothing one does not penetrate. Shu'an and Yue...

An Inscription for the Hall. These words concern the essential principles for a person to cultivate the Way; they are the most correct teaching. Formerly, while traveling on pilgrimage, I visited Yungju and saw Gaosan.
One evening during the night assembly, he said: "The unsurpassed, ultimate Way is direct and straightforward, standing out in its uniqueness.
It does not follow worldly sentiments; one must truly sincerity their heart and rectify their intention. One must not engage in artificiality, falsehood, or decoration, nor fall into partiality."

If one is privately perverse and employs artifice and embellishment, one approaches the class of the deceitful and sycophantic; if one is biased and perverse, one enters the category of the unrighteous and imbalanced.
To compare this with the Unsurpassed Ultimate Way is like trying to fit a square base onto a round lid; they will certainly not harmonize. This I have reflected upon in private.
These words from this informal discourse (xiao-can) accord with principle; therefore, engrave them upon the ground of your mind and put them into practice.

Upon meeting the late Master Fozhi, my mind was opened by a single word, and I finally succeeded in not failing the lifelong aspiration I had cultivated through climbing mountains and wading through waters as a wandering practitioner.
Shui-an said: "When Yue-tang served as abbot, he took the practice of the Way as his sole responsibility. He did not dispatch fundraising emissaries nor did he engage in formal visits to patrons.

Each year, the expenses for the community were met solely from what the monastery’s permanent endowment provided. When many monks with aspirations to serve as fundraisers sought his approval, he repeatedly declined them.
Someone asked: "The Buddha’s precepts for bhikṣus state that one should maintain one's life by carrying an alms bowl. Why does the Master refuse them?"
[The Master] would not tolerate this. Yuet-tang said: "This might have been acceptable when our Buddha was alive;

but were it done today, there would surely be those seeking profit who would go so far as to sell themselves. Thus one reflects that Yuet-tang’s foresight in preventing small evils before they become great was profoundly penetrating and clearly illuminating.
"His words of truth remain in our ears even now. Judging by today’s circumstances, how could it have been merely a matter of self-promotion?
(Dharma Words). Yuet-tang, whose name was Daochang, was the dharma heir of Miaozhan Hui. "Index finger" refers to the second finger of the human hand.
Regarding the infant who has not yet cut its teeth and is constantly suckling at the breast: this refers to the meaning inherently possessed by every person.
To "sell" is to explain that one must not engage in greedy seeking; thus spoke Master Shui-an. Whenever Master Yue-tang arrived at a place...
He took only the practice of the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs as his own primary responsibility.
He did not dispatch monks to solicit money or grain, nor did he visit the doors of the nobility to seek audiences with officials.
Regarding annual expenditures, he provided for his own sustenance from his own portion; whatever the monastery obtained—whether abundant or meager—everyone shared in its use. Among the monastics...
He resolved his will, wishing to serve as a guide for transformation and lead the donors. Yet, Dantang repeatedly rejected him and would not permit it.

Someone from the side remonstrated with him, saying: "When the Buddha was in the world, he once commanded bhikṣus who maintained the precepts to enter the city to collect alms in order to sustain their lives.
For what reason does your master reject you and refuse permission? Dantang—
He then recounted the reasons for his refusal and replied: "When our Buddha was in the world, those who were moved to transformation were many.

They ate but one meal at midday, and the monks devoted themselves solely to investigating their own person, free from distracting thoughts; because ten thousand people shared a single mind, it was permissible.
But people of the present age are mostly greedy for fame and profit and do not apply themselves to matters that concern them personally; they fear only the present day."
If one were to do so, there would inevitably be those who seek profit and take advantage of public office to serve their private interests, even to the point of selling themselves out;

therefore, it was not permitted. I have reflected upon this and realize that Monthang’s meticulousness in guarding against even the slightest transgression and his total prevention of gradual corruption stemmed from a mind that was perilously vigilant and profoundly earnest.
His apprehension of potential calamities was deep-seated and clearly manifest; this truly accords with the ultimate truth.
Truly excellent words! Fortunately, those words still ring in our ears.
Looking at the present times, the maladies of us practitioners go far beyond mere self-promotion; there is something even worse, all of which begins with soliciting donations.
Shuian said to Minister You Yanzhi: "In the past, Dayu, Ciming, Guquan, and Langya formed a group to study under Fenyang.
The region of Hedong was bitterly cold, and everyone else found it unbearable; only Ciming’s resolve was fixed upon the Way. Morning and night he never slackened.
When he sat through the night and felt drowsy, he would pull a needle to prick himself, exclaiming: 'The ancients regarded the matter of birth and death as so great that they did not [seek ease]...'"

He would not sleep while eating. [Chuyuan] asked, "What kind of person am I that I allow myself such reckless indulgence? To live without benefiting the age and to die without leaving a reputation for posterity is to abandon oneself.
Once he took his leave and returned home, Fenyang sighed and said, "With Chuanyuan’s departure today, my Way shall flourish in the East" (*Xihu Jiwen*).
"Hedong" refers to Taiyuan and Fenzhou; it belongs to Taiyuan. "Kuhan" means severe cold. "Danwei" means to dread or find difficult. You Yanzhi:
surnamed You, named Mao, styled Yanzhi, and known as the Layman Suichu. He was one who sought the Way from the monk Shui'an Yi.
"Huangtai" means neglectful, dissolute, and indolent. Shui'an cited the ancients' forgetting... [text ends]

Taking the Dharma as his own body, he practiced with unremitting diligence. Regarding the account of You Yanzhi, it is said that in the past, when Daoyu Zhi, Ciming Yuan, Guquan Dao, and Langya Jue formed a group to join the ranks of the firewood carriers and go to attend upon the Patriarch Fenyang Wuye, the region of Hedong was bitterly cold;
while the spirits of the others were weak and they felt apprehension, only Ciming’s resolve remained firm.
He directed his mind toward the vast and distant. He kept this in mind at all times. Morning and evening he was diligent and vigilant; there was not a single moment of rest or indolence.
During his night sittings, whenever he felt the urge to doze off, he would pull out a sharp awl and prick himself.
This can be called attaining the samādhi of diligence, being able to remain single-mindedly persistent without ceasing. Furthermore, he once sighed, saying: "The ancients..."

I truly feel deep anguish. Not knowing where one comes from when born, and not knowing where one goes when dead—this great matter is so urgent that I forget to eat by day and forget to sleep by night.
Even though it is thus, who am I that I dare to indulge in negligence and indolence? If, during this present life, there is no genuine virtue to benefit others, [what will become of me]?
At the time of his death, he left no fine reputation to be passed down to future generations; this was his own self-abandonment. What kind of person could he have become?
One day, he took his leave of Fenyang, who sighed with admiration and said, "Chu-yuan is now departing;
my Way shall travel eastward, and I too shall go along with him. Thus did Fenyang Zhao, his ancestral master, hold him in high esteem. Furthermore—
"Deeply, I grant that it is exactly as you say; it is not empty praise.
Shuian said, "When ancient worthies served as abbots, they led themselves by practicing the Way, never being lax or self-indulgent.
In the past, Fenyang often lamented that in this degenerate age, students are difficult to transform. Ciming said, 'That is very easy. The only concern is those who preside over the Dharma.'"
"I am unable to guide them well. Fenyang said, "In ancient times, people were sincere and honest; it still took them twenty or thirty years before they could achieve realization.
Ciming said, "This is not the discourse of a sage or a wise man. One who skillfully cultivates the Way requires the effort of a thousand days.

Some claimed that Ciming was arrogant and false and would not listen to him; however, because the region of Fenyang was very cold, he consequently abolished the night assemblies. There was a certain extraordinary bhikṣu...
He said to Fenyang, "There are six great beings (mahāsattvas) within this assembly; why do you not preach the Dharma? Less than three years later, there were indeed six who attained the Way.
Fenyang once had a verse that said: "The foreign monk with the golden staff’s radiance Sought the Dharma at Fenyang.
Six men became great vessels; I entreated him to proclaim it forth. (Recorded in the *Xihu Jiwen* and the *Sengzhuan*.)
"Rude" (sù) means disrespectful; it implies being casual, perfunctory, or negligent. It also conveys a sense of haste, simplicity, or disregard.
"Heterodox bhikṣu" refers to a holy monk. A "Hu monk" is precisely a heterodox bhikṣu. "Golden tongs" refers to the *khakkhara* (staff) held by him. "Radiant descent" refers to the water-bowl.
Shui'an cites these ancient precedents to instruct Zen practitioners: those who would embody the Way through diligent practice must apply themselves with vigor.

It is said that one will surely receive the protection and assistance of the dragons and devas. Since ancient times, those sages who possessed virtue and morality have presided over monastic communities and maintained the Dharma teachings.
They held themselves in high esteem and diligently practiced the Way of the Patriarchs, never being negligent or lax, nor allowing themselves to indulge in self-indulgence.
One need not look further than the frequent sighs of the former patriarch Fenyang Wuye, who lamented that the Semblance Dharma was abiding in the world.
"In these degenerate times, the age has become turbid and the era shallow. Students change with the times and have not remained as they were in antiquity;
therefore, it is difficult to provide them with instruction. Ciming said, "Not so. Man is the most spiritual of beings, and thus it is actually very easy.
The only concern is that those who uphold the Way of the Dharma are unable to exert diligent effort to guide others."
"It is simply a matter of reaching it. Fenyang said further, "The people of ancient times were simple, sincere, and earnest;
yet they still required twenty or thirty years before they could finally achieve unity and master this matter. Ciming said, "This is merely your Reverence’s way of rejecting counsel;
it is not the kind of discourse held by sages and wise men. If one were truly willing..."
For one who has resolved upon the Great Mind and applies courageous diligence with all their might to the Path, a thousand days of practice will suffice for accomplishment.
However, some claimed that this statement by Ciming was deceptive and refused to believe it;
furthermore, as the region of Fenzhou is near the north and frequently cold, they consequently discontinued the night assemblies. Suddenly, there appeared a strange bhikṣu.
Unknown to him, someone came and said to Fenyang, "Within this Dharma assembly, there are six good men who can become great vessels.
Why do you not speak the Dharma to them, instead neglecting the night assemblies?
Not more than three years later, it indeed turned out that six people had accomplished the Way; Fenyang was thus [vindicated].
The verse says: "The Hu monk with the golden staff’s radiance. This refers to the Hu monk who came from the West, arriving with his golden staff as a descent of light.
"He requested the Dharma at Fenyang. This means he came specifically for the sake of the Buddha-dharma.
"Six men became great vessels. These were Ciming Yuan, Dayu Zhi, Langye Jue, Guquan Dao, Fahua Ju, and Tiansheng.
"Tai! These six men are capable of becoming great vessels. I urge you to proclaim their virtues.
By saying this, he urged that they continue to preach the Dharma as before to inspire these six men, and that the night assemblies must not be discontinued.

"If one is willing to exert oneself to the utmost for the Way, the dragons and devas will offer such praise and assistance. Ji then remarked, "Is it not the case that the 'extraordinary bhikṣu' attained the wondrous [state] at Qingliang?"
Is this a manifestation of his virtue? Not so; otherwise, how could his power of knowing future karmic retributions be so unfailing?
Master Touzi Qing painted a portrait of Heshang Shuian and requested a eulogy, saying: "The Dharma-heir Qing Chanren is solitary and resolute, without rival."

He maintained a single fast from dawn until dusk and did not let his side touch the mat. He entered deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and transcended the coming and going of breath.

His reputation reached the ninefold palace, and when the Emperor discussed his meditative virtues and selected him for his excellence, the Dragon Countenance was greatly pleased. The Emperor bestowed upon him gold and silk, but he declined three times; the Sovereign then marveled at him with praise.
A true man of the Way! Grasses and trees blaze forth in radiance as they transmit my humble form. I offer incense and request this eulogy;
this is what is meant by "the green surpassing the blue. (See the portrait.)
Touzi’s name was Yiqing; he was the successor of Shuian. "Xuan-de" (Selected Virtue) is the name of the inner palace hall; "Shang-jun" (Supreme Sovereign) refers to the King.
"The green surpasses the indigo" means that when dyeing for green, it originates from indigo, yet the resulting green is even more excellent than the indigo itself.
This is a metaphor meaning that the disciple excels the teacher. [This concludes] the record of Touzi Qing painting water.
An image of Master Shu’an was sought for a eulogy. Shui’an’s eulogy reads: “His Dharma heir is Yiqing. This Chan practitioner is solitary and lofty, foremost in his steadfastness.
Morning and evening, he takes but one meal a day; he sits upright for long periods, never lying down upon his mat.
He has deeply entered the four dhyānas and nine samādhis, appearing as if dead with no sign of breathing. His fame reached the imperial court, and he expounded the Dharma and discussed Zen.”
His chosen virtue moved the Son of Heaven, who was filled with joy and bestowed upon him gold, silver, silks, and fabrics. He declined these gifts three times with the utmost sincerity.
The Emperor then praised him highly, exclaiming, "Truly, this is a man of the Way. Grasses and trees shone with a brilliant and radiant luster.
Today, as my humble form is being transmitted and incense is being offered, I am asked to offer a self-eulogy.
This is precisely what is meant by the saying that "blue dye originally comes from indigo, yet the blue is deeper than the indigo. One must strictly avoid self-praise;
to praise others is simply to praise oneself, for when the water rises, the boat floats higher.
Shuian said: "Master Fozhi previously stated that the founding ancestor of Dongshan once told Chancellor Geng Longxue:
'I, this mountain monk, have Yuanwu as my companion, like a fish having water or a bird having wings. Therefore, the layman Ziyuan of the Chancellor’s household praised them, saying:
'The compatibility between teacher and disciple is rare to encounter in a single age; who could ever intervene in their bond from beginning to end? Ziyuan resided..."

This gentleman may indeed be said to understand speech. Lately, I have observed that venerable masters in various quarters employ crafty schemes to manage their disciples, while the disciples exploit power and profit to serve these masters.
When host and guest pursue mutual gain, those above and below engage in mutual deception and contempt;
how, then, can the Dharma-gate flourish or the monastic communities prosper?
The Layman Ziyuan was named Zhang Jun, with the courtesy name Dayuan. At the beginning of the Shaoxing era, he was enfeoffed as the Duke of He. He sought the Way from the Patriarch Yuanwu Keqin.

Shuinan cited the karmic affinity between former masters and disciples as being such that no one could intervene; yet he remarked that Meishan Run had said that his late teacher Fozhi once mentioned that Dongshan Yan had previously stated:

[...]* *Note: The source text appears to be a fragmentary historical record concerning the Chan lineage of the Southern Song dynasty, specifically the interactions between lay officials and various Chan masters.*
Geng Longxue said: "When this mountain monk had not yet attained the Way, I was like a fish stranded in a dry rut or a bird without wings.
Now that I have Yuanwu, it is as if the fish has found water and can leap and soar, or as if the bird has regained its wings and can fly upward.
Therefore, Layman Ziyuan praised him, saying: 'The Master transmits the Way to his disciple; the disciple...'"

The student receives from the teacher; when both are in perfect accord and each finds self-approval, this is truly a rare encounter of a thousand-year age—a marvelous meeting that is no mere coincidence. From beginning to end, there is a fixed and inherent lot;
who could possibly interrupt it? Layman Ziyuan may be called one who knows how to recognize a person, for he... [beginning].
Thus he uttered these words of praise. Whenever I observe the venerable masters of recent times, they harbor ulterior motives to control the monks from all quarters;
these monks from all quarters, in turn, wield power and seek wealth and profit to serve the masters.
From the host above to the guests below, they engage in mutual exploitation, with those above deceiving those below.
If those below deceive those above, how can the Dharma assembly attain prosperity?
Is the flourishing of the monastic groves not like fish having water, or like birds having wings?

Shuian said: "To move others with words, one must ensure they are sincere and direct. If words lack sincerity and directness, the resulting resonance will necessarily be shallow; who would be willing to harbor such [teachings]?
In the past, when Master Baiyun saw off his teacher to reside at Simian, he exhorted him, saying:

'The ancestral Way is in decline and as precarious as stacked eggs. Do not indulge in negligence or dissipation, nor waste your time, thereby ruining your supreme virtue. You must be broad-minded and tolerant.'"
To measure [the situation], you must benefit sentient beings and sustain the assembly; uphold this matter to repay the kindness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
At that time, who among those who heard it would not have been moved to grief? Your recent summons to the Imperial Court was truly a blessing for the Dharma-gate.

You should earnestly humble yourself and honor the Way, making the salvation of others your primary concern. You must not boast of yourself or disparage others. The sages of antiquity were all humble, gentle, reverent, and cautious.

Preserving his person and perfecting his virtue, he did not regard power or status as glory; thus he was able to stir purity throughout his time, and his beauty flowed through ten thousand generations.
Fearing that my own life may not be long and that we shall no longer meet face-to-face, I therefore urge you earnestly (as seen in the letter from Touzi).
"Ling" (凌) means ice; "chi" (遲) means slow or lax. It does not mean "ling-lo" (零落) or "chi-shi" (廢弛), which refer to falling into ruin or neglect.

It should be read as "ling-yi" (陵夷), meaning the Way has declined like a mountain leveled to the plain. As for "piling eggs": Duke Ling of Jin constructed a nine-story terrace that remained unfinished after three years.
Xun Xi remonstrated with him, saying, "I can stack twelve chess pieces, and upon them, I can further place nine eggs."
Regarding the passage above, the Duke said, "How perilous! Xixi replied, "It is not perilous. The Duke was constructing a nine-story tower;
after three years it was still unfinished. Men did not plow and women did not weave; thus, the peril was even greater. His statement regarding the peril of the Patriarch’s Way is similar to this.
The Imperial Palace is the domain of the Sovereign; to attack it is to be boastful. Master Shu'an cited the Patriarch’s words to encourage Touzi, saying that one should be humble.
The lower way honors the Path. It is taught with the intention of benefiting and saving others through speech that moves people;

this requires nothing less than being true and appropriate. If one’s words are not true and appropriate, then whatever moves others will necessarily be superficial, and people will be unwilling to hold them in high esteem.
Long ago, the Master Baiyun saw off Master Yan as he went to reside at...
When assuming the four directions [of governance], he earnestly exhorted them, saying:
"The succession of our ancestors is like a mountain ridge gradually eroding away; its peril is as if nine eggs were stacked upon twelve chess pieces.
You must not indulge in negligence or indolence, nor squander the days before you through heedlessness, thereby further diminishing your own great virtue. You should—"
Magnanimous yet not harsh; forbearing yet not narrow-minded. He gauges their comings and goings, and measures what is permissible or forbidden.
He brings vast benefit to the common people and protects the great assembly. He upholds the great matter of birth and death and repays the extraordinary kindness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
At such a time, who among those who hear of this would not be moved with deep emotion and pensive remembrance? You, having recently served the Most Honored One—
To receive a summons and proceed to the imperial court of the Son of Heaven is truly a source of great fortune for the Dharma-gate.
You should especially maintain humility and reverence, valuing the Way, with a mind focused on broadening your transformative influence for the benefit of all beings.

You must not indulge in self-conceit or arrogance, nor flaunt your prestige and power. The sages of antiquity were humble, gentle, and compliant; they were respectful, cautious, and fearful, preserving themselves through wisdom and discernment.
Fully endowed with profound virtue, he never boasted of his power or status for the sake of honor or distinction;

thus, his pure reputation resounded in his own time, and his noble name has spread its fragrance through ten thousand generations. As for myself, I am personally concerned that my allotted span of life is limited.
In my old age, there are not many years remaining; I fear that we may never have another opportunity to meet again. Therefore, I offer these earnest and repeated exhortations.
Shui-an was youthful and unconventional, possessing great ambition and a high sense of integrity. He did not indulge in frivolous luxury nor did he adhere to petty formalities.

His mind was as vast as a mountain valley, and he followed the path of righteousness with total self-devotion. Even when calamities and harms confronted him from all sides, he showed no sign of dejection or distress. He resided at...

He presided over eight monasteries and traveled through four prefectures; wherever he went, he was filled with a sense of solemnity and diligence, making the establishment of the Way his primary concern.
In the fifth year of the Chunxi era, he retired from Jingci Monastery on West Lake, leaving behind this verse: "For six years I swept and cleaned the imperial capital's temple;
The rubble has been transformed into a palace of Śakra and Brahmā. Today, the palace is complete and I depart; From the tip of my staff, a pure breeze rises in all eight directions."
The officials and commoners blocked his way, refusing to let him proceed. When the small boat reached Tianning Temple in Xiuzhou, he fell ill before long;
bidding farewell to the assembly, he passed away. (From the *Xingshi*; "yǔn" is pronounced like "yǔn," and "huò" is a second-tone character).
*Tìtǎng* (倜儻): Pronounced *tī tǎng*. To be extraordinary and eminent. *Fúmǐ*: To be frivolous and extravagant; to indulge in luxury and waste. *Xún*: To follow and comply with. *Lènxùn* (徇殉):

Synonymous with *cóng* (to follow). To follow the Way with one's person. *Yǔn* (殞): It is not appropriate that it should fall. *Yǔn* means to fall from a height. *Huò* (穫): To reap grain. *Yǔnhuò* (隕穫):
To lose one’s composure due to distress and urgency. Citing the *Rúxíng* (儒行) chapter of the *Lǐjì*: "One does not succumb to despondency or loss of integrity because of poverty and low station."
The meaning of this is as follows: "Falling like a withered leaf" refers to falling and drifting away;
"reaping like grain" refers to being harvested and becoming withered and parched. "Not falling or reaping" means not undergoing change or transformation.

It is recorded that when Shui'an was young and immature, he possessed refined elegance and noble resolve, was carefree and unconstrained, and held far-reaching ambitions. His spirit, momentum, integrity, and操守 (conduct) were such that—
Matters tend toward excess and extravagance, failing to observe even the slightest detail with propriety.
Yet, the inner mind is vast and empty, like a high cliff or a deep valley—utterly open and spacious. Devoting oneself to righteousness, one is unaware of the physical body;
thus, even when great calamities and harms converge before one, there is no perception of change or loss of integrity.
He could truly be called one who has attained great fearlessness. He presided over eight monasteries and traveled through four major provinces;
wherever he went, he was ever vigilant and cautious, filled with a sense of solemn responsibility and apprehension.
His sole concern was to practice the ancestral way and establish the Dharma transformation as his core mission. His contribution to this degenerate age was indeed immense. (Chunxi...)
Five years later, he retired to Jingci Temple on West Lake in Lin’an. At the time of his departure from the monastery, he composed a verse which said:

"Six years sweeping and cleaning the imperial capital temple; The rubble has been transformed into the palaces of Śakra and Brahmā. As Emperor Xiaozong resided in Lin’an at that time, it was referred to as the "imperial capital" (huángdū).
What was formerly a place of ruined rubble has suddenly been transformed into the monastic abode of Śākya and Brahmā.
"Your Excellency, today my work is accomplished and I am returning home. When one’s merit is fulfilled and success attained, it is fitting that the person withdraws.
'From the eight directions of the staff-head, a pure wind arises'—this speaks of the freedom to go or stay. 'The staff moves in a single line, while the pure wind rises from all eight directions';

there is no obstruction whether moving vertically or horizontally. This verse contains a hidden meaning of his intention to depart this world. The officials and commoners tried to detain him, but he pressed on."
He remained there, yet could not stay; his single-leafed skiff drifted away, heading directly for Tiantong Temple in Shuixian County, Jiaxing Prefecture.
Before long, he manifested slight illness, ascended the hall to bid farewell to the assembly, and entered the samādhi of cessation.

Venerable Gattō Chō said: "In the past, the Great Wisdom Master (Daichi Zenji), fearing that monks of the末代 (matsudai) would become arrogant and indolent, specifically established rules and regulations to prevent this.

According to their capacities and abilities, he assigned specific offices to each. The presiding master resided in the *chōshitsu* (private quarters), while the assembly resided in the *tsūdō* (common hall).
He established the strict hierarchy of the ten head positions (*jukyushu*), making them as solemn as a government office. Those in superior positions oversaw the general framework."

As for those of lower capacity, they regulate the various aspects of the community so that the superior and inferior support one another, just as the body directs the arms and the arms direct the fingers, such that all follow in obedience.
It is for this reason that former generations followed and upheld the tradition, serving it with earnest devotion; this was because the legacy of the ancient sages had not yet vanished.
Lately, however, I have observed that the monastic communities (conglin) have declined, and students prize versatile talent while disparaging steadfast adherence to the precepts.

The social order was disrupted; people still prized the ornate and superficial while disparaging the true and simple. Day by day and month by month, they gradually entered a state of moral corruption.

Initially, they merely sought security for a brief moment; but as this practice became habitual over time, they came to regard it as the natural course of things, neither deeming it unrighteous nor irrational.
Those above trembled in fear of those below, while those below gazed with bated breath, waiting for their superiors.

In their daily lives, they use sweet words and humble postures to flatter one another; yet when they find an opportunity, they employ cruel hearts and deceitful schemes to slaughter and deceive each other.
Success is deemed "virtue," while failure is labeled "folly. No longer is the order of rank and status questioned, nor the principles of right and wrong.
When the other does it, this person follows suit; when those below speak thus, those above comply; and once the former has acted...

Thereafter, they merely inherited its flaws. Alas! Had it not been for Master Yan-sheng’s reliance on his vow-power (*praṇidhāna-bala*) and his accumulation of merit over a hundred years, this corruption would surely have remained uncorrected.
(Letter to the Monk Shun. [Note: Zhì is pronounced zhì; Kuí is pronounced kuí; Huài is pronounced guǎi].)

These are the offices presided over by the various authorities. The "Ten Bureaus" (*shí jú*) refer to the heads and officials of the administrative divisions. They are the distinct departments through which each official is made to govern their respective bureau.

There are five bureaus for the affairs of the West Wing (*xī xù*): first, the Head Seat (*zhǔzuò*); second, the Secretary (*shūjì*); third, the Librarian (*zhīzàng*); fourth, the Guest Master (*zhīkè*);

and fifth, the Attendant (*shìzhě*). There are five bureaus for the affairs of the East Wing (*dōng xù*): first, the General Supervisor (*dūjiānshì*); second, the Rector (*wéiná*); third, the Vice-rector (*fù...*) [the text here is incomplete].
Temple. Fourth, the *diànzuo* (seat-director). Fifth, the *zhísuì* (year-steward). *Yì* means respectful. *Dài* means to wear upon the head. *Quánquán* means to uphold with earnest devotion.
*Zhùì* means to be anxious and fearful. *Kuī* means to look askance. *Zǎoshā* means to slaughter. *Huài* means to harm. *Xí* means to join together.
Master Getang said: "Those who preside over monastic communities should follow and practice the ritual laws of the former sages.

In the past, Master Baizhang Dazhi, concerned that monks in the age of the Dharma’s decline would become arrogant, extravagant, and indolent, specifically formulated rules for solemnizing the assembly to restrain them.
According to their capacities and talents, he established various departments for them to oversee."
The Dharma Master presides over the Abbot’s quarters, where the assembly gathers in great numbers.

Throughout the hall, the administrative officers (*kṣāntipati*) and heads of departments are arranged in order from east to west, their dignity and solemnity resembling those of an official government office.
Those situated above single-mindedly uphold the essential principles of the Great Dharma; those below manage the myriad affairs and regulations. Thus, between the superior and...
Below, they support one another in turn. It is like a single body employing its two arms, and the two arms employing its ten fingers;

there is nothing that does not respectfully lead and follow as one. For this reason, those of former generations have followed the established statutes and models, supported the rites and laws, and with earnest devotion have worn them upon their hearts and practiced them in their conduct—this being due to the pure and fragrant [teachings] of the Greatly Wise Sages of old.
This is because the lingering influence of his legacy has never been extinguished. Lately, however, I have seen only the decline of the monastic groves and the replacement of the Dharma;
scholars value only broad talent and learning, while regarding the maintenance of integrity and操守 (操守) as base and lowly.

They became accustomed to and esteemed frivolous ornamentation, while they despised and held in low regard plain simplicity and genuine sincerity. Like a snake drinking water, their corruption increased day by day;

like a pestilence spreading through water and moonlight, it gradually became more diluted and decadent until it reached the depths of the vital organs. This rendered both acupuncture and medicinal remedies ineffective.
At first they remained unaware, merely seeking temporary peace and security for themselves and those above them; yet when it came to...
Wasting the months and years in idle play, they have been steeped in defilement for so long that they instead regard this as right and settle into it without shame.
They do not realize that this is contrary to the principle of what is appropriate, nor do they realize that this is contrary to the logic of the True Path.

Those above cannot help but feel anxiety and dread, fearing a downward investigation; those below, meanwhile, peek from the sidelines and watch expectantly, waiting for a lapse by their superiors—all remaining complacent.
When there is no business at hand, they employ clever words and honeyed speech to flatter one another;
yet, once they find a vulnerability, they harbor wolfish hearts and crafty intentions to harm each other. If a matter succeeds through mere luck, both sides boast of it as a mark of their own virtue;
if a matter goes awry and fails, both sides mock and reproach each other as being foolish.
In that place, there is no further order of seniority and juniority, nor the principle of distinguishing between good as right and evil as wrong.

If they commit evil deeds, why do so? This is also done without shame, imitating such behavior. Since those below speak with gibberish and confusion, those above follow them without any sense of shame.
One person sings and a hundred harmonize; one goes before and another follows behind. Alas! How can one not feel deep pain and sorrow at this?

Ah! Were it not for the Three Sages and Ten Saints—the beings of all-encompassing wisdom—who, by means of the ten great vows and the ten powers of wisdom, accumulated merit and virtue over hundreds of years, I fear that these deep-seated and chronic maladies could never have been reformed.
Who else could have suppressed human desire before it had even sprouted and preserved the Heavenly Principle before it had yet manifested?
Yuet-tang resided at Jingci for the longest time. Someone remarked, "The Master has practiced the Way for years, yet we have not heard of a single disciple among his followers.
Do you think he does not measure up to Miaozhan? Yuet-tang did not answer. When the person spoke of this again another day, Yuet-tang said:
Have you not heard of the man of old who grew melons? One who loved them excessively would water them at midday during the height of summer;
before long, the melons would rot and perish. Why was this? It was not that his love for them was not diligent; rather, he watered them at the wrong time, which was precisely what caused their ruin.
When the veteran masters of various regions guide their disciples, they do not consider their spiritual cultivation.
Internally full, his talent and capacity were vast and far-reaching. Yet, he merely desired to hasten his personal development; when one examines his moral character, it is licentious and defiled;
when one scrutinizes his words and deeds, they are perverse and contradictory; when one considers his sense of justice, he is actually sycophantic and devious.

Is this not an excess of affection that has overstepped its proper bounds? This is truly like watering melons at midday. I fear deeply that those who possess true discernment will laugh at me; therefore, I have not composed [this work].
[From the *Beishan Jiwen* (Notes on What Was Heard at Beishan). *Yū* is pronounced like *yū* [in the sense of being stuck];
*qiè* is pronounced with the entering tone. Miao-zhan, styled Siming Huì, was the successor of Fayun Shanben.

He recorded that Master Yuetang had served as the abbot of Jingci Temple in Lin’an for many years. Some have said: "The Master practiced this way of transmission for the longest time; his disciples..."
"Below this courtyard, I see no disciples who continue the life of wisdom. Is it not a betrayal of the entrustment made by Miaozhan?
Yuetang’s intention was that the continuation of the Dharma must value the Dharma, whereas the severance of the Dharma truly arises from disregarding the Dharma.
How could he have known this? Thereupon, he remained silent and did not answer. On another day, [the Master] asked him again with the same weight. Yuetang—
The Master said, "I shall give you a parable. Suppose there is a man who plants melons and cherishes them exceedingly.
When it is the height of summer and the heat is intense, and the sun is at its zenith, he waters them;
yet before his feet have even left the melon garden, the melons have already withered and their roots rotted. Why is this? It is because of his excessive attachment."
I regret my earnest intentions. It is not that I lack diligence; however, my efforts at irrigation have been in vain, for it was truly not the proper season.
Not only did it fail to assist in nurturing the plant, but it has instead harmed its very roots.

Today, when elders from various quarters take up and support monastics, they do not examine whether their practice of the Way and their virtuous achievements are sufficient, nor whether their merit and wisdom are truly fulfilled within, nor their actual talents.
Whether their capacity and conduct will bear fruit on a vast and distant scale is entirely disregarded; they desire only to emerge quickly to pose as men of distinction.
Yet, when one carefully examines their character and morality, they are found to be lewd, excessive, and filthy beyond endurance.

When one scrutinizes their words and deeds, they are inconsistent, contradictory, and improper. As for what is called their integrity and impartiality, it is actually private corruption, sycophancy, and flattery.
Is this not a case of excessive attachment to scholars beyond what is appropriate? To love others in such a manner is like the sun at its zenith shining upon a gourd that has been watered;
it is utterly improper. I fear deeply that those with true discernment will hold me in derision.
For this reason, I would rather incur the displeasure of my late master than dare to act in such a way.
Thus it is. Those who encounter this should be able to discern my heart. [Note: *wěi* (萎) is pronounced like *wěi* (葦);
*náí* (荄) is pronounced like *jiē* (皆). Yuet Tang said: "When Huanglong resided at Jicui, he did not emerge for three months due to illness. Zhenjing prayed earnestly through the nights."

He went so far as to burn his head and cauterize his arm, praying for spiritual protection from the unseen realm. When Huanglong heard of this, he rebuked him, saying, "Life and death are indeed my own lot;
yet you, who practice Chan, have not attained the principle. Zhenjing replied with composure, "The monastic community may do without Kewen, but it cannot do without the Master.
Those who understood the matter remarked that Zhenjing’s reverence for his teacher and gravity toward the Dharma reached such a state of sincerity.
"One day he will surely become a great vessel" (*Beishan Jiwen*).
Master Yuetang Xue told his students: "You should honor your teacher and revere the Dharma.
Formerly, when National Teacher Huanglong Nan was residing at the Jicui monastic community, he contracted a severe illness that did not subside for three months; he had not yet recovered from it.

Zhang. At midnight, Zhenjing purified his body and mind and offered earnest prayers to the Buddhas of the three periods of time, even to the point of carving out lamps from his own scalp and burning incense from both his arms, looking upward in prayer for secret assistance and blessings in the darkness.
When Huanglong heard that Zhenjing had done such things, he rebuked him, saying: "My life and death are fundamentally determined by my own lot. When it was time...
"Let life come as it may; let death come as it may. This is how you should practice Zen. "If this is the principle that does not admit of anything else being passed through, what is it?
Zhenjing replied calmly and gently: "In the monastic community, Kewen is of no benefit to others.
As for those who can be dispensed with, the Master [Dongshan] guides the Zen monks of the ten directions and upholds the Buddha’s wisdom-life."
"Is this not possible in a single day? Those who understand say that it is because he possesses true purity, filial piety, and reverence for his teacher, and holds the Great Dharma in high esteem;
it is because of his sincerity and single-minded devotion that he has reached such a state. In the future, he will surely become a vessel of great beauty.

Furthermore, within the realm of worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are many instances of ministers sacrificing their bodies to serve their sovereigns, and sons exerting all their strength to serve their fathers.
I have never before seen a disciple serve his teacher with such single-mindedness and devotion.
Zhenjing may truly be called the one person in ten thousand years who has realized the supramundane truth.
Yuedang said: "The Imperial Historian Huang Lüzhi once remarked that Chan Master Huanglong Nan possessed a profound and vast capacity that was never swayed by external circumstances.
Throughout his life, he was free from artifice; among his disciples, there were none who ever witnessed him display anger or joy.
Even toward those who served as his messengers or laborers, he treated everyone with absolute sincerity. Thus, he was able to remain unmoved in voice or demeanor."
The Way of Compassionate Enlightenment arises; it is not a matter of mere expediency (according to one edition, this is seen on a stone inscription at Huanglong).
Master Yuetang Xiao, as a successor of the Dharma, should broaden his breast and treat others with sincerity.
The layman Huang Shanggu once remarked that Master Huanglong Nan was unfathomably profound in his capacity and possessed a vast tolerance, never acting in a narrow-minded way.
Regarding the constant flux of all phenomena, throughout his entire life’s conduct, he was entirely devoid of any affectation, ostentation, or artificial refinement.
Among the disciples and students at his gate, each one was a mature individual of genuine character;

they did not exhibit even the slightest signs of frivolous joy or anger, let alone Master Nan himself. This was true even for those who served as minor attendants, performing their labors with total dedication.
Furthermore, by means of his sincere resolve, how could he have failed to attain the stage of "One Child" (ekaputrika-bhūmi)?

This is why he was able to revitalize the Way of the Patriarch Ciming Huiyuan without resorting to loud voices or stern expressions; how could this have been merely a matter of expediency or something undertaken in vain?
"It is because there is capacity and sincerity that such things occur. Yuedang said:
"On the Shangsi day of the Jiyou year of the Jianyan era, Zhong Xiang rebelled in Liyang. Chan Master Wenshu Dao was beset by peril.
As the rebel forces grew formidable, his disciples fled. The Master said, 'Can disaster be avoided? He then stood firm."
However, while staying in his small chamber, he was ultimately killed by bandits. The layman Wugou (Vimala) extracted these words of Dharma from him, saying:
"Now, to love life and loathe death is the common sentiment of humanity. Only the Perfected One realizes that [life] is fundamentally unborn; thus, though living, he has nothing to love.
He penetrates the fact that it has never ceased; thus, though dying, he has nothing to fear. Therefore, he is able to face the calamities of birth and death."
At such a time, he did not waver from his principles; was he not one to whom we should look as a teacher?
He took as his teachers virtue, the Way, integrity, and righteousness—qualities sufficient to transform the monastic community and serve as a model for posterity. The Master’s name was Zhengdao;
he was a native of Danling in Meizhou and a successor of Fojian (according to one version, he is mentioned in the *Record of the Great Master Huishi of Mount Lu*).
*Jiànyán*: The era name of Emperor Gāozōng of the Sòng dynasty. *Shàngjǐ rì*: The third day of the third lunar month.
Zhōng Xiāng: A rebel from Dōngtíng Hú. *Lǐyáng*: Lǐzhōu in Chángdé Fǔ. *Yì*: To flee. *Yì*: Resolute and courageous.
*Qiáng*: Stubbornly persistent. *Zhì*: To arrive at. *Zhìrén*: One who has reached the ultimate ground. Yuètáng Xiǎo.
When a person stands at the juncture of life and death, or amidst calamity and harm, they must possess integrity and a guiding vision.
On the third day of the third month in the Jiyou year of the Jianyan era (1129), Zhong Xiang incited a rebellion in Liyang, causing widespread injury and destruction among the populace.
Chan Master Wenshu Zhengdao met with misfortune during this turmoil. Prior to this, on a spring day in the third year of the Jianyan era, the Master had ascended the hall to address the assembly.
Regarding the account of Linji’s final instructions to Sansheng, it is said: "The treasury of the true Dharma eye is extinguished by a blind donkey.
Where did Linji ever say such a thing? People of all ages have falsely transmitted this; do not believe it, but simply wait until the third month.
Indeed, when the third month arrived and the power of the rebels had become overwhelming, his disciples wished to flee south with their master. The Master—
He said, "One studies the Way in order to understand birth and death. Now that this calamity has arrived, how can it be avoided? Let the assembly depart together.
The Master then remained resolute and decisive within his chamber. When the bandits arrived, the Master said, "Kill me quickly; satisfy your desires.
The bandits raised their spears and stabbed him, yet the blood was all white milk. The bandits were struck with terror and withdrew.
He covered it with mats and departed. The householder Vimala inscribed this verse upon his dharma-speech:

"Ordinary people universally love life and loathe death; this is but the common sentiment of the world. Only those who have reached the ultimate ground realize that the four great elements are fundamentally non-existent.
Since they are non-existent, who is there to undergo birth? Although one shares this birth with the multitude, one is entirely without attachment."
With a heart of goodness, one realizes that the five aggregates are fundamentally empty. Since they are empty, who is there to undergo this death?
Although one shares this death with all beings, one is entirely free from any thought of fear. Thus, one is able to face the calamities of birth and death.

Though calamities converged before him, he foreknew them and offered thanks with such precision that not even a hair’s breadth was amiss; yet throughout, he never wavered from the resolve he maintained.
Was the Master not truly one who had attained the Way? With his lofty virtue and profound dignity, he lived to uphold the precepts and died for the sake of righteousness.
He is surely sufficient to revitalize the degenerate age and provide a model for the monastic community to emulate for generations.
For a thousand years and ten thousand generations, he shall serve as a model for posterity. The Master was a native of Danling County, Meizhou Prefecture, in Sichuan.
His Dharma name was Zhengdao, and he was the successor of the Venerable Fojian Huiqin. Students should know this;
they should also understand the source of the Master’s virtue, conduct, and integrity. [Note: *Shuò* (pronounced *shuò*) means a spear.]
Master Xinwen Ben said: "Among the practitioners of the patched robe, many fall ill because of Zen. There are those whose illness resides in their ears and eyes;
they mistake staring with furrowed brows, bulging eyes, pricking up their ears, and nodding their heads for Zen. There are those whose illness resides in their mouths and tongues;

they mistake nonsensical talk, inverted speech, and wild, chaotic shouting for Zen. There are those whose illness resides in their hands and feet; they mistake stepping forward and retreating, pointing..."

To demarcate east and west as "Chan" is a sickness of the heart and belly. To take the exhaustion of the profound and the investigation of the subtle—transcending emotion and departing from views—as Chan:

when discussed according to reality, this is nothing but a sickness. Only a master of true substance, discerning the subtlest nuances, knows through direct observation whether one has attained realization or not;
he distinguishes through entry whether one has reached the goal or not, and only then applies the single point of the awl.
A single directive: to strip away their finicky attachments, to strike at their stagnations, to verify their authenticity, and to determine their reality;
yet without adhering to a single expedient or being muddled regarding adaptability, so that they may ultimately tread the path of peace and non-action before finally coming to rest (Shilu).
Xinwen (心聞) was named Yunben (雲賁). He was the successor of Yuyang Jiechen (育王介諶). "Cheng" (瞠) refers to a gaze fixed and straight; it means to pierce through.

"Pou" (剖) means to analyze and explain by dividing. "Zui" (錐) means to prick. "Zha" (劄) means to stab or penetrate. "Da" (搭) and "zhi" (滯) describe being stuck and stagnant, meaning one is congealed and fails to be liberated.
Master Xinwen Ben was straightforward in mind and conduct; he shattered the [attachments of] scholars.

On the Illnesses of Chan: An Exposition on the Direct Pointing to the Essential Principle. Among those who study under the patch-robed monks (*nàzǐ*), there are a great many who fall ill due to their practice of Chan meditation.
To speak briefly, there are four such types. First, there are those whose illness resides in the ears and eyes;
they mistake sensory objects for the Way, staring with furrowed brows and bulging eyes, or mistaking auditory objects for the Way, tilting their heads and nodding.
They take this to be Chan. Second, there are those with an affliction regarding the mouth and tongue;
they identify the tongue as the Way and utter perverse words and inverted speech, identifying the mouth as the Way and engaging in wild shouting and chaotic bellowing, taking this to be Chan.
Third, there are those with an affliction regarding the hands and feet; they identify the feet as the Way and take three steps forward and three steps back, identifying the hands [as the Way].
Regarding the path, some point east while marking west, or point west while marking east, taking this to be Chan.
As for those who have the four illnesses within their hearts and bellies: they take the mind that clings to the aggregates as the Way, seeking to exhaust the profound and investigate the subtle;
they take the empty belly as the Way, seeking to transcend views and detach from emotions, taking this to be Chan. To summarize these four types, according to a factual evaluation:
Among all manner of erroneous understandings, there is not one that is not a sickness.

Only a true master of the original essence and original allotment, possessing the eye of perfect luminosity and the wisdom of penetrating observation, who knows the subtle and the minute, can recognize at a mere glance whether another possesses views or lacks them;
and upon merely entering the gate, he knows whether they have reached the ultimate ground or not. Thereafter...
Alternatively, one may use a single awl to pierce the *gāohuáng* (vital organs); or use a single notch to sever the banner of *māna* (self-conceit);
or use the diamond sword to cut through the slightest taint; or use the mechanism of vigorous exertion to sweep away all stagnation;
or use the dustless mirror to reveal the real and manifest the provisional; or use unimpeded eloquence to refine the substantial and crush the hollow. Yet, one must resolutely not...

By abiding in a single skillful means, one causes the attainment of immeasurable skillful means; one certainly ensures that adaptability is not obscured, but rather causes the attainment of immeasurable skillful adaptations.

This leads to the ultimate practice of reaching a place beyond the reach of the three calamities of war, famine, and water or fire—the realm of the three liberations: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
It is all over now.
Xinwen said: "The ancients said that the most outstanding among a thousand people is called an 'Eminent' (ying), and the most eminent among ten thousand people is called a 'Heroic' (jie).
If a patch-robed monk possesses wisdom and conduct renowned throughout the monastic community, is he not one who approximates such an eminent or heroic person? One need only be diligent in inquiry."

Investigate thoroughly: discard the empty and grasp the real; let each find its own function. Then, whether the monastery is large or small, and whether the assembly is numerous or few, all will follow its transformation.
In the past, there was Fengxue’s "White Commoner," Yaoshan’s "Oxen-Pen," Master Chang’s "Great Plum," and Ciming’s "Jingchu.
At such times, if those who are merely worldly and idle had sought [the truth] by means of status or appearance, they would surely have seen [only the outward form].

Thus he transmitted it to others. One day, occupying the master’s seat and ascending the magnificent throne, surrounded by ten thousand fingers [of disciples], he illuminated the light of the Buddhas and Patriarchs for this degenerate age.
Among the monastic communities, who would not bow in submission at his reputation?

How much more so when his predecessors—possessing such extraordinary talent and heroic spirit—were yet able, during their unmet times, to endure shame and tolerate impurity while blending with the world.
If it is thus even for those who shared the same waves, how much more so for those who came after? Alas! The past is like the present; this is like that.
If one must wait for Yàoshān or Fēngxué to take them as teachers, such a person meets with a teacher only once in a thousand years.

If one must wait for Dàméi or Címíng to take them as friends, such a friend appears only once in a hundred generations. Indeed, there are matters that proceed from the subtle to the manifest, and there are achievements that...
Great things are accomplished by accumulating small ones. I have never seen anyone achieve success without learning, nor reach mastery without cultivation.

If one awakens to this principle, then a teacher may be sought, friends may be chosen, the Way may be studied, and virtue may be cultivated; then what task in the world would be impossible to undertake?
As the ancients said: "Knowing people is truly difficult; even the sages found it a source of concern. How much more so for others? (Letter to Zhuan-an)
Fengxue’s name was Yanzhao. He was the son of the Liu family of Yuhang in Qiantang and the successor to Nan’uan Yongzuo.
Baiding was the name of a place where the local people were mostly commoners; Fengxue lived in seclusion among them, and no one knew of him. Daming’s name was Fachang; he was the successor to Mazu.
His appearance and demeanor were ordinary and unassuming, yet his reputation spread far and wide. He was a man of great integrity, free from deceit or madness.
"Deceitful" refers to the degenerate and declining ages. "Míyǎn" means "how much more so. "Guǐwěi" means "vast and great.

This explains that when one hears of the Venerable Master from the heart, one should personally serve the teacher and choose virtuous friends, accumulating merit and piling up righteous conduct to realize the Way and cultivate virtue.
Now, men of outstanding brilliance and heroism—how could they be mere ordinary people?

The ancients said that one must possess the refined beauty of a thousand men before being called a "heroic man," and only when one possesses the extraordinary talent of ten thousand men is one called a "heroic figure.
When a monk possesses the reputation for wisdom and virtuous conduct that spreads throughout the monastic community, is this not already close to such a standard?
These are men of exceptional talent and outstanding brilliance. They need only be diligent without ceasing and advance without retreating;
examining thus in the morning and investigating thus in the evening, they eliminate what is hollow and empty while adopting what is substantial and practical.
Each possesses wisdom and conduct which, once attained, they put into practice—so why then need one discuss whether it be a large or small monastery, or whether the assembly be numerous or few?
All have come to take refuge [in the Dharma] through the transformations they have undergone.
Tracing this back, we observe that before Fengxue appeared in the world, he lived among the common folk; before Yaoshan appeared in the world, he lived in the cattle pen;
when Master Chang saw Mazu, he later went into seclusion at Damei; and before Ciming responded to his calling...
When Master Huang made his request, he was living in a state of unrestrained freedom during the era of the Jing and Chu regions.
At that time, those who were merely ordinary travelers on the road, not yet having reached their destination, how could they have recognized him?

Had they sought him by way of rank—finding no rank—or by way of appearance—finding no appearance—they would surely have seen him and treated him with contempt and arrogance. Yet one day, the Dragon and Heaven pushed him forth, and he ascended the Precious Flower Throne.
Seated upon the fearless throne, surrounded by a thousand followers and with the fourfold assembly taking refuge,

he extended his *mudrā* arm to manifest great function and opened the lion-king’s mouth to clarify the great capacity, thereby revealing the radiance of the Buddhas and Patriarchs in this degenerate age.
Among all the various schools and sects, who would not submit at the mere sight of their reputation? They flow like water toward the lowlands, unstoppable.

Yet even the former sages, though they possessed rare and magnificent talent and a spirit as lofty as a thousand peaks and ten thousand blossoms, were nonetheless reduced to mediocrity when they found no place for themselves; they endured humiliation and tolerated defilement.
To flow with the current and merge with the filth, following the waves and drifting with the surges—this is how it is. How much more so for those who have come after this? Alas!
How can one not be moved to awakening and aspire to emulate them in general? The ancients were like people of today; this time is like that time.
If one must certainly wait for Fengxue to mingle with the vulgar and blend with the dust, or for Yaoshan’s skin...
To have one’s skin sloughed off and yet remain a teacher is not something easily seen; it is a meeting that occurs but once in a thousand years.

Even if one were determined to find someone with the noble resolve of Damei or the unrestrained magnanimity of Ciming to befriend, such a person is likewise difficult to encounter, appearing but once in a hundred generations.
This is because there are matters where even a single subtle dharma remains unclarified.
Yet through diligent investigation, one reaches the point where every phenomenon becomes manifest and nothing remains obscure.

This merit begins with the accumulation of small virtues in a single thought-moment, which eventually perfects a state of uninterrupted mindfulness, culminating in the unfathomably great virtue of the ultimate.

I have never seen anyone who did not accumulate learning in every thought-moment yet desired to achieve the Way of Goodness; nor have I seen anyone who failed to reach mastery in even a single dharma yet desired to attain it.
Regarding "thoroughly penetrating one's own mind": if one fully awakens to this principle, what great teacher could not be sought?
What virtuous friend could not be chosen? What Great Way could not be studied? What meritorious practice could not be cultivated?
Then, regarding all matters and phenomena throughout the world, what could not be applied?
The ancients said: "To know others is truly difficult. Even the sages suffered from the malady of not knowing others; how much more so for those who are not sages or philosophers?
It is certainly difficult to find a teacher and choose friends, yet it is likewise no easy matter to accumulate virtue and cultivate one's conduct.
Xinwen said: "The Way of the Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings is most simple and essential; from the beginning, there has been no other doctrine.

Our predecessors practiced it without doubt and maintained it without alteration. During the Tianxi era, Xuedou, with his brilliant and erudite talent, manipulated its fine principles for effect, seeking novelty and refining artifice.
He followed in the tradition of Fenyang by composing verses on ancient cases (*songgu*), ensnaring the scholars of his time. From this, the ancestral wind..."
This was one transformation. By the time of the Xuanzheng era, Yuanwu again expressed his own views and separated [the text] into the *Biyán jí* (Blue Cliff Record).
At that time, there were masters of ancient integrity and purity, such as the elder monks Ning Daozhe, Siling Lingyuan, and Fojian.

No one was able to turn them from their arguments. Consequently, the younger generation of new students came to prize these words; they recited them in the morning and practiced them in the evening, regarding them as the ultimate learning.
None among them realized their error. How tragic! The mental faculties of the scholars have been ruined. At the beginning of the Shaoxing era, Furi entered Min;
he saw that the scholars were being led away without turning back, galloping forward day by day and month by month, until they had gradually become so steeped in this [error].
It was corrupt. He immediately smashed those wooden blocks and refuted that doctrine; thus, he dispelled delusions and rescued those drowning.

His efforts were arduous and intense as he demolished the heterodox and manifested the orthodox, shaking the world with a sudden and powerful impact. Once the monastics came to recognize its errors, they no longer aspired to it.

However, had it not been for the Buddha-sun’s lofty brilliance and far-reaching vision, and his reliance on the power of compassionate vows to save the corruptions of the Dharma-ending age, there would have been much more that could be lamented within the monastic groves.
"Wei zhe yi" (From the letter to Zhang Zisha, Part 2, from the *Guanglu*; "wu" is pronounced as "wu"). *Tianxi*:
the era name of Emperor Zhenzong of the Song dynasty. A cage for raising birds; a halter for tethering horses—this refers to the meaning of recruiting students.
*Xuanzheng*: the era name of Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty. *Biyan* is the name of a mountain. A collection of writings.

"Name. This refers to the Venerable Yuanwu Keqin, who composed the *Pingchang* (Commentary and Singing) on Xuedou’s *Gonggu* (Verses on Ancient Cases), which constitutes the *Biyuanji* (Blue Cliff Record).
"Dharma Master Ning" refers to Dao Ning, a successor of Master Yan. "Shaoxing" is the era name of Emperor Gaozong of the Song dynasty. "Furi" (Sun of the Buddha) is Miaoxi.
"Min" refers to Fujian Province. To drive swiftly is called "chi"; to drive in a disorderly rush is called [“luan chi”].

*Wu* (騖): To gallop; to rush about. It means that once momentum has been released for a long time, it is difficult to withdraw. *Zi* (漬): To soak or immerse. *Qu* (祛): To dispel or remove. *Kai* (開): To open or reveal. *Ju* (劇): Excessive or extreme.

This explains the "Mind-hearing" (*xīn wén*) for the sake of enlightening students, in order to critique and rectify errors regarding the methods of "discussing," "evaluating," and "singing" [the teachings], thereby clarifying the Way of Direct Pointing.
Regarding the intent of the Direct Pointing when the First Patriarch came from the West: formerly, Ānanda asked Kāśyapa— [The world]... (text continues)
Apart from the transmission of the golden-threaded *kāṣāya* by the Honored One, what else was transmitted? Kāśyapa called out to Ānanda, and Ānanda responded.
Kāśyapa said, "Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate. At these words, Ānanda attained realization and reached the essential point;
this is called the "Special Transmission Outside the Teachings. It was transmitted through twenty-eight patriarchs in the West before coming to this Eastern land. This is...
The First Patriarch maintained only a single flavor. Through these words, he attained realization and met the needs of his disciples; thus, the lineage was transmitted from one to another.

When it came time for his earnest instructions and admonitions, he said only this: "When practice accords with understanding, and understanding accords with practice—when practice and understanding correspond, one is called a Patriarch.
What did he have to say at the beginning? The predecessors of old practiced in this very manner.

They harbored doubts and clung to them without changing. It was not until the Tianxi era of the Song dynasty that Xuedou Xian, with his brilliant, versatile, and erudite talent, his refined disposition, and his unrestrained spirit, began to reinterpret and display the ancient cases with flair.

Seeking ever-fresh insights and refining them for elegance, he followed in the footsteps of Fenyang and composed *songgu* (verses on ancient cases), thereby gathering the scholars of his time as his followers.
Because of this, it is clear that what was directly pointed out has been transformed into a bent finger.

Reaching the period of the Xuanzheng era, the ancestral master Yuanwu Keqin further expressed his own insights to critique and proclaim the "Eulogies on Ancient Cases" by Xuedou, compiling them into a work titled the *Biyán jí* (Blue Cliff Records).
At that time, there were individuals whose minds surpassed the present and whose conduct transcended the past, possessing pure hearts and complete virtue, such as...
Even when the great masters Ningdao, Sishi, Xinling, Yuanqing, Fojian, and Qin all attempted to dissuade him, they could not turn him back from his doctrine.
For this reason, those who have recently entered as beginners, new novices, and junior practitioners regard him as something rare and precious, like jade.
They value these words; they recite them in the morning and practice them in the evening, regarding them as the ultimate of learning.
No one examines them closely enough to realize they are incorrect. How tragic!
The mental disposition of such scholars is like oil soaking into flour—it can no longer be remedied. At the beginning of the Shaoxing era, the monk Furi Gaofeng entered Fujian.

I see that students have been led astray by the *pingchang* (commentaries), refusing to turn their heads. Day after day they gallop and month after month they race, like wild horses fleeing at full speed that are difficult to restrain.
Over time they become gradually steeped in it, like a poisonous water entering the throat and causing illness.
I have therefore smashed and burned the printing blocks of the *Biyán jí*; this was not because the *pingchang* itself was erroneous, but rather to dispel the delusions that had arisen therefrom.

Yun: To rescue those mired in distress and to prune away what has grown excessively; to set aside the perilous and the urgent, and to break open the stone of Jing-shan to reveal the "ten-thousand-strings-of-jewels" treasure.

He raised it up with such distinction that the patch-robed monks gradually came to realize the error of the *pingchang* (commentary and chanting) style and no longer aspired to it. Had it not been for the extraordinary brilliance of Furi, this—

Beholding this from afar, he mounted upon the four immeasurables, the compassionate mind, the ten great practices and vows, and the ten great powers of wisdom to rescue the accumulated corruptions of this final Dharma age.
How could the monastic groves then fail to possess the path of direct pointing once more?
Truly, there is much to be feared [in its absence]. It can be said that the Buddha-Sun has rendered no small service to this Way.

When Master Zhu’an Fozhao Guang first visited Xuedang at Jianfu Monastery, a physiognomist beheld him and recognized his potential, saying to Xuedang, "Among the assembly, the Venerable Guang has a square head, a broad forehead and full jaw, and the seven parts of his face are even and full;
in the future, he will surely become a teacher to an emperor. At the beginning of the Chunxi era of Emperor Xiaozong, [Guang] was summoned for an audience and met with the Emperor's approval.
The Emperor summoned him to reside in the Neiguantang (Inner Contemplation Hall) for seven nights, receiving treatment of such exceptional excellence that it surpassed anything previously accorded.
He was bestowed with the name Fozhao, which became renowned throughout the world. (Jiwen; *lu* pronounced like *lu*; *yi* pronounced like *yi*).
Zhuān’ān Fózào, whose name was Guāng, was a successor of Dàhuì Zǔgǎo. *Lútóu* refers to the skull; *gé* refers to the forehead; *yí* refers to the jaw.
The "seven places" are the two hands, the two feet, the two shoulders, and the crown of the head. This records the Venerable Master Guāng Fózào.
Upon first entering the monastic community, he arrived at Jianfu Temple in Raoyou to attend upon Master Xuetang.

At that time, there was a physiognomist who, upon seeing him for the first time, marveled at his noble bearing and said to Xuetang, "Among this great assembly, the Venerable Deguang has a head that is square and upright;
his forehead and jaw are broad and both well-filled; moreover, his cranial dome is prominent."
His torso was well-proportioned with broad shoulders and long arms, and his two feet were level; these seven parts were perfectly even and complete.
"In the future, he will certainly become a National Teacher (Guoshi); the physical characteristics of such a person have already been fully manifested.

When Emperor Xiaozong of the Song ascended the throne, at the beginning of the Chunxi era, he summoned Guang for an audience. Indeed, it was just as had been foreseen; the Emperor retained him within the Neiguan Hall.
When he first emerged after his seven-year retreat, the reception and hospitality accorded to him were exceptionally generous and extraordinary in this way.

After Guang returned and resided at Yuhuang Temple, the Emperor again dispatched messengers ahead of him to confer upon him the title "Fozhao" (Buddha-Illumination), which was proclaimed throughout the world.
This record states that blessings have causes and effects, and for the most part are cultivated through practice; thus, such signs arise. As for the name, it is not...
"Jiǒu qiú yě" (If one seeks it). [The character] 覯 (gòu) is pronounced *hòu*.
Zhuōān said to Prime Minister Yú Yǔnwén: "The Great Way is transparent and pervasive; fundamentally, there is neither folly nor wisdom.
For example, Yi Yin and Lü Shang rose from plowing fields and fishing to become teachers of emperors and kings. How could they be compared to a hierarchy based on intelligence or folly?"
"Though he was not a great man, who else could have been his equal? (The "yu" in "yú" is pronounced as an oblique tone).
Prime Minister Yú Yǔnwén, whose courtesy name was Bīnfǔ, was able to compose poetry and lyrics from a young age and possessed startling lines.
The Emperor ordered him to establish the Qiāocūn Academy to entertain scholars from all under heaven. Zhuōān then remarked that this was Prime Minister Yú’s selection of worthy men.
The Dharma should be sought through virtue; do not seek it through fame or status.
As for the Great Way existing within heaven and earth and being bestowed upon humanity, its original nature is empty and void; fundamentally, there is neither folly nor wisdom.
It is like Yi Yin, who was plowing in the wilds of Youxin when Tang sent messengers three times to invite him; he bowed and accepted the office of Prime Minister. Furthermore—
It is like Lu Wang (Jiang Shang), who was fishing at the Boxi River when he was discovered by the Earl of Xi during a hunt and appointed as the Imperial Preceptor.
Judging by these two sages, how could one compare them to those ranked on the ladder of intelligence versus folly?
Nevertheless, were it not for such men of boundless capacity who possess a heart of compassion, [this world would not exist].
He is fully prepared for the One Way; as for anything else, who would deign to grant it? Truly so! In selecting the worthy, one must be cautious not to lightly regard fame and rank.
If one lightly grants fame and rank to others, then those who seek fame will arrive; where then will the truly worthy be found?

Zhu’an said: "Xuan, Wan’an often remarked that Master Huanglong Nan was broad-minded and magnanimous, loyal and trustworthy, reverent and compassionate, profound and far-reaching in his discernment, and widely learned with vast erudition.
Once, while traveling through Huxiang with Yunfeng Yue, they took shelter from the rain beneath a tree.
While Yue sat cross-legged facing him, Nan alone sat upright and alert. Yue glared at him and said, 'The wondrous Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs—'"
This was not like the spirit of a village shrine acting out a solemn display; Nan bowed his head in thanks and sat even more uprightly.
Thus, Imperial Historian Huang Ru-zhi praised him, saying: "Master Nan never forgets reverence in either motion or stillness."
He was truly a master of the monastic community (*Huàn'ān jí*).
