"Squatting like a winnowing basket" (*jǐjù*) refers to a haughty sitting posture that resembles a winnowing basket. Regarding the four modes of deportment, Master Xuéxué of Zhuān’ān told his disciples:

"In matters of the heart and mind, you should take Master Nán as your model. Xuányuǎn’ān once remarked that Master Nán was broad-minded, expansive, dignified, and grave, and was characterized by loyalty and sincerity.
He was profoundly faithful; his person was always reverent and solemn, yet he loved all beings with compassion. His mind was expansive and open, yet concentrated and profound.

He had read widely in the fields of learning and possessed a comprehensive and vast knowledge. Once, while traveling together with Master Yunfeng Yue to Xiangyin in Huguang, they took shelter from the rain beneath a tree.
Master Yue stretched out both legs, and his posture resembled a winnowing basket as they sat facing one another.
Nan was sitting alone in a squatting posture, upright and with single-minded concentration; his form was like a wooden stump as he sat cross-legged.
Yue, taking it upon himself to act as a friend, feared that Nan might be harboring biased attachments, so he stared at him with glaring eyes and rebuked him, saying:
The unsurpassed Great Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs—how could it consist of clinging to appearances or being constrained by forms?

If one does not understand its underlying principle, can it ever be realized? If clinging to appearances and being constrained by forms were the Way, then the stone spirits in front of common villages and ancient temples would all be Buddhas. How could one take such a lifeless appearance as the Way?
This, too, is the correct principle for admonishing others toward goodness. Master Nan was indeed one who clarified the principles and possessed a fundamental basis for his conduct.
Seeing that Master Yue’s words were consistent with reason, he bowed his head in gratitude;
yet he remained solitary and secluded as before, becoming even more solemn and dignified. Thus, the Grand Historian Huang Shanggu once praised him, saying: "Master Nan..."
This man who carries a single board is like this in motion and like this in stillness; being of such a character, he never forgets gravity and reverent caution.
Truly, he can serve as a master of instruction within the monastic community.
Zhu’an said: "To lead oneself and preside over the assembly requires wisdom; to dispel delusions and eliminate attachments requires prior awakening.

To turn one's back on awakening and unite with the sensory dust causes the mind to become obscured; when wisdom and folly are not distinguished, affairs fall into disorder. (Written by Dayuan, the Chief Administrative Officer).
Zhu’an Xiaoren’s Discourse on the Principle of Cultivating Oneself to Benefit Others and Eliminating Delusion to Dispel Emotion:
To govern a vast multitude and benefit others by following one’s own inherent principle,
one must ultimately possess great wisdom to cast off the delusions accumulated over immeasurable kalpas, as well as the incessant emotions of every present thought-moment.

Consciousness must ultimately rely on constant awakening and illumination. If one opposes this awakening and illumination, failing to seek to see the Buddha and following neither the guidance of clarity, but instead uniting with worldly defilements, then the mind will become obscured and fail to attain lucidity; wisdom will become dull and ignorant.
If the noble and the petty are not distinguished by their clarity or turbidity, then every matter and every practice will be erroneous and chaotic.
Zhu’an said: "When Fojian resided at Taiping, Gao’an served as the *vina* (steward). Gao’an was young in years and bold in spirit;
he looked down upon those from all quarters, and few could satisfy his mind. One day during the midday meal, when the *ghanṭā* was struck, he saw an attendant using a separate vessel."
He placed the food before the Buddha Mirror (Fujian). Gaofeng An stepped out of the hall and said in a stern voice, "With five hundred monks as spiritual friends, how can you act with such conduct?
How can this serve as a model for future students? Fujian acted as if he had neither heard nor seen it.

When Gaofeng descended from the hall to inquire into the matter, he found it was pickled vegetables. It turned out that Fujian had long suffered from a spleen ailment and did not eat oil; consequently, Gaofeng felt ashamed.
He went to the Abbot’s quarters to take his leave. Fojian said, "What the Rector has said is very appropriate.

Since Huiqin’s illness has reached such a state, I have often heard the words of the sages that one should resolve all obstacles through principle. Since his food is not substantial, he will consequently have no cause for suspicion regarding the assembly.
The Rector’s spirit and character are clear and far-reaching; in the future, he shall serve as a pillar and foundation for our school. I hope you will not harbor resentment over this matter."

When Fodian succeeded to the Dharma and his wisdom-ocean surged high, Gaoan passed through Longmen. He later became the successor of Foyan. "Jian" (pronounced *jiān*) means to lift; "ju" (pronounced *jǔ*) means to strike with a mallet.
A *jianchui* (striking-mallet) refers to the bell, wooden board, chime, fish-shaped gong, and the leading chime;

these are used to regulate the intervals of ritual procedures for beginning and ending [ceremonies]. "Qujù" (departing and approaching) is synonymous with "xingzhi" (walking and stopping). "Zhu" means a pillar; "cheng" means to prop or support.
Furthermore, "pillars and stones" refers to supporting the gates of the Dharma so that they remain as stable as sounding-stones (*kṣaṇa*). "Jièdì" (芥蔕) refers to a small obstruction;

"gěng" (梗) and "gěng" (鯁) share the same meaning of being upright or rigid. In the world, those who speak with bold integrity are called "bone-throated" (*gǔgěng*), meaning their direct speech is difficult to accept, like a bone choking the throat.
Master Zhuàn'ān cited Gaò'ān’s *weina* (steward), who was haughty in spirit yet upright and rigid. Master Fójiàn... [text continues].
There is a story concerning the mountain-and-sea breadth of mind of Master Fojian while he was abbot at Taiping in Shuzhou. At that time, Gao’an served as the *karmadāna*.
Gao’an was young in years, yet his ambition and spirit were bold and vigorous; he looked down upon others, and few could satisfy him according to his own wishes.
One day, while passing through the hall for the midday meal, just as the *ghanṭī* was being struck, he saw [the master] walking...

He presented the dishes before the head of the refectory with an unusual set of utensils. Gao-an then raised his voice loudly, saying, "With five hundred people in the hall, how can the Head of the Monastery conduct himself in such a manner?
How can he serve as a model for future students? At that moment, Gao-an could not restrain his indignation;

he focused solely on what was right in principle, without yet seeing the full details of the situation. This is what is meant by: [The original Chinese text here would be translated as: "This is what is called..."
There are those who gain, and there are those who lose. Taiping’s mind was as lofty as a mountain and as vast as the sea;
it was as if he had never heard or seen anything at all. When Gao’an saw that the Head Monk’s expression remained unchanged, he grew suspicious and questioned the attendant.
Only then did he learn that it was merely water, pickled vegetables, and greens. This was because Fojian already possessed a certain degree of spleen-strength (digestive fortitude).
Regarding the ailment of his stomach, he had no appetite for oil; therefore, he had separately prepared plain pickled vegetables (*kāñjika*).
Gao’an felt ashamed of having made such a remark and subsequently went up to the abbot’s quarters to resign from his post. Fojian, employing the samādhi of loving speech to guide him, said:
"What the *vīnā* has said is extremely appropriate to the facts. It was precisely because of the illness of Huiqin that [the meal] was prepared in such a manner."
I have heard it said that ancient sages used principle to resolve all obstacles.

Now, the *karmadāna* has used words consistent with principle to resolve the matter of my food, without forcing the assembly. Having reported this to the great multitude, what further obstacle could there be?
Whatever the great assembly has doubted shall henceforth be free from doubt. The Venerable Vinaya Master’s aspirations and character are lofty and far-reaching;
in days to come, he shall uphold the Dharma seat with the stability of a sounding stone. A bright future lies before him;
I hope you will not let my words today cause you any internal distress. When the Master Fojian moved to become the abbot of Zhihai Temple, the Vinaya...
He then went to Longmen and succeeded Fuyan as his Dharma heir. *Gěng* (鯁) is pronounced *gěng*;
*jiǎn'è* (謇諤) is pronounced *jiǎn è*; *fù* (咈) is pronounced *fú*.
Zhuōān said: "In general, when discussing the Way with officials and engaging in social exchange, one must strip away intellectual understanding so that it does not interfere."
He sat within his hermitage, intent solely upon clarifying that one phrase which points directly upward.

My late teacher Miaoxi once said: "When gentlemen meet, they respond when questioned; yet even so, they must not respond unless questioned. Furthermore, they must be people of this same school before such a thing is permissible.
These words are beneficial for the times and do not compromise the dignity of a monastic abbot; you should reflect upon them deeply.
The abbot Zhu’an Xue received a high-ranking official and spoke thus to preserve the fundamental dignity of the Dharma:

"In general, when one who presides over the Dharma engages in discussion with an official, during the exchange of greetings and responses, one must ensure that there is resonance within the words and a hidden blade within the phrases.
One must strip away and eliminate their intellectual understanding and conceptual interpretations; do not allow them to fall into [the trap of such attachments]."
Amidst the tangle of vines and the den of doubt, one prizes only the direct and straightforward single-pointed holding up.
This one move of turning back the pivotal bolt toward the higher realm—Master Miaoxi once said:
"When scholars who have not yet entered official service meet with great officers who have already entered service, whenever there is a question, one must respond; even if there is no question,"
Furthermore, one must not respond through mere forced effort; rather, one must be a person of the inner circle before one can speak the words of that inner circle with another.
These words of our former master are precisely beneficial for the present age and do not compromise the fundamental integrity of a Dharma successor.
You should reflect upon and savor them deeply; do not disparage yourselves.
Zhu’an said: "Beautiful land nurtures things well; a benevolent ruler nurtures scholars well. Nowadays, those who hold the position of abbot often do not take the interests of the community to heart.
They are anxious only for their own desires, loathe hearing virtuous words, delight in concealing their faults and evils, and act willfully according to perverse conduct.
In seeking to satisfy their momentary whims, they are instead exploited by petty people who seize upon their likes and dislikes."

If this is the case, how can the way of abbotship not be endangered? (Letter to Old Master Hong. Note: "hào" and "è" are both pronounced with the fourth tone; the "è" in "guò-è" is pronounced with the first tone.)
The abbot Zhu'an Xiao said: "One who occupies the position of abbot must skillfully nurture the scholars in order to preserve the Dharma-gate.

Just as land that is fertile and rich in moisture will inevitably produce excellent crops, a master who is benevolent, compassionate, and gentle will inevitably be able to foster and educate excellent scholars.

There are three things that must not be done by one who dwells in the monastic life: First, regarding all worldly affairs, they are numerous and complex, piling up layer upon layer;
one must not allow them to remain unmanaged, nor should one be intimidated by them. Second, regarding all mundane matters, one should keep them clear and pure, remaining tranquil and self-composed.
One must not seek out others. Third, whether good or bad fortune arrives, let all things be as they are;

one must not dispute them. A monastic leader who thoroughly understands the principle of these three "non-seekings" will naturally not be disturbed by external objects, and will possess a firm, inherent mastery.
Mimian said: "If a monk's conduct is crooked and depraved, and he has long possessed traces of unwholesome behavior, this is known to all within the monastic community;
such a person is not worth resenting. However, when the multitude deems someone virtuous while that person is in fact unworthy within, this is truly something to be resented."
Mimian Xiaoren once said that it is difficult to discern treacherous and wicked people;
he remarked that the daily conduct of monastics is often not upright or straightforward, and that those with a history of misconduct are known by all within the great assembly.

Such a person does not deserve to be resented or loathed; rather, everyone says of them, "He is a good man," while their heart is more treacherous than mountains and rivers, and every thought is unworthy. Such a person is truly one whom one may justly detest and abhor.
Mimian said to Shuian: "When one encounters insult or humiliation, one should accept it with equanimity. How can one lightly listen to mere words and recklessly set forth one's own limited views?

Generally, those who are sycophantic are of a certain type; those who are devious and crafty employ many stratagems. Those harboring treacherous and biased intentions love to indulge their private whims;
those who give rise to suspicion and jealousy will unilaterally suppress public deliberation. This is because such people are narrow-minded in their inclinations and their vision is obscured."
It is short-sighted indeed to consider being different from others as being beyond the common crowd, and to regard the suppression of criticism as being extraordinary.

However, once it is known that what I employ is ultimately correct, then slander will naturally remain with them; after time has passed, the truth will manifest itself of its own accord, requiring no further clarification.
Furthermore, there is no need to insist upon my own correctness and thereby provoke others. Only then may one perhaps be considered a man of the forest hermitage.

"Partial views" refers to narrow perspectives. "Risky and crooked words" refers to speech that is uneven and unjust. "Skepticism" refers to suspicion and resentment. "To obstruct" means to stop or hinder.
"To expose" means to reveal another's hidden faults; it means to attack another's private secrets.

This is from a letter by Monk Mimi to Shui’an, in which he states that one must take the cultivation of virtue through patience as the primary principle. He says: "Suppose there are those who slander, insult, or revile me."

One should comply with the intentions of others and endure them; one must not, upon encountering even a slight adverse wind, be shaken by it and rashly set forth petty views, fearing that this might harm the integrity of the Dharma. Generally, those who are sycophantic will surely have their kindred.
Those who are craftily devious possess many guiles in their mental faculties; those whose hearts harbor resentment delight in displaying their own one-sided private biases.
Those who give rise to suspicion and enmity will unilaterally discard the public deliberations of the multitude.
Indeed, the inclinations of such people are narrow and cramped, and their perspectives are obscure and shallow. This is for certain.
To hold fast to one's own views and differ from others is to stand out from one's peers.
To be headstrong and self-willed, and to exclusively obstruct collective deliberation, is to rise above the multitude.

If one were to realize that what I employ must ultimately be correct, then those who disparage, slander, and insult me would simply be acting according to their own nature. After a long time, right and wrong will become clear without further debate.

It is clear. Why must you strain yourself to distinguish black from white? Furthermore, there is no need to stubbornly insist that your own position is correct and to attack the shortcomings of others, thereby provoking their private resentments. Simply maintain the integrity of your own being and keep your mind equanimous;
then, whether cut by a blade or smeared with incense, neither anger nor joy will arise. In this way, you may perhaps become one of those who dwell beneath the forest trees.
Master Zide Hui said: "In general, if a monastic is sincere and turns toward the correct path, they may be employed even if they are dull-witted;

if they are sycophantic and harbor evil intent, they will ultimately cause harm even if they are intelligent. For the most part, those who dwell in the forest whose minds are not upright cannot establish themselves, despite possessing talent."
Zide himself was named Huiguang (Wisdom Radiance); he was the successor of Tiantong Zhengjue.
When Master Zide wrote to Jiantang, he said: "In employing people, what is valued is uprightness.

Generally speaking, if a monk is sincere in his heart and upright in his conduct, even if he is foolish, dull, or clumsy, he is still usable. However, if one is merely smooth-talking and sycophantic..."
If there is private depravity within the mind, then despite being clever and wise, one will ultimately act like a comet.

In short, for those who dwell beneath the forest trees, their mental application must be upright. If it is not upright, then even if one possesses talent, capability, and administrative skill, in the end nothing can be established.
Zide said: "The Great Master Dazhi specifically established the Pure Rules (qinggui) to rescue and rectify the improper failings of bhikṣus in the Dharma-ending age.
Consequently, former sages have reverently upheld and faithfully practiced them; they possess instruction, they possess order, and they possess a beginning and an end."

At the end of the Shaoxing era, there were still mature elders in the monastic forests who could maintain the established traditions and protocols, never daring to depart from their side for even a moment.
In recent years, however, the ancestral lineage has been lost; the mainstays are no longer mainstays, and the guiding principles are no longer principles.
Even if such principles exist, how can they be rectified? Thus it is said: "Raise one mainstay and all the meshes will open; loosen one mechanism and ten thousand things fall apart."

Matters have fallen into ruin; it is perilous that the fundamental order is not sustained and the monastic communities do not flourish. Only the ancients embodied the principle of rectifying the branches by attending to the root.
They were concerned solely with the lack of strictness in the Dharma regulations, not with scholars losing their proper place. Their focus on what was essential lay in impartiality.
Nowadays, those who hold positions of authority in various quarters confuse the private with the public and subvert the fundamental with the derivative. Those above seek profit regardless of the Way;

those below pursue gain regardless of righteousness. When superiors and subordinates are in disarray and guests and hosts are intermingled, how can monks turn toward what is correct, and how can the monastic community flourish?
(The character *huī* [隳] is pronounced like *huī*.)
"Laxity" means to neglect and abandon such that one does not follow ritual standards; it is ruinous. "Malice" refers to greed.
I have received a letter from Master Dazhi to Assistant Minister You, discussing the flourishing of the Dharma-gate, which states that it depends entirely upon the practice of ritual laws.
Why did Master Dazhi specifically establish the *qinggui* (pure rules)? It was because he wished to maintain and rescue the bhikṣus and others in the age of the Final Dharma.

This is the accumulated corruption of a lack of integrity. Consequently, those who previously possessed virtue and merit followed and upheld [the teachings], earnestly wearing them upon their hearts and reverently practicing them.
Above, they did not fail the great principles and maintained transformative instruction;
below, they did not neglect their respective duties and maintained orderly governance. Those who came before thus opened the way and established the beginning; as for those who came after—

It is likewise that based on practice there is an end. Toward the end of the Shaoxing era of the Song dynasty, within the monastic community (dharma-saṃgha), there were still elderly and experienced men who were able to remain earnest and vigilant, upholding the statutes and precedents of the former sages, not daring to neglect them for even a moment, nor allowing them to depart from their side.
In recent years, however, things have declined more and more with each passing age.
Age after age has not been its equal. The fundamental principles and the thread of continuity have been lost.
The mainstay of the Dharma is entirely absent and thus fails to form a mainstay; the principles of all truths are utterly discarded and thus fail to form a continuity.
Even if there were once again the ritual laws of one of great wisdom, how could they possibly be restored to order? Therefore it is said: "The master of the Dharma is able to uphold [it]."
When the single main rope is taut, the various strands and details naturally extend and spread.
If the one who presides over the Dharma relaxes even a single mechanism, then every matter and every rule will likewise fall into ruin along with it; how could this not be perilous?
The regulations and statutes will be overturned and fail to be upheld; the forest monasteries and their flagpoles will fall to the ground and fail to rise again.
It was simply that the ancients practiced through their own bodies and actions; by rectifying the root and its branches, everything naturally followed suit and became upright.
They feared only that the laws and prohibitions might not be strictly enforced, and they did not worry that later generations or latecomers would fail to find their proper place.
As for the means by which they achieved this rectitude, it lay in impartiality and justice.

Uprightness means being free from private bias and perversity. Today, however, those who preside over the Dharma in various regions entirely abandon public deliberation in favor of their private interests, using the guise of public affairs to satisfy their personal desires. Their actions are inverted and discordant; they subvert the root while exalting the branches.
Those above greedily seek profit and sustenance, violating the Way to pursue fame; those below flatter to gain favor, coveting gain for themselves.

The meaning is lost. Those above are arrogant and extravagant; those below are insolent and profane, leading to confusion and disorder. Guests harbor suspicions, and masters harbor jealousy and malice, resulting in total chaos.
Under such conditions, how could the patch-robed monks (śramaṇas) ever incline toward the Right Path, and how could the monastic communities (saṅghārāma) endure in permanent prosperity?
I believe that this is absolutely impossible.
Zide said: "When fine jade has not yet been cut, it is no different from common tiles and stones; when a famous steed has not yet galloped, it is indistinguishable from a sluggish hack.
Once it is cut and polished, or once it has been put to the test by running, then the jade and stone, and the steed and the hack, are clearly distinguished.
Likewise, when a monk possesses virtuous character but remains unused, he is mixed among the common crowd—how can he be identified? It depends on those of lofty insight."
If one promotes such a person based on public consensus, assigns them official duties, evaluates them by their talent and ability, and holds them accountable for accomplishing tasks,
they will be vastly different from the common run of people (Yíng is pronounced Róng).
Master Zide’s letter to Master He’gan says: "In discussing the promotion of the virtuous and the employment of the capable, consider this:
when a flawless jade has not yet been cut and polished, how indeed does it differ from a piece of pottery or stone? Yet its lingering reputation is like that of a famous steed."
Before they have ever been put to the test, they are indeed indistinguishable from common, sluggish horses; what difference is there?
Yet when the stone is split and the jade reveals its brilliance, or when the horse is galloped and the thoroughbred is recognized, then the jade is truly jade and the stone is truly stone;
the sluggish horse is truly sluggish and the thoroughbred is truly a thoroughbred—thus they become clearly distinct. It is the same for a monk who possesses talent and virtue.
As for those who have not yet manifested their utility, they are intermingled among the vast multitude,
such that in the end it is impossible to distinguish who is good and who is bad. It rests upon the high-minded and far-sighted sages to adjudicate with impartiality and to elevate them,
appointing them to appropriate official duties and entrusting them with responsibilities to examine their talents, capacities, and wisdom.

When affairs are inevitably accomplished, then the myriad mechanisms of principle are harmonized and the ten thousand transformations proceed; when a single virtue inspires trust, the enlightened and the good meet.
This is utterly different from the common run of people. Thus, when tiles, stones, and hackneys are subjected to testing, the jade and the thoroughbred horse reveal themselves;
when the worthy and talented are recruited once, all matters will surely be secure. (The pronunciation of "nútái" [hackney] is *nú*.)
Huìtái. Once, when Master Ān Tǐ first visited Tiantái Hùguó under Cíān Yuán Bùdài, [the latter] ascended the hall and cited Páng Jūnmǎ’s verse on "Selecting the Buddha.
Upon reaching the line, "This is the field for selecting the Buddha," Cíān gave a shout. Huìtái...

He attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse on seizing the opportunity, which says: "At the limit of deliberation, one beholds the title; at the end of the road, one enters the examination hall.
Grasping the tip of the brush, wind and rain rush forth; this time, I shall not act as the 'Plum-Blossom Gentleman'. Thereafter, he concealed his traces at Tiantai.
Prime Minister Qian, admiring his character, urged him to serve the world by appointing him to the abbotship of Tianfeng. Or...
Upon hearing this, Cañ said, "I do not understand hanging up the head of a goat while selling dog meat. He then fled that very night.
Cañ’s name was Fǎtí; he was a successor of Hùguó Jǐngyuán. "Bùdài" (Baguì) was Cañ’s informal nickname.
Prime Minister Qian Gong, whose courtesy name was Zu and style name was Xiangxian, sought the Way from Master Huan’ou. Regarding the term "dun" (遁), it means to withdraw and hide.
This record concerns Master Tiyi of Huan’ou. It recounts when he first attended upon Master Yuan of Bao-dazi at Tiantai Huguo Temple.
At that time, because Master Yuan had ascended the hall and cited the story of Layman Pang asking Mazu:
"Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as companions? The Patriarch said, "When you can swallow up the waters of the West River with a single draught, I shall tell you.

At these words, the scholar attained great enlightenment and presented this verse: "The ten directions gather together, Each one studying non-action (wuwei). This is the field for selecting Buddhas; The original meaning of the Master has been brought forth.

Master Yuan cited this until he reached this point. The meaning is as follows: [The assembly] is gathered together in the ten directions, each person training in non-action. This is the field for selecting Buddhas; the original intent of the Master has been brought forth.
That is to say: the presiding examiner has already passed through the thorny gate and opened the gates of vermilion clouds; why does the candidate not enter?
Thereupon, he let out a sudden shout, like a probing rod or a blade of grass used to gauge depth, thereby luring him forward.

Master Yuan-an was like a shuttle hanging on a wall in a potter’s workshop, or the staff of Zhang Chang at Ge-po; when it shook and struck the ground, it immediately underwent transformation and ascended.
He departed, unaware that at this moment, upon hearing the shout, he attained great enlightenment. This is what is meant by "blowing fire with the wind; it does not require much effort.
He then presented a verse on seizing the opportunity: "At the limit of deliberation, the title is revealed; The eyes are not merely blurred as the path reaches its end.
Entering the examination hall, one falls into pits and ditches; Lifting the tip of the brush, wind and rain arise."
"Quickly, do not harbor deluded thoughts! This time you shall not be a 'Plucking the Flowers' (first-place) scholar; there is a presiding examiner here.

After he had thus found the right opportunity and attained the Dharma, he maintained the Way and righteousness and cherished his reputation and integrity, eventually withdrawing in noble seclusion to Mount Tiantai.
Prime Minister Qian Xiangxian, admiring him from the bottom of his heart and holding him in high esteem for his character, requested that the permanent endowment of Tianfeng Temple be granted to him.
He appeared in the world to transform and guide sentient beings. Once, while at An Mountain, he heard that Master Qian had come to invite him, whereupon he smiled and said:
"I do not know how to make false appearances on the outside to manifest the 'sheep's head' to deceive others, while selling something entirely different within the inner chamber."
It was indeed dog meat. Thereupon, he immediately solidified his resolve; unswayed by the fame and rank offered by the Emperor, he fled into the night.
At the beginning of the Qiandao era, Xiatang was residing at Guoqing Temple. Upon seeing Huikan’s eulogy for the image of Yuancong, he remarked: "He does not rely on the original..."

[He] divided [the teachings], yet he troubled and disturbed sentient beings. Looking up at him, those with eyes were as if blind. The wind and moon of Chang’an have permeated both past and present; what man walks by feeling his way along the wall?
Xuandao was startled and delighted, saying, "I did not expect this Chan master to have such a son.
He immediately searched everywhere and finally found him at the heart of the Yangtze River. He firmly requested him from among the dense crowd to serve as the First Seat (from the *Tiantai Yalu*).
The *Qiandao* era was the reign title of Emperor Xiaozong of the Song dynasty. Xiatang was the abbot of Lingyin Monastery; his name was Huiyuan, and he was a successor of the patriarch Yuanwu Keqin.
This record concerns the time when Xiatang resided at Guoqing Temple at the beginning of the *Qiandao* era.

It was because he saw that Huigan’s praise of a painted image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva stated: "Not relying on one's own fundamental nature—great skillfulness appears as clumsiness. [This] causes disturbance.
Sentient beings—O Great Benevolent One, you who are beyond benevolence! To gaze upon you and look up to you is to fix one’s hopes and yearn for you in the heart.

Having eyes yet being as if blind: regarding this image of Perfect Penetration (Pūrṇa), whether male or female, whether majestic or compassionate—those who gaze and look up at it, though they possess eyes to behold it, fear that they may fail to reach its essence;
are they not, in truth, no different from the blind? This is the capital city of Chang’an.
From afar and near, people flock here. The scenery and the moonlight span from antiquity to the present; all those in the world who possess clever wisdom know only this as a place of pleasure.
What man of integrity and great character would be willing to grope for and practice upon this very wall?
If one were willing to grope for and practice upon this, take it for granted that they would be equal to the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The Great Being Tong saw him with the same eyes and heard him with the same ears as he had gone and stayed.
Upon seeing this, Xiatang was both startled and delighted, exclaiming, "I did not expect that Chan’an would have such an excellent son who so closely resembles him.
He immediately searched everywhere for him and eventually found him at Jiaoshan; there, amidst a vast assembly, he requested him to serve as the head of the human and celestial realms.
He took his seat and served as a guiding eye for future generations.
In the early years of the Qiandao era, Huikan suddenly visited Xiatang at Mount Huqiu.

When the monastics and laypeople of Gusu heard of his lofty reputation, they immediately went to the prefectural administration to petition for him to reside at Juebao Monastery in the city. Upon hearing this, Huikan said, "This is the former master of this hermitage..."
He instructed me, saying, "In the future, you shall encounter Lao-shou-zhi; today, it is as if our seals have met. Thereupon, I joyfully accepted his command.
This was because Juebao’s former name was Lao-shou-an (Recorded in the Tiger Hill Annals).
Biography of Huan’an. At the beginning of the Qiandao era, [the author] visited Master Xiatang Yuan at Huqiu.

Monastics and laypeople throughout Gusu, both high-ranking officials and commoners, having heard of the reputation of Huan’an’s noble conduct, immediately petitioned the local Governor to invite him to serve as abbot of Juebao Temple within the city. Upon hearing this, Huan’an said with joy, "This temple was formerly..."
The Master said, "I was entrusted by him with the instruction that at another time, when the appointed season arrives, it shall coincide with my reaching old age.

Today’s invitation perfectly accords with the late Master’s entrustment, like two bamboo tally-sticks meeting in perfect harmony. Thereupon, he joyfully accepted the summons of the Governor of Suseong-gun, as well as the requests of the monastic and lay communities.
This was because, at that time, Gakbop Temple... [was originally... (Note: The final sentence appears to be incomplete in the source text.)
This is the name of Laośòu Ān (Longevity Hermitage). That the prophecies and instructions of the Perfected One were not in error is thus evident.
After the Abbot had entered the monastery, a donor requested a *xiaocan* (small discourse), saying: "The Way is eternal and never changes, yet affairs have their decay and must inevitably transform.
In the past, the various patriarchs of Nanyue in Jiangxi took the ancients as their model for instruction; let us examine what was appropriate and what was not. He held [the assembly].
By means of the Middle Way, he strove to harmonize with the human heart, taking awakening as his standard; thus, the original spirit remains lofty and has not perished to this day.

Yet, if we speak from the perspective of the patch-robed monks, to gain realization before words would be to do a disservice to our school’s tradition, and to find clarity within a phrase would be to bury the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Nevertheless, it is said: "When walking, one reaches the end of the water; sitting, one watches the clouds arise. For this reason, the monastic community...
Su was delighted to hear what he had never heard before; those who returned were as numerous as at a marketplace (this differs from the *Yulu*).
In the record of Oran’s entry into Laoshou Monastery, a gentleman requested a small-scale sermon (*xiaocan*), saying:

"The Way of the sages and worthies extends throughout the ten directions, yet it remains unchanging as it penetrates the three periods of time; worldly affairs likewise remain unaltered as people pursue them."
People inevitably seek after names; the populace rushes toward profit and is inevitably greedy. Because of these defects, the Way of the sages and worthies has undergone transformation.
In the past, the various patriarchs such as Mazu of Jiangxi, Nanyue, and Shitou merely examined the ancients to formulate their instructions and admonitions;
they verified what was viable or not to establish the fundamental principles, maintaining the Middle Way without partiality.

Without leaning on anything, he points directly to the human mind and teaches only self-awakening; thus, the spirit of pure simplicity remains majestic even today, continuing from antiquity to the present without interruption.
As for those within the lineage of the patch-robed monks, if one realizes this principle before opening one's mouth, it is still considered a humiliation to my ancestral style.
Only when one has clearly understood it beneath words and phrases [is it truly realized].
It is clear. From the very beginning, it has been groundless; yet even so, the Buddhas and Patriarchs have been submerged.
Although this is inherently possessed by every person and is fully manifest in each, one must ultimately practice with genuine steps and real conduct.

One must go until the waters are exhausted and the mountains are spent, letting go of everything with the whole body, and with eyes wide open, look and see: from where does the wind come? From where do the clouds arise?
There must surely be a reason for this. For this cause, the monastic community rejoices and the common people exult;
they delight in hearing of such a rare occurrence, and the fourfold assembly comes to take refuge as if at a bustling marketplace.
Once Huikan had taken charge as abbot, the gentry and commoners flocked to him in great numbers.
When word reached Tiger Hill, Xiatang said, "This mountain barbarian Du Aowu is a blind practitioner of Zen; he is here to deal with that pack of wild fox spirits."
Upon hearing this, Huikang replied with a verse: "Shanman Du Āo has gained the ability to be resentful; He leads his assembly and guides his followers as if he had never done so before.
Transcending the norm, he turns the handle of a broom upside down; With blind Zen, he treats the wild fox monks.
Xiatang merely laughs. (Recorded Notes. *Āo* is pronounced *yáo*.)

*Xi* (翕) means to gather together. *Du* (杜) means to block. To not follow the proper track is called "blocking"; to act contrary to human sentiment is called "obstinate. *Ai* (拗) means to strike or pat.
It refers to being unable to walk oneself and instead walking while patting another's shoulder. *Dui* (隊) means a group or troop. *Kuang* (匡) means to rectify.
The record states that after Ji-ling-an had assumed the abbacy of Laoshou, scholars and commoners vied with one another to advance; they gathered there in great numbers, coming to take refuge in him.
The assembly: Someone once passed on the report that [Xuedou] had arrived at Tiger Hill.

When Huxiang heard this, he was delighted and said jokingly, "This mountain barbarian Du-aozi has no sense of human feeling and understands nothing of ritual propriety. Let him go on practicing his 'blind' Chan;
it is only fit for dealing with you lot of wild fox spirits. What business could such talk possibly accomplish? Thus he spoke.
This story is spoken as an extraordinary discourse; it does not reside at all in words and phrases.
Although it is called a jest, in reality, it is a way of praising and admiring his virtues. When Or-an heard of this, he replied to Huqiu with a verse, saying:
"The mountain barbarian Du-ao is capable of being loathed; there are those who dislike him. Leading a multitude and instructing disciples, it seems he has never [done so properly]."
The sharp edges have already been exposed, transcending all categories. He picks up the broom handle upside down and sets it aside; he strikes with the blindness of Zen to subdue the wild fox monks.
When the lion’s roar sounds, the fragrant grasses are green; Xiatang merely smiles. Where the elephant king walks, the falling flowers are red.
Ji’er drags his draft to this point and asks a monk standing nearby: "Tell me, do you judge that he has hit the mark or not?"
A nearby monk laughed. The Master said, "A true lion cub; he knows well how to roar.
Oran said to Minister Zeng Gong Dai, "The essential point of studying the Way is like using a scale to determine the weight of objects: it is simply a matter of maintaining balance.
Is partiality toward one side permissible? To lean forward or to lean backward—the bias is the same. Understanding this, one may study the Way."
"Righteousness! (As seen in the writings of Lord Zeng).
Or-an addressed the Minister Lord Zeng, saying: "In studying the Way, one must maintain a balanced perspective.
To reach the ultimate essence of this Way is like the scales of a balance beam weighing all things for their lightness or heaviness; it is simply this."
One simply maintains the standard of equilibrium. Is it permissible to lean toward the side of heaviness?
Not only can one not compare with what is light, but even with what is heavy, one may not compare. It is the same if one leans toward the side of lightness;
leaning toward either the former or the latter is equally improper. To understand this principle of maintaining equilibrium is essential.
Such a person may be considered a true student of the Way. Oran said:
"The Way and its virtue are the foundation of the monastic community; the monks are the foundation of the Way and its virtue.

If an abbot treats monks with disdain, he forgets the Way and its virtue. Once the Way and its virtue are forgotten, by what means can he cultivate transformation and edification? To maintain order...

Regarding monasteries (*conglin*): they are established to attract those who come to study. The ancients took the fundamental essence as the standard for correcting the branches; they were concerned that the Way and its Virtue (*daode*) would not be practiced, rather than being concerned that monasteries would lose their proper place.
Thus it is said: "The monastery is preserved by the patch-robed monks (*nazi*), and the patch-robed monks are preserved by the Way and its Virtue.
If the abbot lacks the Way and its Virtue, then the monastery will fall into ruin."
Or, as Anran wrote in a letter to Jiantang: "One who encounters the Dharma-person should know that the fundamental principle of the monastic community is explained as follows:
the Way of emptiness, non-action, and signlessness, along with the virtues of giving, kind speech, and beneficial conduct—these are the very foundation of the monastic community."

Wise and sagacious men are, moreover, the very foundation of morality. If those who preside over the Dharma abandon them, then these wise and sagacious men will have lost the path of virtue consisting of the three liberations and the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).

Once this path of the three liberations and four means of integration has been lost, with what will they go forth to propagate the Way of the Dharma, benefit and deliver sentient beings, and bring order?
To suddenly reform the monastic communities and guide the younger generation, the ancients focused solely on realizing the fundamental nature to thereby rectify the branches and details.
Their only concern was that the three gates of liberation and the four means of attraction were not being practiced;
they did not worry about whether the monasteries were well-managed or not. This is why it is said that the monasteries protect the patch-robed monks, and the patch-robed monks protect...
To protect the Way and its virtue is to preserve both parties. How could a master of the Dharma be without the virtues of the three liberations and the four means of integration?
Without them, it is certain that the monastic community will inevitably fall into ruin.

Master Or’an said: “To be a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), it is essential to recognize those who are worthy; it does not lie in one’s own self-exaltation. Therefore, he who harms the worthy is a fool;
he who conceals the worthy is ignorant; he who envies the worthy is deficient. To attain the glory of a single lifetime is not as good as attaining a reputation that lasts for an entire age.
To attain a reputation that lasts for an entire age is not as good as finding a single worthy monk (śramaṇa) who serves as a teacher for future students within the monastic community.”
[From a letter to Yuanji]: Oran Xiao is my spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

I value obtaining the counsel of virtuous people. Now, for one who transmits the Way, the primary requirement is first to recognize those who possess virtue as being of supreme importance; it does not lie merely in seeking one's own personal excellence.
Therefore, it is said: one who harms the worthy is made out to be a fool;
one who obscures the worthy is made out to be ignorant; one who envies the worthy is made out to be shallow.
It would be even better to attain the glory and distinction of a single lifetime than to attain the beauty of a reputation for a lifetime. To attain [the latter] for a lifetime...
Such a fine reputation is not as excellent as obtaining a single virtuous monk who has realized the mind and seen its nature, one who possesses the Way and virtue.
Why is this? It ensures that future students have a true lineage of masters and that the monastic community has a true leader of the Dharma.
Therefore, it is precious for a *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend) to obtain such a worthy person.
Three years after Huian moved to Jiaoshan—specifically on the fourth day of the eighth month in the sixth year of the Chunxi era—he first manifested a slight ailment.
He then personally wrote a letter, along with a single inkstone, to part from the Governor, Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, Lord Zeng.
By midnight, he passed away. The Lord lamented him in verse, saying: "Lightly fluttering, his single sandal pursues the western wind; Not a single thing remains, not even a cloth."

Left behind in the bag is the ceramic *hong*—what will it be used for? This old man has no brush to judge the void. (From the *Xingzhuang*. *Hong* is pronounced *hú máng*). "Diao" means to mourn and grieve.
*Tao Hong* is the name of a stone inkstone. What does "di" mean? It records the occasion when Huian moved again to Jiaoshan.
After three years had passed—precisely the fourth day of the eighth month in the sixth year of the Chunxi era of the Song dynasty—he was about to enter parinirvāṇa.
Foreseeing his slight illness, he personally wrote a letter and prepared his inkstone, sending someone to deliver it to Lord Zeng of Runzhou to take his leave.
When the Shilang arrived, at the hour of Zi (midnight), he addressed the assembly and passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. By the following morning, Lord Zeng had arrived.
Having seen him, he vanished through transformation. Jiaojian then composed a verse to lament his passing: "Fluttering, the single sandal pursues the western wind;
The comparison is like that of Bodhidharma. The single sandal flutters away to the west—just so. Not a single thing remains within the cloth bag.
This speaks directly of how Jiaoshan has shed his burden and become utterly empty; within the "skin bag," there is not a single thing at all.
"Leaving behind this Tao Hong, what shall it be used for? This refers to when Jiaoshan, upon his departure, left this inkstone with me and asked what it would be put to use.
"This old man has no brush to judge the void"—this was Zeng Gong’s own saying. "I, this old man, have no brush;
empty-fisted and bare-handed," he said. At the end, Jiaoshan’s radiance covered heaven and earth, like the void itself.
It is generally empty and inconceivable; truly difficult to judge. As for Ji'er, he was called He'nan.

It was from this hermitage that he first attained awakening upon being struck by a shout. He concealed his traces at Tiantai. Qian Xiangxian urged him to accept an imperial appointment, but he fled into the night.
Xia Tang received the Dharma at Jiangxin, where his karmic conditions corresponded to those of Lao Shou; he led the assembly and wielded the broom.
A Single Inkstone: Parting from Master Zeng Gong. Truly, this is a monk of transcendent caliber; one may say his head is straight and his tail is straight.
Master Xiatang Yuan said to Huo’an: “The capacities of people naturally vary in size.
It is truly impossible to teach them all. Thus, one with small paper cannot carry a great load; one with a short rope cannot draw from a deep well. An owl can catch its prey at night...”
One may discern the finest tip of autumn hair, yet by day, with eyes wide open in anger, one fails to see hills and mountains;
this is because one's lot is fixed. In the past, Xingjing transmitted the Way of Dongshan at Nantang; his realization was profound and subtle, penetrating and illuminating.

When he came to serve as abbot in the world, however, his influence did not flourish wherever he went. When our late master Yuanwu returned to Shu, he visited Dazui together with Master Fanguan; there they saw Xingjing leading [the assembly].

[Omitted]. Generally, regarding all matters of negligence and laxity, the former master never questioned me about them. Upon my return to Zhonglue, Fan said, "Jing and you are fellow practitioners and dharma friends;

why did he not offer you a single word of instruction? The former master replied, "When responding to the world and presiding over a community, the priority must be the enforcement of rules and regulations.
The implementation of these rules depends on one's intelligence and capability. Whether one is capable or incapable is determined by one's long-standing practice."

"How could such things be taught? Fan nodded his head in agreement. (From the *Jiwen* of the Tiger Hill Record. *Chī* is pronounced as *tái*; *xiū* is pronounced as *xiū*. *Cuō* and *cuàn* are pronounced with the entering tone.)

The *chǔ* (mulberry paper tree) is a species of tree; its bark can be made into paper. A *gěng* (rope) refers to a well-rope; when the *chǔ* is small, the rope is short—this expresses the meaning of having limited talent and shallow capacity.
The *chīxiū* (owl) is a strange bird that sees nothing by day and emerges at night to peck at mosquitoes—this expresses the meaning of seeing only what is small.
Jing is the name of Nantang (South Hall); he was a successor of the founding patriarch of Dongshan (East Mountain). *Yǐng* refers to the sharp point of a chisel.
"Yingwu" (穎悟) means that one’s words emerge like the tip of a grain stalk. Master Xiatang Yuan remarked:
"Huangan Ying’s talent and capacity were destined for greatness; furthermore, he insisted that the Dharma and its precepts must be prioritized.
As for the talent, strength, and capacity of people, some are naturally great while others are small; it is truly impossible to instruct them all."
Thus, how can a small sheet of paper contain a large object? How can a short rope draw water from a deep spring?
An owl, that strange bird, can peck at mosquitoes and fleas at night;
it can discern the tip of a fine autumn hair, yet when the sun rises and it is broad daylight, its two eyes glare in great anger and it cannot see the hills and mountains before it.
How could this not be the innate capacity of one who is not incapable of being taught? Such is the nature of the underlying principle. Formerly, Nantang Yuanjing met Dongshan Yanzu;

having exhausted all ancient and modern *gong'an*, he attained a transcendent awakening, penetrating the profound and subtle with such depth, precision, and appropriateness that it was manifest and clear.
The Patriarch certified him, saying: "The essential points of all quarters are not beyond his grasp."
The disciple has mastered it. Yet, when he appeared in the world, wherever he went, he was unable to revitalize the tradition.
When my late master, Yuanwu, returned from the south to Chengdu, he visited Master Fan at Mount Daisui.
There he saw that [the abbot] was quiet, negligent, and dismissive; all the regulations of the monastic community were completely lax and abandoned. My late master knew his talent...
Such was his character; he ultimately did not utter a single word. On the way back, Huifan asked the former master, "Master Jing and you shared the same gate and were bound by a karmic affinity;
together you served under the Way of the Fifth Patriarch, and thus you were friends.
Why did you not reveal even a single word to inspire and guide me? The former master replied to Master Huifan:
Now, when one leaves the mundane world to benefit sentient beings and stands before a vast assembly, it is essential to prioritize the establishment of prohibitions and commands through the Dharma.
In the application of these laws and decrees, wisdom must serve as the vanguard, while capability must serve as the rearguard.
Wisdom first and capability last is how one achieves both the beginning and the end. That Jing-neng can achieve the end but cannot achieve the beginning is due to this...
This was due to the inherent nature and fixed destiny of that person. He was not unaware; rather, he was unable to act.

How could I have been able to instruct him? Fan understood the reason why he had not been enlightened, and so he silently took note of it. (The character *chài* [嘬] is pronounced with the departing tone.)
Xiatang said: "A student of the Way must first rectify their mind; only then can they rectify themselves and rectify others.
Once the mind is rectified, the myriad things are settled. I have never heard of one whose mind is disciplined yet whose body is in disorder.

The teaching of the Buddhas and Patriarchs proceeds from the internal to the external, and from the near to the distant. To be deluded by sounds and forms is a sickness of the four limbs. [The text continues: "Delusion..."

Emotions arise from within; they are like ailments of the heart and belly. I have never seen one whose mind was not upright yet unable to govern external things, nor one whose person was not upright yet unable to transform others.
Indeed, the single mind is the root, while the myriad things are the branches and leaves. When the root is strong and substantial, [the branches flourish].
When the branches and leaves flourish, the root withers; when the branches and leaves are prematurely severed, it is because the root has failed.

One who studies the Way well first governs the internal to resist the external, and does not covet the external to the detriment of the internal. Therefore, the essential means of guiding beings lies in purifying the mind.
To rectify others, one must first rectify oneself. When the mind is upright and the self is established, there has never been a case where the myriad things do not follow one’s transformation.
A Letter from Chángtáng to Vice Minister Yán on the Discourse: "The Study of the Way Values Rectifying the Mind and Rectifying the Body.
Those who devote themselves exclusively to this principle must first cleanse their own minds, ensuring they are free from even the slightest taint.
Only then can they rectify themselves and, by extension, rectify others. When one's own mind is upright and not deluded, and one's own body is upright and not...

If one is partial [to this], then every matter and every dharma will all be stable and free from disorder. I have never heard of one whose mind and principles are in order, yet whose body is not disciplined.
The teachings of the Buddhas and the Patriarchs first proceed from the single mind within, and only then extend outward to the physical body;

they begin with what is within the span of a few feet before one’s eyes, and thereby reach as far as a thousand li. As for the six sense objects—sounds, forms, and material gain—[they are likewise governed by this principle].

To be deluded and confused by external things is an ailment of the four limbs. For the false imaginings and anxieties of the three poisons to erupt suddenly within is an ailment of the heart and abdomen.

I have never seen one whose mind was not crooked and perverse yet failed to manage all affairs, nor one whose body was upright and dignified yet failed to attract others to submit and be transformed; for the mind is the foundation.
The person is the sovereign, just as a tree has roots, sprouts, trunk, and main branches. All other things are like the twigs, branches, and leaves; they are all of one kind.
If the roots, sprouts, trunk, and main branches are robust and solid, then the twigs, branches, and leaves will naturally flourish and grow beautiful.
If the roots and sprouts wither and dry up, and the trunk and main branches become emaciated, then the twigs, branches, and leaves will certainly wither and decay.

[This leads to] ruin and downfall. Those who are truly capable of devoting themselves exclusively to this principle first cultivate and rectify their single-minded deluded thoughts to resist the sounds and colors of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
By not craving the six sense-objects, they prevent them from destroying the single mind.
Therefore, in benefiting beings and pointing out the way for those lost, what is valued is a pure and single mind. To rectify others at their fundamental source, one must first rectify oneself.

Once one's own mind is upright and the hearts of ten thousand people have become one, and once order has been established among the myriad things, could there be anyone who does not follow such transformation? Certainly, such a thing has never occurred.
Master Jiandang Ji resided at Guanshan in Fanyang for nearly twenty years. He lived on wild herbs and millet, appearing as if he had severed all interest in worldly honor and advancement.
Once, while descending the mountain, he heard the sound of mournful weeping by the roadside; Master Jiandang was moved with compassion, and upon inquiring into it, [he learned...]

A family was stricken by a cold-related illness, resulting in the death of two members. Being too poor to afford the necessary funeral equipment, they specially borrowed coffins from the market to bury them.

The local villagers sighed with unending admiration. Minister Li said to the scholar-officials, "The elder Ji of our district is a monk of great realization who, moreover, bestows compassion upon all beings.
How could he remain long at Mount Guan? At that time, State Councillor Wang...
The Pacification Commissioner of the various circuits reported [Jiandang’s arrival] to Lin Gong, the Prefect of Jiuyang County, who vacated the Dharma seat at Yuan Tong to welcome him.
Upon hearing this command, Jiandang said, "My Way shall now prevail," and immediately came forth with a joyful smile, dragging his staff. Ascending the seat, he preached the Dharma, saying:
"Yuantong does not open a pharmacy for the living; he sells nothing but the heads of dead cats. I do not know which one..."

Without a moment’s hesitation, he bit into it, and cold sweat poured down his entire body. Monastics and laypeople alike were struck with wonder, and from this point on, his Dharma seat flourished greatly.
Jiantang Mingxingji was a successor of Huguo Jingyuan. Fanyang refers to Poyang County in Raozhou; "Guanshan" is the name of a mountain.
"Liluo" refers to the *li* plant: when small, it can be eaten; when large, it can serve as a staff. "Lianju" refers to the coffin.

The *Guōshuō* (Explanations of the Coffin) refers to lending on credit. The *Shūmì Dūcháyuàn* (Chancellery and Court of Judicial Inspection) refers to the Bureau of Military Affairs and the Censorate.
The "Dead Cat" case refers to the legal precedent concerning a dead cat. A monk asked Caoshan, "What thing in the world is most precious?
Caoshan replied, "A dead cat is most precious. This recalls when Master Jiantang was at Guanshan in Poyang for a period of twenty years.
He ate congee made of *qí* and *huò* herbs and rice made of *shǔ* and *sù* millet, appearing as if he had severed all ties to the mundane world and sought no advancement at the imperial court.
Once, while descending the mountain, he heard the sound of lamentation from a house by the roadside.
Jiantang’s compassionate *samādhi* suddenly manifested before him; he personally stepped down the path and inquired about it. The person replied, "At this time, because of..."
Two people died of cold-related illnesses. The family was in extreme distress, lacking even a coffin for the enshrouding.
They went to the market and borrowed the necessary funeral equipment to bury them. Not a single person in that village failed to be moved and submit to his virtue; they praised him incessantly.
Li Chunian, a Senior Secretariat Drafter, circulated this account widely among both those who had not yet entered official service and those who were already serving as officials.
He spoke thus: "The Venerable Master Ji of our own region is truly a monk who has attained the Way.

Furthermore, he possesses a compassionate heart and bestows the kindness of aiding those in distress upon others. Since Mount Guan is narrow and small, how could it be appropriate for him to remain there for so long?
Subsequently, after the Southern Song dynasty had moved its capital, he encountered the Mingyuan, the Censor-in-Chief Wang."
He traveled through the roads of various commanderies until he reached Jiujiang Prefecture.
There, Magistrate Lin Gushuda vacated the Yuantong Chan Monastery to invite him to appear in the world as its abbot. Upon hearing of the invitation, Jiantang said, "The Way shall now prevail.
Knowing that the time had come, he accepted with joy and did not decline. On the day he entered the monastery, the assembly of monastics...
The Layman said: "Please ascend the seat and preach the Dharma. [The Master] replied:
"I, Yuantong, do not open a pharmacy of 'life-giving' medicines to deliver sentient beings by means of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). I sell only 'dead cat's heads.
This alone is the sole reality; the other two are not true. I know not which one is without thought or calculation—only the actions of body, speech, and mind."
Only those who are free from fault can let go over a precipice and personally accept the responsibility;
having consumed [the truth], cold sweat flows over their entire bodies, and having passed away, they are revived once more—this cannot be faked before the Master.
Whether they be monastics in black robes or laypeople in white, all who hear of this are struck with wonder and marvel at the transformation of the Dharma, and thereby it is greatly revitalized.
"Concealing one's brilliance and accumulating virtue; when the time comes, the principle is revealed. This is precisely how it should be—the model for later students. Jiantang said:
"In antiquity, those who cultivated their persons and regulated their minds shared the Way with others; those who initiated undertakings and established enterprises shared the merit with others;
and once the Way was perfected and achievements were manifest, they shared the fame with others. Therefore, there was no [aspect of the] Way that was not shared."
When one’s merit is manifest, there is no achievement that will not be accomplished; when one’s reputation is manifest, there is no glory that will not be attained. People today, however, are not so.

They adhere solely to their own way, fearing only that others might surpass them, and they are further unable to follow what is good or strive for righteousness to broaden themselves. They cling exclusively to their own achievements.
They do not wish for others to possess [virtue], yet they cannot employ the worthy or the capable because of their self-importance.
They monopolize their own reputation and refuse to share it with others, nor can they manifest humble brilliance to guide all things toward their own realization.

Consequently, their Way cannot escape obscuration, their achievements cannot escape diminution, and their reputation cannot escape disgrace. This is the case for scholars of both ancient and modern times.
This is the great principle.
Master Jiandang Xue taught that students should recognize the distinction between the "great body" and the "shared explanation.
Students of old disciplined their persons and subdued their minds; once they had attained understanding themselves, they would explain it to others and share the Way with them, rather than...

One is thus free from selfishness. Once a task has flourished and its work is established, one realizes it was not accomplished by oneself alone, but must have relied on the collective strength of many;

therefore, one shares the merit and does not claim it for oneself. When the Way is perfected and the achievement is manifest, one possesses this reputation and must yield it to others, sharing the fame and not dwelling upon it personally. For this reason, the Way is not—
One may be enlightened alone, yet there is not a single person who is not enlightened; merit is not achieved by oneself alone, yet there is not a single person who does not achieve it;
fame is not glorified by oneself alone, yet there is not a single person who is not glorified. Those who study today, however, are not so:
even if they devote themselves exclusively to the Way for their own benefit, they are unwilling to benefit others; they fear only that others might surpass them in knowledge. Furthermore—

If one is willing to receive good advice with an open mind, to strike at one's own longings and encourage one's shortcomings, and to strive to act in accordance with what is timely and appropriate, thereby broadening oneself; even if one achieves merit,
if one focuses solely on concealing it from others and claiming it as one's own, taking no pleasure in others possessing even a fraction of it,

and if one cannot humble the heart to honor the worthy or delegate tasks to assist them, remaining instead cold, harsh, and discordant rather than being magnanimous— [then such conduct is not true self-cultivation].

Furthermore, even if one’s reputation is established, if one focuses solely on self-exaltation and does not share it with others; if one feels displeasure rather than joy upon seeing others receive praise;

and if one cannot practice humility and accumulate virtue, blending with the light and the dust to guide the ignorant and deluded toward self-enlightenment—then though the Way originally seeks clarity, one instead obscures its efficacy, and though it originally seeks fulfillment, one instead...
To damage one's reputation—seeking honor yet instead bringing oneself disgrace—is a fundamental principle that scholars, both ancient and modern, have found difficult to alter.
This is a matter of public concern.
Jiandang said: "Studying the Way is like planting a tree. If it is felled while just flourishing, it can provide firewood;
if felled when about to reach full maturity, it can be made into rafters and eaves; if felled when somewhat robust, it can serve as pillars and beams;
and if felled when fully grown and large, it can become a ridgepole or a main beam. Is this not taking advantage of the distant utility and the great benefit?"

Because the ancients possessed a Way that was inherently vast rather than narrow, an ambition that was far-reaching and profound rather than mundane, and speech that was sublime rather than base—though they encountered friction with their times and were brought to the brink of ruin by hunger and cold, their lingering influence and enduring legacy have spanned a thousand years;
even today, later generations still take them as a model and transmit their teachings. Had it been otherwise...

To force one's way into a narrow path out of mere expediency, to draw near to others seeking only to find harmony, and to employ humble speech to serve the currents of power—the benefits of such actions stop at bringing glory to a single person.

How could there be any surplus grace to spread far and wide throughout future generations? (Note: *chuī* is pronounced *cuāi*; *jué* is pronounced *jué*; *zhǔ* is pronounced *zǔ*; *yǔ* is pronounced *yǔ*).

*Chuī* and *jué*. In the state of Zhou they were called *chuī*; in Qi they were called *jué*. These are the rafters (*chuán*). *Yíng* refers to the pillars. *Bǎng* and *kēn* refer to the lintels. Regarding "beams" (*liáng*) and "rafters" (*dòng*):
the central support of a roof is called the *dòng*; that which supports the *dòng* is the *liáng*. *Zhǔyǔ* means one tooth is forward and the other recedes; it signifies that the teeth do not meet.
This conveys the sense of being uneven or rugged. *Pǔ* means broad. [This is from] the letter Hall-Simple (Jiǎn Táng) wrote to Minister Li.
It is said that the study of the Way values deep accumulation and substantial cultivation. The practice of studying the Way is like planting trees:
if one cuts them down just as they begin to flourish and grow, they can only serve as firewood for fueling stoves;
yet, if one fells them when they are in full vigor, they can be fashioned into rafters and beams to prepare for roofing and thatching.
When it is somewhat mature and solid, one cuts and fells it; it can then serve as pillars and beams for construction and repair.
When it reaches full maturity before being cut down, it can even withstand the role of main girders and ridgepoles, serving the purposes of palaces and pavilions.
The cultivation of the Way is precisely analogous to this; is this not taking the effort and labor over a long duration?
The benefit [derived] from this condition is many times greater than that.
Therefore, as for the principles that ought to be so, the ancients were both firm and vast; their mental orientation was neither narrow nor constricted.
Furthermore, their presentation of words and phrases was both eternal and profound, rather than shallow or superficial; they were also most reverent.

He was solitary and lofty, yet never base or petty. Although the circumstances of his time were rugged and treacherous, and he suffered the hardships of cold and hunger, even facing mortal danger in the mountain forests and ravines, the legacy of his Way remained so abundant and its fragrance so potent that it has endured from antiquity to the present.
For a thousand years and more, those who came after him have still taken him as a model of self-respect, and his teachings continue to be transmitted throughout the land.
This would cause the ancients to narrow their paths and seek accommodation through expediency; to make their aspirations shallow and superficial, flatter others to seek favor;
and to make their words base and petty, rushing after power and circumstance. Their benefit would consist solely in the glory of a single person.
How could there possibly be vast and profound grace that universally reaches for thousands of millions of generations thereafter? What is more, it would...
This is because the Way prizes the accumulation of cultivation.
In the fourth month of the fifth year of the Chunxi era, Jiantang [Zhaozong] traveled once more from Jingxing Rock in Tiantai to Yijing.
There, the Grand Secretary, Lord Wu, who had retired in leisure at the Xiuxiu Hall, composed thirteen poems in the style of Yuanming (Tao Qian) to see him off; the first of these says:

I have returned to the forest depths and have already grown distant from the world. Fortunately, there is a spiritual friend who frequently visits my humble cottage, accompanying me as we discuss the Way and delighting in my reading of the Buddha’s scriptures.
Since he has ascended to the mountain crags, I too shall prepare the grease for his carriage.
I shall now spread out my bowl and partake of vegetarian food alongside my teacher; casting off these worldly entanglements, I shall dwell forever among the crags and rocks.
This cliff is indeed lofty, rising prominently above the maps of mountains and seas; yet if compared to the loftiness of my teacher, this cliff falls short.

Biographical Note on Master Jiantang. In the fourth month of the fifth year of the Chunxi era of the Song dynasty, he accepted a second invitation from Yijing Temple, departing from Jingxing Rock on Mount Tiantai.
At that time, the retired official Wu Gufu was living in leisure at the Xiuxiu Hall, composing thirteen poems in the style of the Five Willow Master, Tao Yuanming, to be presented to Jian.
Master Tang saw him off as he departed. The first [verse] said: "Since I retired from official service, I have returned to rest beneath the mountains and forests.

I have already grown distant from worldly affairs and the pursuit of profit and honor. Now, fortunately, Master Jian comes from time to time to visit my thatched hut and does not abandon me in my remoteness.
At times, he joins me in discussing the words of the Way; moreover, I am further delighted by him."
While reading the texts of the Śākya school, there were times when the Master returned to the mountain crag. I would also prepare grease for his carriage, oil, salt, tea, and rice.
I would set out my alms bowl; although it was not the same as the Master’s, the vegetarian meal I ate did not differ from his.
Upon reaching this point, I clearly understood that worldly toil and mundane affairs had all been cast off, leaving me free from all entanglements;
my only wish was to dwell forever among these rocky crags. These cliffs are originally sublime and lofty, rising far above the surface of the earth as depicted in the *Ditu*.
Yet, when compared to the loftiness of Master Jian’s virtue and realization, even these cliffs fall short.
He also said, "My birth was within a mountain cave;
on all four sides were rugged crags. There is a cliff named Jingxing (Auspicious Star); I have known it for how many years?"

Only now do I begin to believe in its wondrous and extraordinary nature. Having surveyed Mount Xiaozhong at a single glance, I have further found you, Master, as my guide; these two excellences are not easily described.

The mountain’s appearance is rugged and imposing. [The two words "rugged" and "imposing"] mean: I was born and raised within the caves and hollows of the mountain slopes. To the east, south, west, and north, all are rugged heights.
Amidst these high mountains there is a cavern named Jingxing (Auspicious Star). My heart yearns to reach it.
Many years have passed. Only upon arriving today do I see that this crag is of the utmost extraordinary beauty. Looking down from afar, all the surrounding mountains appear to sink below it.
Furthermore, having Master Jian as the master of this mountain—where both the mountain and the man are sublime—is something that can hardly be fully expressed in words.
(Note: The character *chàn* is pronounced *chán*.)
My home lies upon a mountain by a lake; wherever my eyes turn, there are forests and hills. Were these mountains compared to its splendor, even a small hillock would find it difficult to rival.
From its clouds one sees for a thousand li; springs and rocks flow through the four seasons. Having arrived here but once, I have already surpassed the excursions of the Five Lakes.
A "qiu" is a mound; a "peilu" is a small mound. "Chou" means companions. These are three words. My home is situated upon the lakes and mountains;
wherever my eyes reach, there are nothing but forests, mounds, and hills. Even if this mountain were compared to them, it would be considered beautiful and elegant.
My former dwelling was but a small hillock, hardly worthy of companionship; yet this mountain’s white clouds can be seen for a thousand li—how lofty it is!
This cliff’s clear spring flows unceasingly through the four seasons—how remote it is!

In the past, when I traveled among the Five Lakes, I thought there was nothing to compare with them; who would have known that arriving here all at once today, I have already surpassed them by so much?
I am seventy-five years old; the setting sun clings to the treetops. Even if my life has not yet ended, how could it last much longer?
I still hope to dwell among the groves, sharing the final light with you, Master. Suddenly a solitary cloud emerges for a moment, startling those near and far into a state of hurried agitation.
A state of hurried agitation. Four characters. My age is now seventy-five; it is like the lingering light at the tip of a tree branch about to sink into the earth.
Even were this physical form not yet dead, it could certainly not remain for long.
Why do I especially hope to dwell among the forest retreats? It is because I wish to enjoy my final years together with you, Master. Master.
This journey is like that of a solitary cloud or a wild crane, merely entering and exiting for a brief moment.
When the gentry and commoners near and far see him unexpectedly, they will surely be startled into a state of frantic agitation and distress.
My love for mountain peaks has long been my constant nature; yet to be bound by worldly customs is truly pitiable. Yesterday I governed Dangtu County and did not know of Mount Yinjing;
now I envy you, Master, as you come and go. What words can I utter in my shame? I still hope that you will not stay long, so that you may return and spend the remainder of my life with me.

It is a matter of being bound by attachments. These five lines express a fondness for mountain crags rooted in one’s natural disposition; yet to be constrained and fettered by worldly defilements is truly pitiable.
In former days, one was busily adrift in the sea of officialdom; who would have known that today one would find such sublime excellence in seclusion within the mountains?
What is most admired is that the Master came with such effortless ease and departed with such effortless ease, leaving me feeling ashamed of my own lack [of such freedom].
"I wish to provide you with parting gifts," he said. "I only hope that you will not remain there for long, but will return quickly; I wish to see you before my death.
The Master’s mind was like extinguished ashes and his body like withered wood. Why did he respond to the monk's return as an echo answers from a valley?
Beholding this body of dust and defilement, it truly awaits a bath in the *amṛta* essence. I further pray that you shall kindle the Buddha-lamp to serve as a substitute for my own bright candle.
In six-word verses: Inferring the Master’s mind through my own, his mind is no-mind, like extinguished ashes.
Furthermore, observing his form, his form is no-form, like withered wood. For what reason does he act for the sake of the patch-robed disciples?
The place of ultimate refuge lies within the vast, open expanse of another’s mind, like an echo responding in an empty valley.
Beholding my own body, defiled by the dust of worldly toil, I truly await the *amṛta* (nectar) of the Master to serve as my bath.
Seeing that the eye which perceives beyond form has not yet emerged, I further pray that the Buddha’s lamp of wisdom be extended to act as a candle of insight for me.
The spreading trees atop the crags have all cast their shade by summer’s start; what was once a wilderness of thorns for many years has in a single day become a lush forest.
Here I am with the monks, together listening to the sound of the ocean tides; life is full of gatherings and partings, and this sudden separation strikes the heart with alarm.
