"Spreading and luxuriant" means that the branches and leaves are flourishing. [This is] in seven-character verse. The mountain forests are dense and lush;

when summer arrives, they altogether become a single expanse of coolness. Thorns, brambles, and wild scrub, once they enter the hands of the Benevolent One (Nengren), are entirely transformed into grounds for selecting Buddhas.
At that time, I was just emerging from the mountain peaks with several fellow practitioners of Zen to listen together to the sound of the ocean tides.

I did not recall the sudden request to visit Yijing. I lamented to myself that while the gathering and dispersing of human lives is indeed a natural law, the joy of meeting and the fear of parting are feelings beyond one's control; they startle the heart unexpectedly.
I have associated with my teacher for years, though not for long; yet we have grown into two elders, our refined character likewise extraordinary.
While the teacher sits in tranquil meditation upon the cliff, I am busy gathering provisions. If the teacher could return home early, this joy would still not have reached its end.
This concludes the eighth statement. Master and I have only recently begun our association;
though the time has not been long, we have gazed upon one another with our two eyes and are truly both old men. Yet, our mutual refinement is certainly not like that of ordinary people.
You sit in peaceful meditation upon the cliff, skillfully expounding the Prajñāpāramitā, while I am currently gathering provisions for our sustenance.
I shall depart first. If you, Master, can truly return soon after this journey, these scenes of joy will not yet have come to an end.
Those who study Chan in such numbers carry their bags and rush about in competition; as soon as they can expound some tangled webs of words, their deluded minds immediately become self-important.
Seeking one whose virtue and realization are honored—such a master is truly rare. I pray that you, a successor of the Supreme Vehicle, will forever illuminate the lineage after Linji.

(Nine words. Nowadays, there are those among the various factions of Zen students who wander restlessly in all directions. With their satchels slung over their shoulders and straw hats on their heads, they travel back and forth in haste.
Having learned a few scraps of intellectual entanglement through mere lip-service, they immediately harbor a sense of self-importance and pride within themselves.
To possess the Way in its entirety and be fully endowed with virtue, as was the case with Master Jian, is truly rare.
I only pray that the Master’s Way may be transmitted to those of Mahayana capacity, so that it may never be interrupted and the lineage of Linji may be glorified for future generations.
(Note: The character "fu" [負] is pronounced in the upper tone.)
In my district, there are many monastics, vast as clouds and oceans. The Great Capacity has long since vanished; we rely on the fact that the Small Capacity still remains.

I shall further grant one more [period] to Shenmen; when both are complete, there will be no regrets. These two eminent Chan masters stand forth with dignity, and all within the realm look toward them with expectation.
Daji (Great Capacity) was styled Zhongji (Heavy Capacity); his name was Mingzhen, and he was a successor of Xuansha Shibei.
Xiaoji (Small Capacity) was Jiantang Xingji; Yicen was Yuanji Cen. "Tang-tang" means magnificent and flourishing. Regarding the ten words:
among the local districts, those who have donned the monastic robes are exceedingly numerous; they are vast and expansive, like clouds and like the sea. Although Tianning Daji—
They have long since passed away. Fortunately, their small capacity for the Dharma remains present today;

how much more so, then, in the case of Master Cen, who was a person of singular and complete virtue, entirely free from transgression or regret. The spiritual influence of these two elders was majestic and profoundly flourishing.
Throughout the four seas, all look toward this with shared expectation; it is not like ordinary matters. In antiquity, there was no office of abbot;
one merely transmitted the essential meaning of the Dharma. If one can awaken to the emptiness of form, one may transcend birth and death.

The mediocre monk is oblivious to his original nature; how could he recognize the sandals for returning to the West? He buys a certificate to sit upon the meditation platform—upon what can he rely regarding the Buddha-dharma?
"Mediocre monk" refers to the common sort who merely subsist on rice gruel and food. "Sandals for returning to the West" refers to those worn by Bodhidharma when he was buried at Mount Xiong'er.
Wei Wu Di sent Song Yun on a mission to the Western Regions. Upon his return, he encountered the Master at the Pamir Mountains (Congling), who was carrying a single sandal on his hand.

Yun asked where he was going; the Master replied, "I am going to India. When Yun returned and informed the Emperor, the Emperor ordered the grave to be opened, but there was nothing inside except an empty coffin and the single sandal.
In eleven words: In antiquity, there was originally no institution of abbacy; there was only the transmission of the Dharma.
The fundamental principle of the Buddha-dharma is this: if one can truly awaken to the truth that form is empty, one may thereby transcend birth and death.
Vulgar monks, being ignorant and obscured, do not recognize the Way that is inherently their own; how could they know the sandals left behind by the First Patriarch?
Times have declined and the Way has perished; when the Dharma appears, the wicked arise. They purchase certificates to sit in meditation; such is the state of the Buddha-dharma today.
This is the ultimate of substitution. On what can one rely?
Among the monastics there are eminent monks, and among the laity there are eminent scholars. Although I am not eminent myself, my coarse mind knows how to find contentment.

The Master is one who has realized this; my only regret is that he does not do so for you. How fortunate it is that both I and the Master are sons of neighboring households—though we are but coarse and simple folk.
Within the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, there are truly those who are eminent monks;
within our Confucian scholars, there are truly those who are eminent gentlemen. Although I am not such an eminent gentleman, my mind, in its broad outline, is nonetheless capable.
If one knows when to stop, how much more so should a teacher? A teacher is a virtuous and perfected person within the Way; even a Buddha would not begrudge such a role.

One’s only concern is that they do not humble their dignity to conform to the lowly, nor abandon their treasures to cling to filth. I do not know by what cultivation I have incurred such good fortune as this.
My life and my teacher’s were neighbors from birth; we dwelt together in seclusion upon the same mountain, sharing the same joy in the Way.
The Master was originally a monk of profound poverty; I too am a scholar of deep indigence. Our hearts have already mastered the endurance of poverty, so why would we begrudge not returning?
Though we part from you now for a time, O springs and rocks, do not harbor suspicion. I return to you merely to follow conditions; how could the Master have any ulterior motive?
It is suspicion; it is jealousy. Furthermore, he goes back and forth along the old path. The character "I" (我) at the end is an error;
it is likely the character "You" (爾). These are thirteen words. If you, Master, can firmly maintain this poverty, you are a poor monk.
I too can firmly maintain this poverty; I am a poor scholar. As for the heart that delights in poverty, we have both thoroughly realized it. You grow old, I grow old.
"Why not return? Now that you, Master, and I have met, though we are briefly separated, it is like a flowing spring meeting a rock—fundamentally free of suspicion or doubt.
This present meeting with conditions is merely a matter of passing by one another for a while. How could you, Master, possibly have any intentional purpose?"
It is truly so. From this, one can see the Confucian scholars of Li-xue and the eminent monks of Dao-de.
When Official Wu addressed Jian-tang, he said: "The ancients extinguished their worldly desires and stilled their intellects amidst a thousand crags and ten thousand valleys;

they drank from mountain streams and ate from the trees, as if having severed all intent for fame and office. Yet, one day, they received the imperial edict sealed with purple clay. [He then withdrew his] *tao*...
Guang concealed his traces beneath the lowly labor of a grain-pounder, initially having no thought of honor or advancement, yet in the end he joined the ranks of those who transmit the lamp.
Thus, when attained without intentionality, the Way becomes great and the virtue expansive;
when calculated through seeking, the reputation becomes base and the ambition narrow. Only one whose capacity and measure are profound and far-reaching, who succeeds the ancients, is able to—

He dwelt in seclusion at Guanshan for seventeen years, eventually becoming an excellent vessel for the monastic community. Today’s monks, however, have nothing to maintain within and pursue only external splendor;
their plans are short-sighted and they lack a sense of the greater purpose. Consequently, they are unable to support and sustain the religious teachings.
"This is why he did not reach his teacher; they were worlds apart" (Recorded by Attendant Gao). "Purple-black and red":
purple mud refers to the seal used for imperial edicts; it is red earth. "Zu" means "end.

Gong Zanmei of the Wu court praised Jian Tang, saying that he was able to store [his talents] deeply and nurture them fully, thereby causing his reputation to spread to the ends of the earth. This is the discourse of antiquity.

The hermit has extinguished his mind like cold ashes and obliterated his intellect. He dwells deep within thousands of crags and ten thousand gorges, drinking from mountain springs when thirsty and eating the fruits of trees when hungry;
how could he ever have harbored intentions regarding fame, profit, rank, or emolument?
Yet, in a single moment, unexpectedly, he received the imperial decree sealed with purple clay from the Son of Heaven—a summons for the wise among the monastic forests.
This person concealed his brilliance and hid his traces, sinking like a submerged ox into the lowly service of carrying grain on his back.

How could he have ever harbored thoughts of fame or the realization of the Way? Yet, suddenly, beneath a single word, he grasped the essential pivot and entered the ranks of those who transmit the Lamp.
All of them attained this through a mindless state; thus, their realization of the Way was magnificent and their virtuous conduct vast and far-reaching. Suppose...
If one calculates it thus: if something is obtained through a mind of seeking and wishing, its name will be humble rather than lofty, and its ambition narrow rather than broad.
Only you, Master, possess a Prajñāpāramitā that is profound and deep; your talent and capacity are expansive and open; and you concentrate your spirit in steady tranquility.
His far-reaching insight was boundless; he strove to perpetuate the life of wisdom and follow in the footsteps of the ancients.
Consequently, he found refuge and remained at Guanshan in Poyang for seventeen long years, steadfastly maintaining his integrity and becoming a pillar of the Dharma.
Yet, contemporary practitioners observe that he possessed no inner substance or virtue, nor did they see him engage in cultivation, while outwardly...
They cultivate themselves yet compete for fame and profit; they neglect long-term strategies for the safety of the state and fail to practice the fundamental principles of the teaching.
Consequently, they are unable to maintain the Great Dharma, falling far behind Master Jiantang. The gap between them is vast indeed.
Jiandang said: "In the common sentiments of people, it is rare not to be deluded.

Generally, they are obscured by what they believe, hindered by what they doubt, negligent regarding what they deem trivial, and submerged in what they love. When belief is biased, one does not examine the reality of what is heard;
thus, there arise words that are excessive. When doubt is extreme, one does not listen even to the truth; thus, there arises the loss of reality."
If one holds a person in low esteem, one will neglect the matters that ought to be valued; if one cherishes those matters, one will preserve the person who ought to be discarded.

These are all instances of recklessly indulging private attachments and failing to investigate the underlying principles. Consequently, one forgets the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and loses the spirit of the monastic community.
Thus, what is deemed trivial by ordinary sentiment is precisely what the sages and worthies hold in high regard. As an ancient master said: "In planning for the distant..."

One who seeks to verify the near must first examine what is close at hand; one who strives for the great must be diligent regarding the minute. This lies in gathering extensively and carefully discerning the middle way within it;
it certainly does not consist in admiring loftiness or delighting in the eccentric.
A Letter from Jiantang to Imperial Censor Wu, also showing how people know what is worthy of esteem yet remain unmoved by their own emotions.
Generally, in the ordinary course of daily life, when encountering objects that stir the emotions, there are few who are not deluded by them.
Generally, there are four ways one is deluded: first, hearing words that enter the ear without careful discernment, which obstructs what one believes;
second, seeing a matter and desiring to act upon it yet failing to do so, which causes one to stagnate in doubt; third, harboring pride regarding human relations.
They are negligent regarding what they despise. Fourth, they may seek after objects with extreme intent and become intoxicated by what they cherish.
If my ears hear and believe that which is not upright, then when listening to words, my mind will certainly fail to examine whether their principles are real or unreal;
consequently, there will be speech that is either excessive or deficient—this is the first delusion. Furthermore, if within my heart I harbor suspicion...
To suspect that person excessively means that even if what they say is perfectly reasonable, one is unwilling to listen;
because of this, there is a failure to hear the truth. This is the second delusion. Furthermore, if I treat that person with contempt...
Thus, there may be matters worthy of honor that are nonetheless cast aside and not put to use; this is the third delusion.
Furthermore, if I happen to favor a certain matter, there may be individuals who ought to be discarded, yet they are instead retained and employed;
this is the fourth delusion. These four instances all represent a state of negligence and license, driven by private passions and base inclinations, rather than a careful examination of the truth.
Adhering to biased principles, one consequently forgets the Great Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and acts in opposition to the hearts and minds of the great assembly.
Therefore, it is said that what ordinary people treat with neglect and contempt is precisely what the ancient sages and worthies revered and esteemed.
An ancient master once said: "If you wish to plan and deliberate with mature calculation for the distant future, first examine and verify what is near at hand."
The small is the work of the beginning; one who wishes to devote their efforts exclusively to the great must be cautious during the most subtle and hidden moments.

Furthermore, while gathering knowledge extensively and reading broadly, one must exercise discernment and apply it from within. This is fundamentally not a matter of abandoning what is near to grasp at what is distant, or longing for the lofty;
nor is it a matter of wearying oneself with the ordinary to delight in the strange or craving the unusual.

Jiantang was clear-sighted, upright, and even-tempered. He was compassionate and kind toward all beings; if a monk committed even the slightest error, he would shield and protect him to help him cultivate his virtue.
He once said, "Who among men is without fault? It is in the rectifying of one's errors that beauty lies.

While he was residing at Guanshan on Mount Poyang, it happened that the deep winter brought continuous snow and rain, and provisions such as thick gruel were failing. Yet the Master acted as if he had neither heard nor seen this, and thus there is [this verse]:
The verse says: The hearth is cold and the traveler’s bag is empty; Snow falls like willow blossoms as the year draws to a close.
With his patched robe covering his head, he burns firewood; He knows not that he dwells in solitude. Throughout his life, he had found contentment in the Way and held no urgency for fame or honor.
On the day he accepted the invitation to Mount Lu’s Yuantong Monastery, he carried nothing but a staff and straw sandals. Those who saw him perceived a dignified countenance and a liberated mind.
Lin Gongsuda, the Governor of Jiuzhang Commandery, observed him and remarked, "This man is a bridge and ferry across the waters of the Buddha-dharma.
From this, his reputation spread throughout the four quarters. His conduct in leaving or remaining [in the world] truly embodied the standard of the former masters.
On the day of his death, even the messengers who were striving to assist him shed tears for him. (Guā, zhān, gǔ, duò.)
"Guāiwò" (詿誤) means error or mistake. "Zhān" (饘) refers to thick gruel. "Guǒduò" (榾柮) refers to short pieces of wood, used here as a metaphor.
It is synonymous with the meaning of the "samādhi of true fire. "Zìshí" (自適) and "zìdé" (自得) mean self-contentment and self-attainment. This records how Jiantang’s four deportments were pure;
his mind was clear and bright, his character was broad and level, and his benevolence and kindness extended to all monastics.
Within this [work], should there be even slight errors or faults, I shall conceal and protect them, preserving and cherishing them in order to nurture my virtuous practice.
I have often said that everyone inevitably possesses faults; it is simply a matter of being willing to reform one's errors, for then one is a good person.
During my stay at Mount Rao-po-guan, it was the season of late winter, and rain and snow fell continuously and incessantly, accumulating to a great depth.
Even congee cannot sustain us from moment to moment; how much less can we obtain rice and meat? The Master appears as if he neither hears nor sees. Thus, there is a verse that says:
"The hearth fire is out and the traveler’s bag is empty; hunger is all too evident. The snow resembles willow blossoms as the year draws to a close;
the cold is unsurpassed. Wrapping my patched robe around my head, I burn bits of wood; we practitioners take this as samādhi."
The nature-heaven is blissful; one does not realize that the body dwells within a state of profound stillness. When hunger and cold reach such a point, all else is utterly forgotten.
Since the beginning of this life, I have used only this principle to harmonize and refresh myself, never seeking honor, prestige, or fame.
When he went to attend the invitation at Yuantong Temple on Mount Lu, he carried nothing but a single gourd ladle, a solitary staff, and straw sandals;
he possessed no other belongings. Those who beheld him could not help but have their worldly thoughts dissolve upon seeing his countenance.
Lin Gong Shuda, the Governor of Xunyang, saw him and sighed in admiration, saying: "This man is truly a ferryboat and a bridge within the Buddha-dharma."

For this reason, his reputation was esteemed throughout all quarters. In his conduct—whether in staying or departing, in advancing or withdrawing—he truly embodied the standards and formats of the ancients.
On the day he entered nirvana, even the lowliest of servants who had served him daily could not help but weep with bitter grief and shed tears.
Such was the power of his virtue to move the hearts of others.
Minister Zhang Gong Xiaoxiang sent a letter to the Elder Yan of Fengqiao Bridge, saying: "The patriarchs of old had no affairs of administrative incumbency.
Opening the gates to receive disciples was done only out of necessity. As the Dharma of images declined, there even arose talk of submitting sealed petitions to purchase monasteries.
What has occurred at Fengqiao Bridge recently is entirely of this nature. Thus spoke the Minister.
Those who dwell here know this fully. Like the chick pecking and the hen pecking at the same moment, there is originally no exertion of force. When conditions arise, one remains;

when conditions end, one departs. If those who are like petty merchants wish to create the karma of hell in this place, it would be better to simply hand everything over with both hands (as inscribed on the stone tablet at Hanshan Temple).
"Fengqiao" refers to Fengqiao Bridge in front of Hanshan Temple in Suzhou. "Fenfen" means chaotic and disorderly. "Cuì" is the sound of calling out. "Zhuó" means eating food;
it describes how when a mother hen finds food and crows, her many chicks all arrive to eat it—conveying the sense of one call being answered by a hundred responses.
"Bèi" (稗) should be understood as "bì" (裨), meaning to supplement or attach to. This is as stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "Supplemental peddling... [as in the phrase "裨販如來"].
He came and spoke of those who, within our Buddhist teachings, greedily trade in offerings and sustenance for profit.
The Court Gentleman, Lord Zhang Xiaoxiang, sent a letter to the Elder Yan of Fengqiao Bridge, stating that he should understand the affairs of the times and know when to advance or withdraw, saying:
"From the time of the various patriarchs of old, there was originally no such thing as being an abbot. Whether founding a mountain gate or receiving disciples..."
O Assembly! This is driven by necessity during the age of the Semblance Dharma, at the height of its decline.
There are even those who, seeking fame, form alliances with powerful officials of the state to convert original documents into requests for official seals and bestowed titles.
There are those who, seeking profit, rely upon gentlemen and merchants, describing their desperate circumstances to engage in fraudulent sales and purchases to deceive others out of their money.
Regarding the discourse of those who wear white robes: for generations now, within the temples of Fengqiao, there has been much clamor and endless wrangling;

these are all people of this sort. Whether you go forth or remain at home, leading the assembly in the practice of the Way, everyone knows it as clearly as a hen calling her chicks—the mother pecks and the chicks peck back;
one call brings a hundred responses, requiring no effort at all. Upon reaching [this state],...
It is the same in all places. How can you rely on this? Where there is affinity, one dwells; where there is no affinity, one simply lets go and moves on.
If you are like those who peddle the teachings of the Tathāgata for profit, you will surely create the karma of hell at Fengqiao Bridge.
It would be far better, Master Gong, if you were to constantly accord with sentient beings, handing everything over with both hands; that would truly be excellent.
Master Cishou Shen said to Master Jingshan Nan: "In these two or three decades, the Chan school has become desolate and is truly pitiable to behold.
Elder masters from all quarters have fled south and north in countless numbers; those who have dispersed their followers and scattered their communities fill one's eyes.
Yet you, my elder brother, remain unmoved in spirit, sitting and enjoying ease. How can this be compared to those who are merely mediocre?"
To speak of those who are diligent is to speak of those on the same level. I admire and marvel at this account.
Were it not for one whose Way is full and virtue is substantial, whose practice and understanding are in accord, how could such a cause and condition be easily obtained?

I further hope that you will exert yourself to guide and inspire future generations, so that the Cao River may swell again after drying up, and the Tree of Enlightenment may bloom once more after withering. This is truly the humble hope of my heart. (Note)
Cishou’s name was Huaishen; Jingshan Miaokong’s name was Zhinu. Both were successors of Changlu Chongxin. "Suo" refers to the sound of the *sāṃga* (lute);
"yi" refers to the sound of the *se* (zither). "Xiaose" implies a state of gloom, urgency, and violent, sudden winds. In the *Chuci*, the phrase "xiao se xi caomu yaoluo" (how desolate!
the plants and trees wither and fall) uses this as a metaphor for the decline of the Dharma, which is likewise so. "Dai jiang" means "it will likely come to pass."
"Lululu" (碌碌) refers to those of mediocre character. "Qingong" (欽恭) means to admire and praise. "Heshui" (涸水) means dried-up water.
"Ququ" (區區) denotes a humble and lowly appearance; it carries the sense of modesty. This refers to Chan Master Cishou Shen’s praise for Chan Master Nan of Mount Jing.

His countenance was serene and composed. It is said that he possessed genuine virtue; in recent times, the dharma-gate of the Chan school has gradually declined and withered, to the point that it is almost unbearable to hear or see.
Elders from all directions—coming from the west, the east, the south, and the north—[gathered there].

Like rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds, branching out and spreading in every direction until they cover the earth—how can my elder brother at Mount Jing compare to the mediocre, common folk of all other quarters?
His spirit is concentrated and his mind is settled, remaining unmoved; he enjoys ease and tranquility without ever wavering.
How could he possibly be spoken of on the same day as those ordinary people? I pay my deepest respects, I pay my deepest respects. If this account of our circumstances...
It is not that one has seen the truth of reality; rather, it is through diligent and meticulous cultivation that practice accords with understanding and understanding accords with practice.

When practice and understanding correspond in this way, how could such a person be many? Furthermore, what I hope for is that you will be diligent and energetic in your practice, and take up the guidance of those who follow.
That the source and stream of Caoqi, having once run dry, should overflow once more;
and that the Bodhi tree of awakening, having once withered, should bloom again in spring—this is truly what my humble and ignorant heart has long hoped for.
This is indeed to extol and praise the true virtues of my fellow disciples.
Master Lingzhi Zhao said: "Are calumny and slander the same, or are they different? He replied: "Calumny necessarily relies upon slander to be accomplished.
There may be instances of slander that is not calumny, but one has never seen calumny that does not involve slander. As for the arising of calumny..."
It begins with hatred and envy, and ends in blind credulity; those who act thus are sycophantic and base men.
In antiquity, there were those who offered loyalty to assist their sovereigns, exhausted filial piety to serve their parents, and embraced righteousness to bond with friends.
Although such were the harmony between sovereign and minister, the affection between father and son, and the intimacy between friends, yet for a single day—
When slandered by others, people may turn their eyes away and roll up their sleeves, ostracizing and alienating one another until they regard each other as enemies.
Even among the sages and worthies of antiquity, this could not be avoided. Yet there are those whose innocence cannot be proven at first but becomes clear only after a long time;
those who cannot prove it while alive but have it vindicated after death; and those who cannot prove it even unto death, remaining so forever.
Those who cannot understand this are beyond counting.
The Venerable Lingzhi Zhanran, whose name was Yuanzhao, taught people by saying that enduring slander and ceasing defamation are one and the same.
Furthermore, he asked himself: "Are slander, hatred, and defamation the same thing, or are they two different things? He then answered himself: [They are the same.]
Generally speaking, slander and hatred must rely upon defamation to achieve their end.
There may be those who harbor a singular sense of loathing and suspicion in their hearts but do not voice slanderous words;
however, it has never occurred that one utters slander with their mouth while harboring no hatred or malice in their heart. From what does slander arise? It originates, at its inception, from...
Hating and being envious, they ultimately fall into the error of listening to others too lightly. Such people are those who are sycophantic and flatterers.

This is not only true of the present; even among the people of antiquity, there were those who served as ministers and sacrificed their bodies to face death, remaining loyal to their sovereigns and turning the state toward righteousness.
There were also those who served as sons, submitting themselves with flexibility and obedience.

There are those who serve and nourish their parents; there are those who dwell among friends and associates—men who are upright, loyal, and well-informed, whose bonds of righteousness and trust are firm.
Even when serving a sovereign, they do not flee or hide; even between father and son, though bound by love, they do not desert one another;
and among friends, they remain harmonious and close rather than distant or estranged. Yet, in the space of a single day, they may be slandered by petty men.
Through slander, fathers and sons give rise to anger and glare at one another; brothers quarrel and fight, rolling up their sleeves;
rulers and ministers openly resist and exclude one another, leading to eternal estrangement.
This extends even to the way rulers, ministers, fathers, sons, and friends regard each other, as if they were enemies or bitter foes. Even the sages and worthies of antiquity could not avoid this.
As for the slander and calumny of petty people: there are those who, though unable to clear their names at the outset, eventually attain purity after a long time;
there are those who cannot clear their names during their lifetime, but only achieve purity after death;
and there are those who cannot clear their names even after death, remaining ultimately and eternally [indefensibly].

From the past until now, there have been those who could not maintain purity and integrity; it is impossible to exhaustively enumerate those who were incapable of the task over the course of a few days.
How much less so, then, for the present?
Ziyou said, "To be too frequent in serving one's ruler leads to humiliation; to be too frequent in dealing with a friend leads to estrangement.

This was intended as a warning for people to distance themselves from slander. Alas! Slander and defamation must be scrutinized. Moreover, they are recorded in the Classics and Histories so that they are not obscure.
When scholars read them, none fail to know their wrongfulness; yet often they personally fall into the mouths of slanderers, choking upon it.

To remain resentful until death and fail to clarify one's own innocence must surely stem from the failure of those who receive slander to exercise discernment, and from the flattery and sycophancy of those who slander.
When a multitude of petty people arrive before him and further slander others, he listens again and accepts it as true.
Can this be called being wise? Indeed, those skilled at slandering are clever and artful in inciting strife and discord, seeking only to ingratiate themselves with their superiors.
Obscured and deluded, they become so bewildered as if possessed by demons, such that some cannot discern the truth for the rest of their lives.
Ziyou, whose surname was Yan and given name was Yan, was a disciple of Confucius; "shu" (數) here means "frequently. The word "si" (斯) functions like "suo yi" (所以), meaning "the reason why.

"Rong" (榮) refers to honor, while "ru" (辱) refers to disgrace; "shu" (疏) refers to those who are distant, while "qin" (親) refers to those who are close. [The grief] choked the throat and knotted within the heart, leading to internal strife.
To instigate such strife and resentment is a cause for lamentation. The second section follows from the preceding discussion on loyalty to one’s sovereign and trust in one’s friends;
it states that the harm of slander is no small matter, as it can cause even those who are loyal and trustworthy to be cast out and alienated from their sovereign and friends.
In the *Analects*, Ziyou said: "In serving the ruler of a state, one must offer remonstrance..."
Admonition and remonstrance should not be frequent. If they are repeated too often, one may suddenly be slandered by a petty person;

for such slander easily gains entry, leading to the calamity of being ostracized or expelled. Thus, in seeking honor, one instead incurs disgrace. When living together with friends, admonition and remonstrance likewise should not be frequent.
If they are repeated too often, one may suddenly be slandered by a petty person; and such slander—likewise [easily enters].
It is easy to enter [into such states]. This is why there arises a disposition toward alienation; one seeks intimacy, yet ends up estranged.
These words are precisely intended as a warning for people to distance themselves from slanderous speech. Master Zhi further sighed and said: "Alas!
These two matters of slander and calumny must be deeply scrutinized. Furthermore, regarding the commentaries on the Five Classics and the various Histories..."
I have never failed to clarify this. When students read it, they have never been unaware of the faults of slander and calumny;

yet time and again they lose themselves, falling into the mouths of the slanderous. It becomes choked in their throats and knotted in their hearts, reaching a point where death is certain, and in the end they cannot exonerate themselves. Why is this? It is because they harbor resentment and accept slander.
They slander petty people and refuse to investigate thoroughly. That such slanderers exist is due to the influence of flatterers and sycophants.
Furthermore, when many petty people in turn add slanders against others, their tendency to listen lightly becomes even more entrenched.
Can those of such a sort truly be said to have keen ears or clear eyes? It is simply that they are solely devoted to practicing this kind of slander.
The petty person possesses many devious schemes; they manipulate authority and employ expedients to instigate discord between two parties and curry favor by flattery.
They create a cloud of confusion and obscuration, making things difficult for others to see and leaving them in a state of bewilderment, as if possessed by malevolent spirits.
This is why, in the end, they are unable to discern distinctions or maintain clarity and purity.
Truly this is lamentable.
Confucius said: "Slander that seeps in gradually and accusations based on superficial appearances" refers to the way such gradual infiltration occurs without letting others perceive it beforehand;
even though Zeng Shen was the most filial of sons, his mother would surely have suspected him of murder, and since the marketplace is not a secluded forest, people will surely harbor suspicions.
Among those who encounter tigers, there are some who do not flee; such individuals are called enlightened and far-sighted gentlemen.
Zeng Shen was a disciple of Confucius; his name was Shen and his courtesy name was Ziyu.

The third section follows from the theme of filial piety to state that the harm of slander is no small matter, for it can cause even a son of supreme filiality to be suspected by his own virtuous mother.

This is the meaning. Formerly, Confucius said: "To gradually soak and moisten a person with slander until it reaches their very skin and flesh, and then to lodge a grievance against them—this refers to the gradual soaking and moistening that comes upon one without letting them know beforehand.
Thus, although Ziyu was a great sage and extremely filial, and his mother was likewise clear-sighted and most virtuous, people slandered them three times.

When someone was murdered, the mother also threw down her shuttle and stepped off her loom, leaping over the wall and fleeing. In the midst of the marketplace, how can it be compared to the mountains, forests, marshes, and swamps?
Three people all claimed there was a tiger; the person [who heard them] was likewise divided between doubt and belief.
Suspecting that there must be some ulterior motive, he either made a definitive judgment not to believe, or—such a manner of speaking may be called "wise discernment."
There are gentlemen of far-reaching insight who have perfected their virtue.
Because I am foolish, clumsy, and indolent, I do not delight in flattery or seeking to please others falsely; consequently, I have frequently been the subject of slander and defamation by others.
Upon hearing this, I reflect in private, saying: "Is what they say indeed true? If so, I must reform my faults. As for them, they are... [my teachers].
"The Master said: 'What he says is not the fruit [of realization], is it? He too merely acts in vain; how could he defile me?
Thus, although my ears hear him, my mouth has never debated with him. Whether a scholar or gentleman perceives this or not depends on whether his talent and discernment are clear or not.
Who among us can rectify such distortions and seek to be known by others? Yet even so, after a long time, he remains unaware.'"
"Is it that they become clear later? Or do they become clear in future generations? Or have they never been clear since antiquity?
Wenzhongzi said, "How does one stop slander? By not debating. I shall attend to these words. (From the *Zhizhuanyiji*; the pronunciation of "mǎi" is "měi").
The Master of Wén (Wén Zhōngzǐ): surnamed Wén, given name Tóng, courtesy name Zhòngyān; an ancient worthy.
The fourth section is a self-narrative by the Venerable Zhī concerning the origins of his endurance of slander, citing the case of Duke Wén who quelled defamation to eliminate it himself.
I, for my part, am foolish, rustic, and dull-witted; I am indifferent to wealth and indolent; I do not cherish flattery, nor do I resort to sycophancy, fawning, or deception to seek favor.

When a person is thus hated and envied by petty men, and subjected to gradual infiltration and slanderous calumny, I have heard that one may privately lament and repent, reflecting upon and reforming oneself, saying:
"If this slander is indeed true, I shall surely change my faults and move toward goodness."
"He is truly beneficial to me, for he is a teacher who exhorts one toward goodness. If his slanderous words are indeed false, then they are merely empty sounds;
how could they ever defile me? For this reason, although I have heard them many times, my mouth has never engaged in a dispute or complaint.
Whether wise scholars and virtuous gentlemen examine this matter closely or not, [the truth remains as it is]."
It depends on whether his talent, virtue, wisdom, and knowledge are clear or not; who else could adjudicate its right and wrong?

Who can seek out one who knows the Way? Yet, will this slander remain unknown for a long time until it clarifies itself, or will it wait until after my death before it finally becomes clear, or will it reach a definitive conclusion only from this day forward?
"Will it never be clearly understood throughout the limits of the future? I do not see any statement in the text as to why one should cease this slander;
it says simply, 'There is no defense. This is the discourse of the wise and virtuous, and I shall uphold these words to exercise self-restraint."
Master Làn-ān Shū said: "A student of the Way should take awakening as their goal. They must seek out a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) for definitive discernment.
If even a single thread of emotional views is not exhausted, it is the very root of birth and death. When emotional views are exhausted, one must investigate the reason why they were exhausted.
It is like a person who always lives at home; why worry that the affairs of the household are not being managed? — Míngzhào of Guishan.

The Master said: "People of the present day, although they may attain sudden awakening to the fundamental principle through conditions, still possess habitual tendencies from beginningless time that cannot be immediately exhausted.
They must be taught to purify the flowing consciousness of their current karma; this is precisely what cultivation is.
It is not that there is some separate gate of practice to which they are directed. Only an ancient Buddha such as Guishan could have uttered these words. If it were otherwise,"
When the light of the eyes falls to the ground, one cannot avoid being flustered in hand and foot; it remains like a crab falling into boiling water.
Lan’an, whose name was Dao-shu, was a successor of Daofang Ju-hui. He taught people the necessity of true investigation and actual realization.
For those concerned with birth and death, they must take authentic awakening as their ultimate goal; after all, one must...
One must seek out a true master to discern and distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.

If, within the ground of one's own mind, there remains even a speck of dust of emotional consciousness or the thorns of views that have not been thoroughly cleansed, this is precisely the root, the sprout, and the trunk of the cycle of birth and death within the six realms of existence.
Even if the thorns of emotional consciousness and views were cleansed until reaching a state of total purity, leaving nothing behind—
Furthermore, it must be purified again and again before it can be considered ultimate. It is like a person who is always inside their own house;
what more need they worry about regarding all the affairs of the household that have not been settled?
If you do not believe me, I shall cite another ancient sage’s words as proof. Have you not seen the words of the Patriarch Linyou of Mount Gui?

The Way. People of the present age, although through causes and conditions they may briefly attain a moment of rest from their own restless seeking, still possess the turbid vapors of habitual defilement accumulated over immeasurable kalpas that have not yet been entirely released.
One must cause them to thoroughly cleanse the karmic activities currently manifest before them and eliminate the flowing consciousnesses inherent within their very being. Thus, one proceeds.

This is precisely the method of cultivation. It is not a case of "adding a head atop a head" or creating something out of nothing by seeking some other dharma-gate for practice to drive oneself toward or inspire one to aspire to. Look at Mount Guishan:
from antiquity to the present, everyone calls him an "Ancient Buddha. This praise is not unfounded; were he not an Ancient Buddha, he could not have achieved this.

I have thus revealed these words of Dharma. Should you hear them yet fail to believe, or should you believe yet fail to act accordingly, then at the moment the four elements disperse and the light of the eyes falls to the ground, you will surely find your hands flailing and your feet stumbling—remaining, as it were, like a crab fallen into a cauldron of boiling water. How truly lamentable this would be!
Later, when he was about to take up the study of the Way, he remarked regarding matters that could not be resolved: "The kindness of Master Lán’ān is great and difficult to repay.
His verse says: "This matter has always valued persistence; Having stripped away the banana tree to its very core, one must apply oneself further."
"Awakening is the same as when one has not yet awakened; what need to fear a turtle escaping from within the jar? This is also appended here;
I pray that the benevolent ones will edit and correct it.
Lan’an said: "In the Vinaya it is stated: 'There are four kinds of monastic property: first, the permanently fixed property of the monastery; second, the [property for] ten..."

First is the permanent abiding; second is the permanently abiding of the Dharma-body; third is the permanently abiding that is manifest before one; fourth is the permanently abiding that is manifest before one throughout the ten directions.

Furthermore, regarding these permanently abiding objects, it is not permissible to commit even the slightest transgression against them; the retribution for such an offense is no small matter. From the sages of antiquity to the sages of later times, they have not failed to issue their earnest admonitions.
Often those who hear this are not necessarily able to believe it; those who do believe it are not necessarily able to practice it.

Whether I am in seclusion or amidst the world, I have never failed to keep this matter earnestly in mind, fearing that there may still be something I have not yet attained. Therefore, I have composed this verse to admonish myself:

The property of the Sangha throughout the ten directions is as heavy as a mountain; How could it be easily repaid across ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes? The Golden Mouth [of the Buddha] speaks of it together [with all].
Never having believed, how can one avoid the gates of the Iron City in years to come? This human body is difficult to obtain; reflect upon it well.

When the horns of wisdom first emerge, the years and months have already passed long. It is laughable that for the sake of a single grain of rice, one heedlessly loses half a year’s worth of provisions.
"Vinaya" refers to the Vinaya-piṭaka. "Diligently" means to earnestly exhort one to keep [the teachings] in mind and preserve them within the heart.
This is the golden mouth of the Golden Immortal (the Buddha). Master Lǎn'ān earnestly admonished those who preside over monastic communities, saying:

"One must understand that causes lead to results; this is what is taught in the Vinaya-piṭaka. Within the Vinaya-piṭaka it is said: "There are four kinds of property belonging to the Sangha. The first kind is dwellings."

Fields and gardens, bamboo, trees, vegetables, fruits, servants, livestock, rice, wheat, and the like—these constitute the primary assets of the permanent monastery (saṃghārāma) for the residence of the Master.
They are permitted only for the current co-residents and the monastic community to utilize; not even a single thread or grain may be used for private purposes.
The second type consists of the cooked food and drink provided within the temple for the monks, which embodies the ten directions and is not [for private use].
This belongs to the local monastic community, for it is the property of the permanent residents of the ten directions, each of whom has a share.

The third type refers to that which is both present as an object and present as the monastic assembly; this is because the object was specifically bestowed upon the monastic assembly currently present.

The fourth type refers to the property of deceased monks. Since its substance belongs equally to the present assembly of the ten directions, the monastic community of the ten directions shall share it together;
thus, those who arrive after the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) has been concluded shall not receive a portion.

Regarding these four types of permanent property (*sāṃghika-vastu*), the custodian must absolutely not encroach upon them even by the measure of a mustard seed. Should there be any violation, the transgression is exceedingly grave. From antiquity, all...
From the Buddha down to the patriarchs of today, there have been most earnest and repeated exhortations.
Yet those who hear them often fail to believe them with deep sincerity; and even if there are those who do believe, they may not necessarily act upon them.
Whether I am at a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*) or residing in a temple, how could I ever fail to keep these four types of permanent property in mind?

Between my breast and heart, I am filled with a sense of urgency and trepidation, fearing that there may be something I have failed to reach regarding the ground of the ancient sages and former worthies who clearly understood causes and attained fruits. Therefore, I have composed two four-line verses to admonish myself.
The first says: Let alone the property of the Sangha of the ten directions, even a single grain of rice is as heavy as a mountain. Suppose...
There is a point of divergence: throughout ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, one merely repays debts, which is a great hardship to settle.
This was spoken from the very lips of the Great Awakened Golden Immortal, yet not a single person has been willing to believe it.
At some future time, how can you avoid that iron threshold of the realm of hungry ghosts? Second: among the six paths of existence, being human is supreme.
The spiritual is easily lost and difficult to regain. Why do you not contemplate and deliberate well for yourself?
I fear that with even a slight deviation, you will flow into the animal realm; once you are there, shedding hair and wearing horns, the years and months will be even more vast and distant.
It is truly laughable how some people have insatiable greed, seeking no more than the trivial profit of a tortoise’s hair, like a single grain of rice.
Alas! Without realizing it in our daily lives, we have descended into the deep pit of hell and lost even half a year’s worth of provisions.
How can we not be cautious? How can we not be cautious?

Lan’an said: “The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: ‘If a person hears a single phrase or a single word of the Great Nirvāṇa, and does not form a conception of words, does not form a conception of phrases, does not form a conception of hearing, does not form a conception of the Buddha, and does not form a conception of preaching—such a meaning is called the characteristic of no-characteristic.
That the Great Master Daruma came across the sea and did not establish written words was precisely because of this.”
The principle of signlessness was not something newly devised by Bodhidharma nor a separate school established by him. Yet, scholars of recent times have failed to realize this principle;

they maintain that the Chan school is a distinct dharma-gate, asserting that for those who take Chan as their primary focus, the scriptural teachings are not their doctrine, and for those who take the teachings as their primary focus, Chan is not their practice. Consequently, two schools of thought have emerged, mutually disparaging one another.
They clamor and protest, unable to restrain themselves. Alas! That what I have heard has come to such a state of shallowness—either it is foolishness or madness;
it is truly lamentable. (From the *Cittadharmamukha*; "niǎo" is pronounced as *nǎojiāo*).
Dharmabodhidharma was the second son of King Xiangzhi. In the Western Heaven (India), he was the twenty-eighth patriarch;
in this Eastern Land (China), he is the First Patriarch. Master Lan’an taught that one should treat Chan and the Teachings as a single discourse.
It is said in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "If a person hears the preaching of the profound *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*..."

Regarding the Dharma Jewel: whether it be a single phrase or a single syllable, it does not manifest as the characteristic of a syllable; this is the emptiness of syllables. It does not manifest as the characteristic of a phrase;
this is the emptiness of phrases. It does not manifest as the characteristic of hearing; this is the emptiness of the nature of hearing. It does not manifest as the characteristic of a Buddha;
this means that above there is no Buddha-Path to be accomplished. It does not manifest as the characteristic of speaking; this means that below there are no sentient beings [to be saved].

This is the benefit. Such a principle—that all phenomena possess the characteristic of emptiness—is called "signlessness" (*animitta*). The characteristic is sublated by emptiness, yet it is not non-empty.
The First Patriarch Dharma came from the West across the sea to the East; facing the wall at Mount Song, he pointed directly to the human mind.
To "see one's nature and become a Buddha" and "not rely on words and letters" is because [the First Patriarch] profoundly understood this principle of formlessness;
it was not that he fabricated something new according to his own whims, established a separate dharma-gate, or opened another door and window.
There is indeed a reason for this. Contemporary scholars do not understand this fundamental principle;
they recklessly speculate, claiming that the Chan school possesses a distinct set of rules and a unique pedagogical style.

Consequently, those within the Chan lineage disparage the Teaching (Dharma), while those within the Teaching lineage revile Chan. Thus, the division between the two houses of Chan and Teaching has come about.
He said: "You are not I; I am not you. Without contention, we cannot exist, and it is difficult to find rest. Alas!
Such as these are all merely what has been seen and heard—superficial, base, and vulgar—to the extent that they have become like this.
Are they not either utterly ignorant or wildly arrogant? Is this not truly a matter for deep lamentation and sighing?"
